## 2. Regional highlights

*   Europe remained the largest market globally for personal luxury goods, despite a slight contraction in 2025. The Americas held its position as the second-largest region and stood out as the most resilient this year. Mainland China recorded another significant decline—though less pronounced than in 2024—but maintained its third-place ranking. Japan also saw a marked correction following its 2024 record.

*   In 2025, the European personal luxury goods market declined by 1% to 3% at current exchange rates, totaling about €108 billion. According to Global Blue, sales of luxury goods to international visitors in Europe were flat in the first nine months of the year against a backdrop of euro strength and geopolitical tensions. Chinese tourist spending fell by about 15%, purchases from Gulf visitors rose by 5% to 10%, and spending from US tourists increased by around 5%. However, the nine-month total masked a deterioration in performance after the first quarter, a trend that continued into October and November. Overall luxury performance diverged sharply by country. Southern Europe recorded growth, supported by robust local demand in key Tier-1 cities. Paris and Milan remained the undisputed leaders in terms of tourist sales while Madrid and Barcelona gained traction. Northern cities lost luxury tourist sales momentum. The UK continued to be constrained by the absence of tax-free shopping. Europe’s affluent consumers kept spending, but aspirational buyers postponed purchases. In line with this trend, outlets gained further traction, putting pressure on full-price channels to sharpen their value proposition.

*   Sales in the Americas reached an estimated €101 billion in 2025, up by 0% to 2% at current exchange rates. The average share of total discretionary spending allocated to fashion luxury eased back to pre-Covid levels. The first half of 2025 was constrained by financial uncertainty, but the second half experienced a rebound as the stock market recovered. According to Pyxis by Bain & Company data, the number of US luxury customers declined, shopping frequency remained stable, and average order value increased. Accessible luxury brands thrived. The weak dollar made it more attractive for US consumers to buy some luxury goods domestically, “repatriating” spending that would ordinarily have occurred abroad. US brands also benefited from renewed pride in homegrown labels. Gen Z was drawn back in by the creativity, authenticity, and cultural relevance of winning brands. In Latin America, growth was stable, particularly in Mexico and Brazil, supported by retail expansion and tourism, with Panama also emerging as a hot spot.

*   Mainland China significantly slowed in 2025, albeit by less than last year. The market declined by an estimated 6% to 8% at current exchange rates compared with 2024. Persistently low consumer confidence and challenging macroeconomic conditions—including pressure on the real estate market, rising youth unemployment, and a deflationary environment—continued to weigh on domestic spending. International brands faced intensifying competition from local players across categories, as rising cultural pride and confidence fueled the success of Chinese brands offering better value for money and culturally resonant propositions, particularly among younger consumers. The overall market showed signs of stabilization in the second half of the year.

*   After an exceptional 2024, Japan sharply decelerated from the second quarter of 2025, ending the year down an estimated 6% to 8%. Tourism slowed, and local demand softened, despite resilience in ready-to-wear and jewelry. Global Blue data indicates that tax-free luxury spending fell by 20% to 25%, while the number of shoppers decreased by only about 5%. The growing share of aspirational Chinese visitors shifted the tourist mix toward more value-conscious shoppers. Even so, tax-free spending on personal luxury goods remained well above pre-Covid levels. The preloved segment maintained strong momentum, reinforcing Japan’s position as a secondhand leader in Asia.

*   Excluding mainland China and Japan, Asia-Pacific sales remained broadly stable in 2025, with growth ranging between a decline of 1% and an increase of 1% at current exchange rates. South Korea showed early signs of improvement, supported by favorable currency dynamics and Chinese travelers, though domestic sentiment remained cautious. Hong Kong continued to regain appeal, attracting younger Chinese tourists and a growing ultra-high-net-worth population. Southeast Asia delivered a mixed performance: Thailand lagged, Singapore, and Indonesia held steady, while Vietnam and the Philippines showed strong potential as luxury awareness continued to rise.

*   The rest of the world grew by an estimated 4% to 6% at current exchange rates in 2025, reaching €23 billion. Dubai and Abu Dhabi remained solid, supported by diverse tourism and local demand. Saudi Arabia continued to stand out as a market of exceptional potential. Other Gulf markets were mixed. Australia was held back by subdued Chinese tourism.

*   Globally, tourist spending represented only 30% to 35% of global luxury purchases in 2025, compared with about 40% in 2019.

## 3.Distribution trends

*   Distribution trends in 2025 continued to reflect a focus on value, with outlets outperforming full-price retail. Markdown pressure intensified across channels, forcing brands to navigate difficult trade-offs between inventory monetization and margin protection. Stock levels as a share of revenues were 3 to 4 percentage points higher in 2025 than in 2019. At the same time, discounted sales continued to expand, accounting for 35% to 40% of industry revenues in 2025, an increase of about 5 percentage points compared with 2015.

*   Monobrand store sales declined by an estimated –2% to 0% at current exchange rates, reflecting subdued footfall. Amid pressure on cash flows, brands took a conservative approach to their store footprint. Closures included the loss of about 25,000 square meters of monobrand space since January. In the first 11 months of 2025, the number of monobrand store openings was 15% to 20% lower than in the corresponding period of 2022, although the new locations were significantly larger as average flagship store size increased by more than 30%. The monobrand model needs a strategic reframing. Rising customer expectations are increasing the cost to serve. Within a typical city, consumers are becoming more fragmented in their needs and behavior. Alternative purchase options are multiplying, too. Reenergizing the store and customer engagement will require investment in hyper-personalization beyond traditional clienteling, more localized and store-level assortment strategies, and deeper human connections that extend beyond transactions.

*   The online channel stabilized in 2025, with growth ranging between a decline of 1% and an increase of 1% at current exchange rates as it continued to normalize post-pandemic, slightly increasing share from 20% to 21% of the luxury market. Brand-operated online stores showed encouraging signs, supported by renewed engagement from aspirational clients and AI-powered enhancements to the user experience and interface. Multibrand platforms, however, remained under pressure, with only a limited number of clear winners.

*   The offline multibrand retail channel continued to underperform in 2025, relying increasingly on discounts and loyalty programs as traffic remained muted despite brands’ efforts to introduce experiential formats. In the US, department stores continued restructuring their networks, reducing selling space by roughly 10% since 2024.

*   The outlet channel outperformed the market again in 2025, growing by an estimated 1% to 3% at current exchange rates. Momentum was driven by strong consumer demand for value-for-money purchases, alongside continued network rationalization.

*   The secondhand luxury goods market grew to an estimated €50 billion in 2025, with sales rising by 4% to 6%, aided by consumers’ enthusiasm for treasure hunting and iconic archival pieces. The mix between soft and hard luxury remained broadly stable, with hard luxury (watches and jewelry) representing about 83% of total sales. Innovation also supported growth: AI-powered authentication tools and digital product passports increased trust in online platforms, but physical resellers still anchor the credibility of the preloved market.

This is the Bain & Company 24th annual Luxury Study (Bain-Altagamma Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study), published December 18, 2025, analyzing the global luxury market's performance in 2025 and outlook for 2026 and beyond.

KEY MARKET FIGURES:
- Total global luxury spending in 2025: €1.44 trillion, a marginal decline of 1% to 3% from 2024 (flat at constant exchange rates), still 12% to 14% above 2019 levels
- Personal luxury goods: €358 billion in 2025 (down 2% from €364 billion in 2024, flat at constant exchange rates); improvement in the second half of the year
- Industry lost about 20 million consumers versus 2024, extending a contraction trend since 2022
- Only 40% to 45% of brands reported positive revenue growth in 2025 (vs. 95% in 2022 and 65% in 2023); more than 70% of growth brands were specialists
- Operating margins fell to 15% to 16% (down from 21% in 2022), equivalent to a 20% loss of total industry profit vs. 2023
- Accessible luxury was the most dynamic segment (~50% of brands grew), vs. ~25% in aspirational and ~35% in absolute luxury
- Secondhand luxury grew 4% to 6% to ~€50 billion, outpacing new goods sales; hard luxury represents ~83% of preloved sales
- Discounted sales accounted for 35% to 40% of industry revenues (up ~5 percentage points vs. 2015)

SEGMENT PERFORMANCE (2025, current exchange rates):
- Luxury cars: €545 billion, down 6% (largest luxury segment)
- Luxury hospitality: €251 billion, up 3%
- Fine wines and spirits: €93 billion, down 5%
- Gourmet food and fine dining: €74 billion, up 5%
- High-end furniture/housewares: €51 billion, up 1%
- Fine art: €31 billion, down 9%
- Private jets and yachts: €34 billion, up 9%
- Luxury cruises: €6 billion, up 10%
- Luxury experiences outperformed products, rising ~3%; experience-based goods declined ~5%; luxury products fell ~1%
- Jewelry was the standout category; eyewear maintained momentum; beauty moderated with fragrances most dynamic; watches and apparel stable; leather goods and footwear contracted sharply

REGIONAL PERFORMANCE:
- Europe: €108 billion personal luxury goods, down 1% to 3%; Southern Europe grew, northern markets lost traction; UK constrained by no tax-free shopping
- Americas: €101 billion, up 0% to 2%; most resilient region; weak dollar encouraged domestic spending; Latin America steady (Mexico, Brazil strong)
- Mainland China: down 6% to 8% (milder decline than 2024); signs of stabilization in H2; rising competition from premium domestic brands
- Japan: down 6% to 8% following exceptional 2024; tax-free luxury spending fell 20% to 25%
- Rest of world (incl. Middle East): up 4% to 6% to €23 billion; Saudi Arabia showed exceptional potential
- Emerging regions (Southeast Asia, LatAm, Middle East, India, Africa) collectively represent €40-45 billion in retail sales—equivalent to mainland China's market
- Tourist spending fell to 30% to 35% of global luxury purchases (vs. ~40% in 2019)

DISTRIBUTION TRENDS:
- Outlets outperformed all other physical formats, growing 1% to 3%; all other physical formats weakened
- Monobrand store sales declined 0% to 2%; store openings down 15% to 20% vs. 2022; flagship store size increased by 30%+
- Online stabilized (0% to ±1%), holding 20% to 21% market share; brand-operated online stores gained traction via AI personalization; multibrand platforms struggled
- US department stores cut selling space ~10% since 2024

OUTLOOK:
- 2026 forecast: return to moderate growth (low- to mid-single-digit at constant exchange rates), highly dependent on macro scenarios
- Long-term (2035): positive trajectory anchored in customer base expansion
- Brands advised to: decide future target customers, reestablish creativity/quality/purpose as non-negotiable pillars, invest in product excellence, talent, and storytelling, prioritize precision over scale, and empower local teams

Jewelry Leads Luxury Market Amid Stabilization, Bain Says

[Surveys](/industry/surveys)Jul 27, 2026

# Jewelry Leads Luxury Market Amid Stabilization, Bain Says

Bain & Company delved into the trends shaping the luxury market, the impact of AI, and more in its recent study.

[![](https://uploads.nationaljeweler.com/uploads/7aa17c3727ee24de764af5c00ad5b62b.jpg)](/search_by_authors?query=Lenore+Fedow)[Lenore Fedow](/search_by_authors?query=Lenore+Fedow)[lenore.fedow@nationaljeweler.com](mailto:lenore.fedow@nationaljeweler.com)

A brooch from Mikimoto’s new “L’éclat” high jewelry collection. Jewelry is leading the way as the luxury market stabilizes, according to Bain & Company’s annual study.

New York—The global luxury market is stabilizing after an onslaught of ongoing crises and obstacles in the first half of the year, from the Middle East conflict and spiking oil prices to rising inflation and struggling consumer confidence.  
  
Despite it all, global luxury spending in 2026 is expected to reach €1.44 trillion to €1.47 trillion ($1.64 trillion to $1.68 trillion), with sales growth between flat and up 2 percent at constant exchange rates, according to the spring update to the Bain-Altagamma Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study for 2026.   
  
The personal luxury goods market is expected to grow 2 to 4 percent to €365 billion to €373 billion ($415 billion to $424 billion) in 2026 following [last year’s slowdown.](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/14079-jewelry-stays-strong-as-luxury-market-slows-bain-co-says)  
  
Jewelry is leading the way, according to Bain’s analysis of each category’s performance.  
  
Richemont, which owns Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Vhernier, and Buccellati, saw its [jewelry sales soar](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/15136-richemont-s-jewelry-sales-soar-for-the-seventh-quarter-in-a-row) for the seventh consecutive quarter in Q1.   
  
Kering’s jewelry brands, which include Boucheron and Pomellato, [posted double-digit growth](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/14880-kering-s-jewelry-shines-in-q1-gucci-s-struggle-continues) in Q1.  
  
The apparel, eyewear, and fragrance categories also are performing well, Bain & Co. said in its study, while cosmetics are lagging.   
  
Sales in the leather goods and footwear categories are on track for improvement.  
   
“The luxury market is stabilizing, but this is not a return to the old rhythm, it is the emergence of a new one,” said Claudia D’Arpizio, Bain & Company senior partner and global leader of the firm’s Fashion & Luxury practice and the lead author of the study.   
  
“Consumers are not stepping back from luxury. They are stepping forward into a new relationship with it, one defined by meaning, not just by product. The brands that will win are those that can continuously reinvent their relevance and resonate with both consumers and AI-led ecosystems.”  
  
Released last month, the study delved into what’s shaping the luxury market today and what customers are looking for in a luxury brand.  
  
Here are five key takeaways from the report.   
  
**AI is changing how luxury consumers shop.**  
  
Bain’s study found that half of luxury consumers already use AI in their shopping journey, with nearly all planning to continue doing so.  
  
“Consumers increasingly discover, compare, and validate their purchases of luxury brands through AI and the technology rapidly redefines luxury relevance,” said the study.  
  
Nearly one-quarter of luxury shoppers use AI for brand and product discovery, while two out of three of them use it to compare products.  
  
Luxury brands that are not building “AI-native relevance” risk being left behind, Bain said.  
  
As budgets and preferences change, some shoppers are moving away from luxury, though 70 percent intend to return, but not always to the same brands.   
  
“The question is whether brands are building the meaning and AI-native relevance to be surfaced and chosen when that moment arrives,” said Federica Levato, Bain & Company senior partner, leader of the firm’s EMEA Fashion & Luxury practice, and co-author of the study.  
  
**The luxury resale market is hot.**   
  
The luxury resale market is thriving, the study said, with around half of all luxury shoppers checking the secondhand market before buying something new.  
  
Watch collectors, for example, value connoisseurship over hype, with collectors prioritizing craftsmanship and rarity, which fuels the momentum in the watch resale market.  
  
Online searches for vintage bags have more than doubled year-over-year.  
  
The secondhand luxury goods market grew 4 to 6 percent to an estimated €50 billion ($56 billion) in 2025, Bain said in a [December 2025 study](https://www.bain.com/insights/finding-a-new-longevity-for-luxury/), with growth boosted by “consumers’ enthusiasm for treasure hunting and iconic archival pieces.”

> “The appetite for luxury remains strong. The tolerance for disappointing experiences or products does not. ”  
> - Federica Levato, Bain & Company

**Experiential luxury is evolving.**  
Luxury shoppers are seeking special moments when choosing a luxury experience, shifting toward emotion- and purpose-led moments, Bain said.  
  
Bookings across dining, leisure, and entertainment experiences are up 30 percent year-over-year, with growth driven by “bespoke, slow-travel formats rooted in local culture.”  
  
More travelers also are headed to nontraditional locations, with trips to these locales up 20 percent year-over-year, which Bain attributes to the [“elsewhere-ism” travel trend.](https://www.robbreportindia.com/travel/international/what-are-new-luxury-travel-trends-inheritourism-and-elsewhereism)  
“The appetite for luxury remains strong. The tolerance for disappointing experiences or products does not,” Levato said.   
  
Multi-generational travel is also trending, and, notably, half of Gen Z respondents said their parents influence their luxury brand preferences.  
  
“Consumer sentiment towards experiences is outgrowing tangible goods by 1.5x so far in 2026, reflecting a structural and cultural shift from ownership to lived moments,” said the study.  
  
Within the category, luxury hospitality, private jets, yachts, and cruises are resilient, with fine dining and gourmet food also doing well. The fine arts category is returning to growth.  
  
Luxury assets, like high-end cars, are weaker, while fine wines and spirits hit a snag as alcohol consumption softens.   
  
The design and furniture categories are slowing down, while real estate remains “constrained.”

 Related stories will be right here …

**Luxury sales are surging in America, boosted by younger shoppers.**  
  
Luxury spending in the United States is on the rise, with growth in sales of beauty, apparel, and hard luxury, which includes jewelry and watches.   
  
American luxury brands saw Q1 sales increase about 10 to 15 percent year-over-year, adjusting for currency fluctuations.   
  
Younger shoppers, those under 35, are outspending their elders.  
  
“Perhaps more striking, upper middle-class households are now growing their luxury spending at roughly twice the rate of wealthier cohorts, suggesting that the market is succeeding in broadening its base,” the study said.  
  
Globally, Europe is the luxury market’s “weak link” said Bain, as international tourist spending faltered at the start of the year, particularly as Middle Eastern tourists affected by the regional conflict stayed away.  
  
China’s luxury market is slowly recovering while Japan faces a slowdown due to a drop in tourist traffic, particularly from China.  
  
**The personal luxury goods market is on the road to recovery.**  
  
The overall personal luxury goods market, which includes jewelry and watches, is seeing a gradual recovery, with the possibility of bouncing back this year.  
  
In 2025, sales in the personal luxury goods market fell 2 percent (up 1 percent at constant exchange rates) year-over-year to €358 billion ($407 billion).  
  
In 2026, the market is expected to grow 2 to 4 percent to €365 billion to €373 billion ($415 billion to $424 billion), down slightly from [Bain’s previous forecast](https://www.vogue.com/article/luxury-will-return-to-growth-in-2026-bain-forecasts), which came out before the conflict in the Middle East began.   
  
Bain assigned a 70 percent probability to its most recent forecast, which assumes stabilization in the Middle East, resilient local spending, and recovering demand in China.   
  
There’s a 20 percent probability the market could grow even more, 4 to 6 percent, but this would require further easing of political tensions, renewed momentum in the U.S. market, and an accelerated recovery in China.  
  
It’s even less likely (10 percent probability) that the market will see flat to 2 percent growth. This scenario requires escalation in the Middle East, softer tourism, or weakness in the Americas.  
  
“Around 60 percent of luxury players are already outperforming their Q1 2025 results, and the wide performance gap that defined 2025 is beginning to close, as last year’s winners cool and former laggards recover,” said the study.  
  
Bain’s analysis concluded that it’s a “new era” for the sector as the meaning of luxury evolves.  
  
It’s less about social validation, like being seen with the latest handbag, and more about a sense of personal fulfillment, said the study.  
  
“This new era for the sector means that luxury will no longer define what its consumers own but rather how they live,” it said. “It sees luxury evolving from elitism through aspiration and self-expression to an era characterized by ‘living well’.”  
  
So, what do brands need to do in this evolving market?  
  
The three imperatives, said Bain, are delivering wonder through immersive experiences, building cultural relevance for diverse communities, and offering AI-enabled creativity and personalization.

This is a National Jeweler news article (dated July 27, 2026) reporting on Bain & Company's spring update to the Bain-Altagamma Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study for 2026. The article, written by senior editor Lenore Fedow, outlines that the global luxury market is stabilizing after a turbulent first half of the year marked by Middle East conflict, rising oil prices, inflation, and weakened consumer confidence.

Key findings from the Bain study:
- Global luxury spending in 2026 is expected to reach €1.44-1.47 trillion ($1.64-1.68 trillion), with sales growth between flat and up 2% at constant exchange rates.
- The personal luxury goods market (including jewelry and watches) is expected to grow 2-4% to €365-373 billion ($415-424 billion) in 2026, following a 2% decline in 2025 (€358 billion/$407 billion).
- Jewelry is leading the luxury market's recovery. Richemont (Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Vhernier, Buccellati) saw jewelry sales soar for a seventh consecutive quarter in Q1, and Kering's jewelry brands (Boucheron, Pomellato) posted double-digit Q1 growth.
- AI is reshaping luxury shopping: half of luxury consumers already use AI in their shopping journey, with nearly a quarter using it for brand/product discovery and two-thirds using it to compare products.
- The luxury resale market is thriving—about half of luxury shoppers check secondhand markets before buying new; the secondhand luxury goods market grew 4-6% to ~€50 billion ($56 billion) in 2025.
- Experiential luxury is evolving toward emotion- and purpose-led moments; bookings across dining, leisure, and entertainment are up 30% year-over-year; trips to nontraditional locations are up 20% (the "elsewhere-ism" trend).
- US luxury spending is surging, with Q1 sales up 10-15% year-over-year; shoppers under 35 are outspending elders, and upper middle-class households are growing luxury spending at roughly twice the rate of wealthier cohorts.
- Europe is the "weak link" globally due to faltering international tourist spending; China is slowly recovering; Japan faces a slowdown from reduced Chinese tourist traffic.
- Bain assigned a 70% probability to its forecast (assuming Middle East stabilization and recovering China demand), a 20% probability of 4-6% growth (requiring eased tensions), and a 10% probability of flat-to-2% growth (if Middle East escalates).
- The study concludes it's a "new era" for luxury—moving from social validation to personal fulfillment and "living well."
- Three imperatives for brands: delivering wonder through immersive experiences, building cultural relevance for diverse communities, and offering AI-enabled creativity and personalization.

The article also includes site navigation elements, editors' picks, and a list of recent National Jeweler articles on topics including jewelry crime, retailer news, auctions, and industry events.
args.key_excerpts: "The luxury market is stabilizing, but this is not a return to the old rhythm, it is the emergence of a new one... Consumers are not stepping back from luxury. They are stepping forward into a new relationship with it, one defined by meaning, not just by product." - Claudia D'Arpizio, Bain & Company senior partner and lead study author, "The appetite for luxury remains strong. The tolerance for disappointing experiences or products does not." - Federica Levato, Bain & Company, "Perhaps more striking, upper middle-class households are now growing their luxury spending at roughly twice the rate of wealthier cohorts, suggesting that the market is succeeding in broadening its base," the study said, "Around 60 percent of luxury players are already outperforming their Q1 2025 results, and the wide performance gap that defined 2025 is beginning to close, as last year's winners cool and former laggards recover," said the study, "This new era for the sector means that luxury will no longer define what its consumers own but rather how they live... It sees luxury evolving from elitism through aspiration and self-expression to an era characterized by 'living well'."

# Global Luxury in Transition: Key Findings from the Bain Market Study

Jan 9, 2026

![](https://worldluxurychamber.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Web-WLCC-Feature-Image-1920-x-1280-px-1280x853.png)

The global luxury market stabilized in 2025 following several years of volatility. Total luxury spending reached approximately €1.44 trillion, resulting in a flat to slightly negative year-on-year outcome at constant exchange rates, while remaining materially above 2019 levels. The data indicates a normalization phase rather than a cyclical downturn, as demand patterns, pricing dynamics, and customer behavior adjust after the post-pandemic surge.

This article is a high-level overview of the study conducted by Bain & Company: <https://www.bain.com/insights/finding-a-new-longevity-for-luxury/>

### Demand and Spending Patterns

Luxury spending continued to shift away from goods toward experiences. Categories such as hospitality, fine dining, wellness, and travel delivered the strongest performance and accounted for all net market growth since 2023. This reflects sustained consumer prioritization of social, experiential, and personal well-being-related purchases over product ownership. By contrast, experience-based goods and several core product categories declined as entry-level demand weakened.

Personal luxury goods, the industry’s central segment, remained broadly stable at approximately €358 billion. Performance improved sequentially in the second half of the year, although the category remains under pressure. Repeated price increases since 2019 have reduced perceived value for many consumers, particularly aspirational buyers, contributing to lower purchase frequency and reduced participation.

### Brand and Category Polarization

Market performance remained uneven across brands. Fewer than half of personal luxury goods brands achieved revenue growth in 2025. Specialist players performed materially better than diversified brands, while large global groups reported mixed results. Profitability declined further, with industry operating margins falling to approximately 15 to 16 percent, down from peak levels reached earlier in the decade. Margin pressure stemmed from higher costs, increased markdowns, tariffs, and operating leverage effects from slower top-line growth.

Category outcomes diverged significantly. Jewelry was the strongest performing category across regions, supported by sustained demand and product relevance. Eyewear continued to grow as an accessible category with strong appeal among younger consumers. Beauty was broadly stable, with fragrances leading growth within the segment. Leather goods and footwear declined sharply, reflecting price sensitivity, limited product renewal, and declining appeal among aspirational consumers.

### Regional Performance

Regional trends showed increasing divergence. The Americas remained comparatively resilient, supported by domestic consumption and favorable currency effects. Europe experienced a mild contraction as tourism normalized and local demand softened. Mainland China declined again, although the pace of decline moderated in the second half of the year. Japan corrected following an exceptionally strong 2024, driven by inbound tourism. Emerging regions, including Southeast Asia, the Middle East, India, Latin America, and Africa, collectively represent the most significant source of future market expansion.

### Distribution and Channel Dynamics

Value-oriented channels gained share in 2025. Outlet sales continued to outperform the broader market, while full-price physical retail faced declining footfall and increased promotional pressure. Online sales stabilized, with brand-owned platforms performing better than multibrand marketplaces. The secondhand luxury market expanded to approximately €50 billion, growing faster than the primary market and gaining relevance across both hard and soft luxury categories.

### Customer Base Trends

The luxury market experienced a second consecutive year of customer contraction, losing approximately 20 million active consumers in 2025. Attrition was concentrated among aspirational buyers. High-spending clients maintained absolute spending levels and now account for close to half of total personal luxury goods sales. Generational spending patterns remained stable overall, with Millennials retaining the largest share and Gen Z demonstrating selective engagement combined with lower brand loyalty and higher expectations around authenticity and relevance.

### Forward Outlook

The study projects a return to moderate growth in 2026, followed by a positive long-term outlook through 2035. Growth is expected to be more selective and uneven than in the past decade, favoring brands with strong product discipline, cost control, clear positioning, and consistent execution. Sustained performance will depend less on price increases and more on operational efficiency, product credibility, and customer retention.

Read the full report here: <https://www.bain.com/insights/finding-a-new-longevity-for-luxury/>

Want more news straight to your inbox? Sign up for the WLCC newsletter here: <https://worldluxurychamber.com/wlcc-community>

Source: Bain & Company and Fondazione Altagamma, *Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study: Finding a New Longevity for Luxury*, 2026.

This webpage from the World Luxury Chamber of Commerce (WLCC) provides a high-level overview of the Bain & Company and Fondazione Altagamma "Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study: Finding a New Longevity for Luxury" (2026), published January 9, 2026. Key findings include:

**Market Overview:** The global luxury market stabilized in 2025, reaching approximately €1.44 trillion in total spending—flat to slightly negative year-on-year at constant exchange rates, but materially above 2019 levels. This represents a normalization phase rather than a cyclical downturn.

**Demand and Spending Patterns:** Spending shifted away from goods toward experiences (hospitality, fine dining, wellness, travel), which accounted for all net market growth since 2023. Personal luxury goods remained broadly stable at approximately €358 billion, though under pressure. Repeated price increases since 2019 have reduced perceived value, especially for aspirational buyers.

**Brand and Category Polarization:** Fewer than half of personal luxury goods brands achieved revenue growth in 2025. Industry operating margins fell to approximately 15-16%, down from earlier peak levels, due to higher costs, markdowns, tariffs, and slower top-line growth. Jewelry was the strongest performing category; eyewear grew among younger consumers; fragrances led beauty growth; leather goods and footwear declined sharply.

**Regional Performance:** The Americas remained comparatively resilient; Europe experienced mild contraction; Mainland China declined again with moderated pace in H2; Japan corrected after strong 2024; emerging regions (Southeast Asia, Middle East, India, Latin America, Africa) represent the most significant future market expansion source.

**Distribution and Customer Trends:** Outlet sales outperformed the broader market; online sales stabilized; secondhand luxury market expanded to ~€50 billion. The market lost approximately 20 million active consumers in 2025, concentrated among aspirational buyers. High-spending clients now account for close to half of total personal luxury goods sales. Millennials hold the largest generational share; Gen Z shows selective engagement with lower brand loyalty.

**Outlook:** The study projects moderate growth in 2026 and positive long-term outlook through 2035, favoring brands with strong product discipline, cost control, clear positioning, and consistent execution—depending less on price increases and more on operational efficiency, product credibility, and customer retention.

The page also includes teasers for related WLCC articles: "Luxury 2030 by Matter of Form" (Jun 1, 2026), "The Wealth Report 2026 by Knight Frank" (May 6, 2026), and a 2026 travel industry outlook drawing on Deloitte insights (Apr 14, 2026). Summary by Rapaport AI Jewelry was the top category for global luxury spending in 2025, as the overall market reached EUR 1.44 trillion ($1.64 trillion), according to Bain & Company. Other categories that performed well included apparel, eyewear and fragrances, according to a [report](https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/2026/global-luxury-stabilizes-amid-compounding-disruptions-as-brands-race-to-amplify-meaning-and-rebuild-relevance/) consultancy group Bain released together with Italian luxury goods industry organization Altagamma last week. Cosmetics remained weak, while leather goods and footwear continued to face challenges, though both were on an upward trajectory. In watches, collectors prioritized craftsmanship and rarity over hype, fueling momentum in the resale market. Personal luxury spending dipped slightly to EUR 358 billion ($408.18 billion) in 2025, compared to EUR 364 billion ($415 billion) in 2024. However, sales for 2026 are likely to grow 2% to 4% to between EUR 365 billion and EUR 373 billion ($416.32 billion and $425.44 billion). Bain presented this as the most realistic outcome, with a 70% probability, assuming the Middle East continues to stabilize, local spending remains resilient, and Chinese demand recovers gradually. The luxury consultancy also set out a more optimistic growth scenario of a 4% to 6% rise, but it gives that a 20% chance of eventuating, as it would require geopolitical tensions to ease further, a boost from renewed momentum in the US market and an accelerated rebound in China. Alternatively, the year could see flat to 2% growth – which has a 10% probability of occurring – resulting from renewed Middle East escalations or weakness in the Americas. Meanwhile, overall global luxury spending, which includes cruises, luxury hospitality and fine dining, is expected to be EUR 1.44 trillion to EUR 1.47 trillion ($1.64 trillion to $1.68 trillion), Bain reported. “The luxury market is stabilizing, but this is not a return to the old rhythm – it is the emergence of a new one,” said Claudia D’Arpizio, Bain & Company senior partner and global leader of the firm’s fashion and luxury practice. “Consumers are not stepping back from luxury. They are stepping forward into a new relationship with it – one defined by meaning, not just by product.” However, regional performance in the personal luxury-goods market is diverging sharply. Sales in the Americas are rising, but they are lagging in Europe and the Middle East. Luxury spending in China is beginning to recover, albeit cautiously, as online luxury sales increased 25% to 35% year on year in the first quarter. Younger consumers are driving the trend in the US, with shoppers under 35 increasing their spending about four percentage points faster than older generations. ## Research Approach

## Secondary Research

The secondary research process involved comprehensive analysis of regulatory databases, trade statistics, industry association reports, and authoritative luxury goods publications. Key sources included the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Jewelry Guides and Bureau of Economic Analysis (Personal Consumption Expenditures), UK Birmingham Assay Office and British Hallmarking Council, Swiss Federal Office of Metrology (METAS) for precious metals control, Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) for gold jewelry certification, Dubai Multi Commodities Centre (DMCC) and UAE Ministry of Economy gold trade data, UN Comtrade Database for precious metals and jewelry trade flows, World Gold Council Quarterly Trends Reports, Silver Institute World Silver Surveys, Platinum Guild International market data, CIBJO (World Jewellery Confederation) Blue Books, Responsible Jewellery Council (RJC) certification databases, Jewelers of America consumer preference studies, Bain & Company Global Luxury Goods Reports, Berkeley Research Group luxury market analyses, OECD Trade in Value Added (TiVA) database, US Census Bureau Foreign Trade Statistics (Harmonized System Code 71), EU Eurostat international trade data for precious metals and jewelry articles, and national central bank gold reserve and jewelry consumption reports from key markets. These sources were used to collect import/export statistics, hallmarking volume data, metal price trends, consumer expenditure patterns, sustainability certification tracking, and competitive landscape analysis for luxury necklaces, rings, bracelets, earrings, and specialty jewelry categories.

## Primary Research

During the primary research process, both supply-side and demand-side stakeholders were interviewed to gather qualitative and quantitative data. Supply-side sources included CEOs, Creative Directors, Heads of Sustainability, Chief Gemologists, and Global Retail Directors from luxury jewelry maisons, haute joaillerie houses, precious metal refiners, gemstone mining companies, and high-end OEM manufacturers. High-net-worth collectors (HNWIs and UHNWIs), private wealth managers who focus on tangible assets, chief procurement officers from luxury department stores and duty-free shops, estate jewelry dealers, auction house specialists (jewelry departments), and chief editors of luxury lifestyle magazines were all examples of demand-side sources. Primary research confirmed the timelines for haute joaillerie and high jewelry pipelines, confirmed market segmentation by product type and material, and gathered information on consumer gifting patterns, the demand for investment-grade jewelry, omnichannel retail strategies, and how prices change for gold and platinum pieces.

## Market Size Estimation

Global market valuation was derived through revenue mapping and unit volume analysis. The methodology included:

Identification of 45+ key luxury jewelry maisons and manufacturers across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and Middle East

Product mapping across necklaces, rings, bracelets, earrings, and specialty pieces by material composition (gold, platinum, silver, and high-value gemstone settings)

Analysis of reported and modeled annual revenues specific to watches and jewelry divisions from LVMH (Bulgari, Chaumet, Tiffany & Co.), Richemont (Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels), and independent houses (Harry Winston, Graff)

Coverage of manufacturers representing 70-75% of global market share in 2024

Extrapolation using bottom-up (unit volume × average selling price by country/region) and top-down (maison revenue validation against public filings) approaches to derive segment-specific valuations for fine jewelry versus high jewelry categories

This is a Market Research Future (MRFR) report on the global Luxury Jewelry Market, covering forecast period 2025-2035. The market was estimated at $54 billion in 2024, projected to grow to $123.7 billion by 2035, exhibiting a CAGR of 8.20%. North America holds the largest regional share at approximately 35% (with the US leading at ~29% of global share, driven by high consumer spending, strong brands like Tiffany & Co., and rising demand for lab-grown/sustainable diamonds). Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing region. Necklaces are the largest product type segment (~34% of global share), while rings are the fastest-growing. Gold is the dominant material, with platinum and silver emerging. Women remain the largest end-user segment, with men the fastest-growing.

Key market trends include: (1) a shift toward sustainability and ethical sourcing, with ~60% of luxury consumers willing to pay a premium for sustainable products; (2) rising personalization and customization demand; (3) technological integration and e-commerce expansion, with online luxury sales expected to exceed 25% of total sales by 2026; (4) rising disposable incomes; (5) social media influence (~70% of consumers influenced by social media in luxury purchases); and (6) the cultural significance of jewelry.

Major players include LVMH (FR), Richemont (CH), Chanel (FR), Tiffany & Co. (US), Cartier (FR), Bulgari (IT), Harry Winston (US), Van Cleef & Arpels (FR), and Graff (GB). Recent industry developments (2024-2025) include: Richemont appointing Nicolas Bos as CEO; LVMH opening a new high jewelry atelier in Paris; Tiffany & Co. launching 'Blue Book 2024'; Bulgari partnering with artist Paola Pivi; Chow Tai Fook opening a flagship store in Dubai; Graff acquiring a 100-carat D-flawless diamond; Cartier launching 'Nature Sauvage'; Signet Jewelers acquiring Robbins Brothers; Van Cleef & Arpels opening a Tokyo boutique; Pandora launching lab-grown diamonds in North America; De Beers partnering with Apple for smartwatch jewelry; and Harry Winston opening a Shanghai flagship salon.

Future opportunities include exclusive online platforms for bespoke services, augmented reality virtual try-ons, and partnerships with luxury fashion brands. The research methodology employed both secondary research (regulatory databases, trade statistics, industry reports from sources like FTC, World Gold Council, CIBJO, RJC, Bain & Company, etc.) and primary research (interviews with CEOs, creative directors, gemologists, HNWI collectors, and other supply/demand-side stakeholders). Market size was estimated via revenue mapping and unit volume analysis covering 45+ key luxury jewelry maisons representing 70-75% of global market share in 2024.

The global **luxury jewelry market** was valued at **$52.4 billion** in 2025 and is projected to reach **$89.7 billion** by 2034, expanding at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of **6.2%** during the forecast period from 2026 to 2034. This robust growth trajectory reflects the enduring consumer appetite for prestige, craftsmanship, and investment-grade precious pieces across major global economies. The luxury jewelry sector occupies a distinctive position at the intersection of fashion, heritage, and financial asset management, with high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) and ultra-HNWIs consistently representing the core demand base. Rising global wealth concentration, particularly in Asia Pacific and the Middle East, continues to fuel unprecedented levels of discretionary spending on fine and bespoke jewelry. In 2025, the number of HNWIs worldwide surpassed 22 million, collectively controlling over $86 trillion in wealth, a significant portion of which is directed toward luxury goods and collectible assets including precious metal and gemstone jewelry. The sector benefits further from a vibrant gifting culture, with occasions such as engagements, weddings, anniversaries, and landmark celebrations sustaining consistent demand cycles throughout the year. Digitalization of luxury retail has opened new channels for discovery and purchase, with brands investing heavily in virtual try-on technology, augmented reality-enabled storefronts, and exclusive online drops that generate aspirational demand among younger affluent demographics. Environmental and ethical sourcing considerations are also reshaping supply chains, with leading players committing to traceable diamond sourcing and sustainable gold mining practices, enabling brands to maintain premium pricing while aligning with the ESG expectations of socially conscious luxury consumers. The market also benefits from the resilience of jewelry as a store of value, particularly during periods of macroeconomic uncertainty when precious metals and gemstones serve as inflation hedges. Overall, the convergence of growing global wealth, digital channel expansion, product innovation, and cultural affinity for adornment positions the luxury jewelry industry for sustained and accelerating growth through 2034.

Ultra-HNWIs (net worth exceeding $30 million) increased to approximately 220,000 individuals globally, with this cohort collectively accounting for an estimated 28% of all luxury jewelry spend. Asia Pacific contributed the fastest-growing HNWI cohort, with China and India adding a combined 480,000 new HNWIs in 2025 alone. This demographic expansion directly correlates with elevated spending on investment-grade jewelry including [colored gemstones](/report/colored-gemstones-market), rare diamonds, and bespoke high jewelry (Haute Joaillerie) collections. Brands such as Cartier, Van Cleef and Arpels, and Graff Diamonds have strategically expanded their Haute Joaillerie offerings to capture a greater share of this ultra-premium spending, with individual pieces routinely priced between $500,000 and $10 million. The robust global wealth creation engine, supported by equity market performance, real estate appreciation, and entrepreneurial wealth generation in technology sectors, is expected to sustain HNWI population growth at approximately 4.0-4.5% annually through 2034, providing a reliable demand pipeline for the luxury jewelry sector.

### Digital Channel Expansion and E-Commerce Adoption in Luxury Retail

The digitalization of luxury retail has fundamentally transformed the discovery-to-purchase journey for fine jewelry consumers, with online channels now representing a structurally larger and faster-growing portion of total luxury jewelry sales. In 2025, online channels including brand-owned e-commerce platforms, curated luxury marketplaces such as Net-a-Porter and Farfetch, and social commerce platforms accounted for an estimated **22.3%** of global luxury jewelry revenues, up from approximately 14.5% in 2021. Leading brands have invested aggressively in digital experience enhancement, with Tiffany and Co. launching an AI-powered personalization engine in late 2024, and Cartier deploying augmented reality virtual try-on capabilities across its global e-commerce platform in early 2025. The rise of social media-driven luxury discovery, particularly through Instagram, Pinterest, and Xiaohongshu (Little Red Book) in China, has compressed the consideration cycle and expanded brand awareness among younger affluent demographics. The Gen Z and younger Millennial luxury consumer segments, estimated to represent 35% of total luxury spending by 2030, demonstrate a native preference for digitally-mediated luxury experiences, making continued investment in omnichannel capabilities essential for sustained market competitiveness. Resale platforms including 1stDibs and The RealReal have also introduced a new secondary market dynamic, increasing overall consumer engagement with luxury jewelry categories while creating pricing transparency that benefits informed buyers.

### Bridal and Gifting Culture Sustaining Structural Demand

The bridal jewelry segment represents one of the most structurally resilient demand drivers in the luxury jewelry market, accounting for an estimated **31.8%** of total global jewelry revenues in 2025. Engagement rings and wedding bands remain the highest-value single jewelry purchases in many consumer lifetimes, with the average spend on a luxury engagement ring in the United States reaching approximately $8,400 in 2025, while in key Asian markets such as China and South Korea, premium bridal sets routinely command $15,000 to $50,000 per transaction. Beyond bridal, gifting occasions including birthdays, anniversaries, Valentine's Day, Diwali, Chinese New Year, and corporate gifting programs collectively sustain year-round demand pulses that provide revenue stability across seasonal fluctuations. The corporate gifting segment, often overlooked, has grown significantly as luxury brands develop dedicated B2B gifting programs, with Bvlgari, Cartier, and Chopard all reporting double-digit growth in corporate gift revenues in 2025. The growing trend of self-purchase, particularly among financially independent professional women in their 30s and 40s, has also expanded the addressable demand base, with self-gifting now representing an estimated **29%** of all women's luxury jewelry purchases in North America and Western Europe. This diversification of purchase occasions provides multiple demand vectors that reinforce market stability throughout economic cycles.

### Lab-Grown Diamonds and Sustainable Material Innovation

The emergence of lab-grown diamonds (LGDs) and sustainable material innovations has introduced a disruptive but ultimately growth-accretive dynamic into the luxury jewelry ecosystem. While traditional luxury houses largely continue to position natural diamonds as irreplaceable emblems of rarity and heritage, the broader fine jewelry market has witnessed rapid LGD adoption, with lab-grown [diamond jewelry](/report/global-diamond-jewelry-market) revenues growing at an estimated **18.4% CAGR** between 2021 and 2025. This democratization effect has expanded the overall addressable market by enabling consumers with lower price thresholds to access diamond jewelry aesthetics at dramatically lower price points, effectively enlarging the total consumer pool. Simultaneously, leading luxury brands are responding to ESG-driven consumer preferences by committing to Responsible Jewellery Council (RJC) certification, Kimberley Process compliance, and blockchain-based provenance tracking for diamonds and precious metals. De Beers launched its Tracr blockchain platform for diamond traceability, while several European luxury groups have committed to carbon-neutral supply chains by 2030. The man-made stones for jewelry segment has also expanded the palette of materials available to luxury designers, enabling innovative color and form expressions that complement rather than compete with traditional gemstone jewelry. These sustainability commitments are increasingly cited as purchase drivers by environmentally conscious affluent consumers, particularly in European and North American markets.

## Luxury Jewelry Market Analysis by Product Type

By product type, the global luxury jewelry market is segmented into necklaces, rings, earrings, bracelets, and others (including brooches, anklets, and [body jewelry](/report/global-body-jewelry-market)). **Rings** commanded the largest product type share at **31.4%** of total market revenues in 2025, equivalent to approximately **$16.5 billion**, reflecting the dominant role of engagement rings and wedding bands in sustaining premium category demand. The rings segment benefits from the universal cultural significance of ring-giving in bridal traditions across virtually every global civilization, ensuring that this category maintains structural demand resilience irrespective of broader economic conditions. Diamond solitaire rings from houses such as Tiffany and Co., Cartier, and Harry Winston consistently command premium pricing, with flagship pieces such as Tiffany's Setting and Cartier's 1895 Solitaire remaining among the highest-selling fine jewelry SKUs globally. The rings segment is projected to grow at a CAGR of **6.5%** through 2034, supported by rising engagement rates in Asia Pacific, premiumization trends in bridal spending, and innovation in colored gemstone and fancy-cut diamond ring designs. The growing men's jewelry segment also contributes incremental rings demand, with signet rings, statement bands, and luxury wedding rings for male consumers gaining significant traction in North American and European markets in 2025 and 2026.

**Necklaces** represented the second-largest product category, accounting for **24.8%** of market revenues in 2025, driven by the enduring popularity of iconic pieces such as Cartier's Love necklace, Van Cleef and Arpels' Alhambra collection, and Tiffany's Return to Tiffany pendants. Necklaces serve as highly versatile gifting items, spanning entry-level luxury pendants priced from approximately $1,500 to ultra-high-end Haute Joaillerie pieces exceeding $5 million, providing brands with a broad price architecture that captures spending across multiple affluent consumer tiers. The category is projected to grow at a CAGR of **6.0%** through 2034, with demand particularly strong among younger luxury consumers (aged 25-35) who prefer statement-making, branded necklace designs as self-expression vehicles. **Earrings** held a **20.3%** share, growing at **5.9%** CAGR, while **bracelets** accounted for **16.2%** with a projected CAGR of **5.7%**. The others category, comprising brooches, hairpieces, and body jewelry, held the remaining **7.3%** share and is seeing renewed interest as avant-garde designers and heritage houses revive historically significant brooch and clip jewelry formats as fashion-forward accessories for affluent consumers.

## What Makes Rings the Best-Selling Luxury Jewelry Category Globally?

Rings dominate the luxury jewelry market primarily because of their central role in engagement and wedding traditions worldwide, which are among the highest-value jewelry purchasing occasions. Beyond bridal, rings serve as quintessential statement and collectible pieces, with high-demand collections such as Cartier's Love ring, Bvlgari's B.zero1, and Piaget's Possession ring generating consistent repeat purchase behavior among brand loyalists. The category's strong performance across all major regions, combined with a broad price range that spans from accessible luxury to ultra-premium bespoke commissions, ensures that rings maintain their leading market position through the forecast period to 2034.

## Luxury Jewelry Market Analysis by Material

Material composition is a fundamental value determinant in luxury jewelry, with the choice of metal and gemstone directly influencing product positioning, pricing, and consumer demand patterns. **Gold** retained its status as the most widely used material in luxury jewelry, commanding a **38.7%** market share in 2025, equivalent to approximately **$20.3 billion** in revenues. Gold's enduring dominance is rooted in both its cultural resonance as a symbol of wealth and celebration across Asian, Middle Eastern, and African societies, and its intrinsic value as a store of wealth. Yellow gold experienced a significant resurgence in design preference among affluent consumers in 2024 and 2025, reversing the white metal preferences that characterized the early 2010s, as luxury fashion trends swung back toward warm, opulent aesthetics aligned with maximalist design philosophies. Rose gold, popularized by Cartier's Love and Juste un Clou collections, maintained strong demand among younger affluent consumers globally. Gold-based luxury jewelry is projected to grow at a CAGR of **5.9%** through 2034, supported by sustained gold price appreciation (gold reached $3,100 per troy ounce in early 2025, enhancing the investment appeal of gold jewelry) and deepening cultural demand in Asia Pacific and Middle East markets.

**Diamond**-set jewelry represented the second-largest material category at **28.4%** market share in 2025, growing at a projected CAGR of **6.8%** through 2034. The diamond jewelry category encompasses both natural and lab-grown diamond pieces, with natural diamonds maintaining an overwhelming premium positioning in the luxury segment. Fancy colored diamonds (pink, blue, yellow) have emerged as particularly high-value segments, with individual stones achieving record auction prices at Christie's and Sotheby's in 2025, reinforcing diamond jewelry's status as a collectible investment asset. **Platinum** held a **15.8%** share, driven by its association with bridal and high jewelry, particularly in Japan and North America, growing at **5.6%** CAGR. **Silver** accounted for **10.5%**, largely represented by entry-level luxury and fashion-forward sterling silver collections from brands such as Tiffany, Georg Jensen, and David Yurman, growing at **5.2%** CAGR. The others category (**6.6%**) includes colored gemstones, pearls, and innovative alternative materials, with the pearl jewelry segment experiencing notable renaissance driven by Mikimoto's continued brand investment and growing appreciation for South Sea and Tahitian cultured pearls among Asian and European luxury consumers. Similar to the premium aesthetics of luxury watches, material authenticity and provenance are paramount purchasing criteria for fine jewelry consumers globally.

## Is Online or Offline Retail Growing Faster in the Luxury Jewelry Market?

Online stores are definitively the fastest-growing distribution channel in the global luxury jewelry market, projected to expand at a CAGR of **9.4%** from 2026 to 2034, compared to **4.8%** for traditional offline retail. In 2025, online luxury jewelry revenues reached approximately **$11.7 billion**, representing a near-doubling since 2020. This growth is driven by brand-owned e-commerce platform investments, luxury marketplace partnerships, and the native digital preferences of younger affluent consumers aged 25-40 who are increasingly comfortable purchasing high-value jewelry online. Despite this trend, offline retail remains the dominant channel for purchases above $10,000, where physical verification, personal consultation, and brand experience remain decisive factors. Hybrid omnichannel strategies are therefore the dominant competitive approach among leading luxury jewelry houses through 2034.

## Luxury Jewelry Market Analysis by End-User

End-user segmentation reveals a highly asymmetric demand structure in the global luxury jewelry market, with the **women's segment** representing the clear dominant cohort at **62.5%** of total market revenues in 2025, approximately **$32.8 billion**. Women's luxury jewelry demand is driven by a combination of gifted purchases (from partners, family, and corporate programs) and self-purchase behavior, with the self-purchase trend gaining particularly strong momentum in affluent professional demographics across North America, Europe, and East Asia. Collections explicitly designed for and marketed to independent women, including Cartier's Trinity, Van Cleef and Arpels' Lucky Alhambra, and Bvlgari's Diva's Dream, generate substantial repeat purchase loyalty among brand-conscious female consumers. The women's segment is projected to grow at a CAGR of **6.0%** through 2034, with especially strong incremental demand anticipated from growing female professional classes in Asia Pacific and the Middle East as gender equity in economic participation continues to improve across these regions. Product innovation targeting women, including multi-wear convertible jewelry, colored gemstone sets, and personalized initial and birthstone pieces, further expands consumption frequency and addressable price points within this dominant segment.

The **men's** luxury jewelry segment, while significantly smaller at **22.1%** of global revenues in 2025, is the fastest-growing end-user segment with a projected CAGR of **7.4%** through 2034. This growth is driven by evolving masculine aesthetics, celebrity and influencer normalization of men's jewelry wearing, and the expansion of culturally significant men's jewelry categories including signet rings, chain necklaces, diamond stud earrings, and luxury bracelets and cuffs. The resurgence of men's fine jewelry has prompted leading houses including Cartier, Bvlgari, and David Yurman to substantially expand their men's collections, with dedicated men's jewelry campaigns featuring high-profile male brand ambassadors in 2025 and 2026. The rise of the groom's jewelry market, where male partners increasingly invest in their own luxury wedding jewelry, has added a new demand catalyst within the bridal category. The **unisex** segment held a **15.4%** share in 2025, growing at **6.8%** CAGR, supported by inclusive design philosophies and the luxury market's broader move toward gender-neutral collections. Brands such as Tiffany and Co., Georg Jensen, and several emerging independent luxury jewelers have explicitly positioned key collections as unisex, resonating strongly with younger luxury consumers who reject traditional gender categorization. Similar consumer demographic trends are also reshaping adjacent premium categories including art and sculpture collecting among younger HNWIs.

## Why is the Men's Luxury Jewelry Segment Growing So Rapidly?

The men's luxury jewelry segment is growing at a projected CAGR of **7.4%** from 2026 to 2034, outpacing all other end-user segments, driven by a confluence of cultural, social, and commercial forces. Globally, social norms around male jewelry wearing have liberalized significantly, with celebrities, athletes, and social media influencers normalizing high-end jewelry as an integral component of sophisticated male personal style. In 2025, an estimated **38%** of men aged 25-40 in North America and Europe regularly wore fine jewelry items, up from approximately 24% in 2019. Luxury brands have responded with dedicated men's campaigns, expanded men's product ranges, and in-store experiences tailored to male consumers. Additionally, the groom's jewelry trend, growing popularity of signet rings and identity jewelry, and cross-cultural resonance of men's jewelry in Middle Eastern and Asian markets provide multiple structural growth vectors supporting this segment's outperformance through the forecast period.

## Luxury Jewelry Market Opportunities and Threats 2025-2034

The global luxury jewelry market presents a compelling array of growth opportunities for established heritage brands and emerging luxury jewelers alike. The most significant near-term opportunity lies in the accelerating wealth expansion of Asia Pacific's ultra-affluent consumer base, particularly in China, India, and the rapidly growing Southeast Asian markets. China's luxury consumption recovered strongly in 2024 and 2025 following post-pandemic normalization, with Chinese consumers now accounting for an estimated **30-32%** of global luxury goods expenditure, including jewelry. India's luxury jewelry market is experiencing a structural transformation as younger, internationally-exposed affluent consumers increasingly seek branded fine jewelry as an alternative to traditional unbranded gold jewelry, creating substantial opportunity for global luxury houses to capture share from domestic players. The Middle East's ambitious Vision 2030 program in Saudi Arabia, combined with UAE's continued luxury tourism investments, is creating a high-value new luxury consumption geography that global jewelry brands are actively prioritizing for new boutique investments. The bridal jewelry opportunity in Southeast Asia, particularly in Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines, where rising middle-class incomes and growing acceptance of branded jewelry for weddings is generating entirely new market segments, offers significant upside potential for brands with the agility to localize product and marketing for these culturally distinct markets. The luxury resale and circular economy opportunity also merits strategic attention, with the secondary luxury jewelry market estimated at approximately **$18-22 billion** globally in 2025 and growing at double-digit rates, representing both a competitive threat and a potential revenue stream for brands that develop authenticated resale programs. Similar market expansion trends are visible across related luxury categories including the luxury perfume market and the broader premium goods segment.

Personalization and customization represent arguably the most dynamic frontier opportunity in the luxury jewelry market, with consumers increasingly willing to pay significant premiums for bespoke, one-of-a-kind, or monogram-enabled pieces that express individual identity and narrative. Brands that invest in scalable customization capabilities, whether through in-store engraving and stone selection services or digital configurators enabling customers to design pieces online, are demonstrating meaningfully higher average transaction values and customer lifetime value metrics. The integration of digital technologies including AI-powered design tools, 3D printing for prototype creation, and blockchain-based certificate of authenticity programs are enabling even small luxury jewelers to offer credible customization journeys that rival the bespoke services of heritage houses. The growing interest in colored gemstones, including Paraiba tourmalines, Padparadscha sapphires, alexandrite, and tsavorite garnets, among discerning collectors represents a high-margin niche opportunity where informed brands can achieve significant pricing power through gemological expertise and curated sourcing relationships. Investment in immersive experiential retail, including jewelry master classes, heritage storytelling ateliers, and exclusive high jewelry viewing events, provides brand equity amplification opportunities that reinforce premium positioning while deepening consumer emotional engagement with the brand universe. These experiential strategies are also proving effective in engaging luxury consumers who span multiple premium categories, including those with interest in luxury cars and other aspirational lifestyle assets.

Key threats to the luxury jewelry market's growth trajectory include macroeconomic headwinds such as potential slowdowns in China's economic growth, which would disproportionately impact global luxury demand given Chinese consumers' outsized market share. Geopolitical tensions, trade policy uncertainty, and the risk of tariff escalation between major luxury goods producing countries (principally France, Italy, Switzerland) and key consuming markets (China, United States) could disrupt supply chains and erode profitability. The ongoing pressure on natural diamond prices from lab-grown diamond supply expansion represents a structural challenge for brands heavily reliant on natural diamond jewelry positioning, potentially requiring significant marketing investment to maintain the narrative of natural diamond rarity and desirability. Counterfeit and replica luxury jewelry, increasingly sophisticated in both quality and distribution via social media platforms, remains a persistent brand integrity risk, requiring continuous investment in authentication technology and consumer education programs. Additionally, the growing scrutiny on mining practices and supply chain sustainability from institutional investors and NGOs poses reputational risks for brands that fail to achieve and transparently communicate credible ESG standards in their sourcing and manufacturing operations.

## Luxury Jewelry Market Competitor Outlook 2025-2034

The global luxury jewelry market exhibits a moderately concentrated competitive structure, with the top five brands (Cartier, Tiffany and Co., Bvlgari, Van Cleef and Arpels, and Harry Winston) collectively accounting for an estimated **38-42%** of global luxury jewelry revenues in 2025. This concentration is somewhat lower than adjacent luxury categories such as [haute couture](/report/haute-couture-market) and prestige fragrances, reflecting the market's significant long-tail of regional heritage brands, independent luxury jewelers, and artisan ateliers that serve local affluent markets with culturally specific designs. The competitive landscape is dominated by brands operating within the portfolios of major luxury conglomerates, with LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton owning Bvlgari, Chaumet, and Fred; Richemont Group controlling Cartier, Van Cleef and Arpels, Piaget, Boucheron, and Vacheron Constantin; and Kering owning Boucheron through its luxury fashion arm. This conglomerate structure enables resource sharing in supply chain management, retail real estate, and marketing, creating significant scale advantages over independent competitors. Standalone brands including Harry Winston (owned by Swatch Group) and Graff Diamonds maintain competitive relevance through ultra-premium positioning, exceptional gemstone sourcing capabilities, and a focused high jewelry strategy targeting ultra-HNWI clientele.

**Cartier**, the Paris-based maison founded in 1847 and wholly owned by the Richemont Group, retained its position as the global luxury jewelry market leader in 2025, with estimated annual jewelry revenues exceeding **$9.5 billion**. Cartier's market leadership is underpinned by an unparalleled portfolio of iconic collections including Love, Juste un Clou, Trinity, Panthère, and Clash de Cartier, each generating substantial repurchase and cross-purchase behavior among brand loyalists. The brand's strategic investments in Asia Pacific boutique expansion, immersive exhibition programming, and digital platform development in 2024-2025 have reinforced its market leadership position while extending brand appeal to younger affluent demographics. **Tiffany and Co.**, acquired by LVMH in 2021 for $15.8 billion, has undergone a significant brand revitalization under LVMH stewardship, with CEO Anthony Ledru overseeing a comprehensive retail renovation program, product line expansion, and high-profile ambassador campaigns featuring Beyonce and Jay-Z. The brand's 2025 revenues were estimated at approximately **$5.8 billion**, reflecting the success of the LVMH-led repositioning toward a more overtly ultra-premium brand positioning. **Bvlgari**, headquartered in Rome and owned by LVMH since 2011, maintained strong growth momentum in 2025, with revenues estimated at approximately **$3.4 billion**, driven by Serpenti, B.zero1, and Divas Dream collection strength across Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

**Van Cleef and Arpels**, the Richemont-owned Parisian maison celebrated for its Alhambra, Perlée, and floral high jewelry collections, continued to benefit from a deliberate scarcity-based distribution strategy and exceptional craftsmanship reputation, with estimated 2025 revenues of approximately **$2.9 billion**. The brand's distinctive "invisible setting" gemstone technique remains one of the most recognized and technically demanding achievements in luxury jewelry, commanding significant collector premiums. **Chopard**, the Geneva-based independent luxury brand owned by the Scheufele family, distinguished itself through its commitment to fully ethical gold sourcing via its Fairmined Gold program, with 100% of Chopard's gold procurement certified as Fairmined since 2018, generating strong brand preference among sustainability-conscious affluent consumers. **Graff Diamonds**, the London-based ultra-luxury specialist, continued to set benchmark prices at auction and in private sales for exceptional diamonds, reinforcing its position as the destination brand for ultra-HNWI diamond collectors. **Mikimoto**, the Japanese pearl jewelry specialist, maintained its dominant position in the cultured pearl segment, with global revenues estimated at approximately $800 million in 2025, and expanded its presence in North American and European markets through new boutique openings and collaborations with high-fashion designers. The competitive dynamics in this sector draw parallels to the stratified positioning structures observed in adjacent premium lifestyle markets including the black watches for men segment and high-end personal accessories broadly.

The competitive landscape is expected to intensify through 2034 as luxury conglomerates accelerate their jewelry portfolios through acquisition and organic brand development, while independent players respond with increasingly specialized ultra-premium and bespoke offerings designed to serve the hyper-personalization preferences of top-tier clientele. Strategic priorities for leading players include geographic expansion in Southeast Asia and Africa, digital channel capability building, sustainability certification, and talent development in high jewelry craftsmanship to preserve and transmit artisanal skills to the next generation of master jewelers. M&A activity is expected to remain elevated, with independent luxury jewelers of scale representing attractive acquisition targets for conglomerates seeking to expand their fine jewelry portfolios into new geographic strongholds or material specializations. The competitive intensity is further heightened by the entry of luxury fashion brands including Chanel Fine Jewelry and Hermes Jewelry into more aggressive jewelry-centric positioning, leveraging their parent brand's fashion authority and global retail footprints to compete for share of wallet among luxury consumers who cross-shop fashion and jewelry.

args.summary:
The DataIntelo report on the Global Luxury Jewelry Market (2025-2034) provides a comprehensive analysis of the industry's size, growth, segmentation, and competitive landscape. The market was valued at $52.4 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $89.7 billion by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 6.2% (2026-2034). The report covers segmentation by product type (necklaces, rings, earrings, bracelets, others), material (gold, platinum, diamond, silver, others), distribution channel (online stores, offline retail, specialty stores, others), end-user (men, women, unisex), and region (Asia Pacific, North America, Latin America, Europe, Middle East & Africa).

KEY MARKET STATISTICS:
- Rings hold the largest product type share at 31.4% (~$16.5 billion in 2025), driven by bridal and engagement demand; engagement and bridal rings account for 54% of the rings segment.
- Gold is the leading material with 38.7% share (~$20.3 billion); diamond-set jewelry follows at 28.4%; platinum 15.8%; silver 10.5%.
- Asia Pacific dominates regionally with 36.8% share (~$19.3 billion in 2025), growing at 7.1% CAGR. Europe holds 27.4%, North America 22.1%, Middle East & Africa 8.5% (fastest-growing at 7.8% CAGR), and Latin America 5.2%.
- Women's segment accounts for 62.5% of end-user demand (~$32.8 billion); men's segment is the fastest-growing at 7.4% CAGR (22.1% share); unisex holds 15.4%.
- Offline retail is the dominant distribution channel at 44.6%; specialty stores 28.7%; online stores 22.3% but fastest-growing at 9.4% CAGR; online revenues reached ~$11.7 billion in 2025.

KEY GROWTH DRIVERS: Rising global HNWI population (surpassed 22.4 million in 2025 with $86.8 trillion in wealth, growing ~4.7% YoY; ultra-HNWIs account for ~28% of luxury jewelry spend), digital channel expansion and e-commerce adoption, bridal and gifting culture (bridal represents 31.8% of total jewelry revenues), and lab-grown diamond adoption (18.4% CAGR 2021-2025) plus sustainable material innovations.

COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE: The top five brands (Cartier, Tiffany and Co., Bvlgari, Van Cleef and Arpels, Harry Winston) account for 38-42% of global revenues. Cartier leads with ~$9.5 billion in 2025 jewelry revenues, followed by Tiffany (~$5.8 billion, under LVMH since 2021), Bvlgari (~$3.4 billion), Van Cleef and Arpels (~$2.9 billion), and Mikimoto (~$800 million). Major conglomerates include LVMH (Bvlgari, Chaumet, Fred), Richemont (Cartier, Van Cleef and Arpels, Piaget, Boucheron), and Kering.

OPPORTUNITIES AND THREATS: Key opportunities include Asia Pacific ultra-affluent wealth expansion (China accounts for 30-32% of global luxury expenditure), India's branded jewelry transformation, Middle East Vision 2030 growth, secondary market ($18-22 billion), and personalization/customization. Threats include China economic slowdown risk, geopolitical/tariff tensions, lab-grown diamond price pressure, counterfeiting, and ESG/sustainability scrutiny.

The report is 257 pages, authored by Debadatta Patel (fact-checked by V. Chandola, edited by Shruti Bhat), updated April 2026, covering historical period 2019-2025 with forecast 2026-2034, and covers 20 key companies including Cartier, Tiffany, Bvlgari, Van Cleef and Arpels, Harry Winston, Chopard, Graff Diamonds, Piaget, Mikimoto, Boucheron, Buccellati, David Yurman, De Beers, Rolex, Patek Philippe, Hublot, Omega, Swarovski, Chanel Fine Jewelry, and Hermes Jewelry.
