State of Colored Stones: The Big Three in the Modern World

[Sourcing](/diamonds-gems/sourcing)May 19, 2025

# State of Colored Stones: The Big Three in the Modern World

Sapphires, emeralds, and rubies are finding their place in a U.S. market captivated by the gemstones once referred to as “semi-precious.”

[![](https://uploads.nationaljeweler.com/uploads/7ab280cd0c2b5013fe7890cfe0edf28a.jpg)](/search_by_authors?query=Lauren+McLemore)[Lauren McLemore](/search_by_authors?query=Lauren+McLemore)[lauren.mclemore@nationaljeweler.com](mailto:lauren.mclemore@nationaljeweler.com)

A selection of sapphires, emeralds, and rubies (Photo courtesy of Gemfields, which mines emeralds in Zambia and rubies in Mozambique)

*Editor’s Note: This story first appeared in the print edition of the 2025 State of the Majors. Click* [*here*](https://magazines-nationaljeweler-com.s3.amazonaws.com/stateofthemajors/2025/index.html?page=1) *to see the full issue.*  
  
Sapphires, emeralds, and rubies, the Big Three of the colored gemstone world, have long been revered for their beauty and rarity, coveted for centuries by consumers worldwide.  
  
It wasn’t long ago that the designation of “precious” was reserved for only these three gemstones and diamonds, with everything else deemed to be “semi-precious.”  
  
With a long history of association with royals, the terms Burmese ruby, Colombian emerald, and Kashmir sapphire are familiar references to the most valuable gemstones to exist, and many gem dealers still argue it’s simply just the truth.  
  
The landscape around trading the Big Three is evolving, however, as mining technology advances, sources dry up (and new ones are discovered), tastes change, and the industry [navigates complex global politics](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13879-tariffs-colored-gemstones-relying-on-stock-considering-the-ripple-effect).  
  
The U.S. market, driven in part by higher prices post-COVID and the lack of super-fine material available, has seen dealers recently adjust what they define, and can market, as valuable.  
  
However, the finest untreated sapphires, rubies, and emeralds still command the highest prices of any gemstone, and the appetite for the best and the rarest remains strong.  
  
**A Matter of Price**  
A simple understanding of the law of supply and demand can explain why prices of the Big Three, in the finest quality, are skyrocketing, but there is some nuance.  
  
Gemstone dealer and bespoke jeweler Simon Dussart of Asia Lounges explains, “There used to be three prongs in the market—the low, the mid-range, and the high range. One could argue there was a fourth one, the super high end, but that’s like, an oddity of the high end.   
  
“But the mid-range is dying.”  
  
The loss of interest in this category, which he describes as eye-clean material, the bread-and-butter for the average self-purchaser, is affecting the mining business, Dussart says.   
  
“A lot of the mines are no longer profitable. They needed to have all three segments in order to produce, and now they are stuck producing for the low end, which demands increasingly lower prices, but they can’t really do it [that way], so you’ve got more and more treated materials.  
  
“The trade has an increased demand for higher-quality material that is untreated, which is one of the reasons—but not the only reason—why the price of the material is skyrocketing.”  
  
Since the pandemic, untreated fine sapphires have tripled in price, and Dussart says ruby was inaccessible for him even before the pandemic.   
  
“I seldom go anywhere above 3 carats in the red and blue department,” he says. “Rubies, pre-COVID, that was out of my range anyway because it was already in the six figures, but now it’s like, forget about it. It’s impossible.”  
  
**Red-Hot Ruby**   
Today, untreated fine-quality ruby is exceedingly rare, making it basically a specialized market.   
  
A museum-worthy set of rubies ranging in weight from 7.11-17.88 carats sourced from five different countries—Myanmar, Tajikistan, Thailand, Mozambique, and Madagascar—took longtime collector Jack Abraham more than 40 years to curate, he said in an interview with the American Gem Trade Association’s Prism magazine.   
  
  [![Jack Abraham rubies](https://nationaljeweler.com/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBa3hlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19----ea15daad36a7f7266e7d591867d534d851352260/20250519_Jack%20Abraham%20rubies.jpg "Jack Abraham's quintet of unheated rubies from five different origins")](/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBa3hlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19--1b6bca8c4389bdc5e4c683c278078efc428e32d7/20250519_Jack%20Abraham%20rubies.jpg)  

Jack Abraham's quintet of unheated rubies from five different origins

   
  
To many in the trade, material from Myanmar’s (formerly Burma) Mogok Valley remains incomparable in quality, but production has decreased significantly.  
   
Earlier this year, Gemfields published [“Understanding the Global Supply of Emerald, Ruby and Sapphire.”](https://gemfields.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/20250204-Understanding-the-Global-Supply-of-Emerald-Ruby-and-Sapphire.pdf)   
  
The research reviews the evolution of colored gemstone supply over the past 40 years. It’s also an update to the mining company’s 2022 global market analysis of the Big Three.  
  
The report stated that, as of 2009, more than 90 percent of the rubies with a price above $50,000 per carat auctioned at Christie’s were from Mogok, a testament to the material’s popularity and value.  
  
According to Gemfields’ report, the drop in production can be explained by the depletion of the deposits—the Mogok Valley mines as well as the deposit discovered in 1992 in nearby Mong Hsu—but also the increase in privately owned mines, which aren’t obligated to report production.   
  
The main source of ruby production today comes from deposits in northeast Mozambique, which were discovered in the late 2000s.  
  
Although Gemfields announced a record per-carat price ($321.94) from its [December 2024 auction](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13506-gemfields-reports-record-ruby-auction-results-despite-challenges-at-source) of mixed-quality rough rubies from its Montepuez mine, those who have been attending rough sales in the region report that, generally, the quality and quantity of the material are decreasing.   
  
However, the mine remains the sole option for bigger brands that require coherence in material, such as precisely calibrated melee-size ruby with consistent color.  
  
Rubies are also mined, on a much smaller scale, in pockets across several other countries, such as Vietnam, Tanzania, and Sri Lanka, as well as Afghanistan, though trading involving the latter poses some challenges for U.S. dealers.  
  
Last year in Afghanistan, the Taliban, which took control of the country in 2021, indicated it was going to [focus on minerals](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/22/fashion/jewelry-gary-bowersox-afghanistan-gem-business.html) to help Afghanistan’s economy.   
  
In 2022, the U.S. government issued a license allowing for economic activity in Afghanistan, as long as it was not linked to the Taliban or any persons or entities on the Office of Foreign Assets Control’s sanctions list.  
  
So, if a dealer or a company is not connected to the Taliban and not sanctioned, they could trade legally, though it is not likely, according to the Jewelers Vigilance Committee, because it would be very difficult to prove a business is unlinked to the Taliban, as the entity is the government of Afghanistan.  
  
However, during a [presentation on the colored gemstone market](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13676-colored-stone-market-update-tracking-industry-trends-in-tucson) in Tucson, GemGuide Editor-in-Chief Brecken Branstrator said one of her sources confirmed that rough gemstones are still flowing out of Afghanistan, largely through Pakistan.  
  
International and at-source politics are an unavoidable aspect of dealing in gemstones, from years-long U.S.-imposed sanctions banning Burmese rubies to current-day criticisms of the mining concession in Mozambique as Gemfields navigates heightened illegal activity amid the country’s civil unrest.   
  
Still, there are vendors committed to ethical practices, a surging area of interest within the industry, that are leaning into alternative ruby sources.  
  
  [![Columbia Gem House pomme ruby](https://nationaljeweler.com/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBazFlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19----ea15daad36a7f7266e7d591867d534d851352260/20250519_CGH%20pomme%20ruby.jpg "Columbia Gem House’s “Pomme Ruby” collection features apple-red rubies mined by artisanal miners in Madagascar.")](/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBazFlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19--9912143ffbf94a3fdd207977a363f1127bce226e/20250519_CGH%20pomme%20ruby.jpg)  

Columbia Gem House’s “Pomme Ruby” collection features apple-red rubies mined by artisanal miners in Madagascar.

   
  
A few years ago, wholesaler Columbia Gem House launched its “Pomme Ruby,” collection, featuring “apple red” gemstones produced by artisanal miners in Madagascar.  
  
“For sourcing-conscious designers, Pomme Ruby is the dream gemstone. Its untreated nature and traceable supply chain make it a standout choice for those seeking luxury with responsibility,” says Natasha Braunwart, the company’s brand and corporate social responsibility manager.   
  
At the Ethical Gem Fair in Tucson this year, Virtu Gems debuted rubies mined and cut in Kenya.  
  
While the quality of rubies from these alternative regions tends to be lower, options like these can offer interesting, non-traditional ruby color and peace of mind regarding responsible sourcing.

**The Other Corundum**   
When it comes to sapphires, many consumers are likely to first visualize a classic Kashmir blue.  
  
History, along with mainstream media and pop culture, influence what consumers, many of whom are far removed from the complex business of gemstone trading, believe gems should look like.  
  
When asked about blue sapphire, “[Consumers] most likely tell you that it’s supposed to look like Princess Diana’s sapphire,” says Dussart, who added that the vast majority of the dealers in the trade agree that the beloved British royal’s stone is “too dark.”  
  
Sapphire represents a smaller market value than ruby and emerald, according to Gemfields’ report, and it’s an outlier in the Big Three because it’s available in a rainbow of colors.   
  
The average consumer who assumes sapphires are out of reach for their budget may be surprised at the range of options available to them.  
  
“A lot of sapphires are not that expensive. It depends what color you want,” Dussart says. “A lot of people are exclusively looking at sapphire for the royal blue color … If you’re looking at that, then yes, prices are princess-only department.”  
  
  [![blue sapphire and diamond stud earrings](https://nationaljeweler.com/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBazVlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19----ea15daad36a7f7266e7d591867d534d851352260/20250519_Asia%20Lounges%20sapphire%20studs.jpg "Natural blue sapphire and diamond earrings in 18-karat white gold from Asia Lounges")](/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBazVlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19--3fcdffee884d933f71eb1346a848db0f874f0ec2/20250519_Asia%20Lounges%20sapphire%20studs.jpg)  

Natural blue sapphire and diamond earrings in 18-karat white gold from Asia Lounges

   
  
Fine quality, untreated sapphire is still in limited supply, and therefore, pricey. Gemfields’ report stated that its sources indicate that more than 90 percent of sapphires are treated.  
  
New discoveries have been offset by the depletion of existing mines, leading to inconsistency in overall sapphire supply over the last few decades.   
  
Production of the gemstone is relatively stable, though the overall quantity of sapphires available has decreased significantly since the 1980s, according to Gemfields’ report.  
  
Quality is dwindling as well, according to Dussart, and less material is filtering down into the market.   
  
With ultra-high prices for classic blue sapphires posted throughout [the Tucson shows in 2024](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/12931-state-of-colored-stones-why-the-market-is-more-colorful-than-ever), buyers shifted focus to other shades of blue, opting for teal sapphires from Australia and the earthy, denim-blue material from Montana.  
  
However, several vendors at the 2025 trade shows in Tucson and at the Bangkok Gems & Jewelry Fair in February reported that buyers appear to be leaning back into the Ceylon blue tones.   
  
Not surprisingly, many are still hunting for top-quality material. For these untreated stones, dedicated collectors and investors appear willing to face the sticker shock.   
  
Dealers who have the material are keenly aware that even if they are able to sell, replacing the stone will be a challenge.

 Related stories will be right here …

**Understanding Emeralds**The emerald market has experienced a similar pricing phenomenon in that vendors report buyers looking for untreated fine-quality stones come shopping with apparently no ceiling.  
  
A variety of beryl, emerald has enjoyed a boost from the popularity of green gemstones over the last few years.   
  
It also has become a popular choice for those seeking a colorful engagement ring despite its relative softness (7.5-8) on the Mohs scale when compared with diamonds, rubies, and sapphires.

The emerald mines in Bogotá, Colombia, regarded by many as producing the world’s finest emeralds, have a history dating back more than 800 years, and they’re still producing.   
  
Neighboring Brazil also offers a consistent supply, though it produces less fine quality.   
  
Together with Zambia, these three countries dominate the global emerald supply.  
  
  [![Kagem emerald mine](https://nationaljeweler.com/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBazllIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19----ea15daad36a7f7266e7d591867d534d851352260/20250519_Kagem%20emerald%20mine.jpg "Kagem, an emerald mine in the “Copperbelt” region of northern Zambia that is owned in part by Gemfields")](/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBazllIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19--5437e1a7979ec47344a94393482eaf957ead9719/20250519_Kagem%20emerald%20mine.jpg)  

Kagem, an emerald mine in the “Copperbelt” region of northern Zambia that is owned in part by Gemfields

   
  
In the last 40 years, there have been no major discoveries that have dramatically changed the emerald supply dynamic.   
  
According to Gemfields’ report, the key factors affecting volume and supply in the last four decades have been changes in mining activities, including a shift towards larger, more mechanized and formalized operations.   
  
However, the finer-quality material is becoming rarer as the appetite for untreated gems grows.  
  
“There [are] not enough stones on the market to support the demand for no-oil gemstones [regardless of origin],” says Zoe Michelou, director at Imperial Colors Ltd., a gemstone manufacturing company based in Bangkok.  
  
“The price has come down a little bit [for commercial-quality goods] because of economic conditions and shifting consumer demand, but it’s widely available,” Michelou says. “I don’t buy much of this quality; I go more toward the high-end quality and here, the price has gone up.”  
  
She says that, at the moment, she can’t even guarantee a customer a price for two months because it keeps climbing.  
  
Michelou’s father, the late Jean Claude Michelou, was an emerald specialist with more than four decades of experience mining the verdant gem, so she’s familiar with the public perception of the gemstone.   
  
“In terms of demand and value in people’s minds, because of the history, Colombia will always be No. 1,” she says, adding that Colombian emeralds command premium prices in the market.  
  
However, Imperial Colors has also established a partnership with a licensed miner in the tribal Swat district in Pakistan, which produces smaller crystals than mines in Colombia.   
  
“They’re extremely clean, the luster is extremely high,” she says.   
  
They’re also highly saturated, and their small size makes the material ideal for calibrated melee.  
  
“I call it the Rolls-Royce of emeralds, because it’s what the [luxury] watch companies are using,” she says. “The price also has gone up, but it remains unstable due to inconsistent production, regional factors, and the limited supply, as the mine is not mechanized.”  
  
While the supply is there, it is still artisanal small-scale mining. There is no dynamite being used on the land and many miners work by hand, meaning the process is slow.   
  
  [![swat emeralds](https://nationaljeweler.com/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBbEJlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19----ea15daad36a7f7266e7d591867d534d851352260/20250519_Imperial%20Colors%20emeralds.jpg "Emeralds from the tribal Swat district in Pakistan (Photo courtesy of Imperial Colors)")](/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBbEJlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19--de3b7a597583c4f70b4a263c5c2562a109d0585a/20250519_Imperial%20Colors%20emeralds.jpg)  

Emeralds from the tribal Swat district in Pakistan (Photo courtesy of Imperial Colors)

   
  
While it is legal for U.S. dealers to trade in Pakistan, working in the country’s remote mining regions means navigating bureaucratic and tribal complexities, making trust-based, established partnerships like Michelou’s an important part of the process.   
  
She also enjoys the look of the lighter-colored emerald material from Russia, she noted, and had some specimens at her booth at the Bangkok Gems & Jewelry Fair.  
  
She said Americans attending the show were intrigued by the material, noting, “I find they are more curious [than attendees from Europe].”  
  
More widely available are the emeralds from Zambia, some of which Michelou says are “even more beautiful than Colombian material.”  
  
The oversupply of commercial-quality goods is impacting this African nation.  
  
In December, Gemfields announced it was [temporarily suspending production](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13516-gemfields-to-temporarily-suspend-emerald-mining) at the Kagem mine for up to six months.   
  
Five months later, in early May, the company said it would resume [“focused”open-pit mining at the site](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13902-gemfields-resumes-emerald-mining-in-zambia).  
  
The miner’s most recent emerald and ruby auctions held prior to the announcement had yielded lower-than-expected revenues, which it attributed to an oversupply of Zambian emeralds on the market at “discounted prices,” lower production of premium rubies, a weaker luxury market, and civil unrest in Mozambique.  
  
To address these challenges, the miner announced a package of measures designed to cut costs and streamline its business, which included the months-long suspension of mining at Kagem.  
  
However, some say the use of terms like “discounted prices” can give a skewed perception of the emerald market.   
  
Grizzly Mining (the competitor Gemfields is believed to be referring to when it mentions “discounted prices”), which also mines emerald in Zambia, offered a total of 1.93 million carats in its [December emerald auction](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13483-grizzly-emerald-auction-garners-22-4m).  
  
Dussart noted that while the volume of material in the Grizzly auction was high, in reality, the proportion of gem-quality material was not.  
  
“Because it was a lot, it looked like the prices went down,” he says, when in fact, prices for the high-end material have not gone down at all.  
  
“If you look at the collections from the high jewelers, there are significantly more emeralds, and so it’s like, emeralds must be all the rage,” he says. “But no, there’s just more emerald right now on the market.”

> “Gems, by definition, are freaks of nature. Once you understand that part, you understand that whatever comes out in gem form and gem quality is rare.” — Simon Dussart, Asia Lounges

**The Role Brands Could Play**  
While the luxury jewelry brands once bought only material from top localities—think Colombian emeralds, Ceylon sapphires, and Burmese rubies—they are now a bit more “country agnostic,” according to Dussart, who pointed to Van Cleef & Arpels as an example.  
  
Perhaps, he wonders, the brands are the better way to move the ultra-expensive fine quality material, recalling a recent occurrence with a luxury brand that was looking at an extremely rare, super-clean untreated ruby from Thailand weighing more than 5 carats.   
  
It’s what the trade would refer to as a unicorn stone.  
  
“[The brands] can make phenomenal marketing around it to customers who not only have the firepower to get it but on top of that, don’t have the problem of, ‘Is it going to impact my bottom line next month?’”  
  
  [![Chopard Insofu emerald ring](https://nationaljeweler.com/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBbEZlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19----ea15daad36a7f7266e7d591867d534d851352260/20250519_Chopard%20Emerald%20ring.jpg "An emerald ring from Chopard’s “Insofu” jewelry collection, which features pieces created from the 6,225-carat “Insofu” emerald discovered in Zambia in 2010.")](/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBbEZlIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19--0e8b76f2ecb5be6551a6970f57baadb1abfde43e/20250519_Chopard%20Emerald%20ring.jpg)  

An emerald ring from Chopard’s “Insofu” jewelry collection, which features pieces created from the 6,225-carat “Insofu” emerald discovered in Zambia in 2010.

   
  
The brands have been informed of what is happening at the mines, and they understand the material, the rarity of it, and the sourcing process.   
  
Also, and perhaps more importantly, they understand the psychology of the end buyer and how to educate them.   
  
**Color’s Growing Market Share**  
The colored gemstone market, as a whole, is experiencing a surge in interest.  
  
For years, GemGuide, a trade magazine published by GemWorld International, recognized colored stones as an entire category, usually accounting for somewhere between 9 and 11 percent of the fine jewelry market, but GemWorld International Inc. President Stuart Robertson said in Tucson that isn’t the case anymore.  
  
  [![Niveet Nagpal Spectrum winner 2024](https://nationaljeweler.com/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBbEplIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19----ea15daad36a7f7266e7d591867d534d851352260/20250519_Niveet%20sapphire%20suite.jpg "Niveet Nagpal’s suite of Sri Lankan cushion-cut blue sapphires totaling 114.89 carats that won first place in the “Pairs and Suites” category of AGTA’s Spectrum and Cutting Edge Awards in 2024")](/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBbEplIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJibG9iX2lkIn19--18ddb660a2915259960dd0b4cfa48945d75e39a8/20250519_Niveet%20sapphire%20suite.jpg)  

Niveet Nagpal’s suite of Sri Lankan cushion-cut blue sapphires totaling 114.89 carats that won first place in the “Pairs and Suites” category of AGTA’s Spectrum and Cutting Edge Awards in 2024

   
  
“We’re seeing color increasing its market share. It’s become a major profit center,” he said during the presentation he co-hosted alongside Branstrator, GemGuide’s editor-in-chief.   
  
There’s a refreshing atmosphere of open-mindedness that has developed amid the increase in demand.  
  
Higher prices across the board are encouraging buyers to embrace cool inclusions, unusual colors, and non-traditional cuts.  
  
Suppliers of the Big Three are learning to ride the wave too.  
  
In 2023, Thailand-based gemstone manufacturer and supplier Navneet Gems & Minerals launched a wholesale line of [portrait-cut Mozambican rubies](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/12293-navneet-gems-introduces-portrait-cut-rubies) in non-traditional shapes like kites and hexagons, as well as in calibrated cuts.   
  
The initial collection featured material from ruby mining company Fura Gems, and Navneet recently expanded the collection with a deeper-color material sourced from Gemfields’ ruby mine in Mozambique.  
  
The expansive market is even leading some to playfully predict that a new Big Three is on the horizon.   
  
Jason Stephenson, a gemologist at supplier Pala International, wrote in a recent opinion piece for [Prism, AGTA’s magazine](https://agta.org/category/prism/), that he believes the contenders for the title are rare varieties of garnet, spinel, and Paraíba tourmaline.  
  
People have an appetite for everything beautiful, precious, and rare in general, Dussart says, and those certainly are adjectives that apply to a clean colored gemstone.  
  
“Gems, by definition, are freaks of nature. Once you understand that part, you understand that whatever comes out in gem form and gem quality is rare. It may not be as rare as another, but it’s still rare.”

This National Jeweler article (published May 19, 2025) examines the state of the "Big Three" colored gemstones—sapphires, emeralds, and rubies—in the modern U.S. market. Written by Lauren McLemore, associate editor for gemstones, the piece first appeared in the 2025 State of the Majors print edition.

KEY THEMES AND FINDINGS:

**Pricing Dynamics:** The finest untreated sapphires, rubies, and emeralds continue to command the highest prices of any gemstone. Since the pandemic, untreated fine sapphires have tripled in price. The mid-range market segment is "dying," according to gemstone dealer Simon Dussart of Asia Lounges, as mines struggle with profitability and shift toward treated materials for the low end. Rubies above 3 carats have become effectively inaccessible for many dealers.

**Ruby Market:** Untreated fine-quality ruby is exceedingly rare and now a specialized market. Myanmar's Mogok Valley remains the benchmark for quality but production has decreased significantly—over 90% of rubies over $50,000 per carat auctioned at Christie's (as of 2009) came from Mogok. Today, northeast Mozambique is the main source of ruby production, though quality and quantity are decreasing. Gemfields set a record per-carat price of $321.94 at its December 2024 Montepuez mine auction. Ethical sourcing alternatives include Columbia Gem House's "Pomme Ruby" from Madagascar and Virtu Gems' Kenyan rubies. Trading Afghan rubies remains legally complex due to Taliban sanctions.

**Sapphire Market:** Sapphire represents a smaller market value than ruby and emerald and is unique among the Big Three for its rainbow of colors. Over 90% of sapphires are treated. Overall sapphire quantity has decreased significantly since the 1980s. While classic "royal blue" (Princess Diana-style) sapphires command premium prices, buyers have shifted toward teal sapphires from Australia and denim-blue Montana material, with some movement back to Ceylon blue tones at 2025 trade shows.

**Emerald Market:** Emerald has benefited from the popularity of green gemstones and colorful engagement rings. Colombia, Brazil, and Zambia dominate global supply. There have been no major new discoveries in 40 years. Finer-quality untreated material is becoming rarer—demand for no-oil emeralds outstrips supply. Zoe Michelou of Imperial Colors Ltd. (Bangkok) notes prices keep climbing, sometimes changing within two months. Colombian emeralds still command premium prices due to history. The Swat district in Pakistan produces extremely clean, highly saturated small crystals (dubbed "the Rolls-Royce of emeralds" due to luxury watch company usage). Gemfields temporarily suspended mining at Zambia's Kagem mine (December, up to six months) citing oversupply of commercial-quality emeralds, then resumed focused open-pit mining in early May. Grizzly Mining offered 1.93 million carats at its December emerald auction.

**Role of Brands:** Luxury brands like Van Cleef & Arpels are becoming more "country agnostic" in sourcing and are seen as better positioned to market ultra-expensive fine-quality material (e.g., "unicorn" stones) to buyers with significant purchasing power.

**Market Share Growth:** Colored gemstones now account for more than 9-11% of the fine jewelry market, which was the previous long-standing range, according to GemWorld International President Stuart Robertson. Higher prices are encouraging buyers to embrace inclusions, unusual colors, and non-traditional cuts (e.g., Navneet Gems' portrait-cut Mozambican rubies in kite and hexagon shapes). Some in the trade speculate about a new "Big Three" emerging—rare garnet, spinel, and Paraíba tourmaline, per gemologist Jason Stephenson of Pala International.

**Key Quote:** "Gems, by definition, are freaks of nature. Once you understand that part, you understand that whatever comes out in gem form and gem quality is rare." — Simon Dussart, Asia Lounges
args.key_excerpts: "There used to be three prongs in the market—the low, the mid-range, and the high range. One could argue there was a fourth one, the super high end, but that's like, an oddity of the high end. But the mid-range is dying." — Simon Dussart, Asia Lounges, "Rubies, pre-COVID, that was out of my range anyway because it was already in the six figures, but now it's like, forget about it. It's impossible." — Simon Dussart, "Gems, by definition, are freaks of nature. Once you understand that part, you understand that whatever comes out in gem form and gem quality is rare." — Simon Dussart, "I call it the Rolls-Royce of emeralds, because it's what the [luxury] watch companies are using. The price also has gone up, but it remains unstable due to inconsistent production, regional factors, and the limited supply, as the mine is not mechanized." — Zoe Michelou, Imperial Colors Ltd., "We're seeing color increasing its market share. It's become a major profit center." — Stuart Robertson, GemWorld International President

## Summary of Gemstone Market

### How Will the Gemstone Market Value Evolve by 2036?

According to FMI's estimates, the sector is projected to expand from USD 38.4 billion in 2026 to USD 72.8 billion by 2036, registering a CAGR of 6.6%. This valuation reflects a dual-speed growth engine where the [United States gemstone](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/united-states-gemstone-market) sector anchors high-value natural sales, while emerging markets drive volume in the affordable luxury segment.

**FMI Research Approach:** Based on proprietary modeling of import data (USGS, UN Comtrade) and corporate revenue guidance from major miners (De Beers, Gemfields).

### What Defines the Structural Evolution of the Industry?

FMI analysts opine that the industry is transitioning from a fragmented, inventory-heavy model toward a streamlined, data-driven ecosystem focused on provenance. This evolution is driven by the rapid adoption of tracking technologies and the rising dominance of the [synthetic diamond](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/synthetic-diamond-market), which forces natural players to differentiate through scarcity and verified ethics.

**FMI Research Approach:** Insights derived from analysis of patent filings (Guebelin’s DNA tags), production reports, and strategic pivots announced by market leaders.

### Which Region Anchors Global Demand?

The United States remains the dominant demand center, supported by consistent import values (USD 25 billion in 2023) and a robust bridal jewelry culture. However, the [Japan gemstone](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/japan-gemstone-market) sector and emerging hubs in Southeast Asia are becoming critical for high-quality colored stones and precision manufacturing.

**FMI Research Approach:** Regional weighting based on UN Comtrade import statistics, luxury retail footprint analysis, and consumer spending surveys.

### How Will Lab-Grown Diamonds Impact the Market Structure?

By 2036, the [cvd lab grown diamond](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/cvd-lab-grown-diamond-market) segment is expected to dominate the mass-market jewelry category, fundamentally separating "fashion" from "investment" purchases. This shift forces natural diamond producers to retreat into the hyper-luxury tier, relying on "Origins" strategies to justify significant price premiums over functionally identical synthetic rivals.

**FMI Research Approach:** Analysis of sales volumes from Pandora and Brilliant Earth, alongside pricing trends in the wholesale LGD market.

### What Is the Primary Definition of this Market?

The market encompasses the extraction, processing, and sale of natural and synthetic precious and semi-precious stones, including diamonds, emeralds, rubies, and sapphires. It explicitly includes revenue from [colored gemstones](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/colored-gemstones-market) and pearls used in jewelry and industrial applications, but excludes raw mining output not destined for commercial or industrial finishing.

**FMI Research Approach:** Definition aligned with HS codes for precious stones and metals, filtered for commercial jewelry and industrial grade applicability.

### What Unique Trends Are Shaping Consumption?

A key trend is the "Provenance Premium," where buyers demand forensic evidence of a stone's journey, driving investments in blockchain and physical tracers. Simultaneously, the integration of [crystal products](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/crystal-products-market) into wellness and lifestyle categories is expanding the addressable market beyond traditional adornment.

**FMI Research Approach:** Synthesized from sustainability reports (Pandora, De Beers), consumer sentiment analysis, and technology adoption rates in the midstream.

## Why Is Provenance Technology Becoming a Gatekeeper?

Procurement teams now evaluate traceability not as a marketing add-on but as a fundamental compliance gate that determines market access. The deployment of technologies like De Beers' DiamondProof and Guebelin's "Emerald Paternity Test" creates a mechanism where stones without verified origin are discounted or excluded from premium channels. For retailers, the trade-off is clear: invest in detection hardware and verified supply chains to protect brand equity, or risk reputational damage in a market increasingly sensitive to ethical sourcing. This pressure shifts leverage toward vertically integrated players who can control the data trail from the mine to the [diamond jewelry](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/diamond-jewelry-market) retail counter, effectively marginalizing aggregators who rely on mixed sources.

As per FMI's projection, this technological bifurcation drives a wedge between the "blind" supply chain and the "verified" ecosystem, enabling premium pricing for traceable assets. Lucara’s consistent recovery of high-value stones, such as the 2,488-carat Motswedi diamond, reinforces this dynamic by providing high-visibility assets that justify the cost of provenance tracking. For investors, the signal sits in the widening valuation gap between companies that own their supply integrity and those dependent on the open market. Consequently, the adoption of forensic tagging and blockchain ledgers is expected to accelerate, becoming a standard operating procedure for the [luxury fine jewellery](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/luxury-fine-jewellery-market) sector by 2036.

## What is the Segmentation Outlook of Gemstone Market ?

The segmentation outlook reveals a market defined by product type, application, and origin, where value is concentrating in high-transparency categories. The Emerald segment currently commands a significant position, while Jewelry & Ornaments dominate applications, reflecting the enduring appeal of personal adornment over industrial use. FMI analysts opine that by 2036, the mix will pivot toward "investment-grade" colored stones and branded [industrial diamond](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/industrial-diamond-market) applications, driven by precision manufacturing needs. A standout data point is the 32.0% share held by Emeralds, which signals a robust preference for colored assets that offer visual distinctiveness and perceived rarity compared to the commoditized white diamond sector.

### Why Does the Emerald Segment Command a Leading Share?

## How Is Sustainability Reshaping Manufacturing Economics?

Manufacturing planners face a different constraint: the carbon footprint of production is rapidly becoming a decisive factor in supplier selection for global brands. The shift toward "carbon-negative" materials, exemplified by startups like Aether Diamonds, introduces a mechanism where environmental metrics serve as a proxy for product quality and innovation. This change forces traditional miners to audit their emissions and water usage, as seen in Alrosa’s move to achieve carbon neutrality for its diamond complex. For distributors, the binding constraint becomes the verification of these green claims, as [luxury products](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/industry-analysis/luxury-products) consumers increasingly scrutinize the environmental cost of their purchases.

Pandora transitioned to using 100% recycled silver and gold by August 2024, setting a new baseline for material sourcing in the mass-market jewelry sector. Those dynamic drives a ripple effect upstream, forcing refiners and miners to certify their recycling loops or risk losing contracts with major volume buyers. The emergence of lab-grown diamonds as a sustainable alternative has accelerated this trend, compressing the premium for natural stones that cannot demonstrate a comparable or superior environmental scorecard. Winners in this environment will be those who can integrate sustainability into their core operational model, turning compliance into a marketable asset rather than a regulatory cost.

### What Fuels the United Kingdom's Resurgence?

Demand for gemstones in the United Kingdom is anticipated to grow at a **6.90% CAGR**, buoyed by its status as a global trading hub and a resilient high-net-worth consumption market. The Board of Directors at Gemfields Group Limited noted in April 2025: "Market conditions through 2024 were more challenging than we could have anticipated. Revenues at both emerald and ruby auctions were materially lower than the Group experienced in recent years due to three principal factors." This underscores the volatility even in established markets, yet the UK's robust import value of USD 92.04 billion in 2024 signals a deep underlying capacity to absorb premium supply despite auction-level fluctuations. Consequently, the market is pivoting toward private sales and bespoke commissions to bypass the instability of public auction cycles.

### How Is Germany Maintaining Stability?

The gemstone industry in Germany is projected to expand at a **6.7% CAGR**, reflecting a cultural preference for durability, precision cutting, and certified sustainability. Demand is underpinned by a "Mittelstand" of specialized cutters and polishers who integrate seamlessly with the Swiss watch industry and high-end [united states luxury fine jewelry](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/united-states-luxury-fine-jewelry-market) brands seeking European craftsmanship. While specific country-level corporate data is less volatile, the global trend of rising input costs, Gemfields reported operating costs of USD 172 million, impacts German workshops that rely on imported rough. The implication for local players is a need to secure long-term supply agreements for ethical rough stones to protect their value-add margins against global price shocks.

### Why Is the United States Market Resilient?

The gemstone market in the United States is poised to register a **6.3% CAGR**, serving as the clearinghouse for global production and the primary testing ground for retail innovation. Beth Gerstein, CEO of Brilliant Earth, stated in March 2025: "Despite a competitive, highly promotional holiday season, we not only hit the high end of our net sales expectations but also delivered Q4 profitability that far surpassed our guidance, marking our 14th consecutive quarter of profitability as a public company." This resilience is structurally supported by a massive domestic consumption base, evidenced by USD 25 billion in imports in 2023, which absorbs supply even when other regions falter. Strategically, this forces competitors to maintain heavy inventory positions in the USA to service the "on-demand" expectations of American retailers and e-commerce platforms.

### What Constraints Define the Japan Market?

Gemstone demand in Japan is anticipated to grow at a **5.0% CAGR**, a steady trajectory defined by a mature demographic that prioritizes quality and heritage over fast fashion trends. Import data from UN Comtrade shows Japan imported USD 15.15 billion in pearls and precious stones in 2024, indicating a stable but cautious procurement environment where buyers are highly selective. The mechanism driving this market is the "trust premium," where established department stores and legacy jewelers dominate, creating high barriers to entry for new, unverified players. For exporters, success in Japan requires rigorous quality control and certification, as the market demonstrates near-zero tolerance for undisclosed treatments or ambiguous provenance.

## Market Definition

The gemstone market encompasses the commercial ecosystem dedicated to the exploration, extraction, processing, and retail of precious and semi-precious stones. This includes natural diamonds, emeralds, rubies, sapphires, and a vast array of colored gemstones, as well as the rapidly expanding sector of lab-grown or synthetic counterparts. The definition strictly covers stones that are cut and polished for use in jewelry, ornamentation, and luxury artifacts, measuring revenue at the point of wholesale distribution or initial retail sale.

Included in this market are the revenues generated from the sale of rough and polished stones, as well as the value-added services related to certification, grading, and traceability which are increasingly bundled with the physical asset. It covers all grades of gem-quality stones and near-gem qualities used in "affordable luxury" applications, along with the burgeoning market for branded synthetic stones sold through jewelry channels. The scope also extends to the trading activities in major hubs like Antwerp, Mumbai, and Dubai, capturing the midstream value accumulation.

Excluded from this valuation are industrial-grade diamonds and stones used exclusively for abrasive, cutting, or drilling purposes, unless they are dual-use qualities sold into the jewelry market. The market sizing also excludes the resale of vintage or second-hand jewelry (the secondary market) and the value of the metal settings (gold, platinum) in finished jewelry pieces, focusing solely on the gemstone component's value. Retail sales of generic, unbranded costume jewelry using non-precious simulants (like cubic zirconia or glass) are also explicitly excluded.

The Gemstone Market report from Future Market Insights (FMI), authored by Principal Consultant Rahul Pandita, provides a comprehensive analysis of the global gemstone industry. The market is estimated at USD 38.4 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 72.8 billion by 2036, registering a 6.6% CAGR. Emeralds lead the product segment with a 32.0% share, while Jewelry & Ornaments dominate the application segment with 78.0% share. South Korea (7.2% CAGR) and the United Kingdom (6.9% CAGR) are the fastest-growing markets, followed by Germany (6.7%), the United States (6.3%), and Japan (5.0%).

KEY TRENDS AND DRIVERS:
- The market is shifting from opaque trading toward "verified luxury" with provenance-based value chains, where origin proof and grading quality determine buyer confidence.
- Lab-grown diamonds are expected to dominate the mass-market jewelry category by 2036, fundamentally separating "fashion" from "investment" purchases and forcing natural diamond producers into the hyper-luxury tier.
- Provenance technology (blockchain, forensic tagging, physical tracers like De Beers' DiamondProof and Guebelin's "Emerald Paternity Test") is becoming a compliance gate determining market access, creating a valuation gap between companies that own supply integrity versus those dependent on open markets.
- Sustainability is reshaping manufacturing economics, with carbon footprint becoming a decisive factor in supplier selection. Pandora transitioned to 100% recycled silver and gold by August 2024, and Alrosa achieved carbon neutrality for its diamond complex.
- The "Provenance Premium" trend sees buyers demanding forensic evidence of a stone's journey, driving investments in blockchain and physical tracers.

REGIONAL INSIGHTS:
- United States remains the volume anchor, importing USD 25 billion in gemstones in 2023, with a 6.3% CAGR. Brilliant Earth CEO Beth Gerstein reported 14 consecutive quarters of profitability.
- South Korea leads growth at 7.2% CAGR driven by tech-savvy omnichannel retail and rapid adoption of branded lab-grown alternatives.
- UK growth (6.9% CAGR) is buoyed by its trading hub status with USD 92.04 billion in imports in 2024, pivoting toward private sales and bespoke commissions.
- Germany (6.7% CAGR) benefits from precision cutting and certified sustainability integrated with the Swiss watch industry.
- Japan (5.0% CAGR) is characterized by a "trust premium" with rigorous quality control requirements, importing USD 15.15 billion in pearls and precious stones in 2024.

KEY COMPANY DEVELOPMENTS:
- De Beers reported USD 3.3 billion revenue in 2024 despite a 23% decline; incumbents leverage upstream dominance to enforce traceability standards.
- Gemfields sold the Fabergé luxury jewelry brand for USD 50 million in August 2025 to focus on core colored gemstone mining.
- GIA expanded origin determination services to include opal, peridot, and demantoid garnet (effective January 1, 2026), and overhauled lab-grown diamond grading on October 1, 2025, replacing the 4Cs nomenclature with "Premium" and "Standard" descriptors.
- Lucara recovered the 2,488-carat Motswedi diamond, reinforcing the value of high-visibility traceable assets.
- Pandora reported 13% organic growth in 2024 and 87% growth in lab-grown diamond sales in Q1 2024.

MARKET SCOPE: The market covers extraction, processing, and sale of natural and synthetic precious/semi-precious stones (diamonds, emeralds, rubies, sapphires, opals, spinel, pearls) for jewelry, ornamentation, and luxury artifacts. Segments include product type, application (Jewelry & Ornaments, Luxury Art, Others), end use (Jewelers, Industrial, Personal Investment), and region. Exclusions include industrial-grade stones, secondary/second-hand market, metal setting values, and non-precious costume jewelry simulants. Key players include Gem Diamonds, Kiran Gems, Gemfields, Alrosa, De Beers (Anglo American), Pandora, Brilliant Earth, Lucara, Sarine Technologies, Fenix Diamonds, Guebelin, and Rio2. The report is 324 pages, starting at US$ 5,000, with research based on USGS and UN Comtrade data, corporate revenue guidance from De Beers and Gemfields, and FMI's proprietary forecasting model.

# Inside the Rising Market for Colored Gems

![Yvonne Raley](//www.cecileraleydesigns.com/cdn/shop/users/avatar_250x250_crop_center_5dca233f-e88f-4006-bc83-6e1578054694_54x54.jpg?v=1677682009)

Written by Yvonne Raley

  

![Inside the Rising Market for Colored Gems](//www.cecileraleydesigns.com/cdn/shop/articles/Gem_Market_Blog_Title_c06a0b70-398f-4204-a7f7-bb79a504877b_1024x1024.png?v=1780576509)

The secret seems to be out: colored gemstones have made significant progress catching up to the diamond market in the jewelry world. With lab grown diamonds steadily gaining market share, the value of diamonds is plummeting. Meanwhile the opposite is happening in the colored gem markets, especially when it comes to the most popular higher value gems: blue sapphire, ruby, emerald and Paraiba tourmaline. As a 2025 article by Jennifer Heebner of Spectrum details, many jewelers have shifted from an inventory that previously consisted mostly of diamonds to one with up to 50% colored gems. (The Rise of Color, Volume II, 2025, https://agta.org/from-prism-volume-ii-2025-the-rise-of-color-colored-gemstones-are-gaining-market-share-in-a-diamond-loving-world/).

If you consider availability and supply of colored gems vs diamonds, this shift is huge. While there are no hard figures available that compare production volume of diamonds vs, say, sapphire, minimum estimates are around 100:1 and above. (Most of the diamonds produced are industrial value, and that increases the difficulty of finding a good comparison base). Blue sapphire, meanwhile, is actually a very ubiquitous stone in the fine quality category (so I am leaving out amethyst and other quartz of lower value in this comparison). Sapphire is also one of the largest revenue creators in the colored gem market with total revenue of 1% of the total annual global revenue generated. So if you compare supply and demand, assuming that sapphire goes up from 1% to 2% of the global market because jewelry retailers prefer to have more sapphires in their inventory, pricing has to increase because there is not enough availability.

Anecdote: when I first started making jewelry, I pitched my inventory to jewelry stores and I was asked a few times if I could “create a line” with a particular gem. My answer was always “no” because each gem is unique and I would not be able to create even 5 rings where the center stone looks the same (assuming a larger center stone, say 1 carat and above). It is very hard to match five pieces of the same color blue sapphire in 1 carat round (let’s say 6mm on the nose). It is even harder to do that with ruby or emerald, and nearly impossible with Paraiba. With diamonds, you can easily match a few hundred pieces in that size (and same color, say GH, and same clarity, VS2 for example).

According to the Natural Gem article [here](https://thenaturalgem.com/en/performance-of-gemstones/ "Natural Gem Article on the Performance of Colored Gems"), unheated blue sapphires have tripled in value between 2013 and 2023. Ruby has gone up by a factor of nearly five. Emeralds did not go up as much in that time period, but when I returned to Colombia last month after a 3 ½ year absence, I found prices to have nearly doubled from 2022. Note by the way the miserable performance on diamonds by comparison. Here's the graph from the article:

![]()![](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/1139/4488/files/Gem_graph.webp?v=1779114582)![]()![]()Also note that this graph ends just where it gets interesting, as lab grown diamonds have made quite a splash in the US market since 2023! Since then both market share and value of diamonds has dropped even further.

Now adding Paraiba tourmaline into the mix, we see an even more drastic price increase. A Swiss colored gem company called “Edelsteinkabinett” claims a 45% increase in value in the last year, with the most valuable gems coming from old stock (https://edelsteinkabinett.ch/pages/paraiba-tourmaline-prices-forecast). I can agree insofar as I have noted the the intensity of color in newer inventory has decreased, especially in the larger sizes, but really down to the smallest. For example, last February I wanted to stock up on the greenish colored smaller rounds (2-2.7mm) that I had in stock, as well as ovals of similar quality but bluer color. All that material had sold out in the meantime. I had bought most of it already in the past, not realizing there were no “refills”. Now I cannot replace it.

You can see the gems above [here](https://cecileraleydesigns.etsy.com/listing/4378841447 "Ceylon sapphire Emerald Cut"), [here](https://cecileraleydesigns.etsy.com/listing/1884944061 "Russian emerald round"), [here](https://cecileraleydesigns.etsy.com/listing/4467051599 "Paraiba Tourmaline Pear") and [here](https://cecileraleydesigns.etsy.com/listing/4501700556 "Unheated ruby oval")...

A couple of weeks ago I was asked what a top quality 1.5 carat Paraiba would cost now. Well, I saw one in Tucson, an oval from the old mines, glowing blue and clean. Adding my own margin, I quoted $117,000 net for the gem. Given the buyer’s response, their expectation was about 80% less than what I had quoted.

And the reasons they gave for why the value of one of my gems (which has since sold) should be lower: the cutting is “commercial” quality, my gem is “lighter” in color and more included than the gem for $117K. Aside from the fact that Paraiba are cut for minimal weight loss and maximum value, so that even a very high quality Paraiba does not necessarily look precision cut, the other two points were correct. My gem was lighter in color and more included than the gem that cost 10x as much. But that only justified the sticker price it already had, and not a price lower than that.

Gem dealers that can afford to own higher value inventory know how to evaluate the price of the gems they procure, so it doesn’t usually pay for a buyer that isn’t part of the trade to debate the “value.” If the buyer cannot find anything cheaper out there, then they are most likely mistaken in their assumption that it “should be cheaper.” Secondly, if the next buyer is willing to pay the set price, then that is what determines the value at that time. Just like the housing market. If inventory is low and demand is high, then housing prices increase, and vice versa. And if a buyer cannot bid high enough, it will not help to say that the “real” value of the house should be lower.

True: in 2016 I was able to sell decent two carat paraibas for $5,000 net (per piece). But alas, that time has passed!

# Gemfields Emerald and Ruby Auctions

Wim Vertriest

![Figure 1. Fine emerald (>60 ct) and ruby (13 ct) crystals offered at the 2024 Gemfields auctions in Bangkok. Photos by Wim Vertriest.](/dam/migrated-assets/images/FA24-GNI-Fig1AB-327878-636px.jpg "Figure 1. Fine emerald (>60 ct) and ruby (13 ct) crystals offered at the 2024 Gemfields auctions in Bangkok. Photos by Wim Vertriest.")

Figure 1. Fine emerald (>60 ct) and ruby (13 ct) crystals offered at the 2024 Gemfields auctions in Bangkok. Photos by Wim Vertriest.

In May and June 2024, GIA was able to attend viewings of rough gemstones prior to Gemfields auctionsin Bangkok. The first viewing offered emeralds from Gemfields’ Kagem mine in Zambia, and the second featured rubies from the MRM mine in Mozambique (figure 1). Both viewings were immediately followed by the tender, where bids were submitted online and the winners of each parcel were notified.

Many international buyers attended the auctions, with strong interest from Indian and Israeli companies in the emeralds, while Thai and Indian companies focused mostly on the rubies. Several firms from Europe, China, and other Asian nations also submitted bids on parcels.

![Figure 2. Large emerald crystals from the Kagem mine in Zambia. The three crystals have a combined weight of 106 g, while the large single crystal weighs 479 g. In these stones, visible fractures and inclusions will determine how the pieces are processed into smaller preforms before going to polishing. Photos by Wim Vertriest.](/dam/migrated-assets/images/FA24-GNI-Fig2AB-327864-636px.jpg "Figure 2. Large emerald crystals from the Kagem mine in Zambia. The three crystals have a combined weight of 106 g, while the large single crystal weighs 479 g. In these stones, visible fractures and inclusions will determine how the pieces are processed into smaller preforms before going to polishing. Photos by Wim Vertriest.")

Figure 2. Large emerald crystals from the Kagem mine in Zambia. The three crystals have a combined weight of 106 g, while the large single crystal weighs 479 g. In these stones, visible fractures and inclusions will determine how the pieces are processed into smaller preforms before going to polishing. Photos by Wim Vertriest.

During both auctions, production from recent months was offered in pre-graded parcels. These lots are created by experienced professionals who have often spent decades working with the respective gemstones. The first factor in sorting is the size of the stones. Larger stones usually hold higher value, so these are often in very high demand by companies that specialize in fine single stones. Several substantial emerald crystals were available, including one that weighed 479 g (figure 2).

![Figure 3. Large parcel of smaller emeralds of very high clarity; the average size of the crystals is between 2.8 and 4 mm. ![Opals from Color Source Gems image](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201280%20720'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

A captivating gemstone grabbed headlines at the Sotheby’s Magnificent Jewels sale in New York this past December. The 16.53-carat Brazilian alexandrite was the center stone of a ring that sold for $1.9 million ($116,152 per carat), setting a record auction price for the color-changing mineral.

It was impressive but not surprising, according to industry insiders, considering the strong demand for rare stones that dominated the market in 2024. Wholesaler Omi Gems observes that the year’s top performers were alexandrites, rubies and Paraiba tourmalines.

Dealers who specialize in colored stones are entering 2025 in optimistic spirits. “The market for colored gems in 2025 looks strong, with retail demand in the US expected to remain robust, particularly for rare and high-quality stones,” says [Anup Jogani](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anupjogani), owner of [Jogani](https://jogani.com/) in Silver Lake, California.

## More precious than diamonds?

The ascent of colored gems is directly linked to the challenges the diamond industry is facing, stone dealers say. Although diamonds still represent the majority of jewelry sales, color is increasingly capturing market share thanks to consumers’ desire for novelty and collectors’ desire for a more reliable investment.

“I think the upheaval in the diamond industry right now is helping color,” says [Eric Braunwart](https://www.linkedin.com/in/eric-braunwart-5109437), president and CEO of [Columbia Gem House](https://columbiagemhouse.com/) in Vancouver, Washington. He cites the controversy over Russian diamonds and the embattled state of lab-grown as two factors undermining the sector in favor of the color market.

![A pear-cut, 10.73-carat spessartite garnet from 100% Natural image](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**A pear-cut, 10.73-carat spessartite garnet from 100% Natural. (100% Natural)**

[Leibish Polnauer](https://il.linkedin.com/in/leibish-polnauer-57313834), whose New York- and Israel-based company, [Leibish](https://www.leibish.com/our-story), deals in fancy-color diamonds and colored gems, says the latter category outperforms the former. “Gemstones are selling at a higher price than a year ago, while polished diamonds have gone down…. High-end jewelers make a margin on gemstones of about 80%, but for fancy-colored diamonds, the retailer’s margin is about 40%.” In the bridal segment specifically, he adds, the market share of colored gemstones rose to 15% last year.

Many see colored stones as a safe haven in uncertain times. High-value clients at [Joseph Gad](https://josephgad.com/) have been looking into investment-quality gems as “a way to hedge many of the other assets they currently hold in their portfolios,” reports [Gabriel Ammar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/gabriel-ammar-395b0173), the New-York based company’s vice president of global operations. Known as a leading supplier of Colombian emeralds, sapphires and rubies, the firm has seen stones of over 10 carats become the most covetable among savvy investors.

At the [Swiss Gemmological Institute (SSEF)](https://www.ssef.ch/), 2024 confirmed a more substantial interest in colored gemstones over diamonds, especially untreated, high-quality specimens, says [Laurent Cartier](https://ch.linkedin.com/in/dr-laurent-cartier-22421998), the lab’s head of special initiatives.

Beyond the traditional Big Three — rubies, sapphires and emeralds — high-jewelry houses and independent designers often feature Paraiba tourmalines, black opals, spinels, and garnets. “Recent auction results and campaigns by maisons show that these gems are becoming increasingly noticed by the public,” reports Cartier. “It’s one of the reasons we decided to offer free online courses on some of these gems.”

## The cost of success

The desirability of colored material has caused sharp price rises, with dealers noticing increases of over 10% to 20% in the last decade and skyrocketing highs during the Covid-19 years, starting in 2020. Supply limitations and restrictions in mining operations are driving these prices, as is “the growing demand for specific types and sizes, and stones that have traceability,” explains gemology consultant [Erica Silverglide](https://www.gemologygeek.com/about-the-founder-of-gemologygeek), founder of New York-based company [GemologyGeek](https://www.gemologygeek.com/).

![Image of Constantin Wild’s Dance of the Jungle suite, consisting of tourmaline, peridot and mandarin garnet](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**Constantin Wild’s Dance of the Jungle suite, consisting of tourmaline, peridot and mandarin garnet. (Constantin Wild)**

Price hikes affect every stone category, from fine and extra-fine to lower and mid-tier goods, according to data from GemGuide, a leading gem-pricing and market information provider. Its editor in chief, [Brecken Branstrator](https://www.linkedin.com/in/breckenbranstrator), says price resistance was already growing among the trade last year, becoming most apparent during the September Hong Kong show. “However, supply is still low for most materials…so with a few exceptions, we don’t expect prices to drop any time soon.” Still, she adds, the Tucson gem shows “will be the ultimate test for that.”

A proactive attitude is key when it comes to keeping up with pricing. “Current pricing is strong but stabilizing in everyday goods, while higher-end and finer stones have increased and will continue to increase dramatically,” says [Jeremy Chalchinsky](https://www.colorsourcegems.com/about), director of sales at [Color Source Gems](https://www.colorsourcegems.com/) in New York. “If you want a fine stone, buy it today rather than waiting, because chances are, it either won’t be available or the price will be higher.”

## Digging deep into the problem

The current challenges of the colored-stone market are not that novel for veterans. “Color is generally produced by artisanal miners and smaller operators,” Braunwart points out. “You may have a supply for six months, and then you don’t see anything more for the next six months.”

With the exception of emeralds and rubies from large mining companies, sourcing colored materials is the biggest pain point for dealers. Increased mining costs — some report hikes of up to 50% since the pandemic — are another factor behind the rising prices, and on top of that, the mining workforce is decreasing.

![Paraiba tourmaline from 100% Natural image](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**A 2.19-carat Paraiba tourmaline from 100% Natural. (100% Natural)**

The lack of funding, training and support for small mining communities poses a long-term threat to the industry, argues [Michella Cruz](https://www.linkedin.com/in/michella-cruz-961439229), a graduate gemologist from the Gemological Institute of America (GIA) and a Van Cleef & Arpels sales advisor in New York. “Miners leave, looking for better pay and safer work opportunities. Gem cutters don’t have access to training and tools. There are already some great independent initiatives for colored gems and new ones where ideas are fermenting. But they need support, and we need more of it.”

As artisanal miners leave, more diamantaires are entering the colored-stone market, creating an even more challenging environment for established wholesalers. Other impediments include new bureaucratic regulations and rising worldwide shipping expenses.

## ‘More like art than a commodity’

Dealing with colored stones comes with a learning curve, says [David Nassi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/david-nassi-22898a66), manager at [Mya Nassi](https://www.nassigems.com/) and president of 100% Natural, both gem suppliers in New York. “There is a lot of nuancing when it comes to quality and pricing, which can often be overlooked by a newcomer. Colored gems are more akin to art than a commodity, because there is no agreed-upon pricing list and small details can have quite an impact.”

![Cushion-cut Burmese ruby at Jogani Gallery image](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**A cushion-cut Burmese ruby at Jogani. (Jogani)**

In addition to the aesthetic draw of colored gems, the sector has a strong responsible-sourcing story to share, with a few trailblazers leading the way. One of them is Seattle-based [Monica Stephenson](https://www.linkedin.com/in/monicastephenson), president of [Anza Gems](https://www.anzagems.com/), which works with artisanal miners and cutters in east Africa. Stephenson is optimistic about the segment of “gemstones sourced very intentionally with a beneficial element [for the local communities],” and believes that “transparent stories really resonate with designers, retailers and the end customer. Competing on price or physical attributes alone doesn’t really move the needle.”

## Rising stars: From greens to oranges

Which stones are most likely to rule in 2025? With green achieving a near-consensus among dealers as the most popular shade, many are predicting that emeralds will be the year’s star gem.

“Emeralds, especially from Colombia, could see a surge in demand, supported by increasing awareness of their origins and sustainable mining practices,” says Jogani.

Sapphires in teal and green, which are among Columbia House Gem’s best sellers, are getting a lot of attention. Chalchinsky at Color Source Gems has seen huge demand for Montana and green sapphires in the last two years, and says the trend shows no sign of abating.

“Montana sapphires are still some of the market’s strongest players,” agrees Branstrator. “This year, I think we will see Australian sapphires be even more popular, with their interesting blues and greens, and especially as bicolor stones grow in popularity with buyers.”

![Leibish Cascade rings with diamonds, aquamarine, tourmaline and tanzanite image](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**Leibish Cascade rings with diamonds, aquamarine, tourmaline and tanzanite. (Leibish)**

One gem with a history of falling into and out of favor is the spinel. Today, it is enjoying a revival. Bangkok-based [Vasily Aydov](https://th.linkedin.com/in/vasily-aydov-700a88329?original_referer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bing.com%2F) and [Alexandra Floyd](https://th.linkedin.com/in/alexandra-floyd-a4a44a104), sales managers at [Gemstock.org](https://gemstock.org/), highlight the neon-pink Mahenge spinel from Tanzania as a rising star. Aydov also points to Vietnamese cobalt-blue spinels as “strong competitors to sapphires, appealing to collectors seeking untreated, vibrant stones.” At the softer end of the palette, gray and lavender spinels appeal to consumers as well, says GemologyGeek’s Silverglide.

Unconventional stones such zircons in natural browns and oranges, as well as yellow chrysoberyls, are set to gain momentum. And a strong penchant for vibrant orange shades makes garnets and topazes in that hue a hit.

“Spessartite garnet was one of our best sellers of 2024,” reports Nassi, while Cruz cites the super-saturated Fanta garnet as a standout.

“In 2024, we had stable demand in imperial topaz in the better orange-reddish colors,” affirms Constantin Wild, managing director of the eponymous gem dealer in Idar-Oberstein, Germany. “I expect this trend to continue in 2025.”

*Main image: Opals from Color Source Gems. (Color Source Gems)*

## **The synthetic issue**

Synthetic colored stones have been available on the market for longer than their diamond counterparts and are generally considered a harmless subcategory. However, a rise in cases of synthetics getting mixed in with natural gems could change this feeling of security.

The problem appears to affect small goods more, says Columbia Gem House’s Eric Braunwart, who has been investigating the topic. But because the industry is experiencing a shortage of natural stones, he warns, the issue could become more acute.

“It opens the door for some of the less-ethical players to decide, ‘Well, let’s slide some [synthetics] into the natural parcels,’” he explains. “It’s not a new issue in color, but I think it is something that the industry overall will need…to spend some more time looking at.”

Indeed, the undisclosed mix of stones is one of the most talked-about topics right now in the colored-gem industry, says Monica Stephenson of Anza Gems and [Moyo Gems](https://moyogems.com/). “This issue really highlights the importance of knowing origin and trust in traceable sources.”

# Investment Gems for the Future: Paraíba Tourmaline and Mahenge Spinel in Focus

As the jewelry market evolves in 2025, savvy investors are turning to rare colored gemstones like Paraíba tourmaline and Mahenge spinel for their skyrocketing value and unique beauty. At Jae's Jewelers, we're spotlighting these gems as top investment picks, especially when paired with lab-grown diamonds for affordable luxury. Here's why these stones are stealing the spotlight and how they can elevate your collection with both value and style.

## Why Invest in Colored Gemstones?

The gemstone market is shifting, with colored stones gaining traction as natural diamond prices continue to decline—down nearly 40% in recent years. Rare gems like Paraíba tourmaline and Mahenge spinel are seeing unprecedented demand due to their scarcity and vibrant hues, making them smart choices for collectors and investors. At Jae's Jewelers, we combine these treasures with lab-grown diamonds to offer pieces that are both high-value and ethically crafted.

### Paraíba Tourmaline: The Electric Blue Gem

Paraíba tourmaline, known for its neon blue-to-green glow, is one of the rarest gemstones on Earth, found primarily in Brazil's Paraíba region. Its vivid color, caused by copper inclusions, is unmatched, and its scarcity—only a few mines produce gem-quality stones—has driven prices to rival top-tier diamonds. In 2025, Paraíba tourmaline is a favorite for statement pieces, especially in high-end jewelry markets.

Our Paraíba Tourmaline Ring features a 1.5-carat Paraíba stone encircled by lab-grown diamonds, blending rarity with sustainability. This piece not only dazzles but also holds strong investment potential, with some Paraíba stones appreciating by 20-30% annually.

### Mahenge Spinel: The Rising Star

Mahenge spinel, sourced from Tanzania's Mahenge region, is another gem gaining investor attention. Its vibrant pink, red, and purple hues rival rubies, but at a fraction of the cost—often 70-80% less than comparable rubies. With limited supply and growing demand, Mahenge spinel is a hidden gem for those looking to diversify their portfolios. Its durability also makes it ideal for everyday wear.

Jae's Mahenge Spinel Pendant pairs a radiant spinel with lab-grown diamond accents, offering a bold yet affordable centerpiece. This combination captures 2025's trend toward unique, high-value gems that stand out in a crowded market.

## Why Lab-Grown Diamonds Enhance the Value

Pairing these rare gems with lab-grown diamonds is a game-changer. Lab-grown diamonds, produced with advanced technology, offer identical sparkle to natural diamonds but at 70-90% lower cost. Their ethical production—no mining, minimal environmental impact—aligns with modern values, making them the perfect complement to investment-grade stones like Paraíba and spinel. At Jae's, our lab-grown diamond settings enhance the brilliance of these gems without breaking the bank.

## Styling and Investment Tips

* **Statement Pieces**: Wear a Paraíba tourmaline cocktail ring for evening events, letting its electric hue shine against a lab-grown diamond halo.
* **Everyday Elegance**: Choose a Mahenge spinel pendant for versatile wear, pairing it with neutral tones to highlight its vibrant color.
* **Long-Term Value**: Store your gems in a safe, climate-controlled environment to preserve their clarity and value, as rarity continues to drive appreciation.

## Why Choose Jae's Jewelers?

At Jae's Jewelers, we curate pieces that blend investment potential with [stunning design](https://www.jaesjewelers.com/pages/custom-jewelry-design). Our Rare Gem Collection features ethically sourced Paraíba tourmaline and Mahenge spinel, set with lab-grown diamonds to maximize value and sustainability. As the market shifts away from traditional diamonds, our pieces offer a forward-thinking approach to luxury.

Discover the future of jewelry investment with Jae's Paraíba and Spinel Collection. Whether you're a collector or simply love unique beauty, these gems are your ticket to 2025's most exciting trends.
