--- SOURCE 1: Luxury in Transition: Securing Future Growth - Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/luxury-in-transition-securing-future-growth

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Bain & Company 23rd annual Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study, co-released with Fondazione Altagamma, published on January 17, 2025, by authors Claudia D'Arpizio, Federica Levato, Andrea Steiner, and Joëlle de Montgolfier. The report analyzes the global luxury market's performance in 2024 and forecasts growth through 2030.

**Key Findings for 2024:**
- Overall luxury spending totaled €1.48 trillion globally in 2024, a slight decrease of 1-3% at current exchange rates vs. 2023 (flat to +1% at constant exchange rates), though still above pre-Covid levels.
- Personal luxury goods experienced their first contraction in 15 years (excluding the Covid period), dipping 2% at current exchange rates to €363 billion.
- Only about one-third of brands experienced growth in 2024 (down from 95% in 2021-22 and 65% in 2023).
- The global luxury customer base shrank by approximately 50 million people (from 400 million to ~350 million) between 2022 and 2024 — the first contraction in the 23-year history of the report.
- Top customers (VICs, just over 2% of the customer base) now account for 45% of global luxury purchases, up from 35% in 2021.

**Regional Performance:**
- Japan was the growth champion: +12-13% at current exchange rates to €33 billion, driven by favorable currency and tourist spending.
- Europe grew 3-4% to €110 billion, retaining position as largest region, driven by tourism (Chinese tourist purchases grew 40% and US tourists 10% in the first 10 months).
- Americas declined 1% to €100 billion; US showed upward quarterly trajectory.
- Mainland China declined sharply by 20-22%, dropping to 4th position; only ~5% of brands achieved positive revenue growth in China in the first 10 months.
- Rest of Asia-Pacific declined 1-2%; South Korea improved relatively.
- Rest of world grew 3-4% to €22 billion; UAE showed robust growth.

**Segment Performance (2024):**
- Luxury cars: declined 5% to €579 billion (largest segment).
- Luxury hospitality: rose 4% to €242 billion.
- Fine wines and spirits: stable at €99 billion.
- Gourmet food and fine dining: grew 8% to €72 billion.
- High-end furniture: eroded 2% to €51 billion.
- Fine art: dropped 7% to €36 billion.
- Private yachts and jets: grew 13% to €31 billion.
- Luxury cruises: grew 30% to €5 billion.
- Personal luxury goods categories: Beauty grew 3-5% to €79 billion; eyewear grew 3-5% to €17 billion; jewelry grew 0-2% to €31 billion (most resilient core category); leather goods declined 3-5% to €78 billion; apparel eroded up to 2% to €76 billion; watches declined 5-7% to €51 billion; shoes declined 5-7% to €25 billion (weakest category).

**Distribution Trends:**
- Outlets outperformed, growing 0-3%, as consumers sought value.
- Monobrand stores declined 1-4%; online channel declined 1-4% but maintained 20% market share.
- Secondhand luxury market grew 7% to €48 billion, outpacing new luxury goods.
- Net store openings in 2024 were one-third of 2023 levels.

**Profitability & Outlook:**
- Personal luxury goods profit margins (EBIT) expected at 18-19% in 2024, down from 21% in 2021-22.
- 2025 forecast: personal luxury goods growth of 0-4% (moderate).
- Through 2030: overall luxury spending expected to grow 5-9% per annum to €2-2.5 trillion; personal luxury goods to grow 4-6% annually to €460-500 billion.
- More than 300 million new addressable consumers expected globally in next five years; emerging markets (Latin America, India, Southeast Asia, Africa) expected to add more than 50 million upper-middle-class luxury consumers by 2030.
- Brands are urged to shift toward the "post-elevation era," rebuilding luxury foundations through creativity, craftsmanship, meaningful customer connections, and flawless tech-enabled execution (including generative AI). Key strategic dilemmas include exclusivity vs. broader audience, desire vs. love, and continuing price elevation vs. "high-low" strategies.

**Customer Insights:**
- Generation Z's advocacy for luxury brands continued to decline; their NPS is 25-30 points lower than millennial shoppers.
- More than 50% of consumers consider luxury brands overpriced.
- Customer satisfaction with luxury brands has dipped below pre-Covid levels.
- Experiences grew faster (5%) than goods (down 2%), as consumers prioritized travel and social events.

The study is based on triangulated data from more than 280 luxury companies, macroeconomic data, expert interviews (100+), and sources available as of November 10, 2024.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The market for personal luxury goods—the 'core of the core' of luxury segments—experienced its first contraction in 15 years (excluding the Covid period), dipping to €363 billion in 2024, a 2% decline compared to 2023 at current exchange rates (but flat at constant exchange rates).", "We estimate the market lost about 50 million customers globally between 2022 and 2024, shrinking from 400 million customers to an estimated 350 million at the end of 2024.", "Only about one-third of brands experienced growth in 2024 (compared to 95% from 2021 to 2022 and 65% in 2023).", "These very important clients (VICs), who represent just over 2% of the total customer base, now account for 45% of global luxury purchases, up from 35% in 2021. However, VICs feel less pampered by brands, as their experiences have become more transactional.", "Looking ahead to 2030, we expect overall luxury spending (including goods and experiences) to experience solid growth of 5% to 9% per annum at current exchange rates, rising from an estimated €1.48 trillion in 2024 to an estimated €2 trillion to €2.5 trillion in 2030."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Luxury Stumbles in 2024 but Can Still Return to Solid Growth | Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/luxury-stumbles-in-2024-but-can-still-return-to-solid-growth-snap-chart

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Bain & Company article, published November 13, 2024, by Claudia D'Arpizio and Federica Levato, presents the findings of the 23rd edition of the Bain & Company Luxury Study, released in collaboration with Italian luxury goods body Fondazione Altagamma. The study forecasts that the global personal luxury goods market will dip by 2% to €363 billion in 2024. The decline reflects continued strength in Japan, solidity in southern Europe, and a progressively improving trajectory in the US, but also a rapid slowdown in China and challenging conditions in South Korea. Beauty and eyewear saw the strongest category growth, jewelry was the most resilient core luxury category, while shoes and watches struggled. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Jeweler article (published May 19, 2025) examines the state of the "Big Three" colored gemstones—sapphires, emeralds, and rubies—in the modern U.S. market. Written by Lauren McLemore, associate editor for gemstones, the piece first appeared in the 2025 State of the Majors print edition.

KEY THEMES AND FINDINGS:

**Pricing Dynamics:** The finest untreated sapphires, rubies, and emeralds continue to command the highest prices of any gemstone. Since the pandemic, untreated fine sapphires have tripled in price. The mid-range market segment is "dying," according to gemstone dealer Simon Dussart of Asia Lounges, as mines struggle with profitability and shift toward treated materials for the low end. Rubies above 3 carats have become effectively inaccessible for many dealers.

**Ruby Market:** Untreated fine-quality ruby is exceedingly rare and now a specialized market. Myanmar's Mogok Valley remains the benchmark for quality but production has decreased significantly—over 90% of rubies over $50,000 per carat auctioned at Christie's (as of 2009) came from Mogok. Today, northeast Mozambique is the main source of ruby production, though quality and quantity are decreasing. Gemfields set a record per-carat price of $321.94 at its December 2024 Montepuez mine auction. Ethical sourcing alternatives include Columbia Gem House's "Pomme Ruby" from Madagascar and Virtu Gems' Kenyan rubies. Trading Afghan rubies remains legally complex due to Taliban sanctions.

**Sapphire Market:** Sapphire represents a smaller market value than ruby and emerald and is unique among the Big Three for its rainbow of colors. Over 90% of sapphires are treated. Overall sapphire quantity has decreased significantly since the 1980s. While classic "royal blue" (Princess Diana-style) sapphires command premium prices, buyers have shifted toward teal sapphires from Australia and denim-blue Montana material, with some movement back to Ceylon blue tones at 2025 trade shows.

**Emerald Market:** Emerald has benefited from the popularity of green gemstones and colorful engagement rings. Colombia, Brazil, and Zambia dominate global supply. There have been no major new discoveries in 40 years. Finer-quality untreated material is becoming rarer—demand for no-oil emeralds outstrips supply. Zoe Michelou of Imperial Colors Ltd. (Bangkok) notes prices keep climbing, sometimes changing within two months. Colombian emeralds still command premium prices due to history. The Swat district in Pakistan produces extremely clean, highly saturated small crystals (dubbed "the Rolls-Royce of emeralds" due to luxury watch company usage). Gemfields temporarily suspended mining at Zambia's Kagem mine (December, up to six months) citing oversupply of commercial-quality emeralds, then resumed focused open-pit mining in early May. Grizzly Mining offered 1.93 million carats at its December emerald auction.

**Role of Brands:** Luxury brands like Van Cleef & Arpels are becoming more "country agnostic" in sourcing and are seen as better positioned to market ultra-expensive fine-quality material (e.g., "unicorn" stones) to buyers with significant purchasing power.

**Market Share Growth:** Colored gemstones now account for more than 9-11% of the fine jewelry market, which was the previous long-standing range, according to GemWorld International President Stuart Robertson. Higher prices are encouraging buyers to embrace inclusions, unusual colors, and non-traditional cuts (e.g., Navneet Gems' portrait-cut Mozambican rubies in kite and hexagon shapes). Some in the trade speculate about a new "Big Three" emerging—rare garnet, spinel, and Paraíba tourmaline, per gemologist Jason Stephenson of Pala International.

**Key Quote:** "Gems, by definition, are freaks of nature. Once you understand that part, you understand that whatever comes out in gem form and gem quality is rare." — Simon Dussart, Asia Lounges
</summary>

Key details include: substantial emerald crystals were offered, including one weighing 479 g and three combined weighing 106 g. Production was offered in pre-graded parcels created by experienced sorters, with size being the first sorting factor. Emerald quality is determined by green color richness and clarity, while ruby grading focuses on color intensity, color orientation, and secondary color components (orangy or purplish), ranging from bright pinkish red to darker "closed" burgundy red. Ruby inclusions, especially dense silky bands, add complexity to grading.

Emerald valuation is complex due to abundant fractures (one crystal can yield many polished gems), while one ruby rough typically yields one finished gem.

A notable 500 g parcel of small (0.5 g, 2.8-4 mm average) but unusually clean, richly colored emeralds attracted significant attention due to their rarity and high demand. The article emphasizes that winning or losing parcels can hinge on variations as small as 0.5% of total price. Larger parcels of smaller gems often have greater economic impact than single large stones, as their profits sustain cutting workshops. Buyers bring teams including heat treaters, preformers, and polishers to inspect stones, with preforming/cutting being the most critical value-determining step.

Treatment considerations factor into valuation: fracture filling affects emerald value, and certain ruby grades require heating to improve color (e.g., those with strong purple tint). Results: ruby sales totaled nearly US$69 million with 97% of goods sold; emerald sale (higher quality rough only) totaled US$35 million with 93% of lots sold.

The article provides a "high jewelry crash course" profiling eight major maisons:

1. **Cartier** - "King of Jeweler and Jeweler of Kings." Three key fundamentals: top-quality gemstones, craftsmanship honed since Louis Cartier's workshop on 13 Rue de la Paix, and a distinctive house style. Known for animal-themed pieces (Maria Felix crocodile necklaces, Indomptables collection). 2024 theme was Nature Sauvage, featuring pieces like a flamingo necklace with a 38.5-carat emerald-cut aquamarine (recalling the 1940 Duchess of Windsor brooch) and a cockatoo piece recalling the 1944 Freedom brooch.

2. **Bvlgari** - Roman identity palpable in every piece. Italian design focused on volumes, sculptural gold forms, and large colorful gemstones often in cabochon cut. Signature icons: Serpenti (most recognizable) and Tubogas (evoking Egyptian royalty). Unique Monete collection incorporating ancient coins. 2024 Aeterna collection (marking 140th anniversary) comprises over 500 unique creations including jewelry timepieces, handbags, and fragrances. Notable pieces include a 63.86-carat cabochon Colombian emerald Serpenti necklace.

3. **Boucheron** - Defined by innovation. Founder Frédéric Boucheron first combined rock crystal with diamonds. Introduced the Point d'Interrogation (Question Mark) necklace in 1879, the first necklace requiring no clasp. Creative director Claire Choisne asks "What is the most precious?" — answered with water, leading to the 2024 Carte Blanche collection Or Bleu (26 unique creations interpreting water). Also uses unconventional materials like aluminum, black sand, and palladium.

4. **Chanel** - Ethos of ease of wear and first-person perspective (jewelry designed for how it interacts with the body, presented on mannequins). Her inaugural 1932 Bijoux de Diamants collection broke tradition. Star piece: 55.55 necklace with a 55.55-carat D-IF Type IIa diamond tribute to the No. 5 perfume bottle. 2024 High Jewelry Sport collection brought athleticism to high jewelry for the first time.

5. **Maison FRED** - Founded in Paris 1936, inspired by the French Mediterranean. 2024 Ideal Light collection (continuation of Inner Light tribute to founder Fred Samuel) journeys through Buenos Aires, featuring four high-jewelry sets with signature color palettes. Uses Australian opals, Tanzanian spinels, Colombian emeralds, Sri Lankan sapphires, and lapis lazuli. Signature Hero Cut diamond reappears.

Her style features strong graphic aesthetic, storytelling depth, and reinterpreting maison symbols like trunk clasps and locks. 2024 collection Awakened Hands, Awakened Minds comprises 220 unique creations across 13 themes paying tribute to French craftsmanship. STUDY PURPOSE: The article examines key challenges and opportunities in the high jewelry industry, exploring how brands can address sustainability and diversification demands from consumers on the supply side. It investigates two research questions: (RQ1) How can high jewelry brands enhance supply chain sustainability while maintaining luxury standards and ensuring favorable economic development? (RQ2) How does product diversification help high jewelry brands' market positioning on their way to achieving supply chain sustainability?

METHODOLOGY: The study uses a qualitative approach with semi-structured expert interviews conducted in early to mid-2025. The study achieves 22.22% coverage of all high jewelry companies (8 of the 27 listed by Cognitive Market Research).

KEY FINDINGS: 
- Sustainability has emerged as a key driver in consumer decision-making in high jewelry, with ethical concerns now central to brand strategy and supply chain practices.
- Lab-grown diamonds offer ethical and transparent alternatives to mined diamonds but have not yet entered the ultra-high-end range where rarity and natural provenance remain key value determinants. - Challenges identified include: material traceability and ethical sourcing, lab-grown diamonds not being universally accepted, and balancing craftsmanship, luxury, and sustainability.
- Diversification has emerged as a strategy to meet sustainability demands without losing the brand's luxury essence, including expansion into interior design, bags, accessories, cross-industry collaborations (e.g., watches, haute couture), and limited editions.
- Blockchain technology is increasingly used to verify gemstone origins and trace supply chains.
- Circular economy approaches (recycling gold, upcycling pre-owned jewelry) are gaining traction.
- De Beers faced its most severe inventory backlog since 2008 (approximately $2 billion in inventory) due to weak demand, lab-grown diamond competition, and pandemic-related declines in marriage rates.
- Lab-grown diamond sales in the US grew from 20% to over 50% of all diamond sales between 2021 and 2023, while natural diamond sales fell from 80% to below 50%.

This article from KaterinaPerez.com (published June 16, 2025, by jewellery insider Katerina Perez) reviews Tiffany & Co.'s Blue Book 2025 high jewellery collection, titled "Sea of Wonder." The collection of 50 high jewellery pieces, created under Chief Artistic Officer Nathalie Verdeille, draws inspiration from the archive works of legendary French designer Jean Schlumberger (1907-1987).

The article opens with a biography of Schlumberger: born in Alsace, France into a family of textile manufacturers, he moved to Paris in his early twenties, worked for couturier Lucien Lelong, and created fashion jewellery from antique fragments, corals, shells, cameos, and porcelain flowers. His work for Elsa Schiaparelli (including the 1938 Circus Collection) brought him worldwide fame, alongside surrealist collaborators Salvador Dali, Jean Cocteau, and Louis Aragon. After WWII, he opened a boutique in New York City with childhood friend Nicolas Bongard in 1946, and in 1956 he was invited by Tiffany & Co. chairman Walter Hoving to join the house, where he gained access to precious stones and creative freedom.

The 2025 Sea of Wonder collection is divided into several chapters, each celebrating Schlumberger's beloved sea creatures:
- **Seahorse**: Features blue zircon as the main stone (distinguished from cubic zirconia), combined with moonstones, sapphires, and diamonds. Highlights include a bib necklace and brooch inspired by Schlumberger's famous 1968 seahorse brooch, plus a necklace with over 80 carats of blue zircons.
- **Starfish**: Inspired by a 1956 diamond and pearl brooch from Schlumberger's first year at Tiffany. Includes earrings with over 4 carats of untreated rubies, a 6-carat ruby ring, and a transformable necklace-pendant-brooch.
- **Urchin**: Draws from Schlumberger's signature twisted gold "rope" motif and the sea urchin from a 1960s table clock. Celebrates yellow diamonds (central necklace stone over 18 carats; rings with 12 and 9 carats) and features paillonné enamel, a 19th-century technique revived by Schlumberger.
- **Wave**: Features voluminous diamond jewels with green and blue cuprian elbaite tourmalines. The articulated necklace carries over 17 carats of blue and green elbaite tourmalines and was worn by Natalie Portman at the Cannes Film Festival red carpet. Inspired by Schlumberger's 1956 Leaves necklace.
- **Ocean Flora**: New motif featuring five unenhanced Zambian emeralds totalling over 10 carats.
- **Sea Turtle**: Combines diamond-studded patterns with intricate gold detailing. The standout pendant features a cushion-cut diamond over 4 carats with a hidden mechanism converting it to a brooch, taking over 900 hours to create.

Key quotes include Schlumberger's artistic philosophy ("I'm trying to show things growing unevenly, chaotically, organically, constantly in motion. I want to capture the irregularity of the universe") and commentary from Tiffany's Chief Gemmologist Victoria Wirth Reynolds on the rare unenhanced rubies. The article emphasizes the collection as a testament to Tiffany & Co.'s commitment to creativity, craftsmanship, and appreciation for nature.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Town & Country (October 2024 issue) covers Chanel's new Haute Joaillerie Sport high jewelry collection, which is inspired by sports and athletic themes. The collection was presented in June in Monaco and was inspired by a 1921 Chanel business card discovered in the archives that read "Chanel Couture • Sport," which prompted designer Patrice Leguéreau to launch the concept. The collection's highlights include a one-of-a-kind carbon fiber and diamond cuff designed to fit like a ski boot around the wrist (with four parts and three ways to wear it: all diamond, all carbon, or diamond-carbon), a diamond chain fashioned after a hoodie drawstring created using intricate diamond tubing technique, bright blue lacquered stripes on a chunky diamond ring with a rare red spinel at center, and a necklace of rubies and diamonds with an important sapphire where rubies are scattered randomly "as if in team formation" to convey a perception of speed. The collection includes 80 pieces, featuring materials like colored lacquer, diamond tubing, hand-molded carbon, aluminum, spinels, rubies, sapphires, and mandarin garnet. Many pieces incorporate the word "Chanel" written into the design, inspired by sports jerseys showing team names. Frédéric Grangié, president of Chanel Watch and Fine Jewelry, provides extensive commentary throughout. The article also notes Chanel's historical significance as the first fashion house to present a fine jewelry collection (in 1932), and that Chanel Haute Joaillerie was not reintroduced until 1993. The article highlights that the collection marks a leap of ambition in Chanel High Jewelry history and emphasizes that "the atelier put a premium on joy" — as Grangié says, "We do take fun seriously."

The event took place on Tuesday evening and featured a cocktail, gala dinner, and fashion show with couture gowns designed by Christian Dior creative director Jonathan Anderson, who created 20 specially designed gowns for the presentation.

The collection combines abstract themes with naturalism across three groups: botanical universe, underwater worlds, and celestial bodies—all reflecting founder Christian Dior's personal passions. The designs feature whimsical interplay of shapes, cutouts, colors, overlapping motifs, and sculptural volumes celebrating the art of collage, paying tribute to artists admired by Dior's founder including Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.

De Castellane emphasized the collection's joyful spirit, noting that clients appreciate the playful, childlike elements especially in difficult times, and that the pieces appeal to younger customers. The Diorissima name plays on the original Diorissimo fragrance, offering "a feminine version" and serving as a superlative referencing more color, daring designs, and more precious jewels. Many pieces are modular—brooches can be worn as hair clips and bracelets transformed into chokers—reflecting the collection's timeless, mix-and-match philosophy. Unlike most high jewelry houses, Graff is vertically integrated, controlling the entire journey of its gemstones—from sourcing rough diamonds to cutting, polishing, and crafting finished pieces in-house. --- SOURCE 4: knowledge room | FCRF - Fancy Color Research Foundation ---
URL: https://www.fcresearch.org/lounge-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Knowledge Room section of the Fancy Color Research Foundation (FCRF) website, which serves as an educational and analytical resource hub for the fancy color diamond industry. The site's primary purpose is to provide "Auction Analysis" and "Research & Insights" content to help industry professionals and collectors evaluate fancy color diamonds before auctions.

**Key Sections and Content:**

1. **Auction Analysis (Primary Feature):** The site publishes pre-auction analyses of fancy color diamonds from major auction houses including Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips, and Bonhams across global locations (New York, Geneva, Hong Kong, Paris, Abu Dhabi, Los Angeles). The most recent entries cover auctions from July 2026 back through 2018. Each analysis evaluates diamonds using the proprietary "IDU" method, which examines three key visual characteristics:
   - **Inner-Grade:** The quality and intensity of color within the stone
   - **Color Dispersion:** How color spreads across the face-up view
   - **Undertone:** Any secondary color hues (e.g., green, brown, orange modifiers)

2. **Notable Recent Auction Analyses (2025-2026):** Examples include a 31.68-carat Fancy Vivid Orangy Pink diamond at Sotheby's Abu Dhabi (Dec 2025), a 15.05-carat Fancy Yellow cushion at Christie's New York (Dec 2025), a 2.29-carat Fancy Intense Yellow marquise at Bonhams Los Angeles (July 2026), and a 5.70-carat Fancy Intense Yellow square emerald at Sotheby's Geneva (May 2026).

3. **Research & Insights Articles:** The site includes educational articles covering topics such as:
   - The FCRF I.D.U. Grading Standard
   - The rarity of fancy color diamonds ("One in 10,000??")
   - Lab-grown diamonds versus natural diamonds ("The Eco-Friendly Myth")
   - The storytelling and brand prestige elements in fancy color diamond valuation
   - Industry trends including secondhand market growth and the "last diamond unearthed" supply concerns
   - Investment nuances and market strategy articles (e.g., Alrosa's direct-to-client strategy)
   - Photography tips for capturing authentic diamond images

4. **Key Disclaimers:** Each auction analysis includes a standard disclaimer noting that "This analysis reflects the opinions of the FCRF professional team. It does not constitute a recommendation to buy or not buy a particular diamond." Buyers are advised to verify information with auction houses independently.

5. **Notable FCRF Assessment Framework:** The IDU methodology is used throughout, and articles emphasize that for fancy color diamonds, polish, symmetry, and clarity should not be overemphasized (these are colorless diamond parameters); instead, beauty, color quality, and rarity determine value.

6. **Industry Observations:** Analyses frequently note characteristics like colorless patches/bow-ties across the crown, face-up size versus carat weight discrepancies, color zoning, fluorescence effects, and the impact of cut/facet alignment on color presentation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: The Five Most Expensive Pink Diamonds | Jewelry | Sotheby’s ---
URL: https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/the-five-most-expensive-pink-diamonds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Sotheby's article, authored by Lydia Dokko (Marketplace Jewelry Merchandising Manager at Sotheby's) and published April 8, 2026, explores the five most expensive pink diamonds ever sold at auction, along with the history, rarity, and market dynamics of pink diamonds.

**Brief History:** Pink diamonds were first discovered in India in the early 17th century at the Kollur mine in the Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh (Golconda kingdom). French merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier documented 'The Grand Table,' a large pink rough diamond over 200 carats valued at 600,000 rupees — the largest pink diamond ever recorded. Approximately 80% of recent pink diamond production came from Australia's Argyle mine, which closed in 2020, dramatically reducing new supply.

**The Five Most Expensive Pink Diamonds (sold at Sotheby's):**
1. **CTF Pink Star — $71.2 million** (Sotheby's Hong Kong, April 2017): 59.60-carat oval mixed-cut Fancy Vivid Pink, Internally Flawless. The most expensive diamond/gemstone/jewel ever sold at auction and the largest Internally Flawless Fancy Vivid Pink diamond ever graded by the GIA. Mined by De Beers in Africa in 1999 as a 132.5-carat rough, cut and polished over two years by Diacore.
2. **Williamson Pink Star — $57.5 million** (Sotheby's Hong Kong, October 2022): 11.15-carat cushion-shaped Fancy Vivid Pink, Internally Flawless, Type IIa diamond (the most chemically pure diamond type). Set a world record price per carat for any gemstone. Found in Tanzania's Williamson Mine — the same mine that produced the 23.60-carat Williamson Pink given as a wedding gift to Queen Elizabeth II in 1947.
3. **Graff Pink — $46 million** (Sotheby's Geneva, November 2010): Originally 24.78 carats, Fancy Intense Pink, potentially Flawless, Type IIa. Previously owned by Harry Winston; purchased by Laurence Graff, who recut and renamed it. Now 23.88 carats and Internally Flawless. At the time, the highest price ever bid for a jewel at auction.
4. **The Eternal Pink — $34.8 million** (Sotheby's New York, June 2023): 10.57-carat Fancy Vivid Purplish-Pink, Internally Flawless. Unearthed in 2020 at Botswana's Damtshaa mine, cut by Diacore. Notable for its electrifying fuchsia hue.
5. **Spirit of the Rose — $26.6 million** (Sotheby's Geneva, November 2020): 14.83-carat Fancy Vivid Purple-Pink, Internally Flawless, Type IIa. Unearthed in Russia by ALROSA from a 27.85-carat rough named 'Nijinsky' after the Russian ballet dancer. Named after 'Le Spectre de la Rose,' a celebrated Ballets Russes production.

**Why Pink Diamonds Are Rare:** Unlike most colored diamonds, pink diamonds owe their color to structural distortions from extreme heat and pressure during formation, not trace elements. Fewer than 0.15% of diamonds graded by the GIA are predominantly pink. A 2022 GIA study found only 2% of pink Type IIa diamonds were graded Fancy Vivid Pink. Notable related stones include The Desert Rose (31.68-carat pear-shaped Fancy Vivid Orangy Pink) and a 17.70-carat Fancy Brown-Orange diamond ring by JAR that sold for 3,302,000 HKD (426,000 USD) at Sotheby's High Jewelry auction in April 2025.

**Collecting Today:** Pink diamonds remain among the most sought-after gemstones due to rarity, vivid color saturation, and limited supply following the Argyle mine closure. Collectors focus on vivid color grades, strong provenance, and exceptional size. The article also promotes Sotheby's services for buying/selling pink diamonds, listing retail examples ranging from $17,000 to $330,000, and highlights upcoming jewelry auctions across New York, Hong Kong, Paris, Milan, Geneva, and elsewhere through late 2026.
</summary>

URL: https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/12020-estrela-de-fura-ruby-purplish-pink-diamond-sell-for-30m-each-at-sotheby-s

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Jeweler article reports on Sotheby's Magnificent Jewels auction held on June 8, 2023, in New York, which made history by selling two jewels for more than $30 million each on the same day—a first for any auction house.

KEY SALE RESULTS:
• The "Estrela de Fura 55.22," a 55-carat Mozambiquan ruby, sold for $34.8 million ($630,288 per carat), setting a world record for a ruby and any colored gemstone at auction. It was bought by a private collector from the Middle East. The ruby originated as a 101-carat rough discovered at Fura Gems' ruby mine in Mozambique in July 2022. It is the largest gem-quality ruby to ever appear at auction.
• "The Eternal Pink," a 10.57-carat internally flawless fancy vivid purplish pink diamond, also sold for $34.8 million ($3.3 million per carat). It set a world auction record for a fancy purplish pink diamond and a new price-per-carat record for that color grade. The rough was unearthed by De Beers in partnership with the government of Botswana at the Damtshaa mine and cut by Diacore over six months.

ADDITIONAL DETAILS:
• Total auction sales reached $95.9 million, the highest ever total for any jewelry auction at Sotheby's in New York, surpassing the previous record of $65.1 million set in April 2015.
• Sotheby's found buyers for 91 percent of lots, with more than two-thirds selling above their highest pre-sale estimates. Four additional pieces sold for over $1 million.
• The previous ruby record was held by the 25.59-carat "Sunrise Ruby" ($30.3 million, May 2015). Only two rubies had previously surpassed $15 million at auction.
• Fura Gems founder and CEO Dev Shetty called the ruby "a once-in-a-generation discovery" and said the sale could put Mozambique on the map as a significant ruby source. A portion of proceeds will fund the Fura Training Academy in Mozambique.
• The 11 pieces from the Constance Prosser Mellon and Constance Barber Mellon collections all sold, totaling $6.9 million. Highlights included a Cartier sapphire and diamond ring (33.51-carat royal blue Burmese sapphire, no heating) that sold for $3.3 million after a five-minute bidding battle, and a Cartier sapphire and diamond necklace (five Kashmir sapphires totaling ~34.95 carats) that sold for $2.8 million.
• Additional property from the Mellon collections was scheduled for Sotheby's Fine Jewels sale on June 14, 2023.
• Quig Bruning, Head of Sotheby's Jewelry, Americas, and Catharine Becket, Head of Magnificent Jewels, New York, both commented on the record-breaking results and Sotheby's market leadership position.

The article also includes related stories about other jewelry auctions from the same period, including the 'Light of Peace' Diamond ($13.6M at Christie's), JAR Jewels white-glove sale, and the 'Bulgari Laguna Blu' ($25M).

URL: https://www.fcresearch.org/lounge-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Knowledge Room section of the Fancy Color Research Foundation (FCRF) website, which serves as an educational and analytical resource hub for the fancy color diamond industry. The site's primary purpose is to provide "Auction Analysis" and "Research & Insights" content to help industry professionals and collectors evaluate fancy color diamonds before auctions.

**Key Sections and Content:**

1. **Auction Analysis (Primary Feature):** The site publishes pre-auction analyses of fancy color diamonds from major auction houses including Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips, and Bonhams across global locations (New York, Geneva, Hong Kong, Paris, Abu Dhabi, Los Angeles). The most recent entries cover auctions from July 2026 back through 2018. Each analysis evaluates diamonds using the proprietary "IDU" method, which examines three key visual characteristics:
   - **Inner-Grade:** The quality and intensity of color within the stone
   - **Color Dispersion:** How color spreads across the face-up view
   - **Undertone:** Any secondary color hues (e.g., green, brown, orange modifiers)

2. **Notable Recent Auction Analyses (2025-2026):** Examples include a 31.68-carat Fancy Vivid Orangy Pink diamond at Sotheby's Abu Dhabi (Dec 2025), a 15.05-carat Fancy Yellow cushion at Christie's New York (Dec 2025), a 2.29-carat Fancy Intense Yellow marquise at Bonhams Los Angeles (July 2026), and a 5.70-carat Fancy Intense Yellow square emerald at Sotheby's Geneva (May 2026).

3. **Research & Insights Articles:** The site includes educational articles covering topics such as:
   - The FCRF I.D.U. Grading Standard
   - The rarity of fancy color diamonds ("One in 10,000??")
   - Lab-grown diamonds versus natural diamonds ("The Eco-Friendly Myth")
   - The storytelling and brand prestige elements in fancy color diamond valuation
   - Industry trends including secondhand market growth and the "last diamond unearthed" supply concerns
   - Investment nuances and market strategy articles (e.g., Alrosa's direct-to-client strategy)
   - Photography tips for capturing authentic diamond images

4. **Key Disclaimers:** Each auction analysis includes a standard disclaimer noting that "This analysis reflects the opinions of the FCRF professional team. It does not constitute a recommendation to buy or not buy a particular diamond." Buyers are advised to verify information with auction houses independently.

5. **Notable FCRF Assessment Framework:** The IDU methodology is used throughout, and articles emphasize that for fancy color diamonds, polish, symmetry, and clarity should not be overemphasized (these are colorless diamond parameters); instead, beauty, color quality, and rarity determine value.

6. **Industry Observations:** Analyses frequently note characteristics like colorless patches/bow-ties across the crown, face-up size versus carat weight discrepancies, color zoning, fluorescence effects, and the impact of cut/facet alignment on color presentation.
</summary>

# The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market

Recalibration, resurgence, and more selective consumers are edging China’s personal luxury market toward recovery.

By Bruno Lannes, Priscilla Dell'Orto, and Elle Yang

* Published on January 28, 2026
* min read

![](/contentassets/c02ab855900d427aabf650cae012a533/1950x650.jpg?width=768&height=256&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

###### The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market

en

|  |
| --- |
| Bain & Company |
| At a Glance * In 2025, the mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%–5% but showed signs of recovery, starting in Q3. * Category performance was mixed. Beauty rebounded, while other categories, such as watches, continued to struggle, and fashion outperformed leather goods and bags. * Overseas luxury spending declined sharply. Weak currency and narrowing price gaps between mainland China and key luxury markets curbed demand for spending abroad. Daigou sales increased slightly but were restrained by brand-protection measures. * Domestic brands captured more share by appealing to cultural connections and local preferences. * Although it is a small portion of the total luxury market, the secondhand market showed strong growth (15%–20%). Livestreaming played a key role in the market’s expansion. * More cautious and knowledgeable consumers are driving a transition to a slow growth pattern. Signs of continued recovery are expected in 2026, and the potential for long-term recovery remains great as overall domestic consumption improves.  In 2025, the Chinese luxury market continued to recalibrate, starting a gradual recovery as consumer confidence remained cautious. Discretionary spending was still restrained as consumers became more selective and prioritized value-driven luxury items that balanced quality, exclusivity, and practicality. The trend toward experience-based consumption—including travel and wellness purchases—held steady, reflecting an ongoing preference for emotional and sensory experiences over material goods.  In general, brands catering to affordable luxury and ultra-premium segments emerged as winners, delivering perceived “true value.” These brands demonstrated strong connections with affluent young consumers or ultra-wealthy individuals.  In contrast to 2024, the share of overseas spending declined in 2025. A weaker renminbi narrowed cross-market price gaps, diminishing the appeal of international shopping. In addition, ongoing shopping mall promotions and the expansion of domestic tourism boosted consumption repatriation.  As a result of these multiple trends, the mainland Chinese personal luxury market experienced a more moderate decline of 3%–5%, after a steep decline of 17%–19% in 2024 (see Figure 1).  Figure 1    The mainland China personal luxury market declined by 3%–5% in 2025, easing after a sharp decline in 2024   The mainland China personal luxury market declined by 3%–5% in 2025, easing after a sharp decline in 2024 The mainland China personal luxury market declined by 3%–5% in 2025, easing after a sharp decline in 2024   Note: RMB is renminbi Sources: Bain-Altagamma 2025 Worldwide Luxury Market Monitor; Bain analysis Quarter-by-quarter performance The slowdown persisted through the first half of the year, though the market saw a modest Spring Festival boost. Sequential declines persisted through June.  However, a recovery started to emerge in the third quarter. Recovery in the second half was supported by favorable base effects (second half of 2025 vs. second half of 2024), a robust stock market and a resurgence in consumer confidence.  The trajectory of the recovery was confirmed in the fourth quarter, particularly in the fashion and leather categories (see Figure 2).  Figure 2    2025 is a year of two halves: After a difficult H1, nascent signs of recovery started to surface in H2   2025 is a year of two halves: After a difficult H1, nascent signs of recovery started to surface in H2 2025 is a year of two halves: After a difficult H1, nascent signs of recovery started to surface in H2   Sources: Bain-Altagamma 2025 Worldwide Luxury Market Monitor; financial reports; Bain analysis Beauty is the strongest performer among segments Luxury market performance varied by category. The beauty sector, a standout performer, rebounded with 4%–7% growth (see Figure 3). The demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances has kept steady as consumers increasingly seek emotional and sensory experiences, which remain highly valued even amid economic uncertainty.  The fashion segment demonstrated stronger resilience than leather goods, driven by a higher degree of innovation and stronger engagement with both top and aspirational consumers. Other amplifying factors included accelerated digitalization across the entire value chain and shorter product life cycles. These factors particularly benefited the ready-to-wear category, which aligned itself with consumer demand for self-expression and social experiences. This segment’s resilience reflects the increasing maturity of China’s luxury market.  Leather goods, a segment relatively more dependent on aspirational buyers, continued to struggle, with an estimated decrease of 8%–11% (see Figure 3). The category suffered from past and ongoing price increases and limited innovation, making it difficult for consumers to justify purchases.  Jewelry also showed strong improvement compared to 2024, with its expected decrease narrowed to 0%–5%. Consumers, particularly those focused on value preservation, continued to gravitate to jewelry purchases, especially fine jewelry. The increasing price of rare metals also reinforced the asset value represented by jewelry.  Watches, however, remained under severe pressure, with an estimated decline of 14%–17% (see Figure 3). Consumers became more rational in their watch purchases, influenced by a shift in preferences toward other investment assets, the availability of secondhand alternatives, and the growing appeal of sporty and smart-device alternatives.  Within these categories, the most resilient brands maintained strong brand equity and desirability through innovation and targeted pricing strategies.  Figure 3    Beauty rebounded to positive growth, while other categories continue to grapple with pressure, particularly watches   Beauty rebounded to positive growth, while other categories continue to grapple with pressure, particularly watches  Beauty rebounded to positive growth, while other categories continue to grapple with pressure, particularly watches   Sources: Bain-Altagamma 2025 Worldwide Luxury Market Monitor; financial reports; Bain analysis Luxury market grows with wealth creation In China, personal luxury market penetration is closely linked to consumer confidence and has advanced alongside wealth creation. Over the past 25 years, the first wealth-creating generation has enabled luxury market penetration and expansion, shifting the motivation for consumption from having luxury items to increase status to developing more refined preferences.  This evolving landscape is further shaped by an increasingly discerning, sophisticated, and highly segmented luxury consumer base, with three key segments influencing market dynamics:   * **Top consumers:** Continues to account for a large share of sales for premium brands across the jewelry and ready-to-wear categories * **Middle-aged, upper-middle-class consumers:** Remains deeply rooted and active in the market, with incremental buyers coming from lower-tier cities * **Next generation of aspirational consumers:** Faces limited economic opportunities and weaker upward mobility, and has delayed entry into the luxury category, which is the key factor curbing new consumer acquisition and slowing overall luxury penetration growth  Overseas shopping decreases In 2025, overseas shopping continued to play a significant role, but overall cross-border spending decreased, with only 35% of mainland Chinese luxury purchases made abroad (see Figure 4). Despite a strong recovery in overseas tourism, 65% of Chinese luxury spending occurred within mainland China, reflecting a growing preference for domestic luxury purchases and for travel experiences outside the mainland.  Figure 4    Personal luxury consumption in mainland China benefited from an uptick in repatriation   Personal luxury consumption in mainland China benefited from an uptick in repatriation  Personal luxury consumption in mainland China benefited from an uptick in repatriation   Note: 1) Excludes duty-free sales from inbound tourists Sources: Bain-Altagamma 2025 Worldwide Luxury Market Monitor; Global Blue; Bain analysis  Further reducing the incentive for Chinese consumers to shop abroad was a significantly narrowed price gap between mainland China and key luxury markets (such as Europe and Japan).  Conversely, because of the no-visa policy for many countries, the more fluid tax refund policy, and the broad product choices and shopping experience offered in mainland stores, some foreign consumers bought luxury products in mainland China. However, these inbound travelers’ purchases represented a very small portion of the total mainland China personal luxury market. Daigou market remains strong, but uneven across brands Overall, daigou activity remained elevated in 2025 despite the increased efforts of brands to regulate gray market sales, protect brand equity, and maintain pricing integrity in mainland China. The top 45 brands on daigou platforms tracked by Re-Hub showed a slight increase in sales of 3% in 2025, compared to 5% in 2024. Brands have ramped up anti-daigou measures, narrowing price gaps, controlling their overseas supply chains, implementing ID-based controls, amplifying official offline channels, and limiting access to unofficial sales channels.  To examine the effect of daigou sales on specific brands, fashion and leather goods luxury brands were clustered into three buckets according to their degree of control of the daigou channel, in particular their overseas supply chains. Not surprisingly, brands with limited or tightly controlled wholesale overseas channels have seen their daigou sales decline compared to 2024, and daigou sales represent only 5%–15% of their official sales in mainland China (vs. 15%–25% in 2024) (see Figure 5).  In contrast, for brands with larger and less regulated wholesale overseas channels, daigou sales may represent 65%–75% or even more of their total sales in mainland China (see Figure 5). Deeper discounts for less desirable brands (compared to 2024) have not consistently translated into increased revenue, however, because sales in the daigou market are closely tied to overall brand desirability. Demand can fluctuate, and brand appeal remains the decisive factor.  Figure 5    Daigou revenue increased in the fashion and leather categories, except for brands with highly controlled supply chains   Daigou revenue increased in the fashion and leather categories, except for brands with highly controlled supply chains Daigou revenue increased in the fashion and leather categories, except for brands with highly controlled supply chains   Notes: 1) Selectively tracked brands; GMV is gross merchandise value Sources: Re-Hub; Bain analysis Secondhand-market opportunities Looking ahead, brands can no longer depend on broad market growth and must instead compete through differentiated value in an increasingly stable and regulated landscape. Success will hinge on clear brand differentiation, innovative product offerings, strategic pricing, and an elevated customer experience, all while remaining competitive in an additional critical battlefield: the secondhand luxury market.  In 2025, the secondhand luxury market in China remained significantly underpenetrated, accounting for less than 10% of the total luxury market (well below the levels seen in developed markets: 20%–30%) (see Figure 6). Yet it reshaped the luxury landscape. While the primary luxury market faced challenges, the secondhand market continued to show strong gains, maintaining a 15%–20% growth rate in 2025. This ongoing expansion underscores the increasing importance of the secondhand segment as luxury prices in the primary market continue to rise and drive consumers to seek more affordable alternatives.  Figure 6    Against the soft performance in the primary market, the secondhand luxury market has seen sustained rapid growth with significant room for further expansion   Against the soft performance in the primary market, the secondhand luxury market has seen sustained rapid growth with significant room for further expansion Against the soft performance in the primary market, the secondhand luxury market has seen sustained rapid growth with significant room for further expansion   Note: RMB is renminbi Sources: Analyst reports; literature research; Bain analysis  Between 2020 and 2022, the secondhand luxury market experienced its initial and explosive growth, starting from a low base. Covid-19 travel restrictions, the rise of livestreaming, and overall growing interest in secondhand goods fueled a surge in consumer demand. Significant capital investment by secondhand players enabled them to scale their operations as these platforms emerged as serious players in the broader luxury ecosystem.  However, the market experienced a slowdown in 2023 and 2024, influenced by macroeconomic pressures, regulatory tightening, and the delisting of certain platforms. Despite these challenges, the secondhand market remained resilient, with continued growth in luxury goods liquidity and rising consumer awareness.  In 2025, a combination of factors readied the secondhand luxury market for renewed growth. The supply of pre-owned luxury goods increased. High-net-worth individuals and middle-class consumers continued to sell assets to optimize their portfolios, and resellers offered lower prices to off-load excess inventory under price pressure. In addition, consumer behavior shifted, particularly among younger, price-sensitive buyers who prioritize cost-effectiveness and sustainability over the prestige of new luxury items. This changing mindset is increasing the appeal of pre-owned goods, positioning them as a rational and desirable alternative to new items.  Another significant factor in the market’s growth was the widespread adoption of livestreaming. Livestreaming platforms enable real-time interaction and product verification, building consumer confidence in the authenticity of secondhand luxury goods. This medium has become particularly crucial for engaging consumers in lower-tier cities, where access to luxury items has traditionally been limited.  In 2025, online platforms continued to dominate the market, accounting for the majority of its total share, with livestreaming platforms representing a significantly growing portion. However, the online marketplace has resulted in stronger price transparency, which in turn has eroded the profit margins of purely online players.  As a result, top players are expanding into offline channels. These stores are viewed as key to personalized services, authentic product verification and guarantees, and enhanced customer engagement, helping bridge the gap between online convenience and tangible, experience-driven retail. Furthermore, these spaces function as both sales touchpoints and recycling hubs, foster a circular ecosystem in which consumers can trade in items, and help brands cater to a broader consumer base. Secondhand-market success by category In 2025, the secondhand luxury market in China was concentrated in leather goods and bags, along with watches. Leather goods and bags accounted for 50%–55% of the total market. Watches held the second-largest share at 25%–30%, followed by jewelry and the ready-to-wear segment, each contributing 10%–15% to the market (see Figure 7).  Figure 7    Leather goods and bags constitute the core category, while the lowest price gaps between primary and secondhand markets are seen in watches   Leather goods and bags constitute the core category, while the lowest price gaps between primary and secondhand markets are seen in watches  Leather goods and bags constitute the core category, while the lowest price gaps between primary and secondhand markets are seen in watches   Note: 1) Compared top three SKUs selected for leading brands in each category from online platform; price data recorded in December 2025 Sources: Online e-commerce platform; Bain analysis  The secondhand market also features varying price gaps between classic and seasonal models by category. The classic models maintain strong resale value (lower price gaps with primary market prices) because of their timeless appeal, making them the preferred choice for investment-minded buyers. In contrast, the value of seasonal models tends to drop more quickly because of their reliance on shifting fashion trends.   * **Leather goods and bags:** The leather goods and bags segment is characterized by strong demand and stable supply, thanks to large primary market sales. Classic models in this category are seen as strong value holders. Their long-term appeal and investment value help them maintain high time value. * **Watches:** In the watches segment, consumers consider classic models solid investment pieces. Rare models are especially valued and can command higher resale prices. Seasonal watches, however, see lower value retention and contribute to greater transaction volume. * **Jewelry:** Jewelry suffers from quick depreciation and a short resale window, largely because of its fragility and vulnerability. Unlike watches, which tend to hold their value better, jewelry’s market performance is more influenced by fashion cycles. Unless these pieces possess artistic or collectible merit, or unique craftsmanship, they generally lack the same long-term investment appeal and staying power in the secondhand market. * **Ready-to-wear items:** Secondhand-market penetration in the ready-to-wear segment remains relatively low, despite the large primary market. Expansion is difficult because cheaper alternative channels exist and consumers are often more reluctant to purchase these items, because their appeal is more subjective and a personal fit is hard to ensure. Recently, the ready-to-wear segment has seen rapid growth as increased supply has expanded product variety, lowered price transparency vs. other categories, and enabled stronger margins.   China’s secondhand luxury market is set for sustained growth, acting as an unofficial outlet for some new products and with strong potential to mirror Japan’s mature model, where resale reaches 30%–35% of the primary market. Improving authentication and retailer guarantees will further build trust and accelerate mainstream adoption. Local players emerge across luxury categories Another key 2025 trend was the rise of local players. These emerging Chinese brands are capturing consumer attention with offerings that blend innovation and cultural relevance, positioning them as strong competitors in the luxury landscape (see Figure 8).  Figure 8    Chinese players have forged a long-standing presence in the beauty sector, while emerging front-runners start to appear in other personal luxury categories   Chinese players have forged a long-standing presence in the beauty sector, while emerging front-runners start to appear in other personal luxury categories Chinese players have forged a long-standing presence in the beauty sector, while emerging front-runners start to appear in other personal luxury categories   Sources: Analyst reports; literature research; Bain analysis  They differentiated from international brands through (i) a better understanding of unmet local demand, expressed through product aesthetic, brand values, and storytelling; (ii) tailored (Chinese first) go-to-customer strategies that are digital first, chat native, and engagement oriented; and (iii) increased local access to relevant inputs and raw materials, enabling them to offer lower price points than those of international brands.  Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers. They are transforming the China luxury landscape with their distinctive fusion of global appeal and authentic Chinese identity and redefining what luxury means for modern Chinese consumers (see Figure 9).  Figure 9    Local emerging winners demonstrate resilience while mixing the global luxury playbook with authentic Chinese identity and local relevance   Local emerging winners demonstrate resilience while mixing the global luxury playbook with authentic Chinese identity and local relevance Local emerging winners demonstrate resilience while mixing the global luxury playbook with authentic Chinese identity and local relevance   Sources: Analyst reports; literature research; Bain analysis A look ahead After riding the recovery momentum in the second half of 2025, the personal luxury goods market is expected to show more positive signs in 2026, albeit with continued volatility and uncertainty. It will have help from domestic policy support and geopolitical factors, which are directing more luxury consumption back to the mainland.  The secondhand luxury market—still below the global average in market penetration—is positioned for sustained growth, with an almost stable foundational structure. As a complementary pillar to the primary market, it will enhance the maturity of China’s luxury ecosystem.  Growth remains highly category and brand dependent. More brands are expected to post single-digit gains, while those delivering “true value” will capture stronger consumer advocacy. In a low-growth environment, softer spending widens the gap between winners and laggards, accelerating consumer consolidation toward a few preferred brands.  Adding competition to the market, local luxury players are closing the gap through originality-driven strategies that incorporate distinctive Chinese elements. In parallel, global luxury brands are deepening their local cultural relevance through cross-cultural infusion, including collaborations with local artisans, to better resonate with domestic consumers.  Looking ahead, China will remain a cornerstone of global luxury market growth, despite ongoing macroeconomic challenges and broader societal shifts.  *The authors would like to express their gratitude to Xiaowen Zhang, an associate consultant in Bain’s Shanghai office.* |

The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market report by Bain & Company (published January 28, 2026, authored by Bruno Lannes, Priscilla Dell'Orto, and Elle Yang) examines the state of China's personal luxury market. Key findings:

**Market Performance:** The mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%-5% in 2025, easing after a steep 17%-19% decline in 2024. The slowdown persisted through H1 (with only a modest Spring Festival boost), but recovery emerged in Q3 supported by favorable base effects, a robust stock market, and resurging consumer confidence. Q4 confirmed the recovery trajectory, particularly in fashion and leather categories.

**Category Performance:** Beauty rebounded with 4%-7% growth, the strongest segment, driven by demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances. Fashion demonstrated stronger resilience than leather goods due to innovation, digitalization, and shorter product life cycles. Leather goods declined 8%-11%, hurt by price increases and limited innovation. Jewelry improved (decline narrowed to 0%-5%) as consumers sought value preservation. Watches remained under severe pressure with a 14%-17% decline, as consumers shifted to other investment assets and secondhand or smart-device alternatives.

**Overseas Shopping:** Only 35% of mainland Chinese luxury purchases were made abroad in 2025 (down from 2024), as a weaker renminbi narrowed cross-market price gaps, and domestic mall promotions and domestic tourism boosted consumption repatriation. Inbound foreign tourists' purchases represented a very small portion of the market.

**Daigou (gray market) Sales:** Daigou activity remained elevated but uneven. Top 45 tracked brands showed a slight 3% sales increase (vs. 5% in 2024). Brands with tightly controlled wholesale overseas channels saw daigou sales decline to 5%-15% of official sales (vs. 15%-25% in 2024). Brands with larger, less regulated wholesale channels saw daigou sales reach 65%-75% or more of total mainland sales. Brand desirability remains the decisive factor in daigou demand.

**Secondhand Market:** The secondhand luxury market grew 15%-20% in 2025, remaining under 10% of total luxury market (vs. 20%-30% in developed markets). Online platforms dominate, with livestreaming playing a critical role in building consumer confidence in authenticity and reaching lower-tier cities. Top players are expanding into offline channels for verification, personalized services, and as recycling hubs. Leather goods and bags account for 50%-55% of the secondhand market, watches 25%-30%, and jewelry and ready-to-wear each 10%-15%. The market has strong potential to mirror Japan's mature model where resale reaches 30%-35% of the primary market.

**Consumer Segments:** Three key segments shape the market: top consumers (large share of sales for premium jewelry and ready-to-wear), middle-aged upper-middle-class consumers (deeply rooted, with incremental buyers from lower-tier cities), and next-generation aspirational consumers who face limited economic opportunities and delayed luxury entry—the key factor curbing new consumer acquisition.

**Local Brands:** Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers, differentiating through understanding of unmet local demand, digital-first go-to-customer strategies, and local access to raw materials enabling lower price points.

**Outlook:** The market is expected to show more positive signs in 2026, supported by domestic policy and geopolitical factors directing consumption back to the mainland. Growth remains highly category- and brand-dependent, with "true value" brands capturing stronger advocacy. China remains a cornerstone of global luxury growth despite macroeconomic challenges.

# Global luxury sales are on track for a record decline in 2020, but business is booming in China

![thumbnail](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/106497130-1587401879908img_0254.jpg?v=1587401920&w=60&h=60&ffmt=webp)

[Lauren Thomas](https://www.cnbc.com/lauren-thomas/)[@laurenthomas](https://twitter.com/laurenthomas)

[WATCH LIVE](/live-tv/)

Key Points

* China is on track to become the biggest luxury market by 2025, as wealthy Chinese consumers travel less and splurge more on their home turf, a Bain report said.
* The market for personal luxury goods is expected to contract this year for the first time since 2009.
* Bain expects the global luxury market to return to 2019 levels by the end of 2022 or early 2023, driven by digital sales growth and strength in China.

In this article

* [TPR](/quotes/TPR)
* [CPRI](/quotes/CPRI)
* [FTCH](/quotes/FTCH)
* [BABA](/quotes/BABA)
* [BCSF](/quotes/BCSF)

A view of a person wearing mask passing by a Macy's in Herald Square amid the coronavirus (COVID-19) outbreak on March 24, 2020 in New York City.

John Nacion | NurPhoto | Getty Images

The stage is set for China to become the world's biggest luxury market by 2025, according to a new report.

In a year where global luxury spending has fallen dramatically, China's domestic market is still poised to grow, as the region's wealthy residents stayed close to home due to the [coronavirus pandemic](https://www.cnbc.com/coronavirus/) but splurged on jewelry, leather goods and fine wine.

Historically, luxury markets in Europe and the United States have been fueled by international travel — especially of Chinese tourists. But the new report from Bain & Co. predicts wealthy Chinese consumers are going to be doing much more of their spending locally in the years ahead.

"The overall [luxury] market has basically been shut down," said Federica Levato, a partner at Bain's luxury goods vertical, citing lockdowns and pandemic-induced store closures. "And then the immediate consequence of it was no travel, basically. We've had 11 months of no intercontinental travel whatsoever."

The result: Local luxury consumption has "roared" in China, Levato said.

Chinese consumers were already a known force in the industry, accounting for a third of luxury spending last year, Bain said.

This year, mainland China is expected to be the only region to report year-over-year growth, with the country's luxury market soaring 45% to reach 44 billion euros ($52.21 billion), according to Bain's 2020 Fall Luxury report.

It said sales of personal luxury goods — which includes clothes, jewelry, watches, beauty products and accessories — will contract this year for the first time since 2009. Bain estimates sales will fall 23%, at current exchange rates, to hit 217 billion euros ($257.47 billion) — the largest annual drop ever recorded by Bain.

The overall luxury market — which encompasses luxury goods and experiences such as private jets, yachts and fine wine — is forecast to shrink at a similar pace year over year. It is estimated to be valued at roughly 1 trillion euros ($1.19 trillion), according to the report, which was done in collaboration with the Italian luxury goods manufacturers' foundation Altagamma.

In the Americas, consumers are not offsetting lost sales from global travelers, and department store chains are struggling. Sales in the region are expected to contract 27% to 62 billion euros ($73.56 billion) this year.

Several American department store operators have filed for bankruptcy protection this year, including the high-end chains Neiman Marcus and Lord & Taylor. The latter, the oldest in the nation, is liquidating.

## A 'rebalancing' in the luxury market

Through the busy holiday shopping season and beyond, Bain expects luxury sales to return at a different pace in each region. China is expected to rebound at full speed, while Asia on the whole is still in "recovery" mode, the firm said. The Americas are expected to remain "sluggish," while Europe struggles through new pandemic-related lockdowns. Covid-19 cases are still rising robustly in Europe and the United States.

This, in part, will help China's luxury market overtake Europe and the Americas by 2025, when Chinese consumers will account for almost half of all luxury spending, according to Bain.

"There is going to be a rebalancing between different geographies that, of course, will massively impact the distribution ecosystem, and the size of the distribution networks of the [luxury] brands in these regions," Levato said.

Bain expects the global luxury market to return to 2019 levels by the end of 2022 or early 2023, driven by digital sales growth and strength in China.

Online shopping for luxury goods has doubled to represent 23% of total purchases in 2020, from 12% in 2019, Bain said. The firm expects e-commerce to be the biggest channel for luxury spending globally by 2025.

![Simon: Consumers have stayed engaged despite lockdowns, and additional restrictions won't dampen that enthusiasm](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/106797996-16056152843ED4-WEX-111720-BillSimon.jpg?v=1605615283&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

VIDEO3:5203:52

Simon: Consumers have stayed engaged despite lockdowns, and additional restrictions won't dampen that enthusiasm

[Worldwide Exchange](https://www.cnbc.com/worldwide-exchange/)

Sales of personal luxury goods are forecast to be down about 12% during the holiday quarter worldwide, in line with this category's performance in the third quarter, Bain said.

The consulting firm predicts the luxury market will grow by 10% to 19% next year, depending on the pandemic, effective vaccine distribution and consumers' willingness to return to travel.

"Luxury brands have faced a year of tremendous shifts, but we believe that the industry will come out of the crisis with more purpose and more dynamism than ever before," Levato said.

## Experiences may rebound faster

All personal luxury goods categories have reported declines in 2020, according to Bain, as wealthy consumers have culled their spending on items to treat themselves or loved ones. Watches and apparel are down by 30%. Beauty is down 20%. Shoes, cushioned by demand for expensive sneakers, has fallen 12%.

While experience-based goods — which Bain defines as fine art, luxury cars, private jets and yachts, fine wines and spirits, and gourmet food — have suffered as well, their declines have not been as large, and their outlook is higher than personal items.

"These are the categories that have suffered less, especially the wines and spirits, because they can be consumed at home," Levato said.

Experience-based goods are on track to be down 10% in 2020, compared with a 23% drop for personal luxury goods. Within that, luxury experiences like trips on luxury cruises and fine dining, are on track to fall 56%, according to Bain's report.

Spending on experiences is expected to recover at a faster pace than personal goods like jewelry and leather, Bain said. But experiences that rely on tourism may lag, Levato said.

## 'We're witnessing a paradigm shift'

In recent weeks, luxury retailers have called attention in their earnings reports to rebounding sales in China. The French handbag maker Hermes said in late October its return to growth in the third quarter was aided by "remarkable performance" in mainland China.

Coach and Stuart Weitzman owner [Tapestry](/quotes/TPR/) booked triple-digit e-commerce growth, in addition to double-digit revenue growth in mainland China, for the quarter ended Sept. 26.

[Capri Holdings](/quotes/CPRI/) earlier this month reported "positive global retail sales" at its Versace banner and positive sales in China across its Michael Kors, Jimmy Choo and Versace brands.

And when [Farfetch](/quotes/FTCH/) reported earnings last week, the luxury e-commerce platform noted the pandemic was accelerating a permanent shift to luxury shopping online. Farfetch's third-quarter sales surged more than 70%.

"We believe we're witnessing a paradigm shift in the way people buy luxury," CEO Jose Neves said. "The luxury industry will not go back to the same normal as we did with pre-Covid-19, and it affirms my beliefs that we're witnessing a major acceleration of the sustained online adoption I have anticipated when I founded Farfetch 13 years ago."

args.summary:
This CNBC article reports that global luxury sales are on track for a record decline in 2020, but business is booming in China. According to a new Bain & Co. report (2020 Fall Luxury report, done in collaboration with Altagamma), China is set to become the world's biggest luxury market by 2025, as wealthy Chinese consumers travel less and splurge more on their home turf due to the coronavirus pandemic.

Key findings from the report:
- Mainland China is expected to be the only region reporting year-over-year growth in 2020, with its luxury market soaring 45% to reach 44 billion euros ($52.21 billion).
- Sales of personal luxury goods (clothes, jewelry, watches, beauty products, accessories) will contract 23% in 2020 to 217 billion euros ($257.47 billion) — the first decline since 2009 and the largest annual drop ever recorded by Bain.
- The overall luxury market (including experiences like private jets, yachts, and fine wine) is forecast to shrink at a similar pace to roughly 1 trillion euros ($1.19 trillion).
- In the Americas, sales are expected to contract 27% to 62 billion euros ($73.56 billion); U.S. department store chains like Neiman Marcus and Lord & Taylor have filed for bankruptcy this year.
- Chinese consumers will account for almost half of all luxury spending by 2025.
- Online luxury shopping doubled to 23% of total purchases in 2020 (up from 12% in 2019), and e-commerce is expected to be the biggest channel for luxury spending globally by 2025.
- The global luxury market is expected to return to 2019 levels by the end of 2022 or early 2023, driven by digital sales growth and China's strength.
- The market is predicted to grow 10% to 19% next year, depending on the pandemic, vaccine distribution, and consumer travel willingness.

By category in 2020: watches and apparel are down 30%, beauty down 20%, shoes down 12%. Experience-based goods (fine art, luxury cars, private jets, yachts, fine wines/spirits, gourmet food) are down 10%, while luxury experiences like cruises and fine dining are down 56%. Experiences are expected to recover faster than personal goods, except those relying on tourism.

Retailers confirming the China rebound include Hermes (citing "remarkable performance" in mainland China), Tapestry (Coach/Stuart Weitzman, with triple-digit e-commerce growth and double-digit China revenue growth), Capri Holdings (positive sales in China across Michael Kors, Jimmy Choo, and Versace), and Farfetch (third-quarter sales surged over 70%, with CEO Jose Neves noting a "paradigm shift" toward online luxury buying).

# [Global luxury spending to stay flat at $1.66 trillion in 2025 as shopper base shrinks](https://luxuryroundtable.com/2025/11/global-luxury-spending-to-stay-flat-at-1-66-trillion-in-2025-as-shopper-base-shrinks/)
