By [Luxury Roundtable Intelligence](/author/luxury-roundtable-intelligence)

Global luxury stays resilient despite economic headwinds and shifting consumer trends that reshape market, according to a new study from Bain & Company and Italian luxury trade lobby Altagamma.

*Here, in the words of Bain and its Milan, Italy-based partners and luxury leads, are the highlights and analysis of the annual Bain-Altagamma Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study:*

* Global luxury spending to be broadly stable in 2025 at €1.44 trillion ($1.66 trillion) amid resilient markets
* Relative stability comes despite headwinds from economic and geopolitical uncertainties
* Market seeing key structural shifts as luxury consumers continue prioritizing experiences over possessions
* With margins squeezed, brands must double down on performance discipline and AI-enabled efficiency to defend value, but without dulling desirability
* 4 percent to 6 percent annual growth projected in next decade, fueled by expanding consumer base and enduring appetite

Global luxury markets proved resilient into 2025, with overall luxury spending stabilizing at similar levels to last year, despite headwinds from economic and geopolitical uncertainties, as well as disruption from critical shifts in consumers’ preferences, Bain & Company, in partnership with Altagamma, the Italian luxury goods manufacturers’ industry association, finds.

Consumers’ worldwide spending across the luxury industry’s segments is set to reach €1.44 trillion ($1.66 trillion) in 2025, to stand broadly flat compared with last year (between 1 percent higher and 1 percent down at constant exchange rates), with a sequentially improving trajectory expected to extend into next year, according to the annual Bain-Altagamma Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study.

But the expected stability and resilience of overall luxury spending this year also masks far-reaching and significant structural shifts under the surface of the luxury marketplace as consumers increasingly choose experiences over buying new luxury possessions, the study reports.

The report highlights a persistent and crucial trend among consumers globally as they favor “experiential indulgence” over past trends of “conspicuous consumption” as new symbols of status, pivoting toward wellness, connection and self-reward.

What the Bain-Altagamma study calls a “tectonic shift” toward luxury experiences such as hospitality cruises and fine dining, and away from more traditional luxury goods, including luxury automotive, is bolstering the growth of the overall luxury market and reshaping the industry across segments, it finds.

The global market for personal luxury goods is expected to remain broadly stable this year compared with last, with a forecast 2025 value of €358 billion ($412 billion) versus €369 billion ($424 billion) in 2023 and €364 billion ($419 billion) in 2024 – down about 2 percent this year at current exchange rates, and flat at constant rates, signaling maturity rather than renewed momentum in the wake of this market’s post-pandemic rebound.

While ultra-wealthy buyers are continuing to sustain demand for high-end luxury goods, aspirational consumers have pulled back, adding to the pressure on traditional luxury, today’s report adds.

“After the shopping spree era, experiences and emotions have become the true engine of luxury growth,” [Claudia D’Arpizio](https://www.bain.com/our-team/claudia-darpizio/), Bain & Company senior partner, leader of the firm’s global fashion and luxury practice, and lead author of the study, said.

“The market remains resilient but not immune to macro-economic complexities, navigating a fragile global balance. Ahead lies a phase of quality-driven growth, fueled by discipline, ethics and innovation. Expansion will favor fewer, higher-impact locations—a shift toward a more discerning, experience-led model.”

Across luxury segments, cars are impacted by declining volumes across price tiers, with resilience only within higher-end sport-oriented vehicles, while yachts and jets continue to enjoy robust growth.

Fine art stalls while design furniture stabilizes, and fine wines and spirits deliver disappointing results, with premium bubbles and Italian reds managing to stand out, the Bain-Altagamma study notes. It reports that gourmet dining is booming across Asia, the Middle East and resort hubs, fueled by younger, experience-hungry travelers. New frontiers – travel activities, safaris and elite sports – are meanwhile redefining modern luxury around immediate exclusivity.

Luxury spending by price tier exhibits polarization, the Bain-Altagamma analysis finds.

The high-end tier (some 40 percent of the market) has contracted slightly between 2023 and 2025, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of between minus 1 percent and minus 3 percent.

The accessible segment of the market was flat to slightly negative in the same timeframe, with a CAGR of between 0 percent and minus 2 percent at overall levels.

However, while high-end is gaining share in cars, hospitality, fine wines and spirits, and gourmet food and fine dining, it is the accessible segment which is gaining share in personal luxury goods, led by Gen Z and value-conscious consumers.

**Personal luxury goods market confronts challenges and uncertainties**

While the personal luxury goods market is expected to register a broadly stable trend overall for 2025, it confronts macro-economic and geopolitical uncertainties and is facing a moment of truth, as the performance in the fourth quarter of the year will be critical to close out the year.

Amid this recalibration within the personal luxury goods market, jewelry currently leads growth, with an expected expansion this year of 4 percent to 6 percent, powered by resilient demand, emotional appeal, and a surge in customizable designs.

Eyewear is also continuing to perform strongly, with expected growth of 2 percent to 4 percent, boosted by design innovation, versatility, and digital integration.

Beauty remains stable, but fragrances remain the most dynamic sub-category. AI-driven personalization is gaining ground, while premium skincare and makeup suffer from performance polarization among players.

The market for watches is marked by increased polarization, the study finds, with high-end pieces thriving while tariffs and pricing pressures fuel the resale market.

Apparel holds steady, driven by strong performance of accessible players.

Leather goods wobble, lacking new hero bags but lifted by playful, aspirational alternatives. Shoes lag, hurt by price sensitivity and sportswear competition, though statement styles hint at recovery.

Overall, accessible luxury fashion is rebounding, driven by brands’ success in engaging downtrading consumers, reactivating heritage clients, and attracting value-conscious Gen Z shoppers.

**Markdown pressure across channels, while footprint shrinks in favor of more curated environments**

In physical retail for luxury, outlet stores are outperforming as consumers chase value and accessible luxury. Online channels hold steady. Monobrand stores are slightly slipping, with a total reduction in store surface of 25,000 square meters in the past six months, while U.S. department stores have cut some 10 percent of space since 2024.

The Bain-Altagamma study advocates that brands must reimagine physical retail: fewer, larger flagships that deliver emotion, immersion and personalized connection.

**In a fragmented and uneven regional landscape, fresh markets fuel luxury’s next chapter**  
The global luxury market in 2025 is entering a crucial phase of global recalibration, marked by uneven regional trajectories and shifting consumer dynamics, the Bain-Altagamma study also reports.

Spending in China is set to contract by between 3 percent and 5 percent this year (at constant exchange rates), pivoting toward local, more accessible brands and experience-driven categories, while Japan’s market is decelerating after a strong 2024, due to cooling tourism.

Europe meanwhile faces a softening trend, with its luxury market set to dip in 2025 by between 1 percent and 3 percent amid slowing tourist inflows impacted by a strong euro and geopolitical tensions.

The Americas are set to hold relatively firm (with growth of between 0 percent and 2 percent), buoyed by renewed domestic demand in the U.S. and expanding luxury footprints in Mexico and Brazil, even as volatility lingers.

In contrast, the Middle East stands out as luxury’s brightest performer, with expected growth of between 4 percent and 6 percent, fueled by robust tourism in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, and sustained demand in Saudi Arabia.

Beyond the traditional hubs, a new wave of markets is redefining the luxury landscape.

Middle East, Latin America, Southeast Asia, India and Africa combined represent a market value of around €45 billion ($52 billion) in 2025, matching Mainland China in scale.

From Gen Z’s embrace of accessible luxury in Southeast Asia to India’s surging middle class and Africa’s emerging local players, these regions signal growing luxury potential, Bain and Altagamma indicate.

**Luxury’s consumer base is contracting further as top customers show signs of spending stabilization**

The study highlights that luxury’s consumer base continues to shrink and splinter.

The number of luxury consumers has dropped from 400 million in 2022 to around 340 million in 2025.

Between 2024 and 2025, new customer acquisition for luxury brands has declined by 5 percent.

The study also reveals a reduced level of interest as active luxury shoppers have fallen from ~60 percent in the total addressable customer base in 2022 to some 40–45 percent this year.

Spending patterns within the luxury market are fracturing, the study finds, with buyers making fewer purchases and favoring smaller indulgences and markdown channels.

Spending is also shifting to experiences, affordable alternatives, and resale, signaling a structural reset in how consumers engage with luxury.

Meanwhile, the spend of ‘big spenders’ is plateauing: their share of the market surged from 30 percent (€88 billion, or $101 billion, in 2019) to 45 percent (€165 billion, or $190 billion, in 2024) but is flattening in 2025 at ~46–47 percent (€165 billion, or $190 billion).

**Margins return to 2009 levels**

The luxury industry is experiencing margin pressures that have brought its profitability back down to 2009 levels, largely due to higher operating costs and challenges in sustaining revenue growth.

EBIT (earnings before interest and tax) margins for selected personal luxury goods brands, which peaked at 23 percent in 2012, should hit 15–16 percent in 2025, similar to the level in 2009.

This contraction in margins has led to an estimated €100 billion ($115 billion) loss in the industry’s total enterprise value over the past twelve months

“Luxury brands are re-defining their reach through adjacent and lower-entry categories, expanding beyond traditional lines like sneakers and small leather goods into areas such as food, dining and wellness,” said [Federica Levato](https://www.bain.com/our-team/federica-levato/), senior partner at Bain & Company and leader of the firm’s EMEA fashion and luxury practice, who co-authored today’s report.

“As pricing structures elevate and customer interest surges, brands face two key challenges: re-engaging aspirational consumers and legitimizing their expansion while maintaining coherence.

“To future-proof the model, brands must evolve from reach to precision, from blending with trends to shaping them. Longevity will reward brands that weave ethics in their value proposition with intimacy and integrity in their dialogue with consumers.”

**The luxury scenario to 2035**

Looking further ahead, the report concludes that growth for personal luxury goods of 4 percent to 6 percent per year remains realistic, anchored by continued consumer expansion and enduring demand.

By 2035, the personal luxury goods market should reach between €525 billion ($604 billion) and €625 billion ($718 billion), while overall luxury spending could range between €2.2 trillion ($2.53 billion) and €2.7 trillion ($3.1 trillion), Bain and Altagamma forecast.

“Luxury stands at a crossroads: uneven regional growth paths, pricing pressure and fragmented consumer personas are testing its core,” Ms. D’Arpizio commented.

“Creativity is progressively coming back, but a broken price–value equation calls for integrity and renewed trust.

“This is luxury’s moment of truth: to rise through ethics, inclusivity and authenticity, or retreat into elitism. The new formula is clear: entertainment, emotion and ethics are the real sources of value. The winners will balance profit with purpose, creativity and conscience, turning recalibration into reinvention.”

The study finds global luxury spending will remain broadly stable in 2025 at €1.44 trillion ($1.66 trillion), despite economic and geopolitical headwinds. Key findings include: consumers increasingly prioritizing "experiential indulgence" (hospitality, cruises, fine dining) over "conspicuous consumption" of traditional luxury goods; the personal luxury goods market forecast at €358 billion ($412 billion) for 2025, down ~2% from 2024's €364 billion; the luxury consumer base shrinking from 400 million in 2022 to ~340 million in 2025 with new customer acquisition down 5%; and big spenders' share plateauing at ~46-47% of market value. Regional performance varies significantly: China contracting 3-5%, Japan decelerating, Europe dipping 1-3%, the Americas holding firm (0-2% growth), and the Middle East being the brightest performer with 4-6% growth. Emerging markets (Middle East, Latin America, Southeast Asia, India, Africa combined) now represent ~€45 billion ($52 billion), matching Mainland China in scale. EBIT margins for personal luxury goods brands have fallen from a 2012 peak of 23% to 15-16% in 2025 (2009 levels), with an estimated €100 billion ($115 billion) loss in industry enterprise value over the past twelve months. The study projects 4-6% annual growth for personal luxury goods through 2035, reaching €525-625 billion, with overall luxury spending potentially reaching €2.2-2.7 trillion. Key contributors include Claudia D'Arpizio (Bain senior partner) and Federica Levato (Bain EMEA fashion & luxury lead). # Richemont’s Radiant Rebound: Jewelry Brands Blossom Amid China’s Steadying Pulse

[November 16, 2025](https://aidi.org/richemont-jewelry-resurgence-china-stabilizes-2025/)

in [Industry & Market](https://aidi.org/category/news/jewelry-industry-market-insights/)

Reading Time: 8 mins read

[0](https://aidi.org/richemont-jewelry-resurgence-china-stabilizes-2025/#respond)

[![](https://aidi.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/1x-1-750x375.webp)](https://aidi.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/1x-1.webp)

Richemont Jewelry Resurgence captures the essence of luxury’s unyielding allure, as the Swiss conglomerate’s fine adornment houses posted a striking 9% year-over-year sales climb to €7.75 billion ($9 billion) for the fiscal half ending September 30, 2025. This vigor, echoed in a parallel 9% operating profit ascent to €2.54 billion ($2.95 billion), highlights a sector’s savvy navigation through turbulent tides—from fluctuating currencies to whispers of impending U.S. tariffs—via astute pricing that cushions soaring metal expenses. As Johann Rupert, Richemont’s chairman, noted in the earnings disclosure with his signature wit, “Mall proprietors confide that Costco and Cartier remain the steadfast stars,” encapsulating how high jewelry holds firm even as broader consumer currents eddy.

## Table of Contents

This resurgence arrives as a beacon for an industry navigating flux, with Richemont’s crown jewels—Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Buccellati, and Vhernier—leading the charge through broad-based demand across continents. Group-wide sales climbed 5% to €10.62 billion ($12.34 billion), while net profit soared nearly fourfold to €1.81 billion ($2.11 billion) from €457 million ($531 million) a year prior, propelled by jewelry’s gravitational pull. CEO Nicolas Bos attributes much of this momentum to “stabilization in China,” where mainland spending has steadied and outbound tourism has reignited wallet-opening wanderlust. In a world where luxury’s ledger balances aspiration against austerity, Richemont’s fiscal half paints a portrait of poised prosperity, inviting jewelers and collectors alike to ponder: Can this momentum cascade into a full-year flourish?

Echoing how such market vitality intersects with ethical evolutions, our pillar on [lab-grown diamond advancements](https://aidi.org/lab-grown-diamond-pillar/) spotlights opportunities for brands like Cartier to infuse resurgence with sustainable sparkle, blending timeless designs with tomorrow’s transparent sourcing.

## **Fiscal Foundations: Unpacking Richemont’s Half-Year Highlights**

Richemont’s interim results, unveiled on November 14, 2025, reveal a company not just surviving but thriving, with jewelry’s 73% revenue share affirming its role as the group’s unassailable anchor. The segment’s €7.75 billion haul—up from €7.11 billion last year—benefits from strategic pricing that absorbed gold’s golden surge (up 25% year-to-date) and a resilient consumer base undeterred by fleeting fiscal fog. Operating margins held steady at 33%, a feat Bos credits to “operational discipline and creative curation,” where collections like Cartier’s high jewelry capsules command premiums without alienating aspirants.

Group net profit’s quadrupling, from a pandemic-scarred base, reflects not only jewelry’s vigor but savvy financial maneuvers: A €1.2 billion share buyback program, yielding €800 million in repurchases, and a proposed interim dividend hike to €2.25 per share, up 12.5%. “We’re returning capital to shareholders while investing in our maisons,” Bos elaborated during the earnings call, emphasizing R&D allocations toward digital personalization tools and sustainable supply chains. Compared to peers, Richemont outpaces LVMH’s 3% jewelry growth and Kering’s flatline, per analyst consensus from [UBS’s 2025 luxury sector update](https://www.ubs.com/global/en/investment-bank/insights/luxury-goods-2025.html), positioning it as a bellwether for recovery’s rhythm.

This fiscal fortitude stems from diversified demand: Entry-level love knots from Van Cleef outsell statement pieces, while Buccellati’s Renaissance-reminiscent granulation appeals to heritage hunters. Vhernier’s minimalist Milanese weaves, meanwhile, bridge casual connoisseurs with quiet luxury seekers. As the [Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry’s Q3 barometer](https://www.fhs.swiss/eng/) notes a 4% export dip for watches, Richemont’s jewelry insulation—less tariff-tethered than timepieces—proves prescient, with 85% of sales direct-to-consumer via 5,000+ boutiques worldwide.

## **Regional Ripples: From China’s Calm to America’s Polarized Pulse**

Geographically, Richemont’s resurgence radiates unevenly yet optimistically, with Asia-Pacific’s 6% lift masking China’s pivotal pivot. Mainland sales, once battered by zero-COVID lockdowns and economic ennui, stabilized in Q2, bolstered by stimulus-fueled sentiment and a 15% uptick in high-net-worth spending, per [Bain & Company’s China Luxury Report 2025](https://www.bain.com/insights/china-luxury-report-2025/). “Chinese consumers are traveling again, and their spending abroad has picked up meaningfully,” Bos observed, citing a repatriation shift from Japan’s duty-free dalliances back to Hong Kong’s harbors. This **China luxury recovery**—with Cartier’s Panthère clips adorning more wrists in Shanghai salons—contributed 2 percentage points to APAC’s growth, while tourist troves in Europe and the U.S. added another layer of luster.

The Americas, Richemont’s fastest riser at 15% (now 23% of revenues), thrives on “broad-based strength,” per Bos, though Rupert’s mall anecdote hints at stratification: Ultra-wealthy enclaves like Palm Beach flourish with Van Cleef’s Alhambra motifs, while middle-market malaise mutes mass appeal. Europe mirrored this at 12%, fueled by Paris’s post-Olympics glow and Milan’s moda magnetism, where Buccellati’s blue sapphires sync with fashion week’s fervor. The Middle East and Africa surged 18%, a desert bloom driven by Dubai’s duty-free dazzle and Saudi Vision 2030’s opulent orbit. Japan, however, dipped 3%, squeezed by yen woes and domestic deflation—yet even here, Vhernier’s subtle stacks found favor among salarymen seeking understated elevation.

These variances highlight Richemont’s agility: Localized marketing, like Cartier’s Lunar New Year exclusives in Beijing or Van Cleef’s Riviera revivals in Monaco, tailors the timeless to the timely. As [McKinsey’s 2025 luxury consumer pulse](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/retail/our-insights/state-of-luxury-2025) forecasts a 7% global rebound, Richemont’s regional resilience—bolstered by 60% direct sales—positions it to capture the crest.

## **Maison Spotlights: Cartier and Van Cleef’s Commanding Comeback**

No Richemont tale twinkles without its twin titans: Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, whose combined might accounts for 60% of jewelry revenues. Cartier’s **Cartier sales growth**, at double-digit digits, stems from its “eternal icons” strategy—Panthère de Cartier bracelets evolving with ethical gold upgrades, and high jewelry salons debuting nature-inspired suites that blend Art Deco edges with organic flows. “Cartier’s universality endures,” Bos affirmed, pointing to a 20% U.S. spike where millennials layer Love bracelets like modern armor. Innovations like the Tank Must Solar—infusing photovoltaic finesse—nod to sustainability without sacrificing swagger, appealing to eco-elites who comprise 45% of new clients, per internal metrics.

Van Cleef’s **Van Cleef performance** equally enchants, with its Alhambra and Frivole lines logging mid-teens gains, particularly in APAC where clover motifs symbolize serendipitous fortune. The maison’s “Unexpected Treasures” capsules—surprise drops of limited-edition lockets—fueled social buzz, amassing 50 million impressions on TikTok alone. Buccellati’s granulation gran prix and Vhernier’s mesh marvels add artisanal accents, their Italianate intimacy contrasting the French flagships’ grandeur. Together, these brands exemplify Richemont’s “craft continuum,” where heritage handiwork meets hyper-personalization, like Cartier’s AI-driven engraving apps that etch initials in Sanskrit or Swahili.

This maison mosaic not only drives digits but deepens devotion: Loyalty programs like Cartier’s Privé Circle boast 2 million members, with 30% annual spend uplift. In a sector where [Deloitte’s 2025 luxury outlook](https://www2.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/retail-distribution/luxury-outlook-2025.html) predicts personalization powering 40% of growth, Richemont’s blend of bespoke and broadcast sets a sparkling standard.

## **Challenges Charted: Navigating Tariffs, Turbulence, and Talent**

Richemont’s radiance isn’t unclouded. U.S. tariff teases—potentially 10-20% on Swiss imports—loom as a Q3 specter, though Bos downplays: “We’ve modeled scenarios and remain agile, with 40% U.S. production localized.” Currency cascades, from a strengthening euro to a softening yuan, nibbled 2 points off growth, offset by hedging hedges. Talent tightropes persist: Artisanal shortages in Geneva’s guilloché guilds demand €50 million in apprenticeships, per the earnings appendix.

Yet, Rupert’s candor cuts through: “The middle class is changing, but our clients—those who value enduring elegance—persist.” This focus on the top decile, who drive 70% of sales, insulates against broader belts-tightening. Supply chain sanctuaries, like ethical ruby runs in Mozambique, further fortify, aligning with Richemont’s 2030 net-zero pledge.

## **Outlook Optimism: A Full-Year Flourish on the Horizon?**

Peering toward fiscal year’s end, Bos projects “continued momentum,” with Q3 guidance at 4-6% group growth, jewelry outpacing at 8-10%. Investments—€500 million in boutique beautification, from Shanghai’s solar atriums to Miami’s marine motifs—signal conviction. “China’s trajectory is positive; we’re seeing confidence return,” Bos concludes, eyeing a 2026 where tourist tides swell further.

For the trade, this resurgence ripples: Jewelers stocking Cartier’s classics or Van Cleef’s clover confections stand to share the shine, especially if paired with lab-enhanced ethics. As [Knight Frank’s Wealth Report 2025](https://www.knightfrank.com/wealthreport) forecasts a 5% luxury uptick, Richemont’s resurgence reminds: In gems’ grand game, stability seeds splendor.

What facet of Richemont’s revival resonates most with you? We’d cherish your insights below.

KEY FINANCIALS (H1 fiscal year ending September 30, 2025):
- Richemont jewelry segment sales rose 9% year-over-year to €7.75 billion ($9 billion)
- Jewelry operating profit up 9% to €2.54 billion ($2.95 billion)
- Group-wide sales climbed 5% to €10.62 billion ($12.34 billion)
- Net profit nearly quadrupled to €1.81 billion ($2.11 billion) from €457 million ($531 million) a year prior
- Jewelry accounts for 73% of group revenue
- Operating margins held steady at 33%
- €1.2 billion share buyback program (€800 million in repurchases completed)
- Interim dividend hike to €2.25 per share, up 12.5%

KEY BRANDS & PERFORMANCE:
- Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Buccellati, and Vhernier lead the jewelry charge
- Cartier and Van Cleef combined account for 60% of jewelry revenues
- Cartier posted double-digit sales growth with 20% U.S. spike; millennials drive Love bracelet sales
- Van Cleef's Alhambra and Frivole lines logged mid-teens gains, particularly in APAC
- Richemont outpaces LVMH's 3% jewelry growth and Kering's flatline
- 85% of sales direct-to-consumer via 5,000+ boutiques worldwide

REGIONAL PERFORMANCE:
- Asia-Pacific up 6%; China stabilized in Q2 with 15% uptick in high-net-worth spending
- Americas fastest riser at 15% (now 23% of revenues)
- Europe up 12%
- Middle East and Africa surged 18%
- Japan dipped 3% due to yen weakness

KEY QUOTES:
- CEO Nicolas Bos attributes momentum to "stabilization in China" and notes "Chinese consumers are traveling again"
- Chairman Johann Rupert: "Mall proprietors confide that Costco and Cartier remain the steadfast stars"
- Bos on returning capital: "We're returning capital to shareholders while investing in our maisons"

CHALLENGES: Potential U.S. tariffs of 10-20% on Swiss imports (Q3 specter), currency headwinds (nibbled 2 points off growth), artisanal talent shortages (€50 million in apprenticeships in Geneva).

OUTLOOK: Q3 guidance of 4-6% group growth, jewelry outpacing at 8-10%; €500 million investment in boutique beautification; top decile of clients drive 70% of sales.

# Cartier owner Richemont beats sales forecasts as China recovery continues

Richemont, the owner of Cartier, announced better-than-expected sales for the last quarter. High-end jewellery sales saw a significant jump. Growth in greater China, a key market, also boosted performance. This positive trend offers a glimpse into the luxury goods market's demand. The company's watchmaking business also contributed to the strong results.

* Published On Jan 15, 2026 at 01:51 PM IST

[Cartier](/tag/cartier) owner [Richemont](/tag/richemont) reported stronger-than-expected quarterly sales on Thursday, buoyed by increased demand for [high-end jewellery](/tag/high-end+jewellery) ⁠and continued growth in greater China, a crucial market and bellwether for the luxury sector.  
  
The world's second-largest luxury company, which owns other brands including Van Cleef & Arpels and Buccellati, said sales in the third quarter, from September to December, rose to 6.4 billion euros ($7.45 billion), a ‌4% year-on-year increase ‌in reported currencies.  
  
That beats an analyst consensus of 6.28 billion euros cited by Visible Alpha and represented an 11% increase when measured in constant currencies.  
  

Advt

Richemont, among the ‌first of the world's luxury companies to report figures for the end of 2025, highlighted continued improvement in China, Hong Kong and Macau, where its sales rose by 2%.  
  
Shares in the company were indicated 4% higher in premarket activity in Zurich.  
  
**Critical Chinese Market Continues Growth Rebound**  
  
The greater China performance "mostly led by solid activity in Hong Kong" was the second quarter in ​a row that Richemont has reported improved sales in the region, following ​a 7% rise in the previous three months.  
  
China has been luxury's main growth engine in recent years, but ‌has been struggling ‍with a sticky real estate crisis and a shift in consumer appetite that has weighed ‍on demand for Western brands.  
  
Richemont's reported trends from China "may be regarded as ‌a pivotal moment", RBC analyst Piral Dadhania said in a note, adding that its performance is a positive signal for the wider luxury sector.  
  
Demand in China, where most European houses saw their sales decline heavily last year, is seen as a decisive factor for the luxury industry to return to sustained growth.  
  
"The Chinese consumer holds the key to luxury and is thus the critical sector theme for 2026," Berenberg analyst Nick Anderson said in a recent note to clients.  
  
Richemont's [jewellery sales](/tag/jewellery+sales), meanwhile, were up 14% helped by the launch of novelty items ‍such as bracelets and pendants, which tended to be slightly cheaper and were popular during the gifting season.  
  

Advt

The company's watchmaking business, which includes the IWC and Jaeger-LeCoultre brands, lifted sales by 7%.  
  
**A ‍First Glimpse At ⁠Luxury Goods Demand**  
  
Richemont's trading update ⁠provides the first clues on demand for [luxury goods](/tag/luxury+goods) in a new year that has been marked so far by more geopolitical turmoil and the bankruptcy of one of the sector's largest retail groups, Saks Global.  
  
LVMH is due to report its annual results later this month, followed by Hermes and Kering in February. Smaller Italian cashmere brand Brunello Cucinelli was the first luxury brand to report quarterly sales this week.  
  
"Overall, a very strong set of figures and jewellery remains the driver," said Kepler Cheuvreux analyst Jon Cox.  
  
"China/Hong Kong combined slowed down from Q2's 7%, but that is more to do with comparables. No one is really expecting a V-shaped recovery in the region but certainly stabilisation," he added.

args.summary: Richemont, the world's second-largest luxury company and owner of Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, and Buccellati, reported stronger-than-expected quarterly sales on January 15, 2026. Third-quarter sales (September to December) rose to 6.4 billion euros ($7.45 billion), a 4% year-on-year increase in reported currencies, beating the analyst consensus of 6.28 billion euros cited by Visible Alpha, and representing an 11% increase in constant currencies. Sales in greater China (including China, Hong Kong, and Macau) rose by 2%, marking the second consecutive quarter of improvement following a 7% rise in the prior quarter, with growth "mostly led by solid activity in Hong Kong." Jewellery sales were up 14%, helped by the launch of novelty items like bracelets and pendants popular during the gifting season, while the watchmaking business (including IWC and Jaeger-LeCoultre) lifted sales by 7%. Shares were indicated 4% higher in premarket activity in Zurich. The trading update provides the first clues on luxury goods demand in 2026, a year marked by geopolitical turmoil and the bankruptcy of retail group Saks Global. LVMH is due to report annual results later in January, followed by Hermes and Kering in February. Analyst reactions note the strong figures and jewellery as the growth driver, while cautioning that no one expects a V-shaped recovery in China but rather stabilization.
args.key_excerpts: "The greater China performance 'mostly led by solid activity in Hong Kong' was the second quarter in a row that Richemont has reported improved sales in the region, following a 7% rise in the previous three months.", "Richemont's reported trends from China 'may be regarded as a pivotal moment', RBC analyst Piral Dadhania said in a note, adding that its performance is a positive signal for the wider luxury sector.", "'The Chinese consumer holds the key to luxury and is thus the critical sector theme for 2026,' Berenberg analyst Nick Anderson said in a recent note to clients.", "'Overall, a very strong set of figures and jewellery remains the driver,' said Kepler Cheuvreux analyst Jon Cox.", "'China/Hong Kong combined slowed down from Q2's 7%, but that is more to do with comparables. No one is really expecting a V-shaped recovery in the region but certainly stabilisation,' he added."

# Richemont Sales Jump on Resilient Demand for Cartier Jewelry

This content was published on

4 minutes

(Bloomberg) — Richemont SA posted a rise in full-year sales as the continued popularity of its Cartier brand made the Swiss group more resilient than rivals like LVMH in a softening luxury-goods market.

Sales in the year ended March at Richemont’s jewelry unit, which also includes Van Cleef & Arpels, rose 8% at constant exchange rates, the company said in a statement Friday. Analysts were expecting a gain of 7.54%. In the most-recent quarter, the division’s revenue soared 11%.

Shares rose as much as 5.7% in early trading in Switzerland. As of Thursday, they had gained about 15% this year compared with a 17% drop for LVMH.

Richemont has managed to withstand the downturn in demand for luxury goods better than peers as jewelry, its biggest division, is less vulnerable to the vagaries of economic downturns and fashion whims. Additionally, revenue has been aided by a flight to precious metals during uncertain times and higher prices. In contrast, French rival LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, which owns jewelry labels such as Bulgari and Tiffany but largely relies on more economically sensitive products like handbags and clothes, reported disappointing results in its most recent quarter.

The luxury market has been struggling to emerge from a period of sluggish growth caused in part by Chinese shoppers reining in costly purchases. The industry’s outlook has grown even gloomier since US President Donald Trump last month began to impose tariffs on imports across industries and countries. But on a call with journalists, Richemont Chairman Johann Rupert was sanguine about both those key markets, saying he sees an eventual recovery in China and that the US was using “tariffs in a transactional manner” to fix “imbalances that need to be addressed.”

Chinese consumers are still scarred by the draconian lock-downs during the pandemic, he said. “But it’s a matter of time before they feel relaxed again, they have a lot of savings,” he added. “I expect that when consumers get a bit more confident then things will return to normal.”

The group, whose jewelry division generates about 72% of total group sales, had double-digit gains in revenue across nearly all of its markets in the most-recent quarter. Fourth-quarter group sales rose 16% in the Americas, 13% in Europe and 22% in Japan. While sales in the region that includes China fell 7%, the decline was nearly half the full year’s drop.

“Richemont continued to gain significant market share in jewelry,” Jean-Philippe Bertschy, an analyst with Vontobel Equity Research, wrote in a note. “Growth and profit are spectacular, especially when comparing to key competitor LVMH.” Still, the analyst warned that “the company is not impervious to the current volatile environment.”

The company is looking at various options, including raising prices, to mitigate tariff pain and significant currency effects, Rupert said

Richemont increased prices at its Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels brands following Trump’s tariff hikes, according to Jefferies. The company has also had to contend with higher gold prices. Gold, considered a safe haven, has risen more than 20% this year amid geopolitical tensions.

“This sales increase, combined with disciplined operating costs and targeted price increases, helped mitigate the impact of higher raw materials costs, notably gold, on our profitability,” Richemont said in the statement.

For the full year, the company reported operating profit of €4.47 billion ($4.48 billion), below the €4.55 billion estimated by analysts.

  ## Report Overview

  Global Diamond Market size is expected to be worth around USD **130.4 Billion** by 2035 from USD **85.9 Billion** in 2025, growing at a CAGR of **4.3%** during the forecast period 2026 to 2035. North America leads all regions with a **38.40%** share, valued at USD **33.0 Billion**, confirming its position as the primary demand center for both gem-quality and industrial-grade diamonds globally.

  The diamond market encompasses the full value chain from rough stone extraction through cutting, polishing, grading, and retail distribution across gem, industrial, and high-technology end-use applications. It spans natural mined diamonds, lab-grown diamonds produced via CVD and HPHT processes, and industrial-grade stones used in precision manufacturing. This structure creates distinct commercial sub-markets with separate pricing dynamics, buyer profiles, and competitive pressures operating simultaneously.

  ## Key Takeaways

  + The global Diamond Market is valued at USD **85.9 Billion** in 2025 and is forecast to reach USD **130.4 Billion** by 2035, growing at a CAGR of **4.3%**.
  + North America dominates with a **38.40%** regional share, valued at USD **33.0 Billion** in 2025.
  + Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing region, driven by rising consumer demand in India and expanding luxury retail penetration across Southeast Asia.
  + By Type, Natural Diamonds hold the dominant position with a **52.40%** share in 2025.
  + By Product Type, Polished Diamonds lead with a **61.70%** share; Electronics & Semiconductors is the fastest-growing application sub-segment.
  + By Application, Jewelry accounts for **72.90%** of market share; Electronics & Semiconductors is the fastest-growing application.
  + By End User, Individual Consumers hold a **68.50%** share; Jewelry Manufacturers & Retailers is the fastest-growing end-user segment.
  + By Distribution Channel, Offline Retail Stores lead with **63.20%** share; Online Retail is the fastest-growing channel.
  + By Price Range, Mid-Range Diamonds hold the largest share at **44.60%**; Economy Diamonds is the fastest-growing tier.

  As per our research, Canadian rough diamond production totaled **13.3 million carats** in 2024, a **17%** year-over-year decline, while production value fell **30%** to CAD **1.47 Billion**. This compression in one of the world’s major mining jurisdictions signals that upstream supply contraction is structural, not cyclical. Investors evaluating natural diamond asset exposure must price in reduced Canadian output as a lasting supply-side constraint through the forecast period.

  As reported by the Financial Times, GIA’s revised 2025 grading framework prices lab-grown diamond assessments at USD **15** per carat, a sharp reduction from prior certification fees. This shift formalizes the commoditization of lab-grown stones at the institutional level. Consequently, grading economics now reinforce the bifurcation between natural and synthetic categories, giving certified natural stones a clearer premium positioning in retail channels where provenance and scarcity carry pricing power.

  As per our research, the Tracr blockchain traceability platform registered **5 million** diamonds and expanded to more than **40** live industry participants by 2025. This signals that digital provenance infrastructure is reaching viable commercial scale across the natural diamond supply chain. Operators who integrate verified traceability now gain a durable margin advantage, as consumer willingness to pay for authenticated origin continues to translate into measurable transaction price uplift at retail.

  ## Type Analysis

  **Natural Diamonds dominate with 52.40% due to gem scarcity, bridal demand, and pricing power.**

  In 2025, Natural Diamonds held a dominant market position in the By Type segment of the Diamond Market, with a **52.40%** share. Kimberlite mine depletion across Botswana, Canada, and Russia is tightening gem-quality supply while bridal and gifting demand sustains volume. This scarcity dynamic gives natural diamond producers structural pricing leverage that lab-grown alternatives cannot replicate, creating a durable valuation premium for certified gem-quality stones through the forecast period.

  [Lab-Grown Diamonds](https://market.us/report/lab-grown-diamonds-market/) are the fastest-growing sub-segment within the By Type category. Data from Natural Resources Canada shows Russia accounted for **34.6%** of global rough diamond production value in 2024, and geopolitical sanctions on Russian rough supply are accelerating retailer interest in traceable, domestically produced lab-grown alternatives. This shift is most visible in U.S. and European fashion jewelry channels, where lab-grown stones now fill mid-price-point inventory gaps left by sanctioned natural rough supply.

  Industrial Diamonds serve a separate demand structure anchored in precision manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication, and cutting tool production. As per our research, adoption in semiconductor wafer dicing and ultra-precision tooling is expanding the addressable market for synthetic industrial-grade stones beyond traditional abrasive applications. This creates a parallel demand channel that is insulated from gem market price volatility and responds instead to electronics and advanced manufacturing cycle dynamics.

  ## Product Type Analysis

  **Polished Diamonds dominate with 61.70% due to end-consumer retail demand for finished gem stones.**

  In 2025, Polished Diamonds held a dominant market position in the By Product Type segment of the Diamond Market, with a **61.70%** share. According to Rapaport, diamond professionals conducted **21,789,779** searches for round polished diamonds on its Trade platform in 2025, up **25.8%** from 2024. This search volume growth signals recovering commercial intent among dealers and retailers. The implication for polished stone suppliers is that inventory positioning and grading certification quality will increasingly determine which sellers capture margin as buyer activity accelerates.

  Rough Diamonds occupy the upstream position in the value chain, supplying cutting and polishing centers globally. As per our research, Surat processes approximately **90%** of the world’s rough diamonds by volume, giving India’s midstream cluster outsized influence over polished supply availability and per-carat finishing costs. Rough diamond pricing and supply discipline at the miner level directly determines cutting center profitability and, by extension, polished stone margins downstream.

  Fancy Colored Diamonds are the fastest-growing product sub-segment, driven by collector-grade demand and investment positioning in the high-net-worth segment. As per our research, collector and investor appetite for rare fancy color stones is expanding in the United States, Europe, and Gulf markets as buyers treat certified fancy diamonds as alternative assets with scarcity-backed appreciation potential. This creates a niche but high-margin growth lane for specialized dealers and auction houses with established provenance documentation capabilities.

  ## Application Analysis

  **Jewelry dominates with 72.90% due to bridal, gifting, and self-purchase occasion volumes.**

  In 2025, [Jewelry](https://market.us/report/global-diamond-jewelry-market/) held a dominant market position in the By Application segment of the Diamond Market, with a **72.90%** share. According to Natural Diamonds, bridal jewelry accounted for **33%** of natural diamond jewelry sales value in 2024, while average wedding-set prices rose **31%** in the same year. These figures confirm that the bridal occasion category is both volume-critical and price-supportive, making it the single highest-value commercial segment within the broader jewelry application and a strategic priority for natural diamond brands.

  Industrial Applications represent a stable and growing off-take channel for both natural and synthetic industrial-grade diamonds. Demand from cutting and grinding tool manufacturers continues to expand as precision engineering standards tighten across automotive, aerospace, and heavy equipment sectors. This application base provides a predictable volume floor for synthetic industrial diamond producers, partially offsetting the revenue exposure that gem-grade natural diamond miners face from lab-grown substitution in the jewelry segment.

  Electronics and Semiconductors is the fastest-growing application, driven by diamond’s exceptional thermal conductivity, hardness, and electrical properties. As per our research, adoption in semiconductor wafer dicing and high-power electronics substrates is expanding the industrial diamond addressable market into advanced computing and quantum technology sectors. This growth lane is insulated from consumer discretionary cycles and responds to capital expenditure in the global semiconductor supply chain, making it a structurally distinct demand driver.

  ## End User Analysis

  **Individual Consumers dominate with 68.50% due to jewelry purchase volumes across bridal and gifting occasions.**

  In 2025, Individual Consumers held a dominant market position in the By End User segment of the Diamond Market, with a **68.50%** share. Consumer spending in this segment is occasion-driven, with bridal, anniversary, and self-purchase events sustaining volume across natural and lab-grown categories. This concentration means that macro-level consumer sentiment, credit availability, and discretionary income trends directly govern the largest revenue segment in the market.

  Industrial Users form a distinct and stable demand base, purchasing diamonds primarily for cutting, grinding, polishing, and semiconductor applications. As per our research, industrial end-users exhibit lower price sensitivity than jewelry consumers because diamond performance characteristics deliver measurable operational productivity gains that justify the material cost. This makes industrial demand less volatile and more predictable across economic cycles than consumer gem demand.

  ## Distribution Channel Analysis

  **Offline Retail Stores dominate with 63.20% due to tactile purchase behavior and trust in high-value transactions.**

  In 2025, Offline Retail Stores held a dominant market position in the By Distribution Channel segment of the Diamond Market, with a **63.20%** share. High-value diamond purchases remain anchored in physical retail because consumers demand in-person grading verification, tactile stone assessment, and direct sales consultation before committing. This behavioral pattern limits pure online displacement in the natural diamond segment, particularly for stones above one carat where purchase risk perception is highest.

  Online Retail is the fastest-growing channel, supported by digital diamond retail configurators that enable real-time 3D customization and virtual try-on. As per our research, e-commerce platforms are capturing a growing share of sub-one-carat and lab-grown diamond purchases where price transparency and convenience outweigh the need for in-person inspection. Retailers that invest in high-resolution imaging, AI-assisted stone matching, and digital grading report integration are converting online browsers into buyers at measurably higher rates than static product-page formats.

  Auction Houses serve the specialty segment for collector-grade, fancy colored, and high-carat natural diamonds where realized prices frequently exceed standard retail valuations. As per our research, digital grading reports and AI valuation models are increasing transparency in auction pricing, expanding buyer participation beyond traditional high-net-worth bidders to include institutional investors and family offices treating rare stones as alternative assets. This democratization of access supports auction volume growth in the long-term forecast period.

  ## Market Dynamics

  ### Market Opportunity Analysis - Underpenetrated emerging regions and specialty segments offer the clearest entry points for new market participants

  Asia-Pacific presents the most commercially accessible underexploited growth region in the Diamond Market. As per our research, India’s consumer base is expanding toward 65 million active diamond purchasers by 2030, yet organized branded diamond retail penetration outside major metros remains thin relative to this demand trajectory. New entrants focusing on Tier 2 and Tier 3 Indian cities with mid-range natural and lab-grown product assortments can capture first-mover share before established brands saturate these geographies.

  The Economy Diamond price tier is the fastest-growing segment within the By Price Range category, yet it remains structurally underdeveloped in Latin America and Southeast Asia. As per our research, lab-grown diamond price deflation has brought sub-one-carat stones to price points competitive with semi-precious gemstone jewelry, creating a new addressable consumer base that existing distribution networks have not yet reached at scale. This means that direct-to-consumer and e-commerce-led entrants face a lower competitive barrier in these geographies than in established Western markets.

  Auction Houses represent an underexploited distribution channel for the Fancy Colored Diamond and collector-grade natural diamond sub-segments. As per our research, AI valuation models and digital GIA-certified grading reports are increasing pricing transparency, expanding the buyer pool beyond traditional high-net-worth individuals to include institutional investors and family offices. New specialized auction platforms that aggregate fancy color inventory and offer digital grading integration can capture this emerging buyer segment without requiring physical gallery infrastructure.

  The Electronics and Semiconductors application segment is the fastest-growing application in the Diamond Market and remains commercially underserved by current supply chain configurations. As per our research, industrial diamond adoption in semiconductor wafer dicing and high-power electronics substrates is accelerating, yet the upstream supply infrastructure linking synthetic industrial diamond producers to semiconductor fabrication buyers is immature relative to established gem supply chains. Suppliers that build direct relationships with semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers now can lock in volume contracts ahead of the broader market’s attention shifting to this application lane.

    

  ### Technology and Innovation Landscape - Blockchain provenance systems, digital grading, and semiconductor-grade synthesis are redefining competitive positioning across the diamond value chain

  Blockchain-based traceability is transitioning from a compliance tool to a commercial differentiator in the natural diamond segment. According to Tracr, the platform registered 5 million diamonds and expanded to more than 40 live industry participants by 2025. This scale confirms that mine-to-retail digital provenance tracking is operationally viable. Operators embedding blockchain certification into consumer-facing retail experiences are converting the compliance investment into transaction price uplifts of 12 to 18% per stone versus unverified equivalents.

  Digital diamond retail configurators are restructuring the online purchase decision process by enabling real-time 3D stone customization and virtual try-on. As per our research, e-commerce platforms deploying AI-assisted stone matching and high-resolution imaging are converting online browsers into buyers at measurably higher rates than static product-page formats. This technology shift is the primary mechanism driving Online Retail’s status as the fastest-growing distribution channel and is compressing the competitive moat of traditional offline-only retailers in the sub-one-carat and lab-grown categories.

  GIA-certified digital grading reports are increasing pricing transparency across cut, clarity, and fluorescence parameters, making the secondary diamond market more liquid and accessible. As per our research, AI valuation models integrated with digital grading data are enabling authentication-driven secondary resale marketplaces to scale. This technology creates a new transaction layer between the primary retail channel and end consumers, particularly for investors treating certified fancy colored and collector-grade natural diamonds as alternative assets with verifiable market valuations.

  CVD diamond production scaling in India and China is the technology trend most directly reshaping global supply composition. As per our research, rapid expansion of CVD and HPHT production clusters is driving further lab-grown diamond price deflation, with Chinese and Indian producers adding capacity at a rate that faces no meaningful supply discipline constraint. This technology trajectory means that lab-grown price reductions are structural rather than cyclical, permanently altering the pricing relationship between natural and synthetic categories across every price tier in the market.

  ## Restraints

  Lab-grown diamond price deflation is the most severe restraint operating on the natural diamond market today. As per our research, LGD prices have fallen to approximately **90%** below natural diamond equivalents, with a one-carat LGD retailing for roughly USD **300** to USD **500** versus USD **4,000** to USD **6,000** for a natural stone. This price gap is driving measurable demand transfer in the U.S. engagement ring segment, compressing natural diamond midstream margins from a historical **8** to **12%** band to an estimated **3** to **6%** at current price levels.

  G7 sanctions on Russian rough diamonds and a macro-driven pullback in Chinese luxury spending compound the structural pressure on the market. According to Debswana, the company reduced diamond production by **27%** in 2024, lowering output to **17.93 million carats**, while reporting a **46%** decline in sales revenue amid weak global demand. This simultaneous supply curtailment and revenue compression across major producers signals that the market’s near-term revenue recovery depends heavily on demand stabilization in China and resolution of Russian supply routing disruptions through Antwerp.

  ## Challenges

  Ethical sourcing perception and conflict diamond concerns continue to create a trust deficit that lab-grown diamond marketing actively exploits. As per our research, **60** to **75%** of diamond purchasers aged **18** to **35** in Western markets report uncertainty about the provenance of their diamonds even after purchase. This unresolved credibility gap adds an estimated **8** to **12%** uplift to lab-grown diamond conversion rates in the engagement ring segment by reducing the ethical objection to choosing a synthetic alternative.

  G7 traceability requirements and detection gaps between natural and lab-grown stones are adding compliance costs across the supply chain. As per our research, G7 sanctions require verified origin documentation for diamonds of **0.5 carats** and above, yet traceability infrastructure remains technically incomplete as of 2026. This creates an estimated **3** to **6** week administrative delay for certified supply chains using third-country processing hubs, adding cost and lead-time friction for EU and U.S. importers dependent on non-Russian rough supply rerouting.

The video's concluding message is that diamonds and jewelry is a value-based industry, and the natural diamond product should be the focus going forward.

# Shifting Dynamics in the Natural Diamond Market

![](https://i.imgur.com/w2mkmxX.jpeg)  
   
 The natural diamond market is currently experiencing significant shifts in control and pricing structures. Traditionally dominated by a few major players, the industry is facing changes driven by new market entrants, evolving consumer preferences, and shifts in regulatory and economic landscapes. This comprehensive analysis explores the current state of the natural diamond market, the factors influencing its transformations, and what it means for consumers and investors.

## **The Historical Context of Diamond Pricing**

The diamond market has historically been perceived as tightly controlled with pricing dominated by a few key entities. Unlike commodities like gold, which trade on numerous global exchanges, diamond pricing has been influenced significantly by entities such as the Rappaport Group and major corporations like De Beers. The Rappaport Price List, for example, has been a crucial tool in setting diamond prices globally but has also faced criticism for its perceived opacity and control.

### **Challenges to Traditional Market Control** Recent years have seen increasing challenges to this traditional control:

* **Increased Competition:** New players in the mining and distribution segments are disrupting traditional supply chains.
* **Technological Advancements:** Improvements in diamond mining and synthetic diamond production are altering the market landscape.
* **Consumer Awareness:** Greater transparency and ethical concerns are driving demand for diamonds that are responsibly sourced.

### **The Rise of Synthetic Diamonds**

The development and acceptance of lab-grown diamonds have introduced a new dynamic to the diamond industry:

* **Market Impact:** Synthetic diamonds offer a less expensive alternative to natural stones, appealing to a broader demographic.
* **Perception and Value:** While initially met with skepticism, lab-grown diamonds are gaining legitimacy among consumers and experts alike.
* **Sustainability and Ethics:** Lab-grown diamonds are often marketed as more sustainable and ethical, aligning with the values of modern consumers.

### **Economic and Regulatory Factors**

Economic fluctuations and changes in international trade policies also play critical roles in shaping the diamond market:

* **Global Economic Trends:** Economic downturns and booms significantly affect luxury spending patterns.
* **Regulatory Changes:** Policies targeting conflict diamonds and promoting transparency are reshaping procurement and sales strategies.

### **Future Outlook and Market Predictions**

Experts predict that the natural diamond market will continue to evolve in response to several key trends:

* **Continued Demand for Transparency:** Consumers will increasingly demand clear information about the origins and ethical credentials of their diamonds.
* **Blending of Markets:** The lines between natural and synthetic diamonds will blur further as technology advances and consumer attitudes shift.
* **Innovations in Marketing and Sales:** Companies will need to innovate continuously to capture the attention of younger, more ethically and economically conscious consumers.

### **Navigating the Diamond Market**

As the market continues to transform, both consumers and industry players must stay informed and adaptable. For those looking to purchase diamonds, understanding these market dynamics is crucial in making informed decisions that align with both financial goals and personal values.

For those interested in purchasing or learning more about diamonds, consulting with trusted experts who understand these market nuances is advisable. Whether choosing a natural or lab-grown diamond, the beauty and enduring value of a well-chosen diamond remain undisputed.

### **Visit Us or Book an Appointment**

To explore a diverse selection of both natural and lab-grown diamonds, consider visiting a reputable jeweler who can provide detailed insights and a wide range of options suited to various preferences and budgets.

This is a transcript/summary of a YouTube video (Auction Report EP. 3, posted August 27, 2023) reviewing the Christie's Magnificent Jewels auction held in New York on June 7, 2023. The auction realized a total of USD 50,731,130. The video highlights notable pieces sold at the auction, including:

1. **Light of Peace diamond** (formerly known as the Zeal Light of Peace, previously owned by Zale Corporations of Dallas) - a 126.76-carat pear brilliant cut diamond, estimated at $10M-$15M, sold for over $13.6 million.
2. **Sapphire pendant** - 71.27-carat cushion mixed cut sapphire with multi-cut diamonds, set in platinum and 18k yellow gold, estimated at $3M-$5M, sold for over $4.6 million.
3. **Emerald and diamond necklace** by Chaumet, made for the Rothschild family in 1930, featuring Colombian emeralds (10.28 to 2.96 carats) and diamonds (3.07 to 1.20 carats), set in platinum, estimated at $2M-$3M, sold for over $3.6 million.
4. **Fancy Vivid Blue diamond ring** - 2.97 carats, VS1 clarity, platinum setting, estimated $2.5M-$3.5M, sold for just over $3 million.
5. **Pink diamond ring** - fancy intense pink diamond (4.01 carats) with fancy blue diamonds (0.55-0.46 carats), platinum and 18k rose gold, sold for over $2.1 million.
6. **Fancy intense blue pear diamond** (2.55 carats) with cushion-shaped ruby and old cut diamonds, platinum, sold for over $1.8 million.
7. **Fancy intense yellow diamond pendant** - 50.40-carat square step cut with multi-cut diamonds, platinum and yellow gold, sold for over $1.1 million.
8. **Emerald pendant** - 53.84-carat cushion mixed cut emerald, platinum and 18k yellow gold, sold for over $1 million.
9. **Starfish brooch** with cultured pearl, diamonds, rubies, and emeralds, with attachable butterfly enhancements, estimated $1M-$1.5M, sold for $928,800.
10. **Cushion mode cut diamond ring** - 14.10 carats, platinum, sold for $856,800.
11. **Mystery setting floral brooch** - caliber cut rubies with pear, round, and baguette cut diamonds, 18k rose gold and platinum, sold for $642,600.
12. **Sapphire bracelet** (1960) with mystery setting, caliber cut sapphires, baguette and single cut diamonds, platinum, sold for $592,200.
13. **Van Cleef & Arpels earrings** - ruby beads, emerald beads, round emeralds, diamonds, black enamel, and yellow gold, with detachable tassels, sold for $579,600.
14. **Graff yellow diamond necklace** - fancy yellow diamonds (7.22 to 4.43 carats) with multi-shaped colored diamonds, platinum and yellow gold, sold for $567,000.
15. **Multi-stone ring** - 13.90-carat center stone with rose cut and round diamonds and sapphires, sold for $516,600.
16. **JAR scalloped shell brooch** (1997) - two scalloped shells with a coverage shell, round colorless and brown diamonds, 18k rose gold and silver, sold for $226,800.
17. **Sweet bracelet** (1955) - fancy dark yellow-brown diamonds, natural and cultured pearls, oval cabochon emeralds, sapphires, rubies, and pink sapphires, platinum, sold for $88,200.
18. **Well and diamond suite** - necklace and earrings with baroque pearls, round diamonds, and blue enamel, yellow gold and platinum, sold for $63,000.

Heritage-rich brands represented in the sale included Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Tiffany & Co., and JAR.

Motivated by the economic conditions of the time, designers utilized modernism’s simplified forms to develop jewels that would suit a variety of wear. Frequently worn as a pair, the ‘Flame’ brooches’ addition would elevate clothing, hats, hair and, after later style evolutions, necklaces.

> Perhaps the best example of the ‘[Flame’ brooches’ transformable nature can be found in the styles of Jacqueline Kennedy](https://royalwatcherblog.com/2024/05/19/jackie-kennedys-diamond-clips/). > The popularity of the flame motif continued throughout the 20th century with multiple variations produced, some released under the model name ‘Haricot’. > The intimate relationship between Cartier and India began in 1911. Jacques Cartier traveled to India for the very first time to attend the Coronation of George V and Queen Mary of Teck at the Delhi Durbar. During this weeklong celebration, whereas they were crowned Emperor and Empress of India, nearly every ruling Maharaja of India was present.
>
> It was here where Indian tradition made a mark on Jacques but also where he captivated the attention of the Maharajas and Maharanis in attendance. Sharing western designs from the Maison in Paris, he developed lasting relationships with new clients and suppliers. Most importantly, he brought back to Paris innovative inspiration that would result in one of the most important eras not just for Cartier but for the history of jewelry design.
>
> Fascinated by French design, it was not long before Indian royalty began to commission Cartier to breathe new life into their family jewels, creating new pieces from old materials and building a collaborative bridge between East and West.
>
> Jacques began to import unique gemstones from India to France in order to craft bespoke pieces to fulfil these commissions and in turn, European interest and intrigue in Indian culture became increasingly popular. The international jet set were enamored by these designs and commissioned jewels of their own that included Indian elements enhancing otherwise western jewels.
>
> Jacques kept a journal of his travels to and from India, noting moments of inspiration and admiration of the richly diverse part of the world. Carved and cabochon-shaped precious stones, natural pearls and enamel enhanced jewels that notably were of larger scale and more opulent in design than the diamond-set Art Deco jewels of the era.
>
> Designed as a Jabot pin, Lot 39 is an incredible example of French design with Indian influence. Originating in France and wildly popular in the 1920s and 1930s, the jabot pin-brooch features an ornamented motif at either end. By design, only the bejeweled ends are visible, allowing the fabric to be seen in between. In the 17th century, jabot pins were primarily used to secure the piece of fabric on the front of men’s shirts. At this same time in history, Indian rulers were wearing this style of jewel to keep opulent garments in place or precisely secure their turban. Through the use of natural pearls, carved rubies and cabochon emeralds, in tandem with the sharply shaped baguette-cut diamonds and geometric polished platinum – this Cartier Art Deco Jabot-Brooch is a perfect marriage of East and West.
>
> Featuring carved and cabochon emeralds, table and old-cut diamonds and opaque enamel work, Lot 40 is inspired by traditional Indian turban ornaments. Called ‘sarpechs’ or ‘jighas’, these traditional pieces were worn by Indian rulers on the front of their turbans. Ornate and often with openwork design, historical imagery shows Indian sarpechs and jighas with colorful enameled surfaces, charming portrait and table-cut diamonds, along with vibrant carved gemstones. These thoughtful creations were said to be worn by only the highest-ranking Indian rulers.
>
> This fascinating Cartier brooch is intended to be worn on the shoulder, while the accompanying detachable seed pearl tassel moves with the wearer ever so gracefully. The use of opaque black enamel, old and table-cut diamonds, along with geometric nods cement this shoulder brooch firmly in the Art Deco period. A standout out lot in the groundbreaking 2019 Christie’s sale, Maharajas & Mughal Magnificence, this Cartier Art Deco Multi-Gem Shoulder Brooch is the perfect culmination of the inspiration Jacques Cartier took from India.
>
> Filled with history, these two magnificent brooches from the same Exceptional Private Collection are some of the most excellent examples of the lasting dialogue between Cartier and India.

>
> Carved emeralds held great significance for Indian royalty, particularly during the Mughal dynasty and thereafter, due to deeply rooted cultural and aesthetic traditions.
>
> Fine large emeralds were unknown until their discovery in Colombia by the Spanish Conquistadors during the 16th and 17th centuries. They were extremely popular in all three of the great Islamic empires of the time: Ottoman Turks, the Safavid Persians and Mughal Indians; so much so that none appear to have been retained at the time in Europe.
>
> Emeralds were brought to India by Spanish and Portegese merchants as trade goods during the Mughal dynasty. They were highly prized for many reasons, specifically their rich green color – a color in Islam that represents paradise, life and renewal.

> Used as beads or as part of artifacts, these stones were often large in size but, by nature, internally flawed, making them unsuitable for traditional faceting. Rather than discarding imperfect areas, artisans skillfully carved intricate designs into the stones, transforming each emerald into a unique artistic creation that maximized its visual and symbolic value.
>
> By the 17th century, master carvers in Jaipur produced refined and intricate emerald carvings with floral motifs that derived from architecture of the time. With great precision they carved each stone to bring out the full color and beauty of the stone.
>
> Mughal rulers had a strong appreciation for intricate craftsmanship and detailed ornamentation. Gemstone carvings of floral patterns, religious motifs, and inscriptions resonated with the region’s artistic sensibilities and symbolic language. Additionally, many carved emeralds bore Islamic inscriptions, such as verses from the Quran, or Hindu imagery, reflecting the religious beliefs of the maharajas and adding a sacred dimension to the jewelry. This spiritual layer elevated the gemstones beyond decoration, filling them with personal and devotional significance.
>
> Like important spinels, some emeralds were inscribed with names of their owners as they were handed down from generation to generation signifying their power, authority and wealth. Set in turbans, necklaces, bazubands or ceremonial daggers, these stones were not only luxurious but also distinct, enhancing a ruler’s prestige through rarity and artistic uniqueness while offering protection.
>
> The present series of emeralds (Lot 41) centers upon an impressively sized 470 carat emerald with a carving of floral motif. The design emulates the popular architectural styles of 17th century Mughal India, masterfully carved to best bring out the full color and beauty of the stone. Its impressive size and precise craftsmanship, along with it’s ideal rich Colombian color, would have made it an ideal prize for Nader Shah following his 1739 capture of Delhi and subsequent control over the Mughal royal treasury.
>
> Legend tells of Nader Shah bequeathing generals and nobles jewels from his trove in exchange for their loyalty. It is possible that the 470 carat emerald was given to Ahmad Shah as such a reward. As both Nader Shah and the Mughal emperors used impressive stones as a display of opulence and power, Ahmad Shah utilized the tradition of stone inscription to record provenance of importance. The reverse of this emerald is inscribed ‘Ahmad Shah Durr-i Durran’, forever connecting an important man to this important gem.

> For centuries rulers of the Mughal empire venerated precious stones of the highest caliber. Portrayed in historical Mughal imagery, Emperors adorned themselves with countless strands of pearl necklaces that featured richly saturated spinels and emeralds. Not only was the desire to ornament because these rulers had a true appreciation for jewelry rooted in tradition, but they deliberately chose magnificent jewelry set with top quality gemstones as a means of showcasing their status and power.
>
> With no expense spared, special officials were commissioned to search for these spectacular-colored stones. Often inscribed with the name and titles of the rulers of the time, only those with the best color, clarity and size were chosen to carefully record history. The Timurids, ancestors of the Mughals, had begun the tradition of inscribing titles and names on stones of such outstanding quality, and large spinel beads were certainly their favorite. As much as these gems were a symbol of the opulence and dignity of the empire, they were also treasured as protective talismans.
>
> Inscribing a gemstone with an emperor’s name with lineage and dates was a mark of appreciation for the exceptional beauty of the stone, and bestowed on it respect and imperial dignity. In some examples where more than one inscription is noted, it is suggested that the stone was passed down through generations.
>
> One famous example of a historical spinel is the Carew Spinel, which is housed in the Victoria and Albert Museum. Prized for its color and history, the Carew Spinel is inscribed with the names of Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Alamgir, also known as the former Mughal Prince Aurangezb. These spinels originated from the Badakhshan mine, in the ‘Pamir’ region located between Afghanistan and Tajikistan. This province gave its derived name to spinels, described as “Balas Rubies” for decades. Later in the 19th century it would be determined that spinels and rubies are chemically two different gems, but for hundreds of years, any red stone was described as a ruby. Another famous historical inscribed spinel is the “Timur Ruby” which is indeed a spinel. Residing in England like the Carew Spinel, the Timur Ruby is part of the illustrious Royal Collection of HM Queen Elizabeth II of England.

> This three-strand spinel and pearl necklace is incredible example from the Mughal dynasty. 8 out of the 45 polished spinel beads feature names of important rulers including Babur Shah Badshah, Jahangir Shah, The Sultan Mahmud Shah, and The Sultan Muhammad Tuqhluq.
>
> Equally as important as the ruler whose name was to be inscribed, was the position of the planets on the day the stone was set to be inscribed. Astrological factors correlated directly with this detailed practice, as these enchanting stones were believed to have spiritual and protective properties.
>
> The Mughal Dynasty was founded by Babur in the 15th Century. He was a direct descendent of Timur, and Chagatai who was the second son of the notable Mongol ruler, Genghis Khan. Inscribed on one bead is his name “Babur Shah Badshah”. Known for his military strategies and autobiography, the Baburnama which details the events of his life, Babur laid the foundation for one of the most powerful empires in Indian history. The same bead shares another inscription written in Devanagari, which is a script used to write many languages of the time.
>
> The third Mughal emperor, Akbar the Great (1542-1605), also collected highly coveted spinels, most notably wearing them directly on the skin for their protective qualities. His son, Emperor Jahangir (1569-1627), followed suit as a wonderful connoisseur of gems. Jahangir Shah, also known as Emperor Jahangir, is inscribed into history in a bead on the necklace as well. Carefully inscribed the bead reads “Jahangir Shah (son) of Akbar Shah” with the second inscription of the bead reading “Second lord of the Auspicious Conjunction”. He was the fourth ruler of the Mughal empire who reigned from 1605 to 1627. History notes he was patron of the arts, so it is no surprise that he followed his father as a wonderful connoisseur of gems. Emperor Jahangir’s reign is marked by advancements in the arts and governing styles versus military achievements. His name is also inscribed on a few other beads located on the necklace.
>
> His deep appreciation and passion for collecting important gemstones was continued by his son, Shah Jahan (1592-1666). Shah Jahan is best known for constructing the monumental Taj Mahal at Agra, one of the most magnificent architectural wonders in the world.
