# The millionaire jewels of Bulgari Aeterna

Collectors flock to the Terme di Diocleziano in Rome to seek out high jewellery and watches that celebrate 140 years of the Roman jeweller.   

04 June 2024   by  [RACHAEL TAYLOR](/about-us/team/#author_38)

[![Serpenti Aeterna diamond necklace by Bulgari on model](/media/images_thumbnails/filer_public_thumbnails/filer_public/54/f9/54f9eb9d-7b00-4994-8e2b-a9d9748d0ac3/serpenti_aeterna_diamond_necklace_by_bulgari_on_model.png__1536x0_q75_crop-scale_subsampling-2_upscale-false.jpg)](/shop/product/serpenti-aeterna-necklace-by-bulgari/)

The Eternal City of Rome has fallen plague to fleets of blacked-out cars this past week, zipping between chic hotels and one of the city’s most treasured monuments, the Terme di Diocleziano. The reason for this hive of activity? [Bulgari Aeterna](https://www.bulgari.com/en-int/high-jewellery/aeterna).

The Italian jeweller took over the ancient Roman baths, which first opened to the public in 306, to showcase its latest high jewellery and watch offering, Aeterna. The collection, released in the brand’s 140th anniversary year, is a love letter to its city of origin. The diverse jewels are united by classic Bulgari design codes that pick up the history of Rome; from the shapes of the tiles decorating its monuments, to the emperors that ruled it, and the dawn light that seeps in each day to bathe its streets.

![ ](/media/images_thumbnails/filer_public_thumbnails/filer_public/23/e7/23e7c9a9-345a-4b40-b93d-4e3a2fa7ed83/aeterna_the_collection_released_in_the_brands_140th_anniversary_year_on_the_catwalk.jpg__760x0_q75_crop-scale_subsampling-2_upscale-false.jpg)

Bulgari showcased its latest Aeterna high jewellery and watch collection at the historic Roman baths, open to the public since 306.

Aeterna is also Bulgari’s most lavish high jewellery collection to date. The brand’s high-roller clients have been largely protected from the financial instability that has rocked the rest of the world, its chief executive Jean-Christophe Babin says, while fanning out gouache illustrations of some of the star lots in his makeshift office in the [Terme di Diocleziano](https://museonazionaleromano.beniculturali.it/terme-di-diocleziano/). “Hence, we are not afraid to propose more millionaire pieces than we ever did,” he says. Babin estimates that about 100 of the jewels locked behind glass in the adjacent hall (once a grand entrance to welcome 3,000 Roman bathers at a time) have a price tag in excess of €1 million.

The star of these millionaire jewels is the Serpenti Aeterna diamond necklace, which is in fact priced at €40 million. It features seven pear-shaped diamonds that total 140 carats to mark 140 years of Bulgari, held by a serpentine swathe of baguette-cut diamonds. All of the seven diamonds were cut from a single rough stone of more than 200 carats, which was sourced in the Kingdom of Lesotho.

[![Serpenti Aeterna Necklace by Bulgari](/media/images_thumbnails/filer_public_thumbnails/filer_public/98/3f/983fcf6a-7946-438d-bde2-8503c75f612f/serpenti_aeterna_necklace_by_bulgari.png__760x0_q75_crop-scale_subsampling-2_upscale-false.jpg)](/shop/product/serpenti-aeterna-necklace-by-bulgari/)

The highlight of Bulgari's 140th-anniversary collection is the Serpenti Aeterna diamond necklace, valued at €40 million, featuring seven pear-shaped diamonds totalling 140 carats and a serpentine design of baguette-cut diamonds.

The celebratory carat weight was carefully considered. Babin later that evening regaled guests at the Aeterna catwalk and gala dinner – which included Bulgari ambassadors Anne Hathaway and Priyanka Chopra – with a tale of how the rough could have yielded a further 10 carats, but he chose not to use them, so as to achieve the symbolic number. Of course, it is likely those 10 carats will simply pop up in another Bulgari creation.

The Serpenti Aeterna necklace was unusual for Bulgari in that it celebrated colourless diamonds. The house is very much revered for its bold use of coloured gemstones, and the rest of the collection stayed true to that DNA.

The Terra Mater Serpenti necklace – modelled by Zendaya in campaign shots that lit up the city over the 10-day high jewellery event – coiled a diamond and emerald snake around an enormous cabochon emerald.

[![Terra Mater Serpenti necklace by Bulgari](/media/images_thumbnails/filer_public_thumbnails/filer_public/2f/f2/2ff2f21f-1ca6-405b-b6a6-a3c99e85fa00/bulgari-terra-mater-serpenti-necklace.jpg__760x0_q75_crop-scale_subsampling-2_upscale-false.jpg)](/shop/product/terra-mater-serpenti-necklace-by-bulgari/)

The Terra Mater Serpenti necklace by Bulgari features a gold and diamond snake coiled around a large cabochon emerald.

The Bvlgari Lotus Cabochon necklace was a bib of turquoise, emerald, rubellite, and amethyst cabochons, secured in the maison’s tappetino setting style that makes the stones appear pebble like.

High jewellery watches were also a keen focus within Aeterna. These ranged from simple dials secreted within Serpenti mouths, to elaborate timepieces that were more jewel than watch.

The Fuochi D’Artificio cuff watch recreated fireworks in the night sky with an explosion of precious and semi-precious gems atop black onyx. Its smaller Fuochi D’Artificio Petite sister created the night sky with aventurine inserts.

The Fenice watch, which took craftsmen more than 3,000 hours to complete, used pink and purple sapphires, amethysts, rubies, pink garnets, tanzanites, iolites, aquamarines, and diamonds to create a phoenix inspired by Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s altarpiece in the Roman church of Santa Maria della Vittoria. A tiny dial, fitted with Bulgari’s miniscule Piccolissimo movement, is hidden beneath a hinged 9.78-carat Paraiba tourmaline.

[![Fenice secret watch by Bulgari](/media/images_thumbnails/filer_public_thumbnails/filer_public/ef/8f/ef8fe04e-03fe-427b-9223-5af0205fbf46/fenice_secret_watch_by_bulgari.jpg__760x0_q75_crop-scale_subsampling-2_upscale-false.jpg)](/shop/product/fenice-secret-watch-by-bulgari/)

The Fenice secret watch by Bulgari, crafted in over 3,000 hours, showcases a phoenix design with various gemstones and a tiny dial hidden under a 9.78-carat Paraiba tourmaline.

“We love to own this field,” says Antoine Pin, managing director of Bulgari’s watch division of the elaborate high jewellery watches. “There are a handful of brands that can do it, but very few dare to go that far.”

Bulgari is not a brand that could ever be accused of failing to be daring, and it would seem that in its 140thyear – marked by its most lavish collection in history – the bold spirit of Rome’s foremost jeweller is as eternal as the city it calls home.

args.summary:
This article from The Jewellery Editor, written by Rachael Taylor on 4 June 2024, covers Bulgari's Aeterna high jewellery and watch collection, unveiled at the Terme di Diocleziano (ancient Roman baths open to the public since 306) in Rome. The collection marks Bulgari's 140th anniversary and is described as its most lavish high jewellery collection to date, acting as a tribute to Rome with pieces reflecting the city's history, architecture, and dawn light.

Key pieces highlighted include:
- The Serpenti Aeterna diamond necklace, the star piece, priced at €40 million. It features seven pear-shaped diamonds totalling 140 carats (symbolizing 140 years of Bulgari), held by a serpentine swathe of baguette-cut diamonds. All seven diamonds were cut from a single rough stone of over 200 carats sourced from the Kingdom of Lesotho. CEO Jean-Christophe Babin deliberately left 10 carats uncut to achieve the symbolic 140-carat weight.
- The Terra Mater Serpenti necklace (modelled by Zendaya), featuring a diamond and emerald snake coiled around a large cabochon emerald.
- The Lotus Cabochon necklace, a bib of turquoise, emerald, rubellite, and amethyst cabochons in the maison's tappetino setting style.
- The Fuochi D'Artificio cuff watch, recreating fireworks with precious and semi-precious gems on black onyx, and its smaller Petite sister using aventurine inserts.
- The Fenice watch, which took craftsmen over 3,000 hours, featuring a phoenix (inspired by Bernini's altarpiece) made from pink and purple sapphires, amethysts, rubies, pink garnets, tanzanites, iolites, aquamarines, and diamonds, with a hidden dial beneath a 9.78-carat Paraiba tourmaline.
- The Sapphire Aeterna Waves necklace featuring a 38.93-carat cushion-cut Sri Lankan sapphire.

CEO Jean-Christophe Babin stated that high-roller clients have been protected from global financial instability, so the brand is "not afraid to propose more millionaire pieces than we ever did." Approximately 100 jewels in the collection carry price tags exceeding €1 million. The launch event featured Bulgari ambassadors Anne Hathaway and Priyanka Chopra. Antoine Pin, managing director of Bulgari's watch division, emphasized the brand's dominance in elaborate high jewellery watches. The collection also notably departed from Bulgari's signature coloured-gemstone aesthetic with the colourless diamond Serpenti Aeterna necklace.
args.key_excerpts: "Hence, we are not afraid to propose more millionaire pieces than we ever did." — Jean-Christophe Babin, Bulgari CEO, estimating about 100 jewels in the collection are priced over €1 million.

<webpage_content>
[![Options](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/all/themes/options_theme/logo.png)](/ "Options")

# Cartier's 2025 high jewellery showcase encapsulates the Swedish concept of balance

Unveiled in Stockholm, the maison's latest creations focuses on balanced opulence and simplicity from a distinctively Scandinavian perspective.

By

[Diana Khoo](/authors/diana-khoo)

7 July 2025 - 6:08am

![](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/default/files/field/featured-image/2025/cartier_banner.png)

Models stand against lush woods decked out in pieces by Cartier, appearing as artworks come to life (Photo: Cartier)

At first, it seems utterly contrarian to base a high jewellery collection on the Swedish philosophy of *lagom*. Translated simply as “not too much, not too little”, *lagom* means balance whereas, to the uninitiated, high jewellery is the finest and most luxurious expression of jewellery that money can buy, characterised by the rarest gemstones and consummate craftsmanship and design. Several steps up from fine jewellery, this rarefied realm of precious, exceptional stones fit for only pashas and potentates seems a literal world away from what *lagom* espouses but somehow, the house of Cartier made it work.

Christening its 2025 high jewellery showcase [En Équilibre](https://www.cartier.com/en-my/high-jewellery/latest-collections/en-equilibre/) (French for “in balance”) and selecting Stockholm, Sweden, as the venue for the collection’s global unveiling, caught many off guard. In the previous year, when the Nature Sauvage collection was presented in Vienna, Austria, no one raised an eyebrow as the former seat of the Habsburgs, a city practically laden with numerous sumptuously appointed palaces — a perfect bedfellow for the iconic jeweller’s offerings — made complete sense.

“We chose Stockholm not for the weather,” jokes Arnaud Carrez, senior vice president and chief marketing officer at Cartier. “We believe this city embodies the perfect balance between tradition and innovation, between urban life and nature, and also comfort and durability.”

**The destination**

## [hotel.jpg](https://www.optionstheedge.com/file/hoteljpg)

![](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/default/files/assets/2025/hotel.jpg)

The Grand Hotel Stockholm (Photo: Diana Khoo/The Edge)

While Stockholm, at first glance, has nothing in common with the jewel box-like Vienna or Cartier’s famously red-hued opulence, it has its own allure. Nestled between the sea and lush nature, the Swedish capital is generally considered a “cool” city by most, blending its famously minimalist style and preference for a soft neutral colour palette with a thriving design and fashion scene. It boasts numerous homegrown labels, sought-after in every corner of the globe. From Fjällräven backpacks to Acne Studios jeans, not forgetting democratic homeware brand Ikea and the Hennes & Mauritz clothing empire, with its diffusion labels like Arket, Cos and & Other Stories, to Gunnar Asplund architecture, long seen as the flagbearer of 1920s Nordic Classicism, Sweden has cultivated a distinctive yet diverse aesthetic.

And so it was the city built on 14 islands and connected by 57 bridges that the world’s luxury media and a coterie of handpicked guests descended upon, for a few fairy-dusted days. Dotted with more than 24,000 islands, islets and skerries, Stockholm is also the country’s largest archipelago, justifiably living up to its nickname, the “Venice of Scandinavia”. Dig a little deeper and you will discover that Sweden’s monarchy is among the world’s oldest, dating back to the 10th century and whose present King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia spend time between the Royal Palace in Stockholm’s old city of Gamla Stan and another castle in Drottningholm.

Those who visit Stockholm invariably tell of a vibrant yet relaxed city that has achieved the perfect balance between nature and urban life, and where creativity and design consciousness are juxtaposed against understated yet authentic architecture. In short, a palpable sense of equilibrium.

## [boutique.jpg](https://www.optionstheedge.com/file/boutiquejpg-0)

![](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/default/files/assets/2025/boutique_0.jpg)

Cartier's first boutique in Stockholm (Photo: Cartier)

“We must not forget that Cartier has had a relationship with Sweden since the beginning of the 20th century,” says Pierre Rainero, the maison’s director of image, style and heritage. And indeed it has. Despite opening its first standalone boutique in Scandinavia (along Stockholm’s Smålandsgatan) only seven years ago, Cartier has records of a tiara being created for the Swedish royal family in 1904. “And in terms of art and history, Sweden and France’s links go back even further,” he adds.

The presentation of En Équilibre is yet another link in the shared story of two countries. Comprising 115 exquisite pieces, the collection was unveiled at the Nacka Strandsmässan, a former car factory turned atmospheric events space, a short drive from the city centre. Going one step further to ensure a Swedish sense of place was maintained amid the flurry of diamond, sapphire and emerald perusals, the maison even thoughtfully set up its own *fika* café, paying a respectful nod to the Swedish tradition that blends a coffee and snack break with socialising and forming connections. Visitors to the jewellery showcase could catch their breath over a cuppa (Swedes apparently consume the most cups of coffee per capita, with a daily average of three to four cups), preferably accompanied by a *kanelbulle* (cinnamon bun), the indisputable king of *fika* treats. Socker Sucker, one of Stockholm’s most innovative patisseries, was chosen to helm the café.

**The collection**

## [dentelee.jpg](https://www.optionstheedge.com/file/denteleejpg)

![](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/default/files/assets/2025/dentelee.jpg)

The Panthère Dentelée, fashioned from 800 facaeted Colombian emerald beads (Photo: Cartier)

The En Équilibre journey opened with the Panthère Orbitale, a necklace of amethyst and coral beads with a diamond and onyx panther at its heart, perched on a coral cabochon. Particular attention was paid to the threading technique for this piece while a special coral spot setting was introduced for the very first time. Lovers of emeralds would not fail to miss the Panthère Dentelée, fashioned using a cascade of 800 faceted beads made from Colombian emeralds, totalling almost 275 carats for both necklace and matching earrings. Word has it that the threader took a year to perfect the necklace’s harmony, as its asymmetry and different strands proved a major challenge initially.

The attention-arresting Pavocelle, whose name is inspired by the Latin pavo or “peacock” and the French ocelle (the eyespots of a peacock’s tail) is underscored by one remarkable 58.08-carat oval-shaped cabochon-cut sapphire from Sri Lanka. Sculptural elements, composed using platinum and diamonds, echo the sapphire and are also reminiscent of a peacock’s ocelli. But what makes the necklace or jewelled collar additionally noteworthy is that its reverse side is as beautiful and complex as the front. And although carat-heavy, Cartier’s extraordinary workmanship has resulted in a suppleness that sits it beautifully and comfortably on the skin. The modular necklace’s main motif is removable and may be easily transformed into a collar brooch. If the Pavocelle is a little beyond reach, there is the Azulejo to consider, a white gold ring with sapphire beads, tapered and brilliant-cut diamonds, and best of all, a single and singular 15.35-carat sugarloaf Ceylonese sapphire as its star.

## [pavocelle.jpg](https://www.optionstheedge.com/file/pavocellejpg)

![](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/default/files/assets/2025/pavocelle.jpg)

A single 58.08-carat sapphire on the Pavocelle draws the eye (Photo: Cartier)

Those with a penchant for marine life would surely gravitate towards Janolus, inspired by and named for a genus of sea anemone. As always, with design dictated by the key stone, here the necklace shines with opals, garnet beads and brilliant-cut diamonds. But two gems vie for attention: a 5.74-carat cabochon light opal, below which is an astonishing 23.48-carat cushion-shaped blush green tourmaline. Whichever the jewel, what cannot be reinforced enough is Cartier’s dedication to savoir faire or, succinctly put, “know-how”. The Panthère Dentelée necklace consumed a total of 1,678 hours of work while the Pavocelle and Panthère Orbitale necklaces took 5,739 and 1,424 hours, respectively.

Another masterpiece is Shito, whose impressive twin emerald drops from Zambia, weighing 49.36 carats in total, dangle seductively from a long, gem encrusted strand. With its clasp positioned to the side, leaving the sliding system at the back, this spelt a true technical feat for the jeweller who had to integrate it into a small space without compromising on either aesthetics or mechanism.

**The event**

## [models.jpg](https://www.optionstheedge.com/file/modelsjpg)

![](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/default/files/assets/2025/models.jpg)

'Tableaux vivants' dressed in Giambattista Valli and the latest masterpieces from En Équilibre (Photo: Vanessa Tryde/Cartier)

Undoubtedly, the apex of the event was the crisp evening at Artipelag, the renowned art museum founded by Björn Jakobson, the tycoon behind infant care brand BabyBjörn. Guests were ferried from Stockholm to the museum, located on 22 acres of pristine land in Hållauden and right by Baggensfjärden, a serene bay surrounded by pine forests, aboard the *Östanå I*, a 120-year-old listed historic ship of Sweden.

After sailing past the *Solar Egg*, Artipelag’s famous cliffside landmark in the form of an ovoid sauna that doubles as a social sculpture by the Swedish duo of Bigert & Bergström, passengers disembarked at the seashore jetty before being led up a path flanked by sentinel-like large oaks. Along the way, Cartier had taken the time and trouble to establish delightful *tableaux vivants*, where models, dressed in Giambattista Valli and, naturally, the latest masterpieces from En Équilibre, appeared as artworks come to life.

It was the late Johan Nyrén (son of Carl, regarded as the most Swedish of Swedish architects of the second half of the 20th century) who earned Jakobson’s commission to create a destination where nature and culture could be melded into a wholesomely singular experience. Lush woods and meadows continue to surround, even camouflage, Artipelag’s organic, treasure-rich form. And seeing as it was the end of spring, flowers remained in bloom, offering the eye charming little pops of colour set against a backdrop of vivid green.

## [sawai\_and\_valli.jpg](https://www.optionstheedge.com/file/sawaiandvallijpg)

![](https://www.optionstheedge.com/sites/default/files/assets/2025/sawai_and_valli.jpg)

Anna Sawai (left) and Giambattista Valli during dinner in Artipelag (Photo: Diana Khoo/The Edge)

Once within Artipelag’s sleek interior, a quartet of renowned actors — friends of the maison, Zoe Saldaña and Alexander Skarsgård, and brand ambassadors Deepika Padukone and Anna Sawai — appeared, to join in a dinner of Nordic char, turbot and nettle broth. It was only when dessert was served that the northern sun finally gave way to night.

As the evening wound down, guests proceeded to an upper level for more merry-making, fuelled by music from Canadian rock band The Beaches and a set by DJ Dorion Fiszel. Conversations continued to veer from the upcoming Midsommar festival — a major celebration in Sweden whose origins are tinged with mystery and where bonfires and flower wreaths are de rigueur — to the perfection of Stockholm as a choice of venue for an astounding jewellery collection that encapsulates the essence of balance.

Perhaps it is no coincidence that Cartier chose the magical weeks leading up to Midsommar to launch En Équilibre. The summer solstice is seen in many cultures as a time of rebirth and renewal, as the Earth’s tilt shifts and transition into the next season begins. The extra-long daylight hours of midsummer are a reminder that the sun sustains life and how everything, sooner or later, bows to the cycles of life. Rainero, before parting, offered a final pearl of wisdom. “We must remember that the way we define balance is also how we define ourselves.” As the maison continues to evolve, it has never overlooked the elements of nature in all that it does — as a source of inspiration, as a resource and unveiling things when they should be unveiled, always in perfect rhythm, in harmonious cadence. In equilibrium.

*See more of the high jewellery collection [here](https://www.cartier.com/en-my/high-jewellery/latest-collections/en-equilibre/).*

args.summary:
Cartier unveiled its 2025 high jewellery collection, "En Équilibre" (French for "in balance"), in Stockholm, Sweden, on a philosophy rooted in the Swedish concept of *lagom* — "not too much, not too little." The collection comprises 115 pieces, presented at the Nacka Strandsmässan (a former car factory turned events space), with a *fika* café set up by the maison featuring Swedish cinnamon buns and coffee. Cartier selected Stockholm because it embodies "the perfect balance between tradition and innovation, between urban life and nature," according to Arnaud Carrez, senior vice president and chief marketing officer.

Key pieces in the collection include: the Panthère Orbitale (amethyst and coral beads with a diamond and onyx panther, taking 1,424 hours to craft); the Panthère Dentelée (800 faceted Colombian emerald beads totaling nearly 275 carats, taking 1,678 hours and a year to perfect the threading); the Pavocelle (featuring a 58.08-carat Sri Lankan sapphire, taking 5,739 hours, with a removable modular motif convertible into a collar brooch); the Azulejo ring (with a 15.35-carat sugarloaf Ceylonese sapphire); the Janolus necklace (inspired by sea anemones, with opals, garnet beads and a 23.48-carat cushion blush green tourmaline); and the Shito necklace (with twin Zambian emerald drops totaling 49.36 carats and a technical side-clasp design).

The highlight event took place at Artipelag, the art museum founded by BabyBjörn tycoon Björn Jakobson on 22 acres in Hållauden, with guests ferried aboard the 120-year-old historic ship *Östanå I*. Tableaux vivants featured models in Giambattista Valli wearing the collection. Celebrity guests included Zoe Saldaña, Alexander Skarsgård, Deepika Padukone and Anna Sawai, with music from Canadian rock band The Beaches. Pierre Rainero, Cartier's director of image, style and heritage, noted Cartier's Swedish ties date back to 1904 when a tiara was created for the Swedish royal family. The article concludes with Rainero's reflection: "We must remember that the way we define balance is also how we define ourselves."

"We believe this city embodies the perfect balance between tradition and innovation, between urban life and nature, and also comfort and durability.", "We must not forget that Cartier has had a relationship with Sweden since the beginning of the 20th century," says Pierre Rainero, the maison's director of image, style and heritage., "We must remember that the way we define balance is also how we define ourselves." — Pierre Rainero

This webpage from Luxferity (dated June 6, 2025) announces Cartier's new High Jewellery collection called "En Équilibre" (In Balance). The collection embodies the Maison's creative philosophy of equilibrium—balancing symmetry and asymmetry, purity of line with strength of volumes, and the space between full and empty. According to Jacqueline Karachi, Director of High Jewellery Creation, the collection reflects "the art of equilibrium, engraved at the heart of our creative approach."

The collection features several notable pieces, each with distinctive design narratives:

1. **SHITO NECKLACE** (Platinum, emeralds, diamonds): Created from two 49.37-carat Zambian emerald drops selected for volume harmony, suspended in asymmetrical pendants forming a line of emeralds and diamonds.

2. **HYALA NECKLACE** (Rose gold, fancy coloured diamonds, coloured sapphires, diamonds): Rose gold workmanship gives the impression stones are set directly onto the neck; features a 5.71-carat oval-cut diamond pendant with a pear-shaped diamond below.

3. **PANTHÈRE ORBITALE NECKLACE** (Platinum, coral, amethyst, emeralds, onyx, diamonds): Features the iconic panther perched on a coral cabochon, sculpted with diamonds and onyx, blending coral with amethyst.

4. **PANTHÈRE DENTELÉE NECKLACE** (White gold, emeralds, onyx, diamonds): Lace-like panther body with onyx spots, diamonds, and openwork motifs; features Colombian emeralds transformed into cascading faceted beads using a threading technique.

5. **TSAGAAN NECKLACE** (White gold, onyx, diamonds): Inspired by the elusive snow leopard, with a trompe-l'oeil effect making the feline's head appear or disappear depending on viewing angle; uses kite-, lozenge-, and triangle-cut diamonds with onyx.

6. **TRAFORATO NECKLACE** (White gold, emeralds, onyx, diamonds): Three octagonal Colombian emeralds form the central axis of a geometric mesh, with emerald and onyx touches creating optical effects and movement.

7. **PAVOCELLE NECKLACE/BROOCH** (Platinum, sapphire, diamonds): Inspired by a Ceylon sapphire cabochon (58.08 carats) evoking peacock eye-spots; transformable design where the centre stone can become a collar brooch.

8. **SUMMAE SET** (White gold, onyx, emeralds, diamonds): Ring, earrings, and necklace combining troïdia-cut diamonds, onyx, and emerald beads with Cartier's signature black, white, and green chromatic trio; produced in limited quantities.

Alexa Abitbol, Director of the High Jewellery Workshops, noted that nearly 100,000 hours of work went into the collection, with each piece representing a technical challenge preserving the essence of Cartier High Jewellery—combining suppleness, lightness of touch, and clean lines.

It is the art of looking at things differently, but it is also the art of creating the right balance. It is the art of equilibrium, engraved at the heart of our creative approach, that reveals Cartier's sense of harmony." - JACQUELINE KARACHI, DIRECTOR OF HIGH JEWELLERY CREATION

# Chopard’s Latest High Jewelry Collection Is Full of Quirky Designs Inspired by Fairy Tales

#### [Carol Besler](https://robbreport.com/author/carol-besler/)

#### Carol Besler's Most Recent Stories

![Chopard Red Carpet Collection](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/RR_Chopard_Lead.jpg?w=1024)

Chopard artistic director and co-president Caroline Sheufele gets busier every year. Back in 2007, she pledged to match the number of pieces in her annual Red Carpet high jewelry collection to the edition number of the Cannes International Film Festival – of which Chopard has been the Official  
Sponsor since 1998. This year is the 77th edition, and true to her word, Chopard is introducing 77 new one-of-a-kind designs. The pieces will be worn by stars on the red carpet throughout the festival, which runs until May 25.

The Red Carpet collection usually follows a theme, with past inspirations including architecture, painting, art, literature, and cinema. This year’s theme is *Contes de Fées*, or Fairy Tales. The designs combine a whimsical blend of realism and fantasy that involves fairies going about their magical business in natural settings. Scheufele works her own magic, including setting the pieces with rare, often difficult-to-source gems, sometimes in lavish quantities and bold color combinations. In a twist from the usual gold-focused designs, many of this year’s pieces are made using titanium, which has the advantage of being extremely light: She tends to design on a large scale, and titanium allows her to create pieces that would be impossible to make (and wear) in gold because of their size and weight. Another advantage of titanium is that it can be tinted in various colors by anodization, so it can take on on the color of the stones it surrounds or simply stand alone as a color element. The gold used in the collection is certified Fairmined. Here is a sneak peek of 8 of the quirkiest pieces from this year’s Red Carpet collection.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Oak Necklace

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/810468-3001_Red-Carpet-Collection.png?w=300)

Oak-themed necklace with 18-karat gold and titanium leaves set with tsavorites, and tinted titanium acorns. The necklace is also set with briolette-cut yellow sapphires and emeralds.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Lily of the Valley Brooch

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/9000106-9001_Red-Carpet-Collection.png?w=300)

Lily of the valley brooch in titanium and 18-karat gold, set with 3.90 carats of tsavorites and 2.24 carats of diamonds. The diamond bell-shaped flowers are given tiny yellow gold pistils.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Fairy Tiara

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/870304-1001_Red-Carpet-Collection.png?w=300)

Tiara in 18-karat white gold, set with 17.06 carats of brilliant-cut diamonds and 15.16 carats of pear-shaped diamonds, with a detachable fairy made with mother-of-pearl wings that also serves as a brooch.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Fairy Earrings

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/840499-3001_Red-Carpet-Collection.png?w=300)

Oak leaf and acorn motif earrings, with a fairy perched on each acorn, in titanium with emeralds, tsavorites and cognac diamonds.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Butterfly Earrings

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/840487-1001_Red-Carpet-Collection.png?w=300)

Butterfly motif earrings in 18-karat white gold set with set with two pear-shaped aquamarines totaling 27.57 carats and a gradient of blue, pastel and pink sapphires, as well as topaz aquamarine emerald, and brilliant-cut diamonds.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Mushroom Ring

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/828977-5001_Red-Carpet-Collection-2.png?w=300)

Mushroom-shaped ring in 18-karat rose gold, set with brilliant-cut diamonds in shades of white, orange-brown, and cognac, totaling 9.08 carats.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Frog Ring

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/828974-9001_Red-Carpet-Collection.png?w=300)

An 18-karat gold ring centered with a 17.7-carat, round-cut rubellite, framed by two titanium frogs set with two pear-shaped emeralds. It is also set with white and yellow diamonds.

## Chopard Red Carpet Collection Flower Sautoir

![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/plugins/lazy-load-0.7/images/1x1.trans.gif)
![](https://robbreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/810469-9001_Red-Carpet-Collection-1.png?w=300)

Sautoir necklace in 18-karat gold and titanium with colored sapphires, rubies, colored diamonds, tsavorites, pearls and rock crystal, with rubellite, and amethyst beads.

# First Look At Chopard’s 2023 High Jewels To Be Unveiled At Cannes Film Festival

By[Anthony DeMarco](https://www.forbes.com/sites/anthonydemarco/ "https://www.forbes.com/sites/anthonydemarco/"),

Senior Contributor.

![Jewelry watch 18k Fairmined gold, set with diamond, sapphires. Blue mother-of-pearl dial](https://imageio.forbes.com/specials-images/imageserve/64596f28522a9156e3be84e7/Jewelry-watch-18k-Fairmined-gold--set-with-diamond--sapphires--Blue-mother-of-pearl/0x0.jpg?width=960)

Chopard provided a peek at several of its high jewelry pieces that will grace the red carpet during the 12-day Cannes Film Festival, May 16 - 27. Chopard first became a major sponsor of the event in 1998 and since then it has created a high jewelry piece for each year of the film festival’s existence. This is the 76th edition of the famed film festival so this means Chopard created 76 high jewels for its “Red Carpet Collection,” which is always a major highlight of the international and influential Cannes red carpet parade.

All the pieces are designed by Caroline Scheufele, Chopard’s co-president and artistic director, chose “art” as the theme for this year’s Red Carpet Collection. It is also the theme of the luxury brand’s annual “grande soirée” Chopard hosts each year at the festival.

Her inspiration comes from architecture, museums, galleries, conversations, nature and other patterns of the life she experiences each day. The highly evocative pieces are produced at Chopard’s workshops in Switzerland combining old world craftsmanship with new technological innovations.

### [Best Travel Insurance Companies](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/travel-insurance/best-travel-insurance/?utm_source=forbes&utm_medium=recirc&utm_campaign=tirecircnov "Best Travel Insurance Companies")

![Graphic Best Travel Insurance Companies](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/tropical-vacation.jpeg.jpg)

### [Best Covid-19 Travel Insurance Plans](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/travel-insurance/best-pandemic-travel-insurance/?utm_source=forbes&utm_medium=recirc&utm_campaign=tirecircnov "Best Covid-19 Travel Insurance Plans")

![Graphic Best Covid-19 Travel Insurance Plans](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/couple-traveling-2-e1608019949550.jpg)

It's a challenging undertaking each year and it’s more daunting as the number of high jewelry pieces continue to grow as the festival celebrates another year. The high jewels this year range from pure sparkling diamond earrings and necklaces to bold pieces featuring a variety of colored gems. Metals range from Fairmined certified 18k gold to titanium, known for its strength and lightness.

As already mentioned, Chopard became the official partner of the Cannes Film Festival in 1998. The reason is because the luxury brand was commissioned to create a new Palme d’Or trophy, the top prize of the festival. The look of the Palme d’Or has remained consistent over the years, using 18k yellow gold and rock crystal. In terms of design, the luxury brand instills volume and movement into the 19 leaves of the ‘divine’ golden palm branch that appears to be undulating in a sea breeze, while the stem is tipped with a heart, the signature of the Geneva-based luxury brand. The Palme d'Or rests on a block of rock crystal in the form of an emerald-cut diamond, whose natural inclusions render each piece unique.

The one major change to the trophy was in 2014 when it was first crafted out of Fairmined certified gold, reinforcing Chopard’s commitment to sustainability. The trophy is crafted in Chopard’s artisan’s workshop, the same one used for producing the jewels, taking approximately 70 hours to craft the trophy.

Over the years, Chopard has expanded the number of trophies it produces. This year, it created eight other awards for the closing ceremony: the Best Actress Award, the Best Actor Award, the Grand Prix, the Best Director Award, the Screenplay Award, the Jury Prize, the Short Film Palme d'Or and the Caméra d'Or.

There’s one other trophy presented at the film festival: The *Trophée Chopard*, an award handed out since 2001 to persons at the start of their acting career. Award-winning actress, Natalie Portman, was chosen as the “godmother” of the trophy, meaning she will be handing the trophy to the two 2023 winners.

Additionally, the Trophée Chopard (an award for emerging actors given since 2001) will be presented by Natalie Portman, who was chosen as its "godmother" for 2023.

"The one major change to the trophy was in 2014 when it was first crafted out of Fairmined certified gold, reinforcing Chopard's commitment to sustainability." "The trophy is crafted in Chopard's artisan's workshop, the same one used for producing the jewels, taking approximately 70 hours to craft the trophy." "Award-winning actress, Natalie Portman, was chosen as the 'godmother' of the trophy, meaning she will be handing the trophy to the two 2023 winners."

# RED CARPET COLLECTION 2026

## 'MIRACLES'

A sunray piercing a clouded sky, a moon shimmering in rosy hues, the delicate unfurling of a flower… These fleeting and extraordinary moments of life inspired the 2026 Red Carpet Collection : 79 Haute Joaillerie creations united under the theme of MIRACLES.

![High Jewelry necklace: white gold and emerald choker](https://objects-prod.cdn.chopard.com/q_auto,f_auto,dpr_auto/q_auto,f_auto,dpr_auto,c_fill,ar_9:16/Campaigns/Cannes_2026/Making%20of/desktop_16_9_1920x1080px_necklace)

> “Miracles are often modest: they are born of a detail, a light, an unexpected emotion. This collection is an invitation to look at them differently”.

Caroline Scheufele

Creativity

## A visionary approach

The Red Carpet Collection 2026 captivates with airy volumes, sky‑borne hues, and miniature bestiaries alive with motion. Among its 79 creations, a necklace inspired by the meeting of earth and sky unfolds in Ethical white gold around an 88‑carat Royal Blue sapphire, cascaded with sapphires, aquamarines, and diamonds. Elsewhere, a phoenix brooch embodies rebirth, while diamond‑set watches, emerald‑centered cuffs, and an emerald choker complete this celestial panorama of Haute Joaillerie brilliance and imagination alike.

## Unparalleled expertise

Year after year, the jewelers at the Haute Joaillerie workshops, led by Caroline Scheufele, accomplish the remarkable challenge of making as many pieces of jewelry as there have been years of the Cannes Film Festival, of which Chopard is an Official Partner. A true combination of talent, resulting in masterpieces destined to dazzle on legendary actresses.

args.summary:
This is the Chopard official website (US region) page showcasing the Red Carpet Collection 2026, created in partnership with the Cannes Film Festival. Key highlights include:

**Red Carpet Collection 2026 - "MIRACLES":**
- 79 Haute Joaillerie creations united under the theme of "MIRACLES"
- Inspired by fleeting, extraordinary moments of life (a sunray piercing a clouded sky, a moon shimmering in rosy hues, the delicate unfurling of a flower)
- Led by Caroline Scheufele, Chopard's creative director
- Notable pieces include: a necklace in Ethical white gold with an 88-carat Royal Blue sapphire (cascaded with sapphires, aquamarines, and diamonds), a phoenix brooch symbolizing rebirth, diamond-set watches, emerald-centered cuffs, and an emerald choker
- Jewelers create as many pieces as there have been years of the Cannes Film Festival, of which Chopard is an Official Partner

**Cannes Film Festival Partnership:**
- Chopard has been an Official Partner since 1998
- The collection is unveiled at the Cannes Film Festival

**Navigation/Menu Structure (key site sections):**
- Watch collections: Happy Sport, Alpine Eagle, L'Heure du Diamant, Mille Miglia, L.U.C, Happy Diamonds, IMPERIALE, Grand Complications, Métiers d'art, Poinçon de Genève, High Jewelry watches
- Jewelry collections: Happy Hearts, Ice Cube, Happy Diamonds, L'Heure du Diamant, Precious Lace; categories include rings, necklaces & pendants, bracelets, earrings, and wedding rings
- High Jewelry collections: Red Carpet, Precious Lace, Animal World, The Queen of Kalahari, Caroline's Dreams, Insofu
- Accessories: bags, small leather goods, fragrances, sunglasses, scarves, bracelets, cufflinks, key holders, writing instruments, Haute Parfumerie, clocks, games, gifts for baby
- La Maison section: history, legacy, artisans, Place Vendôme
- Sustainability initiatives: Sustainable Luxury, Rethinking Our Products, Acting Collectively, Engaging Our Employees
- Services: warranty extension, boutique finder, appointment booking, order tracking, contact
- Popular searches: Happy Sport, Happy Diamonds, Ice Cube, Happy Hearts, Alpine Eagle

**Quote:**
"Miracles are often modest: they are born of a detail, a light, an unexpected emotion. This collection is an invitation to look at them differently." - Caroline Scheufele

The page also includes standard e-commerce features (wishlist, shopping bag, registration, checkout) and country/region selection for multiple international markets.

## 

### 

During the Haute Couture in Paris, Buccellati presented The Mosaico High Jewelry collection. Bracelets, bib-necklaces, cocktail rings, and pendant earrings inspired by the colors and shapes of Byzantine-era mosaics are skillfully reinterpreted by the Maison's creative director Andrea Buccellati.

During the Mosaico presentation, a short movie directed by Yuri Ancarani was unveiled. A little piece of art that silently narrates what it is like to create a precious piece from scratch with your own hands. The result is magical: the film captures the moment when light springs from the creations, making them look almost alive.

The space had an immersive circular installation, with Yuri Ancarani's Film set on a 360° video of the sparkly Mosaico creations into a night sky full of stars.

--- SOURCE 1: Luxury in Transition: Securing Future Growth - Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/luxury-in-transition-securing-future-growth

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Bain & Company 23rd annual Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study, co-released with Fondazione Altagamma, published on January 17, 2025, by authors Claudia D'Arpizio, Federica Levato, Andrea Steiner, and Joëlle de Montgolfier. The report analyzes the global luxury market's performance in 2024 and forecasts growth through 2030.

**Key Findings for 2024:**
- Overall luxury spending totaled €1.48 trillion globally in 2024, a slight decrease of 1-3% at current exchange rates vs. 2023 (flat to +1% at constant exchange rates), though still above pre-Covid levels.
- Personal luxury goods experienced their first contraction in 15 years (excluding the Covid period), dipping 2% at current exchange rates to €363 billion.
- Only about one-third of brands experienced growth in 2024 (down from 95% in 2021-22 and 65% in 2023).
- The global luxury customer base shrank by approximately 50 million people (from 400 million to ~350 million) between 2022 and 2024 — the first contraction in the 23-year history of the report.
- Top customers (VICs, just over 2% of the customer base) now account for 45% of global luxury purchases, up from 35% in 2021.

**Regional Performance:**
- Japan was the growth champion: +12-13% at current exchange rates to €33 billion, driven by favorable currency and tourist spending.
- Europe grew 3-4% to €110 billion, retaining position as largest region, driven by tourism (Chinese tourist purchases grew 40% and US tourists 10% in the first 10 months).
- Americas declined 1% to €100 billion; US showed upward quarterly trajectory.
- Mainland China declined sharply by 20-22%, dropping to 4th position; only ~5% of brands achieved positive revenue growth in China in the first 10 months.
- Rest of Asia-Pacific declined 1-2%; South Korea improved relatively.
- Rest of world grew 3-4% to €22 billion; UAE showed robust growth.

**Segment Performance (2024):**
- Luxury cars: declined 5% to €579 billion (largest segment).
- Luxury hospitality: rose 4% to €242 billion.
- Fine wines and spirits: stable at €99 billion.
- Gourmet food and fine dining: grew 8% to €72 billion.
- High-end furniture: eroded 2% to €51 billion.
- Fine art: dropped 7% to €36 billion.

URL: https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13928-state-of-colored-stones-the-big-three-in-the-modern-world

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Jeweler article (published May 19, 2025) examines the state of the "Big Three" colored gemstones—sapphires, emeralds, and rubies—in the modern U.S. market. Written by Lauren McLemore, associate editor for gemstones, the piece first appeared in the 2025 State of the Majors print edition.

KEY THEMES AND FINDINGS:

**Pricing Dynamics:** The finest untreated sapphires, rubies, and emeralds continue to command the highest prices of any gemstone. Since the pandemic, untreated fine sapphires have tripled in price. The mid-range market segment is "dying," according to gemstone dealer Simon Dussart of Asia Lounges, as mines struggle with profitability and shift toward treated materials for the low end. Rubies above 3 carats have become effectively inaccessible for many dealers.

**Ruby Market:** Untreated fine-quality ruby is exceedingly rare and now a specialized market. Myanmar's Mogok Valley remains the benchmark for quality but production has decreased significantly—over 90% of rubies over $50,000 per carat auctioned at Christie's (as of 2009) came from Mogok. Today, northeast Mozambique is the main source of ruby production, though quality and quantity are decreasing. Gemfields set a record per-carat price of $321.94 at its December 2024 Montepuez mine auction. Ethical sourcing alternatives include Columbia Gem House's "Pomme Ruby" from Madagascar and Virtu Gems' Kenyan rubies. Trading Afghan rubies remains legally complex due to Taliban sanctions.

**Sapphire Market:** Sapphire represents a smaller market value than ruby and emerald and is unique among the Big Three for its rainbow of colors. Over 90% of sapphires are treated. Overall sapphire quantity has decreased significantly since the 1980s. While classic "royal blue" (Princess Diana-style) sapphires command premium prices, buyers have shifted toward teal sapphires from Australia and denim-blue Montana material, with some movement back to Ceylon blue tones at 2025 trade shows.

**Emerald Market:** Emerald has benefited from the popularity of green gemstones and colorful engagement rings. Colombia, Brazil, and Zambia dominate global supply. There have been no major new discoveries in 40 years. Finer-quality untreated material is becoming rarer—demand for no-oil emeralds outstrips supply. Zoe Michelou of Imperial Colors Ltd. (Bangkok) notes prices keep climbing, sometimes changing within two months. Colombian emeralds still command premium prices due to history. The Swat district in Pakistan produces extremely clean, highly saturated small crystals (dubbed "the Rolls-Royce of emeralds" due to luxury watch company usage). Gemfields temporarily suspended mining at Zambia's Kagem mine (December, up to six months) citing oversupply of commercial-quality emeralds, then resumed focused open-pit mining in early May. Grizzly Mining offered 1.93 million carats at its December emerald auction.

**Role of Brands:** Luxury brands like Van Cleef & Arpels are becoming more "country agnostic" in sourcing and are seen as better positioned to market ultra-expensive fine-quality material (e.g., "unicorn" stones) to buyers with significant purchasing power.

**Market Share Growth:** Colored gemstones now account for more than 9-11% of the fine jewelry market, which was the previous long-standing range, according to GemWorld International President Stuart Robertson. Higher prices are encouraging buyers to embrace inclusions, unusual colors, and non-traditional cuts (e.g., Navneet Gems' portrait-cut Mozambican rubies in kite and hexagon shapes). Some in the trade speculate about a new "Big Three" emerging—rare garnet, spinel, and Paraíba tourmaline, per gemologist Jason Stephenson of Pala International.

**Key Quote:** "Gems, by definition, are freaks of nature. Once you understand that part, you understand that whatever comes out in gem form and gem quality is rare." — Simon Dussart, Asia Lounges

The Gemstone Market report from Future Market Insights (FMI), authored by Principal Consultant Rahul Pandita, provides a comprehensive analysis of the global gemstone industry. The market is estimated at USD 38.4 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 72.8 billion by 2036, registering a 6.6% CAGR. Emeralds lead the product segment with a 32.0% share, while Jewelry & Ornaments dominate the application segment with 78.0% share. South Korea (7.2% CAGR) and the United Kingdom (6.9% CAGR) are the fastest-growing markets, followed by Germany (6.7%), the United States (6.3%), and Japan (5.0%).

KEY TRENDS AND DRIVERS:
- The market is shifting from opaque trading toward "verified luxury" with provenance-based value chains, where origin proof and grading quality determine buyer confidence.
- Lab-grown diamonds are expected to dominate the mass-market jewelry category by 2036, fundamentally separating "fashion" from "investment" purchases and forcing natural diamond producers into the hyper-luxury tier.
- Provenance technology (blockchain, forensic tagging, physical tracers like De Beers' DiamondProof and Guebelin's "Emerald Paternity Test") is becoming a compliance gate determining market access, creating a valuation gap between companies that own supply integrity versus those dependent on open markets.
- Sustainability is reshaping manufacturing economics, with carbon footprint becoming a decisive factor in supplier selection. Pandora transitioned to 100% recycled silver and gold by August 2024, and Alrosa achieved carbon neutrality for its diamond complex.
- The "Provenance Premium" trend sees buyers demanding forensic evidence of a stone's journey, driving investments in blockchain and physical tracers.

REGIONAL INSIGHTS:
- United States remains the volume anchor, importing USD 25 billion in gemstones in 2023, with a 6.3% CAGR. Brilliant Earth CEO Beth Gerstein reported 14 consecutive quarters of profitability.
- South Korea leads growth at 7.2% CAGR driven by tech-savvy omnichannel retail and rapid adoption of branded lab-grown alternatives.
- UK growth (6.9% CAGR) is buoyed by its trading hub status with USD 92.04 billion in imports in 2024, pivoting toward private sales and bespoke commissions.
- Germany (6.7% CAGR) benefits from precision cutting and certified sustainability integrated with the Swiss watch industry.
- Japan (5.0% CAGR) is characterized by a "trust premium" with rigorous quality control requirements, importing USD 15.15 billion in pearls and precious stones in 2024.

KEY COMPANY DEVELOPMENTS:
- De Beers reported USD 3.3 billion revenue in 2024 despite a 23% decline; incumbents leverage upstream dominance to enforce traceability standards.
- Gemfields sold the Fabergé luxury jewelry brand for USD 50 million in August 2025 to focus on core colored gemstone mining.
- GIA expanded origin determination services to include opal, peridot, and demantoid garnet (effective January 1, 2026), and overhauled lab-grown diamond grading on October 1, 2025, replacing the 4Cs nomenclature with "Premium" and "Standard" descriptors.
- Lucara recovered the 2,488-carat Motswedi diamond, reinforcing the value of high-visibility traceable assets.
- Pandora reported 13% organic growth in 2024 and 87% growth in lab-grown diamond sales in Q1 2024.

MARKET SCOPE: The market covers extraction, processing, and sale of natural and synthetic precious/semi-precious stones (diamonds, emeralds, rubies, sapphires, opals, spinel, pearls) for jewelry, ornamentation, and luxury artifacts. Segments include product type, application (Jewelry & Ornaments, Luxury Art, Others), end use (Jewelers, Industrial, Personal Investment), and region. Exclusions include industrial-grade stones, secondary/second-hand market, metal setting values, and non-precious costume jewelry simulants. Key players include Gem Diamonds, Kiran Gems, Gemfields, Alrosa, De Beers (Anglo American), Pandora, Brilliant Earth, Lucara, Sarine Technologies, Fenix Diamonds, Guebelin, and Rio2. The report is 324 pages, starting at US$ 5,000, with research based on USGS and UN Comtrade data, corporate revenue guidance from De Beers and Gemfields, and FMI's proprietary forecasting model.
</summary>

The author explains that gem dealers who hold high-value inventory know how to price their gems, and value is determined by what the next buyer is willing to pay—comparing it to the housing market.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Gems & Gemology (Fall 2024, Vol. 60, No. 3) by Wim Vertriest, GIA's manager of field gemology in Bangkok, describes the May and June 2024 Gemfields rough gemstone auctions in Bangkok. Two separate viewings were held: emeralds from the Kagem mine in Zambia, and rubies from the MRM mine in Mozambique. Bids were submitted online following the viewings.

Key details include: substantial emerald crystals were offered, including one weighing 479 g and three combined weighing 106 g. Production was offered in pre-graded parcels created by experienced sorters, with size being the first sorting factor. Emerald quality is determined by green color richness and clarity, while ruby grading focuses on color intensity, color orientation, and secondary color components (orangy or purplish), ranging from bright pinkish red to darker "closed" burgundy red. Ruby inclusions, especially dense silky bands, add complexity to grading.

All products were offered untreated except for oiling (used for inspection only). Gemfields previously offered treated parcels but discontinued this practice. Emerald valuation is complex due to abundant fractures (one crystal can yield many polished gems), while one ruby rough typically yields one finished gem.

A notable 500 g parcel of small (0.5 g, 2.8-4 mm average) but unusually clean, richly colored emeralds attracted significant attention due to their rarity and high demand. The article emphasizes that winning or losing parcels can hinge on variations as small as 0.5% of total price. Larger parcels of smaller gems often have greater economic impact than single large stones, as their profits sustain cutting workshops. Buyers bring teams including heat treaters, preformers, and polishers to inspect stones, with preforming/cutting being the most critical value-determining step.

Treatment considerations factor into valuation: fracture filling affects emerald value, and certain ruby grades require heating to improve color (e.g., those with strong purple tint). Results: ruby sales totaled nearly US$69 million with 97% of goods sold; emerald sale (higher quality rough only) totaled US$35 million with 93% of lots sold.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Jewelry Leads Luxury Spending in 2025 – Bain ---
URL: https://rapaport.com/news/jewelry-leads-luxury-spending-in-2025-bain

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Jewelry was the top-performing category in global luxury spending in 2025, according to a report by Bain & Company released jointly with Italian luxury goods industry organization Altagamma. The overall global luxury market reached EUR 1.44 trillion ($1.64 trillion) in 2025. Other strong categories included apparel, eyewear, and fragrances, while cosmetics remained weak and leather goods and footwear faced challenges but showed upward trajectories. In watches, collectors prioritized craftsmanship and rarity over hype, boosting the resale market.

Personal luxury spending dipped slightly to EUR 358 billion ($408.18 billion) in 2025, down from EUR 364 billion ($415 billion) in 2024. However, sales for 2026 are projected to grow 2% to 4% to between EUR 365 billion and EUR 373 billion ($416.32 billion and $425.44 billion), with a 70% probability, assuming Middle East stabilization, resilient local spending, and gradual Chinese recovery. A more optimistic 4% to 6% growth scenario has a 20% chance, while a flat to 2% growth outcome has a 10% probability.

Regional performance is diverging sharply: sales in the Americas are rising but lagging in Europe and the Middle East. Luxury spending in China is cautiously recovering, with online luxury sales up 25% to 35% year on year in the first quarter. Younger US consumers under 35 are increasing spending about four percentage points faster than older generations. The resale market continues gaining momentum, with about half of luxury consumers considering secondhand purchases before buying new items.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The luxury market is stabilizing, but this is not a return to the old rhythm – it is the emergence of a new one," said Claudia D’Arpizio, Bain & Company senior partner and global leader of the firm’s fashion and luxury practice. "Consumers are not stepping back from luxury. They are stepping forward into a new relationship with it – one defined by meaning, not just by product."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market | Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/the-2025-chinese-personal-luxury-goods-market

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market report by Bain & Company (published January 28, 2026, authored by Bruno Lannes, Priscilla Dell'Orto, and Elle Yang) examines the state of China's personal luxury market. Key findings:

**Market Performance:** The mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%-5% in 2025, easing after a steep 17%-19% decline in 2024. The slowdown persisted through H1 (with only a modest Spring Festival boost), but recovery emerged in Q3 supported by favorable base effects, a robust stock market, and resurging consumer confidence. Q4 confirmed the recovery trajectory, particularly in fashion and leather categories.

**Category Performance:** Beauty rebounded with 4%-7% growth, the strongest segment, driven by demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances. Fashion demonstrated stronger resilience than leather goods due to innovation, digitalization, and shorter product life cycles. Leather goods declined 8%-11%, hurt by price increases and limited innovation. Jewelry improved (decline narrowed to 0%-5%) as consumers sought value preservation. Watches remained under severe pressure with a 14%-17% decline, as consumers shifted to other investment assets and secondhand or smart-device alternatives.

**Overseas Shopping:** Only 35% of mainland Chinese luxury purchases were made abroad in 2025 (down from 2024), as a weaker renminbi narrowed cross-market price gaps, and domestic mall promotions and domestic tourism boosted consumption repatriation. Inbound foreign tourists' purchases represented a very small portion of the market.

**Daigou (gray market) Sales:** Daigou activity remained elevated but uneven. Top 45 tracked brands showed a slight 3% sales increase (vs. 5% in 2024). Brands with tightly controlled wholesale overseas channels saw daigou sales decline to 5%-15% of official sales (vs. 15%-25% in 2024). Brands with larger, less regulated wholesale channels saw daigou sales reach 65%-75% or more of total mainland sales. Brand desirability remains the decisive factor in daigou demand.

**Secondhand Market:** The secondhand luxury market grew 15%-20% in 2025, remaining under 10% of total luxury market (vs. 20%-30% in developed markets). Online platforms dominate, with livestreaming playing a critical role in building consumer confidence in authenticity and reaching lower-tier cities. Top players are expanding into offline channels for verification, personalized services, and as recycling hubs. Leather goods and bags account for 50%-55% of the secondhand market, watches 25%-30%, and jewelry and ready-to-wear each 10%-15%. The market has strong potential to mirror Japan's mature model where resale reaches 30%-35% of the primary market.

**Consumer Segments:** Three key segments shape the market: top consumers (large share of sales for premium jewelry and ready-to-wear), middle-aged upper-middle-class consumers (deeply rooted, with incremental buyers from lower-tier cities), and next-generation aspirational consumers who face limited economic opportunities and delayed luxury entry—the key factor curbing new consumer acquisition.

**Local Brands:** Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers, differentiating through understanding of unmet local demand, digital-first go-to-customer strategies, and local access to raw materials enabling lower price points.

**Outlook:** The market is expected to show more positive signs in 2026, supported by domestic policy and geopolitical factors directing consumption back to the mainland. Growth remains highly category- and brand-dependent, with "true value" brands capturing stronger advocacy. China remains a cornerstone of global luxury growth despite macroeconomic challenges.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2025, the mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%–5% but showed signs of recovery, starting in Q3." "The beauty sector, a standout performer, rebounded with 4%–7% growth... The demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances has kept steady as consumers increasingly seek emotional and sensory experiences." "In 2025, the secondhand luxury market in China remained significantly underpenetrated, accounting for less than 10% of the total luxury market (well below the levels seen in developed markets: 20%–30%)... Yet it reshaped the luxury landscape... maintaining a 15%–20% growth rate in 2025." "Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers. They are transforming the China luxury landscape with their distinctive fusion of global appeal and authentic Chinese identity." "Looking ahead, China will remain a cornerstone of global luxury market growth, despite ongoing macroeconomic challenges and broader societal shifts."
</key_excerpts>

This is a video analysis by Avi Krawitz (journalist and diamond industry commentator, published July 28, 2025) examining the state of the lab-grown diamond market at a crossroads in 2025, presented from a natural diamond industry perspective. The video covers several major developments:

**Key Developments in 2025:**
1. **Terminology shift**: The term "synthetic" has returned to use, previously considered taboo due to a misunderstanding of FTC guidelines. The FTC (as explained by Sarah Yu at the World Federation of Diamond Bourses president's meeting in June) recommends three terms—laboratory grown, laboratory created, or manufacturer name created—but "synthetic" is scientifically accurate and acceptable. De Beers and GIA executives have both embraced the term again, signaling an attitude shift.

2. **De Beers shuts down Lightbox**: CEO Al Cook declared "job done" in Vegas regarding Lightbox's role as a disruptor. Launched in 2018 at a fixed $800/carat price point, Lightbox was meant to differentiate lab-grown from natural diamonds. Over its 7-year lifespan, wholesale prices for lab-grown diamonds plummeted more than 90% to well below $800/carat. De Beers now says synthetics' future lies in technology and industrial applications, not jewelry. However, Lightbox's launch gave a green light for others to enter the space, and its closure sends the opposite message.

3. **GIA stops 4Cs grading for lab-grown**: The GIA announced it will stop assigning traditional color and clarity grades for lab-grown diamonds, instead using descriptive terms and categorizing stones as "premium" or "standard." The GIA argues that over 95% of lab-grown diamonds fall in a very narrow quality range (D-F color and VS clarity or better), making the 4Cs scale irrelevant. Krawitz argues the 4Cs are an economic measure—they guarantee a natural diamond's rarity and value, which lab-grown stones lack because they're replicable and mass-produced.

4. **Battle of the labs**: HRD Antwerp followed GIA's lead, announcing it will stop certifying lab-grown diamonds entirely from 2026. IGI doubled down on synthetics grading with 4Cs, as it issues two-thirds of all lab-grown reports and saw 30% revenue growth from the segment last year. Krawitz criticizes IGI for protecting the "illusion of value."

5. **Retail shift**: Retail jewelers in the US are quietly pivoting away from synthetics due to unsustainable diminishing returns. While wholesale prices have collapsed, retail prices haven't followed, leaving jewelers with "tremendous margins" that the video argues are misleading consumers. Retail pricing of synthetics is wildly inconsistent across Walmart, chain jewelers, Pandora, Swarovski, and local jewelers—for essentially identical products. Unlike natural diamonds (where no two stones are alike), a synthetic is "a synthetic is a synthetic."

6. **Volume versus value dilemma**: The retail jewelry sector faces a classic volume-versus-value dilemma. Top-tier independents focused on authenticity and relationship selling are thriving, while mid-tier jewelers are pushed toward lower price points and higher volume. The video predicts the strongest synthetics players will be mass-market brands like Pandora and Swarovski.

**Core Argument**: Krawitz argues the diamond industry lost its "mojo" over the past 7 years by losing sight of value, and that the industry (De Beers, GIA, and now retailers) is course-correcting back to natural diamonds. The video's concluding message is that diamonds and jewelry is a value-based industry, and the natural diamond product should be the focus going forward.

**Brief History:** Pink diamonds were first discovered in India in the early 17th century at the Kollur mine in the Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh (Golconda kingdom). French merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier documented 'The Grand Table,' a large pink rough diamond over 200 carats valued at 600,000 rupees — the largest pink diamond ever recorded. Approximately 80% of recent pink diamond production came from Australia's Argyle mine, which closed in 2020, dramatically reducing new supply.

**The Five Most Expensive Pink Diamonds (sold at Sotheby's):**
1. **CTF Pink Star — $71.2 million** (Sotheby's Hong Kong, April 2017): 59.60-carat oval mixed-cut Fancy Vivid Pink, Internally Flawless. The most expensive diamond/gemstone/jewel ever sold at auction and the largest Internally Flawless Fancy Vivid Pink diamond ever graded by the GIA. Mined by De Beers in Africa in 1999 as a 132.5-carat rough, cut and polished over two years by Diacore.
2. **Williamson Pink Star — $57.5 million** (Sotheby's Hong Kong, October 2022): 11.15-carat cushion-shaped Fancy Vivid Pink, Internally Flawless, Type IIa diamond (the most chemically pure diamond type). Set a world record price per carat for any gemstone. Found in Tanzania's Williamson Mine — the same mine that produced the 23.60-carat Williamson Pink given as a wedding gift to Queen Elizabeth II in 1947.
3. **Graff Pink — $46 million** (Sotheby's Geneva, November 2010): Originally 24.78 carats, Fancy Intense Pink, potentially Flawless, Type IIa. Previously owned by Harry Winston; purchased by Laurence Graff, who recut and renamed it. Now 23.88 carats and Internally Flawless. At the time, the highest price ever bid for a jewel at auction.
4. **The Eternal Pink — $34.8 million** (Sotheby's New York, June 2023): 10.57-carat Fancy Vivid Purplish-Pink, Internally Flawless. Unearthed in 2020 at Botswana's Damtshaa mine, cut by Diacore. Notable for its electrifying fuchsia hue.
5. **Spirit of the Rose — $26.6 million** (Sotheby's Geneva, November 2020): 14.83-carat Fancy Vivid Purple-Pink, Internally Flawless, Type IIa. Unearthed in Russia by ALROSA from a 27.85-carat rough named 'Nijinsky' after the Russian ballet dancer. Named after 'Le Spectre de la Rose,' a celebrated Ballets Russes production.

**Why Pink Diamonds Are Rare:** Unlike most colored diamonds, pink diamonds owe their color to structural distortions from extreme heat and pressure during formation, not trace elements. Fewer than 0.15% of diamonds graded by the GIA are predominantly pink. A 2022 GIA study found only 2% of pink Type IIa diamonds were graded Fancy Vivid Pink. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Jeweler article reports on Sotheby's Magnificent Jewels auction held on June 8, 2023, in New York, which made history by selling two jewels for more than $30 million each on the same day—a first for any auction house.

KEY SALE RESULTS:
• The "Estrela de Fura 55.22," a 55-carat Mozambiquan ruby, sold for $34.8 million ($630,288 per carat), setting a world record for a ruby and any colored gemstone at auction. It was bought by a private collector from the Middle East. The ruby originated as a 101-carat rough discovered at Fura Gems' ruby mine in Mozambique in July 2022. It is the largest gem-quality ruby to ever appear at auction.
• "The Eternal Pink," a 10.57-carat internally flawless fancy vivid purplish pink diamond, also sold for $34.8 million ($3.3 million per carat). It set a world auction record for a fancy purplish pink diamond and a new price-per-carat record for that color grade. The rough was unearthed by De Beers in partnership with the government of Botswana at the Damtshaa mine and cut by Diacore over six months.

ADDITIONAL DETAILS:
• Total auction sales reached $95.9 million, the highest ever total for any jewelry auction at Sotheby's in New York, surpassing the previous record of $65.1 million set in April 2015.
• Sotheby's found buyers for 91 percent of lots, with more than two-thirds selling above their highest pre-sale estimates. Four additional pieces sold for over $1 million.
• The previous ruby record was held by the 25.59-carat "Sunrise Ruby" ($30.3 million, May 2015). Only two rubies had previously surpassed $15 million at auction.
• Fura Gems founder and CEO Dev Shetty called the ruby "a once-in-a-generation discovery" and said the sale could put Mozambique on the map as a significant ruby source. A portion of proceeds will fund the Fura Training Academy in Mozambique.
• The 11 pieces from the Constance Prosser Mellon and Constance Barber Mellon collections all sold, totaling $6.9 million. Highlights included a Cartier sapphire and diamond ring (33.51-carat royal blue Burmese sapphire, no heating) that sold for $3.3 million after a five-minute bidding battle, and a Cartier sapphire and diamond necklace (five Kashmir sapphires totaling ~34.95 carats) that sold for $2.8 million.
• Additional property from the Mellon collections was scheduled for Sotheby's Fine Jewels sale on June 14, 2023.
• Quig Bruning, Head of Sotheby's Jewelry, Americas, and Catharine Becket, Head of Magnificent Jewels, New York, both commented on the record-breaking results and Sotheby's market leadership position.

The article also includes related stories about other jewelry auctions from the same period, including the 'Light of Peace' Diamond ($13.6M at Christie's), JAR Jewels white-glove sale, and the 'Bulgari Laguna Blu' ($25M).

--- SOURCE 10: A History of European Royal Jewel Sales, Including Sotheby’s 2018 Auction of Marie Antoinette’s Jewels | Gems & Gemology ---
URL: https://www.gia.edu/gems-gemology/fall-2020-european-royal-jewel-sales

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Russell Shor, published in Gems & Gemology (Fall 2020, Vol. 56, No. 3), chronicles the history of European royal jewel sales, culminating in Sotheby's 2018 auction of 100 lots from the House of Bourbon-Parma, including 10 items belonging to Queen Marie Antoinette.

KEY HISTORICAL CONTEXT:
- European royals amassed gemstones and jewels for over a millennium, but by the late 18th century monarchies were weakening and major jewel sales began.
- Gemstones were historically rare and costly in Europe, arriving via Silk Road trade routes from India, Ceylon, and Burma. Vasco da Gama's 1498 sea route to India opened new trade channels.
- Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, the era's most famous gemstone trader, purchased a 112 3/16 ct blue diamond for 70,000 livres (~US$1 million) on his sixth voyage (1664-1668), selling it to Louis XIV for 220,000 livres (~US$3.3 million). The king had it recut to 67.12 ct; it was stolen in 1792 and resurfaced in London 20 years later recut to 45.52 ct as the Hope diamond.
- The Diamond Necklace Affair (1782-1785) involving Marie Antoinette, Cardinal de Rohan, and Countess de La Motte helped catalyze the French Revolution.

NOTABLE ROYAL JEWEL SALES:
1. DU BARRY AUCTION (1795): Christie's sold 65 lots of Madame du Barry's jewels (who was executed in 1793 during the Reign of Terror). The collection realized only 8,788 British pounds (~US$1.1 million), far below its appraised value, as many wealthy French exiles had flooded London with jewels.
2. FRENCH CROWN JEWELS SALE (1887): Following a December 1886 law, France sold its crown jewels at the Louvre (May 12-23, 1887) in nine sessions, realizing 7,221,560 francs (~US$107 million today). Tiffany & Co. purchased over two-thirds of lots. The Grand Mazarin diamond (19.07 ct Fancy Light pink), one of only a few pieces from this sale to return to market, sold at Christie's in 2017 for US$14,463,493.
3. RUSSIAN CROWN JEWELS (1926-1927): The Soviet government cataloged seized jewels in 1925 and held a 124-lot tender auction via Christie's in early 1926, with a French consortium winning most lots for over US$3 million.
4. Other notable sales: 1931 Bavarian crown jewels (including the Wittelsbach Blue diamond, which failed to sell), 1987 Duchess of Windsor collection (realized $50.3 million, a record at the time), 1989 Countess du Boisrouvray, 1992 Thurn und Taxis, and 2006 Princess Margaret sale (800 items, realized US$17.7 million, nearly double the presale estimate).

THE 2018 BOURBON-PARMA AUCTION:
- The Bourbon-Parma dynasty descends from France's House of Capet (987-1328) and is related to the Habsburgs through Marie Antoinette's marriage to Louis XVI.
- In March 1791, Marie Antoinette entrusted her jewels to Count Mercy d'Argenteau, who sent them to Brussels, then Vienna. The collection passed to her daughter Marie Thérèse, and after her death in 1851, portions went to Louise de Bourbon-Parma and other family members.
