--- SOURCE 3: State of Colored Stones: The Big Three in the Modern World | National Jeweler ---
URL: https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13928-state-of-colored-stones-the-big-three-in-the-modern-world

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Jeweler article (published May 19, 2025) examines the state of the "Big Three" colored gemstones—sapphires, emeralds, and rubies—in the modern U.S. market. Written by Lauren McLemore, associate editor for gemstones, the piece first appeared in the 2025 State of the Majors print edition.

KEY THEMES AND FINDINGS:

**Pricing Dynamics:** The finest untreated sapphires, rubies, and emeralds continue to command the highest prices of any gemstone. Since the pandemic, untreated fine sapphires have tripled in price. The mid-range market segment is "dying," according to gemstone dealer Simon Dussart of Asia Lounges, as mines struggle with profitability and shift toward treated materials for the low end. Rubies above 3 carats have become effectively inaccessible for many dealers.

**Ruby Market:** Untreated fine-quality ruby is exceedingly rare and now a specialized market. Myanmar's Mogok Valley remains the benchmark for quality but production has decreased significantly—over 90% of rubies over $50,000 per carat auctioned at Christie's (as of 2009) came from Mogok. Today, northeast Mozambique is the main source of ruby production, though quality and quantity are decreasing. Gemfields set a record per-carat price of $321.94 at its December 2024 Montepuez mine auction. Ethical sourcing alternatives include Columbia Gem House's "Pomme Ruby" from Madagascar and Virtu Gems' Kenyan rubies. Trading Afghan rubies remains legally complex due to Taliban sanctions.

**Sapphire Market:** Sapphire represents a smaller market value than ruby and emerald and is unique among the Big Three for its rainbow of colors. Over 90% of sapphires are treated. Overall sapphire quantity has decreased significantly since the 1980s. While classic "royal blue" (Princess Diana-style) sapphires command premium prices, buyers have shifted toward teal sapphires from Australia and denim-blue Montana material, with some movement back to Ceylon blue tones at 2025 trade shows.

**Emerald Market:** Emerald has benefited from the popularity of green gemstones and colorful engagement rings. Colombia, Brazil, and Zambia dominate global supply. There have been no major new discoveries in 40 years. Finer-quality untreated material is becoming rarer—demand for no-oil emeralds outstrips supply. Zoe Michelou of Imperial Colors Ltd. (Bangkok) notes prices keep climbing, sometimes changing within two months. Colombian emeralds still command premium prices due to history. The Swat district in Pakistan produces extremely clean, highly saturated small crystals (dubbed "the Rolls-Royce of emeralds" due to luxury watch company usage). Gemfields temporarily suspended mining at Zambia's Kagem mine (December, up to six months) citing oversupply of commercial-quality emeralds, then resumed focused open-pit mining in early May. Grizzly Mining offered 1.93 million carats at its December emerald auction.

**Role of Brands:** Luxury brands like Van Cleef & Arpels are becoming more "country agnostic" in sourcing and are seen as better positioned to market ultra-expensive fine-quality material (e.g., "unicorn" stones) to buyers with significant purchasing power.

**Market Share Growth:** Colored gemstones now account for more than 9-11% of the fine jewelry market, which was the previous long-standing range, according to GemWorld International President Stuart Robertson. Higher prices are encouraging buyers to embrace inclusions, unusual colors, and non-traditional cuts (e.g., Navneet Gems' portrait-cut Mozambican rubies in kite and hexagon shapes). Some in the trade speculate about a new "Big Three" emerging—rare garnet, spinel, and Paraíba tourmaline, per gemologist Jason Stephenson of Pala International.

This blog post, written by Yvonne Raley of Cecile Raley Designs, discusses the rising market for colored gemstones and how they are gaining market share against diamonds. Key points include:

Blue sapphire is the largest revenue creator in the colored gem market at 1% of total annual global gem revenue. If demand rises (e.g., sapphire going from 1% to 2% of global market), prices must increase due to limited availability.

- The author shares an anecdote about how unique each gem is—she cannot match even 5 rings with similar center stones in the same color (e.g., 1 carat blue sapphires), whereas hundreds of matching diamonds can be easily sourced.

- Performance data (per Natural Gem article): Unheated blue sapphires tripled in value between 2013 and 2023; rubies increased by nearly five times; emeralds rose more slowly but nearly doubled from 2022 prices in Colombia. Diamonds performed poorly by comparison, and lab-grown diamonds have further depressed diamond value since 2023.

- Paraiba tourmaline has seen dramatic price increases: Swiss company Edelsteinkabinett claims a 45% value increase in the last year, with the most valuable gems coming from old stock. The author notes newer inventory has decreased in color intensity, and her previous stock of smaller Paraiba rounds and ovals is no longer replaceable.

- The author recounts quoting $117,000 net for a top-quality 1.5 carat Paraiba from old mines seen in Tucson, while the buyer expected about 80% less. The buyer's objections (commercial cutting, lighter color, more inclusions) were partially valid but only justified the sticker price, not a lower one. The author explains that gem dealers who hold high-value inventory know how to price their gems, and value is determined by what the next buyer is willing to pay—comparing it to the housing market.

<summary>
This article from Gems & Gemology (Fall 2024, Vol. 60, No. 3) by Wim Vertriest, GIA's manager of field gemology in Bangkok, describes the May and June 2024 Gemfields rough gemstone auctions in Bangkok. Two separate viewings were held: emeralds from the Kagem mine in Zambia, and rubies from the MRM mine in Mozambique. Bids were submitted online following the viewings.

Key details include: substantial emerald crystals were offered, including one weighing 479 g and three combined weighing 106 g. Production was offered in pre-graded parcels created by experienced sorters, with size being the first sorting factor. Emerald quality is determined by green color richness and clarity, while ruby grading focuses on color intensity, color orientation, and secondary color components (orangy or purplish), ranging from bright pinkish red to darker "closed" burgundy red. Ruby inclusions, especially dense silky bands, add complexity to grading.

All products were offered untreated except for oiling (used for inspection only). Gemfields previously offered treated parcels but discontinued this practice. Emerald valuation is complex due to abundant fractures (one crystal can yield many polished gems), while one ruby rough typically yields one finished gem.

A notable 500 g parcel of small (0.5 g, 2.8-4 mm average) but unusually clean, richly colored emeralds attracted significant attention due to their rarity and high demand. The article emphasizes that winning or losing parcels can hinge on variations as small as 0.5% of total price. Larger parcels of smaller gems often have greater economic impact than single large stones, as their profits sustain cutting workshops. Buyers bring teams including heat treaters, preformers, and polishers to inspect stones, with preforming/cutting being the most critical value-determining step.

Treatment considerations factor into valuation: fracture filling affects emerald value, and certain ruby grades require heating to improve color (e.g., those with strong purple tint). Results: ruby sales totaled nearly US$69 million with 97% of goods sold; emerald sale (higher quality rough only) totaled US$35 million with 93% of lots sold.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Jewelry Leads Luxury Spending in 2025 – Bain ---
URL: https://rapaport.com/news/jewelry-leads-luxury-spending-in-2025-bain

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Jewelry was the top-performing category in global luxury spending in 2025, according to a report by Bain & Company released jointly with Italian luxury goods industry organization Altagamma. The overall global luxury market reached EUR 1.44 trillion ($1.64 trillion) in 2025. Other strong categories included apparel, eyewear, and fragrances, while cosmetics remained weak and leather goods and footwear faced challenges but showed upward trajectories. In watches, collectors prioritized craftsmanship and rarity over hype, boosting the resale market.

Personal luxury spending dipped slightly to EUR 358 billion ($408.18 billion) in 2025, down from EUR 364 billion ($415 billion) in 2024. However, sales for 2026 are projected to grow 2% to 4% to between EUR 365 billion and EUR 373 billion ($416.32 billion and $425.44 billion), with a 70% probability, assuming Middle East stabilization, resilient local spending, and gradual Chinese recovery. A more optimistic 4% to 6% growth scenario has a 20% chance, while a flat to 2% growth outcome has a 10% probability.

Regional performance is diverging sharply: sales in the Americas are rising but lagging in Europe and the Middle East. Luxury spending in China is cautiously recovering, with online luxury sales up 25% to 35% year on year in the first quarter. Younger US consumers under 35 are increasing spending about four percentage points faster than older generations. The resale market continues gaining momentum, with about half of luxury consumers considering secondhand purchases before buying new items.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The luxury market is stabilizing, but this is not a return to the old rhythm – it is the emergence of a new one," said Claudia D’Arpizio, Bain & Company senior partner and global leader of the firm’s fashion and luxury practice. "Consumers are not stepping back from luxury. They are stepping forward into a new relationship with it – one defined by meaning, not just by product."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market | Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/the-2025-chinese-personal-luxury-goods-market

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market report by Bain & Company (published January 28, 2026, authored by Bruno Lannes, Priscilla Dell'Orto, and Elle Yang) examines the state of China's personal luxury market. Key findings:

**Market Performance:** The mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%-5% in 2025, easing after a steep 17%-19% decline in 2024. The slowdown persisted through H1 (with only a modest Spring Festival boost), but recovery emerged in Q3 supported by favorable base effects, a robust stock market, and resurging consumer confidence. Q4 confirmed the recovery trajectory, particularly in fashion and leather categories.

**Category Performance:** Beauty rebounded with 4%-7% growth, the strongest segment, driven by demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances. Fashion demonstrated stronger resilience than leather goods due to innovation, digitalization, and shorter product life cycles. Leather goods declined 8%-11%, hurt by price increases and limited innovation. Jewelry improved (decline narrowed to 0%-5%) as consumers sought value preservation. Watches remained under severe pressure with a 14%-17% decline, as consumers shifted to other investment assets and secondhand or smart-device alternatives.

**Overseas Shopping:** Only 35% of mainland Chinese luxury purchases were made abroad in 2025 (down from 2024), as a weaker renminbi narrowed cross-market price gaps, and domestic mall promotions and domestic tourism boosted consumption repatriation. Inbound foreign tourists' purchases represented a very small portion of the market.

**Daigou (gray market) Sales:** Daigou activity remained elevated but uneven. Top 45 tracked brands showed a slight 3% sales increase (vs. 5% in 2024). Brands with tightly controlled wholesale overseas channels saw daigou sales decline to 5%-15% of official sales (vs. 15%-25% in 2024). Brands with larger, less regulated wholesale channels saw daigou sales reach 65%-75% or more of total mainland sales. Brand desirability remains the decisive factor in daigou demand.

**Secondhand Market:** The secondhand luxury market grew 15%-20% in 2025, remaining under 10% of total luxury market (vs. 20%-30% in developed markets). Online platforms dominate, with livestreaming playing a critical role in building consumer confidence in authenticity and reaching lower-tier cities. Top players are expanding into offline channels for verification, personalized services, and as recycling hubs. Leather goods and bags account for 50%-55% of the secondhand market, watches 25%-30%, and jewelry and ready-to-wear each 10%-15%. The market has strong potential to mirror Japan's mature model where resale reaches 30%-35% of the primary market.

**Consumer Segments:** Three key segments shape the market: top consumers (large share of sales for premium jewelry and ready-to-wear), middle-aged upper-middle-class consumers (deeply rooted, with incremental buyers from lower-tier cities), and next-generation aspirational consumers who face limited economic opportunities and delayed luxury entry—the key factor curbing new consumer acquisition.

**Local Brands:** Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers, differentiating through understanding of unmet local demand, digital-first go-to-customer strategies, and local access to raw materials enabling lower price points.

**Outlook:** The market is expected to show more positive signs in 2026, supported by domestic policy and geopolitical factors directing consumption back to the mainland. Growth remains highly category- and brand-dependent, with "true value" brands capturing stronger advocacy. China remains a cornerstone of global luxury growth despite macroeconomic challenges.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a video analysis by Avi Krawitz (journalist and diamond industry commentator, published July 28, 2025) examining the state of the lab-grown diamond market at a crossroads in 2025, presented from a natural diamond industry perspective. The video covers several major developments:

**Key Developments in 2025:**
1. **Terminology shift**: The term "synthetic" has returned to use, previously considered taboo due to a misunderstanding of FTC guidelines. The FTC (as explained by Sarah Yu at the World Federation of Diamond Bourses president's meeting in June) recommends three terms—laboratory grown, laboratory created, or manufacturer name created—but "synthetic" is scientifically accurate and acceptable. De Beers and GIA executives have both embraced the term again, signaling an attitude shift.

2. **De Beers shuts down Lightbox**: CEO Al Cook declared "job done" in Vegas regarding Lightbox's role as a disruptor. Launched in 2018 at a fixed $800/carat price point, Lightbox was meant to differentiate lab-grown from natural diamonds. Over its 7-year lifespan, wholesale prices for lab-grown diamonds plummeted more than 90% to well below $800/carat. De Beers now says synthetics' future lies in technology and industrial applications, not jewelry. However, Lightbox's launch gave a green light for others to enter the space, and its closure sends the opposite message.

3. **GIA stops 4Cs grading for lab-grown**: The GIA announced it will stop assigning traditional color and clarity grades for lab-grown diamonds, instead using descriptive terms and categorizing stones as "premium" or "standard." The GIA argues that over 95% of lab-grown diamonds fall in a very narrow quality range (D-F color and VS clarity or better), making the 4Cs scale irrelevant. Krawitz argues the 4Cs are an economic measure—they guarantee a natural diamond's rarity and value, which lab-grown stones lack because they're replicable and mass-produced.

4. **Battle of the labs**: HRD Antwerp followed GIA's lead, announcing it will stop certifying lab-grown diamonds entirely from 2026. IGI doubled down on synthetics grading with 4Cs, as it issues two-thirds of all lab-grown reports and saw 30% revenue growth from the segment last year. Krawitz criticizes IGI for protecting the "illusion of value."

5. **Retail shift**: Retail jewelers in the US are quietly pivoting away from synthetics due to unsustainable diminishing returns. Unlike natural diamonds (where no two stones are alike), a synthetic is "a synthetic is a synthetic."

6. **Volume versus value dilemma**: The retail jewelry sector faces a classic volume-versus-value dilemma. Top-tier independents focused on authenticity and relationship selling are thriving, while mid-tier jewelers are pushed toward lower price points and higher volume. The video predicts the strongest synthetics players will be mass-market brands like Pandora and Swarovski.

**Core Argument**: Krawitz argues the diamond industry lost its "mojo" over the past 7 years by losing sight of value, and that the industry (De Beers, GIA, and now retailers) is course-correcting back to natural diamonds. --- SOURCE 1: China’s personal luxury market contracts 3%–5% in 2025 but shows signs of recovery | Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/2026/chinas-personal-luxury-market-contracts-35-in-2025-but-shows-signs-of-recovery

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Bain & Company's China Personal Luxury Report (published January 29, 2026, in Shanghai) finds that mainland China's personal luxury goods market contracted by 3%–5% in 2025, a significant moderation compared with the sharp decline in 2024. While consumer confidence remained cautious for much of the year, early signs of recovery emerged in Q3 2025, supported by favorable base effects, a more robust stock market, and gradual sentiment improvement. The report characterizes 2025 as a year of recalibration, with consumers becoming more selective and prioritizing value-driven luxury items balancing quality, exclusivity, and practicality, while experience-based consumption (travel, wellness) remained favored.

Category performance varied significantly: Beauty rebounded to 4%–7% growth (strongest performer, driven by ultra-premium skincare and fragrances); Fashion declined 5%–8%; Leather goods declined 8%–11% (due to past price increases and limited innovation); Watches declined 14%–17% (as consumers turned to investment assets, secondhand, and smart devices); and Jewelry narrowed its decline to 0%–5% (supported by gold prices and value-preservation considerations).

Key trends in 2025 included: (1) Overseas luxury spending declined sharply, with 65% of Chinese luxury consumption occurring in mainland China versus 35% overseas, reflecting consumption repatriation driven by narrowed price gaps and currency movements; (2) Daigou (gray-market) activity showed structural restraint, with sales among top 45 brands tracked on daigou platforms rising only 3% versus 5% in 2024; (3) The secondhand luxury market expanded 15%–20% but remains underpenetrated at less than 10% of the primary market, supported by livestreaming and growing consumer acceptance among younger buyers; (4) Local Chinese luxury brands gained traction in beauty and select categories through culturally relevant aesthetics, digital-first strategies, and competitive pricing; (5) The gap between winners and laggards is widening as consumers consolidate spending toward fewer preferred brands.

Bain expects modest growth in 2026, with continued volatility, aided by a growing middle class, improving consumer confidence, and favorable policies, though growth will remain highly category- and brand-dependent. Report contributors include Bruno Lannes (senior partner), Priscilla Dell'Orto (partner), and Elle Yang (partner) at Bain & Company.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"After the turbulence of 2024, the market in 2025 began to stabilize, although consumer confidence remained fragile," said Bruno Lannes, senior partner at Bain & Company. "What we are seeing is not a broad-based rebound, but the start of a recalibration phase, with early signs of recovery emerging in the second half of the year."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market | Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/the-2025-chinese-personal-luxury-goods-market

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market report by Bain & Company (published January 28, 2026, authored by Bruno Lannes, Priscilla Dell'Orto, and Elle Yang) examines the state of China's personal luxury market. Key findings:

**Market Performance:** The mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%-5% in 2025, easing after a steep 17%-19% decline in 2024. The slowdown persisted through H1 (with only a modest Spring Festival boost), but recovery emerged in Q3 supported by favorable base effects, a robust stock market, and resurging consumer confidence. Q4 confirmed the recovery trajectory, particularly in fashion and leather categories.

**Category Performance:** Beauty rebounded with 4%-7% growth, the strongest segment, driven by demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances. Fashion demonstrated stronger resilience than leather goods due to innovation, digitalization, and shorter product life cycles. Leather goods declined 8%-11%, hurt by price increases and limited innovation. Jewelry improved (decline narrowed to 0%-5%) as consumers sought value preservation. Watches remained under severe pressure with a 14%-17% decline, as consumers shifted to other investment assets and secondhand or smart-device alternatives.

**Overseas Shopping:** Only 35% of mainland Chinese luxury purchases were made abroad in 2025 (down from 2024), as a weaker renminbi narrowed cross-market price gaps, and domestic mall promotions and domestic tourism boosted consumption repatriation. Inbound foreign tourists' purchases represented a very small portion of the market.

**Daigou (gray market) Sales:** Daigou activity remained elevated but uneven. Top 45 tracked brands showed a slight 3% sales increase (vs. 5% in 2024). Brands with tightly controlled wholesale overseas channels saw daigou sales decline to 5%-15% of official sales (vs. 15%-25% in 2024). Brands with larger, less regulated wholesale channels saw daigou sales reach 65%-75% or more of total mainland sales. Brand desirability remains the decisive factor in daigou demand.

**Secondhand Market:** The secondhand luxury market grew 15%-20% in 2025, remaining under 10% of total luxury market (vs. 20%-30% in developed markets). Online platforms dominate, with livestreaming playing a critical role in building consumer confidence in authenticity and reaching lower-tier cities. Top players are expanding into offline channels for verification, personalized services, and as recycling hubs. Leather goods and bags account for 50%-55% of the secondhand market, watches 25%-30%, and jewelry and ready-to-wear each 10%-15%. The market has strong potential to mirror Japan's mature model where resale reaches 30%-35% of the primary market.

**Consumer Segments:** Three key segments shape the market: top consumers (large share of sales for premium jewelry and ready-to-wear), middle-aged upper-middle-class consumers (deeply rooted, with incremental buyers from lower-tier cities), and next-generation aspirational consumers who face limited economic opportunities and delayed luxury entry—the key factor curbing new consumer acquisition.

**Local Brands:** Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers, differentiating through understanding of unmet local demand, digital-first go-to-customer strategies, and local access to raw materials enabling lower price points.

**Outlook:** The market is expected to show more positive signs in 2026, supported by domestic policy and geopolitical factors directing consumption back to the mainland. Growth remains highly category- and brand-dependent, with "true value" brands capturing stronger advocacy. China remains a cornerstone of global luxury growth despite macroeconomic challenges.
</summary>

Other strong categories included apparel, eyewear, and fragrances, while cosmetics remained weak and leather goods and footwear faced challenges but showed upward trajectories. In watches, collectors prioritized craftsmanship and rarity over hype, boosting the resale market.

Personal luxury spending dipped slightly to EUR 358 billion ($408.18 billion) in 2025, down from EUR 364 billion ($415 billion) in 2024. Regional performance is diverging sharply: sales in the Americas are rising but lagging in Europe and the Middle East. Luxury spending in China is cautiously recovering, with online luxury sales up 25% to 35% year on year in the first quarter. The resale market continues gaining momentum, with about half of luxury consumers considering secondhand purchases before buying new items.

--- SOURCE 4: Luxury market in mainland China to stay flat in 2025 | Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/2024/luxury-market-in-mainland-china-to-stay-flat-in-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Bain & Company's 2024 China Luxury Report, released January 21, 2025 from Shanghai, reveals that China's luxury market experienced an 18-20% year-on-year decline in 2024, reverting to 2020 levels. The downturn is attributed to low consumer confidence driven by economic uncertainty and declining real estate values, increased overseas spending as international tourism recovers, and consumer reluctance to accept frequent price increases without well-justified value propositions. The market is expected to stay flat in 2025, with continued decline in the first half followed by cautiously optimistic outlook in the latter half.

Key findings include: All luxury categories declined in 2024, with jewelry and watches facing the most significant challenges. Hainan's duty-free sales fell approximately 29% in 2024 due to reduced traffic and basket value from global tourism recovery (especially Japan and Southeast Asia competition) and intense competition from domestic e-commerce platforms. Overseas luxury spending by Chinese tourists recovered significantly, accounting for 40% of total Chinese luxury spending in 2024, with spending in Europe reaching about 50% of 2019 levels and exceeding 2019 levels to around 120% in Asia Pacific. However, this did not offset onshore declines, resulting in an overall 7% decrease in total Chinese luxury goods spending. Price disparities between mainland China and other markets (particularly Japan) drove overseas shopping, with price gaps reaching up to 30% at the Yen's lowest point versus the RMB. South Korean duty-free sales declined 3% year-on-year with average baskets dropping around 40% due to government/brand actions against Daigou and tourism shifts to Japan. The grey market grew approximately 5% in 2024, with Daigou revenues representing 15-25% to 60-70%+ of official mainland China sales depending on brand size and wholesale channel control. Discounts on Daigou platforms deepened by approximately 8 percentage points in 2024.

Bain advises brands to prioritize strategies against Daigou operations, optimize wholesale operations globally, harmonize price gaps, and enhance customer relationship management and overall client experience in mainland China. Featured experts include Bruno Lannes (Advisory Partner, Shanghai) and Weiwei Xing (Alumni, Hong Kong).
</summary>

"The downturn is primarily driven by lukewarm consumer confidence driven by economic uncertainty and a decline in real estate value, a shift in spending toward overseas markets, and a reluctance to accept frequent price increases by brands without well-justified value propositions," said Bruno Lannes, a Greater China-based senior partner at Bain & Company.

- Counterfeit and authentication risk (no universal certification standard)
- Price sensitivity and luxury cyclicality (mid-tier segments most exposed)
- Platform fragmentation and margin compression
- Consumer education gaps on authentication standards

### Market Opportunities
- Branded certified pre-owned programs (LVMH, Richemont, Kering) that could add 15-25% incremental market volume by 2034

- AI and blockchain technology investment (real-time authentication, provenance certificates, dynamic pricing, AR visualization)

### Competitive Landscape

Market concentration: Moderately fragmented. Top-5 digital platforms hold approximately 55-65% of online channel revenue; offline consignment is highly fragmented with no single operator commanding more than 3-5% of national offline resale.

### Emerging Trends
1. Digital platform dominance and AI authentication advancement
2. Strategic retail-resale partnerships (e.g., Fashionphile with Neiman Marcus)

   - **Undertone:** Any secondary color hues (e.g., green, brown, orange modifiers)

--- SOURCE 9: The Five Most Expensive Pink Diamonds | Jewelry | Sotheby’s ---
URL: https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/the-five-most-expensive-pink-diamonds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Sotheby's article, authored by Lydia Dokko (Marketplace Jewelry Merchandising Manager at Sotheby's) and published April 8, 2026, explores the five most expensive pink diamonds ever sold at auction, along with the history, rarity, and market dynamics of pink diamonds.

**Brief History:** Pink diamonds were first discovered in India in the early 17th century at the Kollur mine in the Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh (Golconda kingdom). French merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier documented 'The Grand Table,' a large pink rough diamond over 200 carats valued at 600,000 rupees — the largest pink diamond ever recorded. Approximately 80% of recent pink diamond production came from Australia's Argyle mine, which closed in 2020, dramatically reducing new supply.

**The Five Most Expensive Pink Diamonds (sold at Sotheby's):**
1. **CTF Pink Star — $71.2 million** (Sotheby's Hong Kong, April 2017): 59.60-carat oval mixed-cut Fancy Vivid Pink, Internally Flawless. The most expensive diamond/gemstone/jewel ever sold at auction and the largest Internally Flawless Fancy Vivid Pink diamond ever graded by the GIA. Mined by De Beers in Africa in 1999 as a 132.5-carat rough, cut and polished over two years by Diacore.
2. **Williamson Pink Star — $57.5 million** (Sotheby's Hong Kong, October 2022): 11.15-carat cushion-shaped Fancy Vivid Pink, Internally Flawless, Type IIa diamond (the most chemically pure diamond type). Set a world record price per carat for any gemstone. Found in Tanzania's Williamson Mine — the same mine that produced the 23.60-carat Williamson Pink given as a wedding gift to Queen Elizabeth II in 1947.
3. **Graff Pink — $46 million** (Sotheby's Geneva, November 2010): Originally 24.78 carats, Fancy Intense Pink, potentially Flawless, Type IIa. Previously owned by Harry Winston; purchased by Laurence Graff, who recut and renamed it. Now 23.88 carats and Internally Flawless. At the time, the highest price ever bid for a jewel at auction.
4. **The Eternal Pink — $34.8 million** (Sotheby's New York, June 2023): 10.57-carat Fancy Vivid Purplish-Pink, Internally Flawless. Unearthed in 2020 at Botswana's Damtshaa mine, cut by Diacore. Notable for its electrifying fuchsia hue.
5. **Spirit of the Rose — $26.6 million** (Sotheby's Geneva, November 2020): 14.83-carat Fancy Vivid Purple-Pink, Internally Flawless, Type IIa. Unearthed in Russia by ALROSA from a 27.85-carat rough named 'Nijinsky' after the Russian ballet dancer. Named after 'Le Spectre de la Rose,' a celebrated Ballets Russes production.

**Why Pink Diamonds Are Rare:** Unlike most colored diamonds, pink diamonds owe their color to structural distortions from extreme heat and pressure during formation, not trace elements. Fewer than 0.15% of diamonds graded by the GIA are predominantly pink. A 2022 GIA study found only 2% of pink Type IIa diamonds were graded Fancy Vivid Pink. Notable related stones include The Desert Rose (31.68-carat pear-shaped Fancy Vivid Orangy Pink) and a 17.70-carat Fancy Brown-Orange diamond ring by JAR that sold for 3,302,000 HKD (426,000 USD) at Sotheby's High Jewelry auction in April 2025.

**Collecting Today:** Pink diamonds remain among the most sought-after gemstones due to rarity, vivid color saturation, and limited supply following the Argyle mine closure. Collectors focus on vivid color grades, strong provenance, and exceptional size. The article also promotes Sotheby's services for buying/selling pink diamonds, listing retail examples ranging from $17,000 to $330,000, and highlights upcoming jewelry auctions across New York, Hong Kong, Paris, Milan, Geneva, and elsewhere through late 2026.

URL: https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/12020-estrela-de-fura-ruby-purplish-pink-diamond-sell-for-30m-each-at-sotheby-s

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Jeweler article reports on Sotheby's Magnificent Jewels auction held on June 8, 2023, in New York, which made history by selling two jewels for more than $30 million each on the same day—a first for any auction house.

KEY SALE RESULTS:
• The "Estrela de Fura 55.22," a 55-carat Mozambiquan ruby, sold for $34.8 million ($630,288 per carat), setting a world record for a ruby and any colored gemstone at auction. It was bought by a private collector from the Middle East. The ruby originated as a 101-carat rough discovered at Fura Gems' ruby mine in Mozambique in July 2022. It is the largest gem-quality ruby to ever appear at auction.
• "The Eternal Pink," a 10.57-carat internally flawless fancy vivid purplish pink diamond, also sold for $34.8 million ($3.3 million per carat). It set a world auction record for a fancy purplish pink diamond and a new price-per-carat record for that color grade. The rough was unearthed by De Beers in partnership with the government of Botswana at the Damtshaa mine and cut by Diacore over six months.

ADDITIONAL DETAILS:
• Total auction sales reached $95.9 million, the highest ever total for any jewelry auction at Sotheby's in New York, surpassing the previous record of $65.1 million set in April 2015.
• Sotheby's found buyers for 91 percent of lots, with more than two-thirds selling above their highest pre-sale estimates. Four additional pieces sold for over $1 million.
• The previous ruby record was held by the 25.59-carat "Sunrise Ruby" ($30.3 million, May 2015). Only two rubies had previously surpassed $15 million at auction.
• Fura Gems founder and CEO Dev Shetty called the ruby "a once-in-a-generation discovery" and said the sale could put Mozambique on the map as a significant ruby source. A portion of proceeds will fund the Fura Training Academy in Mozambique.
• The 11 pieces from the Constance Prosser Mellon and Constance Barber Mellon collections all sold, totaling $6.9 million. Highlights included a Cartier sapphire and diamond ring (33.51-carat royal blue Burmese sapphire, no heating) that sold for $3.3 million after a five-minute bidding battle, and a Cartier sapphire and diamond necklace (five Kashmir sapphires totaling ~34.95 carats) that sold for $2.8 million.
• Additional property from the Mellon collections was scheduled for Sotheby's Fine Jewels sale on June 14, 2023.
• Quig Bruning, Head of Sotheby's Jewelry, Americas, and Catharine Becket, Head of Magnificent Jewels, New York, both commented on the record-breaking results and Sotheby's market leadership position.

The article also includes related stories about other jewelry auctions from the same period, including the 'Light of Peace' Diamond ($13.6M at Christie's), JAR Jewels white-glove sale, and the 'Bulgari Laguna Blu' ($25M).
</summary>

URL: https://www.fcresearch.org/lounge-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Knowledge Room section of the Fancy Color Research Foundation (FCRF) website, which serves as an educational and analytical resource hub for the fancy color diamond industry. The site's primary purpose is to provide "Auction Analysis" and "Research & Insights" content to help industry professionals and collectors evaluate fancy color diamonds before auctions.

**Key Sections and Content:**

1. **Auction Analysis (Primary Feature):** The site publishes pre-auction analyses of fancy color diamonds from major auction houses including Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips, and Bonhams across global locations (New York, Geneva, Hong Kong, Paris, Abu Dhabi, Los Angeles). The most recent entries cover auctions from July 2026 back through 2018. Each analysis evaluates diamonds using the proprietary "IDU" method, which examines three key visual characteristics:
   - **Inner-Grade:** The quality and intensity of color within the stone
   - **Color Dispersion:** How color spreads across the face-up view
   - **Undertone:** Any secondary color hues (e.g., green, brown, orange modifiers)

2. **Notable Recent Auction Analyses (2025-2026):** Examples include a 31.68-carat Fancy Vivid Orangy Pink diamond at Sotheby's Abu Dhabi (Dec 2025), a 15.05-carat Fancy Yellow cushion at Christie's New York (Dec 2025), a 2.29-carat Fancy Intense Yellow marquise at Bonhams Los Angeles (July 2026), and a 5.70-carat Fancy Intense Yellow square emerald at Sotheby's Geneva (May 2026).

3. **Research & Insights Articles:** The site includes educational articles covering topics such as:
   - The FCRF I.D.U. Grading Standard
   - The rarity of fancy color diamonds ("One in 10,000??")
   - Lab-grown diamonds versus natural diamonds ("The Eco-Friendly Myth")
   - The storytelling and brand prestige elements in fancy color diamond valuation
   - Industry trends including secondhand market growth and the "last diamond unearthed" supply concerns
   - Investment nuances and market strategy articles (e.g., Alrosa's direct-to-client strategy)
   - Photography tips for capturing authentic diamond images

4. **Key Disclaimers:** Each auction analysis includes a standard disclaimer noting that "This analysis reflects the opinions of the FCRF professional team. It does not constitute a recommendation to buy or not buy a particular diamond." Buyers are advised to verify information with auction houses independently.

5. **Notable FCRF Assessment Framework:** The IDU methodology is used throughout, and articles emphasize that for fancy color diamonds, polish, symmetry, and clarity should not be overemphasized (these are colorless diamond parameters); instead, beauty, color quality, and rarity determine value.

6. **Industry Observations:** Analyses frequently note characteristics like colorless patches/bow-ties across the crown, face-up size versus carat weight discrepancies, color zoning, fluorescence effects, and the impact of cut/facet alignment on color presentation.
</summary>

URL: https://www.fcresearch.org/lounge-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Knowledge Room section of the Fancy Color Research Foundation (FCRF) website, which serves as an educational and analytical resource hub for the fancy color diamond industry. The site's primary purpose is to provide "Auction Analysis" and "Research & Insights" content to help industry professionals and collectors evaluate fancy color diamonds before auctions.

**Key Sections and Content:**

1. **Auction Analysis (Primary Feature):** The site publishes pre-auction analyses of fancy color diamonds from major auction houses including Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips, and Bonhams across global locations (New York, Geneva, Hong Kong, Paris, Abu Dhabi, Los Angeles). The most recent entries cover auctions from July 2026 back through 2018. Each analysis evaluates diamonds using the proprietary "IDU" method, which examines three key visual characteristics:
   - **Inner-Grade:** The quality and intensity of color within the stone
   - **Color Dispersion:** How color spreads across the face-up view
   - **Undertone:** Any secondary color hues (e.g., green, brown, orange modifiers)

2. **Notable Recent Auction Analyses (2025-2026):** Examples include a 31.68-carat Fancy Vivid Orangy Pink diamond at Sotheby's Abu Dhabi (Dec 2025), a 15.05-carat Fancy Yellow cushion at Christie's New York (Dec 2025), a 2.29-carat Fancy Intense Yellow marquise at Bonhams Los Angeles (July 2026), and a 5.70-carat Fancy Intense Yellow square emerald at Sotheby's Geneva (May 2026).

3. **Research & Insights Articles:** The site includes educational articles covering topics such as:
   - The FCRF I.D.U. Grading Standard
   - The rarity of fancy color diamonds ("One in 10,000??")
   - Lab-grown diamonds versus natural diamonds ("The Eco-Friendly Myth")
   - The storytelling and brand prestige elements in fancy color diamond valuation
   - Industry trends including secondhand market growth and the "last diamond unearthed" supply concerns
   - Investment nuances and market strategy articles (e.g., Alrosa's direct-to-client strategy)
   - Photography tips for capturing authentic diamond images

4. **Key Disclaimers:** Each auction analysis includes a standard disclaimer noting that "This analysis reflects the opinions of the FCRF professional team. It does not constitute a recommendation to buy or not buy a particular diamond." Buyers are advised to verify information with auction houses independently.

5. **Notable FCRF Assessment Framework:** The IDU methodology is used throughout, and articles emphasize that for fancy color diamonds, polish, symmetry, and clarity should not be overemphasized (these are colorless diamond parameters); instead, beauty, color quality, and rarity determine value.

6. **Industry Observations:** Analyses frequently note characteristics like colorless patches/bow-ties across the crown, face-up size versus carat weight discrepancies, color zoning, fluorescence effects, and the impact of cut/facet alignment on color presentation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: A History of European Royal Jewel Sales, Including Sotheby’s 2018 Auction of Marie Antoinette’s Jewels | Gems & Gemology ---
URL: https://www.gia.edu/gems-gemology/fall-2020-european-royal-jewel-sales

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Russell Shor, published in Gems & Gemology (Fall 2020, Vol. 56, No. 3), chronicles the history of European royal jewel sales, culminating in Sotheby's 2018 auction of 100 lots from the House of Bourbon-Parma, including 10 items belonging to Queen Marie Antoinette.

KEY HISTORICAL CONTEXT:
- European royals amassed gemstones and jewels for over a millennium, but by the late 18th century monarchies were weakening and major jewel sales began.
- Gemstones were historically rare and costly in Europe, arriving via Silk Road trade routes from India, Ceylon, and Burma. Vasco da Gama's 1498 sea route to India opened new trade channels.
- Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, the era's most famous gemstone trader, purchased a 112 3/16 ct blue diamond for 70,000 livres (~US$1 million) on his sixth voyage (1664-1668), selling it to Louis XIV for 220,000 livres (~US$3.3 million). The king had it recut to 67.12 ct; it was stolen in 1792 and resurfaced in London 20 years later recut to 45.52 ct as the Hope diamond.
- The Diamond Necklace Affair (1782-1785) involving Marie Antoinette, Cardinal de Rohan, and Countess de La Motte helped catalyze the French Revolution.

NOTABLE ROYAL JEWEL SALES:
1. DU BARRY AUCTION (1795): Christie's sold 65 lots of Madame du Barry's jewels (who was executed in 1793 during the Reign of Terror). The collection realized only 8,788 British pounds (~US$1.1 million), far below its appraised value, as many wealthy French exiles had flooded London with jewels.
2. FRENCH CROWN JEWELS SALE (1887): Following a December 1886 law, France sold its crown jewels at the Louvre (May 12-23, 1887) in nine sessions, realizing 7,221,560 francs (~US$107 million today). Tiffany & Co. purchased over two-thirds of lots. The Grand Mazarin diamond (19.07 ct Fancy Light pink), one of only a few pieces from this sale to return to market, sold at Christie's in 2017 for US$14,463,493.
3. RUSSIAN CROWN JEWELS (1926-1927): The Soviet government cataloged seized jewels in 1925 and held a 124-lot tender auction via Christie's in early 1926, with a French consortium winning most lots for over US$3 million.
4. Other notable sales: 1931 Bavarian crown jewels (including the Wittelsbach Blue diamond, which failed to sell), 1987 Duchess of Windsor collection (realized $50.3 million, a record at the time), 1989 Countess du Boisrouvray, 1992 Thurn und Taxis, and 2006 Princess Margaret sale (800 items, realized US$17.7 million, nearly double the presale estimate).

THE 2018 BOURBON-PARMA AUCTION:
- The Bourbon-Parma dynasty descends from France's House of Capet (987-1328) and is related to the Habsburgs through Marie Antoinette's marriage to Louis XVI.
- In March 1791, Marie Antoinette entrusted her jewels to Count Mercy d'Argenteau, who sent them to Brussels, then Vienna. The collection passed to her daughter Marie Thérèse, and after her death in 1851, portions went to Louise de Bourbon-Parma and other family members.
- The collection was inherited by Archduchess Marie Anne of Austria (wife of Prince Elias de Bourbon-Parma), who made detailed inventories in 1907 and 1932.
- Sotheby's spent nearly a decade convincing over 120 scattered descendants to agree to the sale.
- The Farnese Blue diamond (6.16 ct, Fancy dark gray-blue, GIA-graded) was sold separately in May 2018 for US$6.7 million (estimate: $3.7-5.2 million).
- The November 14, 2018 Geneva auction sold 100 lots for a total of US$53 million. The first 26 lots were royal orders, badges, and medals; the final 10 lots belonged to Marie Antoinette. Her signature drop-shaped natural pearl pendant alone sold for US$36 million.

CONCLUSION: Gems and jewels with true royal provenance command high premiums at auction today, unlike early royal jewel sales when prices were often disappointing. The Bourbon-Parma auction was one of the largest sales of jewels with royal provenance in modern history.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Sotheby's article (by Lydia Dokko, Marketplace Jewelry Merchandising Manager, dated May 20, 2026) explains why natural and cultured pearl jewelry is highly collectible. Key points include:

**Natural vs. Cultured Pearls:** Natural pearls form entirely without human intervention when an irritant enters a mollusk and it secretes layers of nacre (aragonite and conchiolin). Cultured pearls use the same nacre-producing process but begin with intentional human insertion of a bead or tissue. Natural pearls are far rarer and thus more valuable.

**Why Natural Pearls Are Expensive:** Value is determined by size, shape, color, surface quality, luster, and nacre thickness. Natural pearls over 10mm are considered rare and highly desirable, ranging from ~$1,000 to over $10,000 per pearl depending on quality. Luster (sharp, mirror-like reflective surface with soft inner glow) and thick nacre are top indicators of value. Classic white-to-cream pearls with rosé overtones remain most sought after, though gray, silver, green, pink, and lavender are growing in popularity.

**Key Collectibility Factors (summary table):** Natural pearl rarity (formed without human intervention, increasingly scarce); historic provenance (antique pieces achieve strong prices due to craftsmanship and documented ownership); luster and nacre thickness; size (over 10mm considered rare); signed jewelry (Cartier, Tiffany & Co., Van Cleef & Arpels command premiums); and strong auction performance at Sotheby's.

**Notable Recent Auction Results (May 2025):**
- Natural Pearl, Ruby and Diamond Devant-de-Corsage Brooch (circa 1865): sold for 406,400 CHF. Features entwined serpents grasping a button pearl, suspending three baroque drop-shaped natural pearls up to 26.20mm.
- Natural Pearl and Diamond Necklace (1950s): sold for 508,000 CHF. Features foliate design with baroque oval and drop pearls (13.45-14.80 x 19.90mm to 10.90-13.10 x 14.20mm) and marquise, brilliant-cut, tapered baguette, and baguette diamonds.
- Pair of Natural Pearl and Diamond Earrings (1950s): sold for 495,300 CHF. Drop-shaped natural pearls with brilliant-cut and marquise diamonds.

**Upcoming Auction (Sotheby's Fine Jewelry, London, closing June 3, 2026):** Includes a two-row graduated natural pearl and diamond necklace (circa 1920, with SSEF and Gem & Pearl reports confirming natural saltwater origin), a pair of natural pearl and diamond drop earrings (early 20th century design), and a four-row natural pearl and diamond necklace. All are certified for natural saltwater origin.

**What Collectors Look For:** Natural origin (most important rarity driver), pearl size, luster, surface quality, and matching (especially in multi-strand necklaces). Antique/early 20th century designs with intricate diamond settings and signed pieces command premiums. Condition and certification from major labs (SSEF, GIA, Gübelin) confirming natural saltwater origin dramatically influence value.

**Sotheby's Services:** Sotheby's offers buying and selling of pearl jewelry, with pieces ranging from ~$3,000 (cultured pearl and diamond) to over $500,000 (natural pearl necklaces and antique jewels). Purchases available online or in person in New York, Paris, and Hong Kong. Upcoming auctions are scheduled across London, New York, Paris, Geneva, and Milan through late 2026.

**Author:** Lydia Dokko, Marketplace Jewelry Merchandising Manager at Sotheby's.

1. **Auction Analysis (Primary Feature):** The site publishes pre-auction analyses of fancy color diamonds from major auction houses including Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips, and Bonhams across global locations (New York, Geneva, Hong Kong, Paris, Abu Dhabi, Los Angeles). The most recent entries cover auctions from July 2026 back through 2018. Each analysis evaluates diamonds using the proprietary "IDU" method, which examines three key visual characteristics:
   - **Inner-Grade:** The quality and intensity of color within the stone
   - **Color Dispersion:** How color spreads across the face-up view
   - **Undertone:** Any secondary color hues (e.g., green, brown, orange modifiers)

2. **Notable Recent Auction Analyses (2025-2026):** Examples include a 31.68-carat Fancy Vivid Orangy Pink diamond at Sotheby's Abu Dhabi (Dec 2025), a 15.05-carat Fancy Yellow cushion at Christie's New York (Dec 2025), a 2.29-carat Fancy Intense Yellow marquise at Bonhams Los Angeles (July 2026), and a 5.70-carat Fancy Intense Yellow square emerald at Sotheby's Geneva (May 2026).

4. **Key Disclaimers:** Each auction analysis includes a standard disclaimer noting that "This analysis reflects the opinions of the FCRF professional team. 5. **Notable FCRF Assessment Framework:** The IDU methodology is used throughout, and articles emphasize that for fancy color diamonds, polish, symmetry, and clarity should not be overemphasized (these are colorless diamond parameters); instead, beauty, color quality, and rarity determine value.

6. **Industry Observations:** Analyses frequently note characteristics like colorless patches/bow-ties across the crown, face-up size versus carat weight discrepancies, color zoning, fluorescence effects, and the impact of cut/facet alignment on color presentation.

- The Wings section introduces a new symbol in the House's fine jewelry universe, featuring the "WINGS OF CHANEL necklace" and "FULL SWING head jewel" (elevated by a 3.08-carat pear-cut DFL diamond, with spread wings in 18K gold set with round-cut and navette-cut diamonds).
- The Lion section presents striking sculptural creations, including the "Strong as a lion ring" and "Strong as a lion necklace."

The webpage also covers the creation process from design to production — from the initial sketch by the CHANEL Fine Jewelry Creation Studio, to sourcing exceptional gemstones, to final production by the House's artisans at 18 Place Vendôme in Paris (featuring the WINGS OF CHANEL necklace). Related collections referenced include LES SIGNATURES DE CHANEL, PLUME DE CHANEL COLLECTION, COMÈTE COLLECTION (including the 1932 CHANEL COMÈTE bracelet adapted by Lorenz Bäumer), and LION COLLECTION.

The page also includes standard CHANEL navigation for Fashion, High Jewelry, Fine Jewelry, Watches, Eyewear, Fragrance, Makeup, Skincare, and Corporate sections, plus client care information (available Monday–Friday 9 AM–10 PM ET, weekends 10 AM–6 PM ET, via email, phone at 1.800.550.0005, or live chat).

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
[WHERE FASHION GETS CREATIVE](https://theimpression.com)

* [Subscribe](#)

![Chanel Unveils New Jewelry Collection](https://theimpression.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Chanel-Spring-2025-News-The-Impression-003-standard-v2-2x.jpeg)

# Chanel Unveils New Jewelry Collection

## “Reach for the Stars” collection focuses on recurring motifs and historical references

[Chanel](https://theimpression.com/?s=chanel) introduced its latest high jewelry collection titled “Reach for the Stars” on Monday, citing influence from the early Hollywood work of Gabrielle Chanel. The collection, presented at the Kyoto National Museum, revolves around references to celestial and animal symbolism.

The label continues to incorporate founder Gabrielle Chanel’s life story into its jewelry releases. Her time designing costumes for Hollywood actors like Gloria Swanson during the late 1920s and early 1930s was used as a central reference point.

“It’s all about this idea found across the house that whatever theme we explore, it becomes inscribed in the history of the house but it also brings us back to Gabrielle Chanel,” said Frédéric Grangié, president of Chanel watches and fine jewelry.

The collection consists of 110 pieces grouped into three thematic sections, 90 of which were unveiled during the Kyoto event. One segment references comets as symbols of autonomy, connecting to the house’s earlier “Bijoux de Diamant” designs. Another segment highlights lions, associated with strength and Chanel’s Leo zodiac sign.

The “Dreams Come True” set exemplifies the comet theme. It includes a necklace designed to resemble a high fashion neckline with diamond clusters arranged like lace and a black line across the design to create visual contrast.

In the lion-themed segment, Chanel used the motif to communicate authority. The “Be the One” and “Strong as a Lion” pieces employed radiant arrangements with lion features encircled by glitter and star details.

Chanel included 27 pieces in the collection priced in the million-dollar range, with some extending into eight-figure values.

Wings also appeared prominently for the first time in the house’s high jewelry, a choice explained by both Chanel’s 1930s design references and a quotation from 1938.

“If you were born without wings, do nothing to prevent them from growing,” said the founder, a phrase used by Patrice Leguéreau, who led Chanel’s jewelry creation studio until his death in November at age 53.

Though wings were new to Chanel high jewelry, Grangié said they were previously seen in couture. He also noted their presence in the original “Bijoux de Diamants” collection.

“[Her] short period in Hollywood certainly had an enormous impact on the presentation in 1932 because [it] was very cinematographic, with mannequins positioned like actresses,” he said. “Given those [designs] and a staging that could be a film set, it certainly influenced in the way she conceived and saw high jewelry.”

A necklace titled Wings of Chanel was included to represent Leguéreau’s work. It features openwork elements framing the neck and includes a detachable pendant that converts into a bracelet.

The diamond layout on the wing’s segments is designed to move and fit different body shapes. Technical aspects such as mixed prong settings contribute to the visual impression of lightness, even with over 45 carats of diamonds.

A Padparadscha sapphire of 19.55 carats appears in the center, selected partly for its alignment with Chanel’s numeric themes. Its orange-pink color aligns with the broader visual tone.

Leguéreau “imagined pieces kissed by the light of the sun at sunset and dawn, with these colors that blaze on the horizon,” said the house. “It’s about that magical moment between day and night when the high jewelry sparkles on the skin.”

The set includes a wide range of colors and stones. The “Sunny Days” set features garnets and a 20.64-carat imperial topaz. The “After Midnight” necklace showcases sapphires from Sri Lanka, and the “Dreams Come True” design uses black DLC-coated gold.

A series of five brooches titled “Five Wings” reflects the wing theme further. Each includes a component painted by a Kyoto lacquer artist with generational expertise in the medium.

Leguéreau had “long been fascinated by this idea of excellence pushed to its pinnacle,” recalled Grangié. He had previously worked with lacquerer Yūji Shihou Okada and his son Yoshio Okada, who continues the family practice and was honored by the Japanese government.

The brooches were intended to express Leguéreau’s interpretation of high jewelry as “an art form, a language, and a legacy,” as written by Grangié in a note distributed to attendees in Kyoto.

“It is absolutely essential that we transcribe the creations of Patrice [Leguéreau] and the studio at the highest level of excellence so that these pieces sit in a patrimony on a 20-, 30-, 50-year scale and that one day, when a magistral exhibition on Chanel in our days takes place, they are part of it,” said Grangié. “That’s a clear goal for us.”

Before the collection enters museum spaces again, the priority is transferring it to private collectors. The jewelry division at Chanel, created in 1993, continues to define itself in contrast to older competitors.

Grangié noted familiar themes at Chanel being repurposed — for example, stars integrated into wing elements or used alongside lion designs.

“For Chanel, it is important to always bring themes that constitute this living patrimony that will have a capital importance in high jewelry,” the executive said. “But we are still in this creation phase and that’s what’s different compared to more institutional houses who have two centuries of history and revisit themes that are their own.”

Following 2023’s “Haute Joaillerie Sport,” this collection is presented as a display of the label’s interpretation of technical and aesthetic standards.

“It’s about creations pushed [to their utmost] but with the iron discipline of being a pure player” in terms of craft, gem sourcing and execution,” Grangié said.

This method targets a cross-section of clients interested in both Chanel’s apparel and high-end jewelry. Grangié estimates the audience for such pieces is composed of several hundred collectors globally.

A clock with a figure of Gabrielle Chanel on a base made of diamond-studded black jade — resembling an award statuette — was reportedly sold prior to the public launch.

“The priority of high jewelry is brand elevation, brand equity, so going higher and higher in terms of know-how, exceptional stones in service of a creation that will always be uniquely Chanel,” he said. “The top line is a consequence that follows, that grows, but that’s not the [primary focus] in high jewelry, which is about pulling the activity upwards.”

Grangié added that market volatility has made planning more complex, though development remains on track.

“Instability is likely to persist for a good long while so we are very vigilant,” the executive continued. “But we are staying the course regarding launches, all the programs [planned] for 2026 and 2027 and more than ever, in terms of investment — there’s no change there.”

Plans include new collections as well as continued movement toward vertical integration and expanding retail presence.

Grangié pointed to evenly distributed global demand and sector stability as encouraging signs.

“Not only is it a category that is resilient but it remains afloat and continues to generate growth,” the executive said. “I believe this will continue in years to come and the category itself is very, very, very positive.”

Luxury jewelry brands now account for around 35 percent of a market projected to reach $90.2 billion in 2025, with continued growth expected, according to Statista. Grangié said the potential for further expansion remains “very significant.”

The Kyoto event also marked a recognition of Leguéreau’s contributions. The evening concluded with a drone display above the Shogunzuka Seiryuden temple. Attendees included Japanese actress Nana Komatsu, Thai actress Chutimon “Aokbab” Chuengcharoensukying, and South Korean actress Kim Go-eun.

Grangié described Leguéreau as “the soul of the collection…gone too soon” and suggested that the house’s technical practices and stylistic choices going forward would be shaped by his influence.

“What you have here is a very, very important collection,” the executive said. “I think it will make a lot of sense 20 years from now, 30 years from now because when you think about high jewelry, only the long term prevails.”

Luxury jewelry brands now account for around 35 percent of a market projected to reach $90.2 billion in 2025. The Kyoto event ended with a drone display above Shogunzuka Seiryuden temple, with attendees including actresses Nana Komatsu, Chutimon Chuengcharoensukying, and Kim Go-eun. A clock featuring Gabrielle Chanel on a diamond-studded black jade base was reportedly sold before the public launch.
args.key_excerpts: "It's all about this idea found across the house that whatever theme we explore, it becomes inscribed in the history of the house but it also brings us back to Gabrielle Chanel," said Frédéric Grangié, president of Chanel watches and fine jewelry. "If you were born without wings, do nothing to prevent them from growing," said the founder, a phrase used by Patrice Leguéreau, who led Chanel's jewelry creation studio until his death in November at age 53. "It is absolutely essential that we transcribe the creations of Patrice [Leguéreau] and the studio at the highest level of excellence so that these pieces sit in a patrimony on a 20-, 30-, 50-year scale," said Grangié. "The priority of high jewelry is brand elevation, brand equity, so going higher and higher in terms of know-how, exceptional stones in service of a creation that will always be uniquely Chanel," said Grangié. "What you have here is a very, very important collection. I think it will make a lot of sense 20 years from now, 30 years from now because when you think about high jewelry, only the long term prevails," said Grangié.

## PREMIÈRE

Debuted in 1987, the PREMIÈRE precedes all others. More than a watch, it is an exercise in style: The dial evokes the stopper of the N°5 fragrance bottle and the absence of hour markers underlines the essential, a spirit of freedom unique to CHANEL.

Explore Haute Horlogerie timepieces in 18K yellow or white gold\*, entirely hand-set with diamonds by the artisans at the Manufacture in Switzerland, or fitted with the Caliber 2, a 3-dimensional skeleton watch movement.
\*White gold with a thin layer of Rhodium plating for color

## J12

Created in 2000, the J12, the first unisex sports watch by CHANEL, has revolutionized the world of watchmaking, asserting itself as a 21st-century icon.

In Haute Horlogerie interpretations, highly resistant matte or glossy ceramic is paired with the sparkle of 18K gold and diamonds. Snow-set or baguette-cut stones adorn the bezel, the dial or the links of the bracelet. Creations equipped with remarkable mechanisms, such as the Caliber 5, the first Flying Tourbillon movement by CHANEL.

args.summary:
This is the CHANEL Haute Horlogerie (High Watchmaking) webpage from the official CHANEL website, showcasing the "Les Signatures de CHANEL" collection. The page highlights five iconic watch collections that combine avant-garde creativity with eternal allure, featuring exceptional timepieces set with precious gemstones and powered by precisely crafted movements from the House's Watch Creation Studio and Manufacture.

**PREMIÈRE**: Debuted in 1987 as CHANEL's first watch, the PREMIÈRE is more than a timepiece—it's an exercise in style. Its dial evokes the stopper of the N°5 fragrance bottle, and the absence of hour markers underscores a spirit of freedom unique to CHANEL. Available in 18K yellow or white gold (white gold with rhodium plating), hand-set with diamonds by artisans at the Swiss Manufacture, or fitted with the Caliber 2, a 3-dimensional skeleton watch movement.

**J12**: Created in 2000, the J12 is CHANEL's first unisex sports watch and has revolutionized watchmaking, becoming a 21st-century icon. Haute Horlogerie interpretations pair highly resistant matte or glossy ceramic with 18K gold and diamonds, featuring snow-set or baguette-cut stones on bezels, dials, or bracelet links. Some creations are equipped with the Caliber 5, CHANEL's first Flying Tourbillon movement.

**MADEMOISELLE PRIVÉ**: This collection represents an encounter between Haute Horlogerie and artistic expertise, drawing inspiration from the intimate universe of Gabrielle Chanel. It reinterprets the House's signature symbols, colors, and materials through creations such as a long necklace with a camellia in mother-of-pearl marquetry set with a diamond, a bracelet featuring Mademoiselle's silhouette sculpted in 18K gold, and a secret ring crowned by a lion. New pieces are flagged as "NEW" on the page.

The webpage also includes standard CHANEL site navigation covering Haute Couture, Fashion, High Jewelry, Fine Jewelry, Watches, Eyewear, Fragrance, Makeup, Skincare, and Corporate sections (including CHANEL Culture Fund, CHANEL Connects, Our History, Heritage Sites, Our Commitments, and Careers). The page indicates availability in boutiques for certain collections from September 2026 and November 2026.

# All The Best High Jewellery Collections To Come Out Of Couture Week

 BY   [10 Magazine](https://10magazine.com/author/10magazine/)

Each season, alongside Paris’s prodigious haute couture shows – the zenith of fashion – comes the unveiling of the fresh-from-the-atelier high jewellery collections. And last week, the industry’s best in the biz, with their extraordinary adornment offerings, did everything except disappoint. From [Dior](https://10magazine.com/dior-couture-ss26/)’s modular creations to [Chaumet](https://10magazine.com/chaumet-bee-my-love-jewellery-collection-10-magazine-73/)’s birds of flight, here we catalog the best high jewellery offerings to come out of couture week. Prepare for glitz, glam and a whole lot of technical glory. *Emily Phillips*

#### **Dior**

[Victoire de Castellane](https://www.instagram.com/victoiredecastellane/?hl=en)’s Belle Dior haute joaillerie collection for 2026 treats Dior’s heritage as something active, not ornamental. Comprising 57 pieces, the collection centres on movement – jewellery designed to sway, convert and respond to the body, borrowing its logic from couture as much as from the garden.

Braiding, a signature of de Castellane’s work, is pushed into vertical forms that hang and fringe rather than sit flat. These elongated pendants and articulated lines recall the swing of Dior’s ball gowns or the upward pull of a flowering stem. Gold, diamonds and coloured gemstones are arranged to suggest growth and lightness, creating a flora that feels constructed rather than literal.

Symbolism takes centre stage in Soleil Céleste, a set inspired by Monsieur Christian Dior’s interest in divination. Yellow diamonds form radiant points, while stars and moons carved from black opal doublets rest on turquoise. The pieces are deliberately versatile: a bracelet becomes a choker, a brooch doubles as a hair ornament, each transformation handled with restraint.

Elsewhere, Jardins Multicolores reappears in bright green and powder pink, while Dearest Dior gains depth through tanzanite. The collection culminates in a ring set with a 6.50k pink spinel, cut to shift from cushion to flower – an understated statement of de Castellane’s precise, restless approach to high jewellery. *EP*

#### **Cartier**

[Cartier](https://10magazine.com/cartier-reopens-sloane-street-boutique/)’s En Équilibre high jewellery collection is an exercise in control wherein balance is not treated as an abstract idea but as a discipline – of line, volume, colour and space. Nothing is added without purpose, meaning symmetry and asymmetry coexist, simplicity edges toward complexity and precision keeps everything in check.

This approach runs through the key necklaces. Euphonia brings together two rare, perfectly matched batches of rubies and diamonds, united by emerald cuts that give the piece its graphic clarity. Square, baguette and brilliant-cut diamonds sharpen the rhythm, while a sliding clasp at the back allows the double strand to move and adjust, reinforcing the sense of fluid structure. With Splendea, Cartier pushes restraint further, arranging matched diamonds into a continuous ribbon of light. Almost imperceptible settings create the sensation of an uninterrupted wave, driven by meticulous construction rather than visual excess. Parcae distills the idea of “nothing in excess” to its core: three pear-shaped Madagascar sapphires, totalling 16.59k, align at the necklace’s centre, anchored by diamond strands cut to introduce tension and movement. Colour takes a more expressive turn in Ondora, where chrysoprase, spinels and turquoise are balanced against diamonds in a composition inspired by the drifting motion of jellyfish. Light, mobile and transformable, the necklace reveals Cartier’s technical mastery while remaining rigorously composed – a study in harmony held firmly in place. *EP*

#### **Chaumet**

Chaumet takes to the sky with its new capsule collection Envol. In its nearly 250 years of history, the 12 Place Vendome maison’s dialogue with its French royal heritage has never ceased to deliver true gems of savoir-faire (pun intended). The initial alchemy that brought forth the partnership between Marie-Etienne Nitot, Chaumet’s founder, and Empress Josephine Bonaparte, was a shared fascination with the natural world. Their predilection? Birds – at once a symbol of power and elegance.

It is in the maison’s archival bird-inspired neo-antique style tiaras that the 2026 Envol collection found its inspiration. The aigrette tiara, capable of being worn four different ways, glitters with brilliant-cut pavé diamonds adorning a pair of grand feu enamel wings. Equally versatile is the pavé diamond white gold necklace adorned with a 10.96k, cushion-cut Madagascar sapphire. Glowing with its strongly contrasting dégradé of blues, the piece required over 650 hours of work to manufacture, but takes only a second to fall in love with. With its nine new majestic winged figures, Chaumet flies straight to the peak of greatness. *Cecilia Nuvola Bechini*

#### **Bvlgari**

[Bvlgari](https://10magazine.com/bvlgari-to-open-a-glittering-exhibition-in-tokyo/) has one of the most awe-inspiring archives in the landscape of high jewellery, and its latest offering has cracked it open to glorious avail. Entitled Bvlgari Icons Minaudière, the collection marks Bvlgari’s first-ever dedicated evening accessories line. Exploring the dialogue between jewellery created in the past compared to now, creative director [Mary Katrantzou](https://www.instagram.com/marykatrantzou/?hl=en) has incorporated the Roman house’s time-honoured codes into a series of objet d’arts that strike the balance between shining jewels and opulent accessories. Reimagining five distinct symbols from Bvlgari’s history – Monete, Serpenti, Tubogas, Divas’ Dream and Bvlgari Bvlgari – each piece adapts high jewellery techniques, like hand enameling and pavé settings to create small, decorative handbags (or minaudières). A beautiful marriage between heritage and contemporary design, the offering is Bvlgari doing what it does best – pushing the boundaries to create something exquisite. *Bella Koopman*

#### **Graff**

Water, and its fluid, rippling beauty, has long inspired those who create works of art. This season, there’s a new, glittering addition to this canon. [Graff](https://www.graff.com/uk-en/home/?srsltid=AfmBOoot0wQw1JIT-3WL-Hgzy-k64FT8f4VQZiwGkmeDi6vqQoLQ51OE), the British heritage jeweller, turned to “the moment a single droplet meets a still, iridescent pool of water” as the foundation for its latest high jewellery collection. Comprised of a pair of earrings and a wide-band choker, Graff’s skilled artisans have turned this moment of natural grace into a shimmering symphony of sculptural artistry. The choker is the hero piece. In its centre sits a rare 31k sapphire, chiselled to perfection into the surrounding mosaic of square-cut diamonds. Smaller sapphires are peppered across the rest of the band, whimsically positioned to emulate the delicate splash of the single droplet that started it all. It’s a poetic ode to nature’s dichotomy and how it can be equal parts delicate and fierce. The same spirit is embraced for the design of the earrings, although this time the sapphire droplets splash upwards. Powerful in both presence and message, this is high jewellery at its towering peak. *BK*

#### **Messika**

In July of last year, [Messika](https://www.messika.com/uk_en) unveiled its exquisitely exotic jewellery collection, Terres D’Instinct. Inspired by Namibia, where beyond golden sand dunes and burning winds, zebras and lions roam, the rich assemblage celebrated 20 years of the brand’s ethical creations.

This year, the brand delivers four fresh jewellery suites, building off of the original Terres D’Instinct offering. Zooming out, the first iteration takes inspiration from the deep rosy-red hue of Namibian skies at dusk. Also inspired by the Art Deco movement, the Groove Necklace boasts a hypnotically rhythmic arrangement of over 4000 diamonds and 43k. Designed for modular wear, the neck piece is made up of a choker and sautoir that can be worn separately or together.

Next up is Magnetique, a shorter necklace of 3057 diamants and one 3.52k brilliant-cut diamond. Inspired by the fairy circles of Southern Africa’s landscape, the stones are set in a diamond rivière. Also available as a bracelet boasting 1277 diamonds or 26.12k, the radiant design aims to capture the power of attraction.

The Divine Enigma pavé choker, meanwhile, sets its sights on the Namibian desert night sky. Like an infinite constellation, the piece features snow settings and a singular pendant drop set with an 18.88k oval-cut diamond.

Seeing off the collection, the Velvet Rope line – a choker, a necklace and a pair of earrings – offers an escape from normality. Sinuous strands of golden tiger’s eye make their debut at the maison, intermingling with diamonds for a feline piece inspired by Africa’s mineral heat. *Fi Munday*

#### **De Beers**

With Vibrations, [De Beers](https://10magazine.com/de-beers-tantalising-talisman/) unveils its latest array of high jewellery, inspired by the “quiet yet inspiring forces of inland water”. Emulating the shape and natural beauty of meandering streams and cascading waterfalls, the new collection interprets the eternal allure of the great outdoors through peerlessly polished diamonds and precious metals.

It features four sets of diamond-adorned pieces, each dedicated to their places of origin – Namibia, South Africa, Botswana, Canada – and their respective bodies of water. The collection’s cornerstone is Echo, a capsule of five resplendent designs evoking water’s hypnotic fluidity and sunlit glimmer. At its heart lies a showstopping necklace set with a rare 1.12k blue Zambian diamond. Its bright, brilliant blue hue mirrors the waters of Zambia’s Fish River, posing a striking contrast to the 193ks of baguette-cut white diamonds clustered around it. A first of its kind feat for the London-based high jewellery house, the necklace is a work of technical sophistication – with expertly articulated draping that snakes around one’s neck just like a rambling river. Adding to its already impressive complexity is its transformative, modular ability to be engineered into a contemporary tiara, a diamond bracelet or into a pair of luxurious earrings, via its detachable tassels. Crafted using artisanally mined diamonds discovered by independent artisans on ancient riverbeds in Sierra Leone, its symbolic designs and materials signal nature’s continuity, vitality and abstract beauty.  

Vibrations’ Riverborn series traces the river’s source through a dozen unique sculptural pieces before culminating in Modern Lines, which draws from De Beers signature Diamond Lines, combining polished round diamonds and portrait-shaped rough diamonds with discreet white-gold fil couteau links in a series of necklaces, bracelets and drop earrings. Set using a unique ‘spectacle’ technique, the diamonds appear to float like water droplets on the skin, recalling the fluid movement of the rivers in which they were discovered. The one-of-a-kind pavé-set Toi et Moi ring’s curvaceous shape also recalls a river, and entices with intertwining satin-finished white-gold bands complete with Florentine engraving. *Ella O’Gorman*

#### **Louis Vuitton**

Another expansion comes through via [Louis Vuitton](https://10magazine.com/louis-vuitton-menswear-aw26/), where the Virtuosity collection – first unveiled in May of last year – receives 12 new themes that count 110 one-of-a-kind necklaces, bracelets, earrings and rings. Starting with Savoir, a guarded expression of secret knowledge where geometry, symbolism and rare stones establish the maison’s technical authority, and stretching to Eternal Sun, wherein creative freedom is distilled into a radiant, solar composition of yellow diamonds, the range is split into two distinct universes: The World of Mastery and The World of Creativity.

In the former, standouts include the Savoir necklace, anchored by a 30.56k triangle-cut Australian black opal paired with a 28.01k emerald drop, its sharp chevrons and nail-set diamonds nodding to Louis Vuitton’s trunk-making heritage. Protection follows with shield-shaped ruby and pearl jewels that balance strength and refinement, while Keeper introduces an all-seeing eye motif across unisex designs, including a bold chain necklace set with a 10.12k sapphire cabochon and a signet ring featuring a colour-shifting grey-blue diamond. Elsewhere, Maestria and Monumental push technical complexity further through architectural high-collar necklaces dense with emeralds, onyx and Damier-inspired stone mosaics, before Apogée reaches a summit in a transformable masterpiece centred on a 30.75k Brazilian emerald and an LV Monogram Star-cut diamond.

The World of Creativity meanwhile loosens structure in favour of movement, colour and transformation. Motion explores fluidity through undulating sapphire and diamond forms, while Florescence erupts in multi-strand tourmaline necklaces built from thousands of hours of work. Joy amplifies chromatic abundance with yellow sapphires and pink tourmalines set into spiralling gold ropes, Aura reframes the LV Monogram flower in blush-toned gems and Eternal Sun closes the journey with a meticulously sourced constellation of yellow diamonds arranged in a necklace that can be worn six different ways. *EP*
