# Emerging Trends in Jewelry Material Innovations for 2026

![Emerging Trends in Jewelry Material Innovations for 2026](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20viewBox%3D%220%200%201283%20733%22%20xmlns%3D%22http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg%22%3E%3C%2Fsvg%3E)

Sustainability, performance, and transparency are no longer separate conversations in jewelry; they are converging into one material-first approach that is reshaping design, sourcing, and manufacturing. In 2026, the biggest shifts in materials are driven by two forces moving in parallel. On one side, brands, studios, and consumers increasingly prioritize [recycled metals](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-design-trends-2026), [lab-grown](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond) and [ethically sourced stones](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond), and traceable supply [chain](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/necklace-layering-techniques)s. On the other, price volatility—especially in [gold](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-selection-guide-for-occasions)—pushes makers toward weight-efficient forms, diversified material mixes, and agile, digital supply networks. Research communities are adding a third axis by bringing rigorous methods and predictive tools to materials choices: academic work maps practical scenarios for sustainable materials, and data-driven models start to quantify the real environmental trade-offs behind each design decision. What follows is a practical field guide to these changes, with definitions, pros and cons, care and buying advice, and signposts to credible standards and resources.

## Sustainability Becomes the Baseline, Not a Niche

Across independent ateliers and larger workshops, the definition of [eco-friendly jewelry](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/high-quality-jewelry-materials-guide) has converged on the same pillars: recycled metals, [lab-grown diamonds](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/lab-grown-diamonds-sustainable-luxury-blue-noon-ring), [ethically mined gemstones](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond), and [upcycling](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-design-trends-2026) or repair programs that keep materials in circulation. That approach directly tackles resource depletion, pollution, and labor abuses and aligns with slow fashion’s emphasis on durability and long life over disposability. The industry conversation has matured from “should we” to “how we prove it,” with the Responsible Jewellery Council (RJC), Fairmined, Fairtrade, and the Kimberley Process supporting traceability and worker safeguards. Sustainability also includes operational choices: lower-emission energy, small-batch or made-to-order production to curb waste, and credible carbon actions for shipping and travel footprints.

While the case for lower-impact materials is ethical and environmental, it is also backed by consumer demand. A recent brand report notes that roughly seven in ten global consumers are willing to pay more for products from companies with a positive environmental impact, and market-facing resources highlight that lab-grown [diamonds](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond) use far less water than mined stones and that recycled precious metals can deliver significantly lower carbon footprints without any drop in material quality. [Vintage and secondhand pieces](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/bohemian-artistic-jewelry-pairing-guide), along with professional upcycling, add historic and aesthetic value while reducing demand for new extraction. The direction of travel is clear: in 2026, sustainability is not a differentiator; it is the default expectation.

## Materials at a Glance: Performance, Proof, and Care

A practical way to choose among 2026’s leading options is to weigh what each material is, where it excels, and what to verify before buying. The comparisons below reflect reported practices and claims from industry and academic sources.

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Material | What It Is | Advantages | Cautions | Care and Buying Notes |
| [Recycled gold and silver](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-design-trends-2026) | Precious metals recovered from old jewelry, electronics, and industrial sources | Avoids new mining; preserves quality; widely available in sheet and wire | Recycled chain and [findings](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/practical-jewelry-matching-guide) can be harder to source; recycled claims must be substantiated | Ask suppliers for documentation; align with RJC; clean with mild dish soap and a soft cloth |
| [Fairmined gold and silver](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-design-trends-2026) | Small-scale mined metals verified to rigorous environmental and social standards | Improves mining-community livelihoods and safeguards ecosystems | Not all sellers are certified; premiums may apply | Look for Fairmined marks and supplier documentation |
| Lab-grown diamonds | Chemically and physically identical to mined diamonds, grown in controlled environments | Lower measured impacts in many cases; reported far lower water use; avoids conflict mining | Energy intensity varies by producer; verify renewable-powered, carbon-neutral claims | Expect the same daily-wear durability and standard [diamond care practices](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond) |
| [Ethically sourced gemstones](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond) | Stones with verified provenance and fair labor conditions | Transparency, reduced social harm, often strong color and clarity at accessible prices | Proof of origin and labor conditions varies widely | Seek Kimberley Process for diamonds and clear chain-of-custody; ask sellers for mine-to-market documentation |
| [Vintage and secondhand jewelry](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/styling-vintage-jewelry) | Pre-owned or [heirloom](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/seasonal-styling-tips-vintage-jewelry) pieces professionally restored or repurposed | Circular by default; unique aesthetics; avoids new extraction | Hidden wear in [prongs](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond) and [settings](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond); [resizing](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-size-golden-ratio-body-shape) may be needed | Ask for condition reports; plan for professional repairs and prong retipping where needed |
| [Titanium](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/high-quality-jewelry-materials-guide) and [stainless steel](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/high-quality-jewelry-materials-guide) | Durable, lightweight, and stylish metals used in contemporary designs | High durability; widely regarded as [hypoallergenic](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-pure-metals-minimalist-jewelry); strong value | Specialized repair or resizing may require specific tools | Clean with gentle soap and water; dry thoroughly to prevent spotting |
| [Platinum](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/platinum-for-cool-undertone-skin) and palladium | Noble metals known for longevity and recyclability | Exceptional durability and [tarnish](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/maintaining-jewelry-color-guide) resistance; fully recyclable | Primary mining can be energy-intensive; source matters | Prefer recycled or responsibly mined sources; use mild cleaners and soft cloths |
| [Moissanite](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/yellow-jewelry-pairing-guide) | Diamond-like gemstone alternative with high brilliance | Aesthetic similar to diamond at lower cost; ethical appeal | Not a diamond; disclosure and expectation-setting are important | Buy from transparent sellers; clean as you would other hard gemstones |

## Four Pathways Guiding Material Innovation

Academic analysis has started to codify how sustainable materials enter jewelry through four clear scenarios. A Sustainability journal framework maps materials on two axes: natural versus lab-created on one axis, and design-driven versus invention-driven innovation on the other. From that mapping, four practical pathways emerge that are highly visible in 2026 collections.

Designing sensibly centers on circular design principles and recognizes a crucial fact of product development: a very large share of environmental impact is locked in during the design phase. In practice, this means specifying repairable settings and [clasps](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/practical-jewelry-matching-guide), minimizing adhesives and unnecessary components, and designing for disassembly so metals and stones can be reclaimed. For brands, it also means clear take-back and repair programs that keep materials and pieces in circulation.

Reshaping waste takes usable streams—agricultural byproducts, industrial offcuts, ocean plastics—and turns them into inputs for jewelry components. This pathway is closely aligned with the circular economy and anchors many boho-chic and textural pieces that incorporate reclaimed wood, cork, bamboo, and other non-traditional elements. The practical test is longevity and wearability; in 2026, makers are demonstrating that reworked waste can meet both.

Modeling nature applies bio-based inputs responsibly, drawing on renewable feedstocks to reduce extractive pressure. Wood, shell, natural fibers, and bio-derived composites enable lightweight structures and tactile surfaces with lower processing intensity. The scenario is not about rustic aesthetics; it is about material science guided by low-impact sourcing.

Making in lab focuses on engineered biomaterials and lab-born alternatives that reduce reliance on scarce or high-impact natural inputs. From mycelium-derived “leathers” to algae-based polymers, these options expand the design vocabulary and can be precisely tuned for weight, stiffness, and finish. Within gemstones, the most visible lab pathway remains diamonds grown with consistent properties, supported by third-party assurances on energy and carbon.

These scenarios are not trend labels so much as routes that designers and manufacturers can choose based on their capabilities and markets. A single brand often combines them by, for example, using lab-grown [center stones](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond) in settings fabricated from recycled metals and packaging those pieces in bio-based materials.

## Digital Design, AI, and Measured Impact

The next wave of material innovation is not just new inputs; it is better measurement before production. A recent peer-reviewed study trained an artificial neural network to predict key environmental metrics—carbon footprint, water usage, and recyclability potential—based on material type and design configuration. The model reported strong performance in carbon prediction and consistently showed that streamlined, modular pieces have lower impacts than complex ones. It also found that ligno-cellulosic biomaterials generally exhibit lower emissions than precious metals and gemstones due to renewable feedstocks and less energy-intensive processing.

For studios and brands, the practical implication is powerful: simulate the environmental consequences of designs while they are still on screen, compare scenarios, and adjust geometry, settings, or materials to drive down impact without trial-and-error on the bench. That is the same logic behind rapid CAD approvals, laser-welded micro-adjustments, and additive manufacturing for intricate forms. When paired with traceable sourcing and small-batch production, AI-supported design becomes a credible path to faster launches with fewer environmental regrets.

## Economics and the Golden Squeeze

Material innovation in 2026 is also a response to price volatility. Sharp increases in gold prices compress margins, raise inventory risk, and nudge consumers toward lower-weight or alternative-material pieces. Brands are responding by shifting to weight-efficient silhouettes, optimizing perceived volume per gram, and mixing materials to deliver visual presence without heavy precious-metal content. The manufacturing side is investing in hedging, dynamic pricing, and more agile sourcing calendars, while retail teams are explaining metal-price swings to customers so that price changes do not look arbitrary.

A helpful way to translate volatility into action is to consider how the same pressure plays out for different stakeholders and what practical steps can follow.

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stakeholder | Pressure in 2026 | Practical Response |
| Designer | Rising gold costs make traditional heavy silhouettes expensive to produce | Favor weight-efficient forms, hollow constructions, and open-backed settings; emphasize craftsmanship over raw metal mass |
| Manufacturer | Tighter cash flow and higher inventory risk | Pre-book or hedge metal; diversify into [recycled gold and silver](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-design-trends-2026); lean on small-batch runs and fast restocks |
| Retailer | Frequent price changes risk confusing buyers | Implement transparent, dynamic pricing and explain market-linked adjustments at point of sale |
| Consumer | Higher retail prices for gold-heavy pieces | Explore lab-grown diamonds, [moissanite](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/lab-grown-diamonds-sustainable-luxury-blue-noon-ring), [titanium](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/titanium-jewelry-for-cool-undertones), stainless steel, and recycled-metal designs to meet budget and values |

For buyers, a simple rule helps during volatile periods. Ask what percentage of a piece’s value is in raw metal versus craftsmanship and stones, then compare across options. In many cases, you will find that design intelligence and finishing quality—rather than raw grams—deliver more style per dollar.

## Ethics, Traceability, and Real-World Risks

Materials decisions carry social consequences. Several reputable sources document the scale and risk profile of mining across low-income regions, including child labor, unsafe working conditions, and community health harms linked to cyanide and mercury use in gold extraction. Diamonds, gold, and [silver](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-design-trends-2026) have been used to fund conflict, and illicit mining has been tied to instability. Environmental tolls are substantial as well, with massive earth movement per diamond carat, significant greenhouse emissions, and deforestation impacts documented in vulnerable ecosystems.

Real progress is possible when material choices and social safeguards connect. Fairmined and Fairtrade frameworks support worker rights and community benefits. The RJC provides standards that brands adopt to improve transparency and labor practices. On the ground, initiatives focused on mercury-free extraction for artisanal and small-scale miners offer portable, affordable alternatives that protect miners and waterways. Retailers are tightening sourcing policies, with some publicly declining to buy from geographies they associate with persistent child-labor risks; such policies should be transparently explained and periodically reviewed against credible, up-to-date data.

For consumers, practical steps include prioritizing recycled metals and lab-grown stones, confirming traceability claims, and considering [vintage purchases](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/vintage-jewelry-cultural-history) that add character without new extraction. If you want to support remediation, some brands tie purchases to cleanup initiatives and publish impact reports. As with any claim, ask for evidence; genuine traceability often includes digital certificates, supplier names, and clear documentation from mine to market.

## Factory and Bench Practices That Matter

Material innovation is not only what you buy; it is also how pieces are made. Studio programs that center sustainability show that safer chemistry and smarter resource use are achievable without sacrificing quality. Galvanic etching replaces traditional acids, and a pickle bath mixed as 20 percent citric acid and 80 percent water can support clean outcomes while keeping shop air safer. Replacing tanked oxygen/acetylene torches with piped oxygen and natural gas reduces storage hazards and burns cleaner. Cross-discipline reuse—such as using ceramic glaze waste as gemstone-like caps—converts studio byproducts into materials.

At the bench, simple habits compound into real reductions. Keep scrap bins and collect “sweeps” from benches and floors; over time, that dust refines back into usable metal. Reuse packaging when possible and turn to vendors that make recycled or biodegradable mailers when buying new. Verify recycled content with suppliers; many listings do not clearly state it, so a phone call or email to confirm chain of custody is normal practice. Some makers note that 100 percent recycled sheet and wire are easy to source from major suppliers, while 100 percent recycled chain and findings can be trickier, which is precisely why documentation matters.

Compliance also belongs in every sustainable studio’s vocabulary. Environmental marketing claims are regulated, and recycled-content assertions must be substantiated. Familiarity with the relevant green guides helps avoid overstatement and keeps communications honest. In practice, robust documentation strengthens brand trust and can be reused in sales and packaging copy.

## Regional Manufacturing Spotlight: Thailand’s Silver Strength

For [silver jewelry](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/silver-jewelry-minimalism-digital-innovation), Thailand remains a premier hub, combining craftsmanship with transparent sourcing practices. In 2026, eco-certification is becoming a non-negotiable expectation for buyers working with Thai partners, who are also moving quickly on digital supply chains that compress launch cycles. Cloud-based order tracking, rapid CAD approvals, and real-time inventory make it easier to test small runs without overcommitting. Forecasts point to elevated silver prices around the mid-thirties per ounce in early 2026, which is reinforcing a move toward daintier, lightweight designs that still deliver daily-wear value. To keep costs predictable, buying teams are working earlier with flexible minimum order quantities and prioritizing [recycled silver](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/jewelry-design-trends-2026) when available. Transparency—supplier disclosures, material traceability, and impact reporting—has become a competitive edge, particularly with Gen Z customers who actively seek proof.

## Care, Longevity, and Buying Tips

Materials become more sustainable when they last longer, and routine care is the simplest way to extend life. For gold and [platinum](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/platinum-for-cool-undertone-skin), a soft cloth and mild dish soap are appropriate for most cleaning. [Plated](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/high-quality-jewelry-materials-guide) and painted [costume pieces](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/color-in-vintage-jewelry-styles) need extra gentleness to avoid finish wear, so skip harsh abrasives and ultrasonic machines. Stainless steel and titanium respond well to gentle soap and water; consistent drying prevents water spotting. For wire-based and delicate pieces, choose chemical-free cleaners and soft brushes, then store in a dry place to minimize tarnish. Sensitive skin often prefers titanium, stainless steel, or palladium and platinum alloy choices; if you experience sensitivity, ask explicitly about [alloys](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/high-quality-jewelry-materials-guide) and [plating](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/high-quality-jewelry-materials-guide).

Longevity also comes from professional maintenance. Prong retipping, secure solder joints, gemstone replacement, [pearl stringing](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/styling-silver-jewelry-with-pearls), and watch servicing keep heirloom and daily-wear pieces out of the waste stream. When buying, request repair guidance and recommended intervals, and consider whether the design allows future resizing and stone changes. Packaging is part of the impact picture too. Reusable and biodegradable boxes, soy-ink printing, and minimalist inserts cut waste, and some brands offer seed-paper tags that add a small delight to the unboxing without plastic.

One final buying lens is proof. Lab-grown producers should be able to state how they power growth and what certifications back their carbon-neutral claims. Recycled-metal products should come with documentation that aligns with recognized guidance on recycled content. For gemstones, insist on traceability and [conflict-free](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/choosing-the-perfect-diamond) assurances, and do not hesitate to ask sellers to name their suppliers. Good actors expect those questions and will answer them with specifics.

## Definitions You Will See in 2026

As materials evolve, precise language makes conversations easier. Circular economy in jewelry refers to keeping metals and stones in circulation through reuse, recycling, repair, and upcycling rather than pulling new resources from the earth. Slow fashion means investing in durable, repairable, and timeless pieces rather than trend churn. Eco-certification is third-party verification that a product or supply chain meets defined environmental and social standards. Fairmined is a certification program for small-scale mining that verifies responsible extraction and fair labor. The Responsible Jewellery Council is an industry body whose standards and certifications support traceability and worker rights across the supply chain. The Kimberley Process addresses conflict diamonds and aims to prevent profits from fueling violence. Conflict-free and ethical are broader terms that cover transparent, responsible sourcing across people and planet. MOQ, or minimum order quantity, is the smallest purchase a manufacturer accepts and is often flexible in digitally enabled partnerships. [Fancy-colored diamonds](https://mvraki.com/blogs/style-guide/fancy-yellow-diamond-engagement-ring-guide) are diamonds that naturally or synthetically express non-white hues. Moissanite is a lab-created gemstone used as a brilliant, diamond-like alternative.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Are lab-grown diamonds “real,” and how do their impacts compare with mined stones?

Lab-grown diamonds are chemically and physically diamond. Reports highlight that they can use far less water than mined stones and avoid the social risks tied to extraction. As with any manufacturing, impacts vary by producer, which is why it is important to prefer makers who disclose energy sources and publish carbon accounting. Routine care matches that of mined diamonds.

### Is recycled gold the same quality as newly mined gold?

Yes. Recycled gold preserves all the metallurgical properties of gold; it simply comes from an existing stock rather than new mining. The value comes from verified chain of custody and reduced environmental impact. A practical consideration is that some components such as chain and findings can be harder to source in fully recycled form, which makes supplier documentation critical.

### What certifications or proofs should I ask for when buying sustainable jewelry?

Look for RJC alignment, Fairmined or Fairtrade for precious metals, and the Kimberley Process for diamonds. Recycled-content claims should be backed by detailed documentation, and some brands now offer digital certificates and blockchain-verified provenance to show mine-to-market pathways. If a listing lacks clarity, ask the seller directly; reputable makers expect that conversation.

### Which materials are best for sensitive skin?

Titanium and stainless steel are widely regarded as hypoallergenic and deliver strong daily-wear durability. Palladium and platinum also have excellent skin-compatibility profiles when responsibly sourced. If you are sensitive, ask about specific alloys and any coatings, and try on pieces briefly before committing.

### How does gold price volatility affect what I should buy in 2026?

Volatility often pushes prices higher for heavy gold pieces and intensifies interest in weight-efficient designs and mixed materials. If you want the look and longevity without overpaying for grams, consider recycled precious metals and balanced designs that prioritize craftsmanship. Alternatives like lab-grown diamonds, moissanite, titanium, and stainless steel can also deliver strong style with a different cost structure.

## Takeaway

In 2026, the most interesting jewelry material innovations are not only about what is new, but about what is proven. Recycled and Fairmined metals, lab-grown diamonds, and ethically sourced gemstones are mainstream options supported by credible standards, while biomaterials and engineered alternatives expand creative possibilities. Data-backed design and agile digital supply chains make launches faster and more responsible. On the ground, safer studio chemistry, robust documentation, and long-term care keep pieces beautiful and in circulation. If you are buying, do three things and you will be ahead of the curve. First, ask for proof and read it. Second, choose designs that are repairable and timeless. Third, match materials to your life—durable enough for daily wear, gentle enough for your skin, and aligned with the values you want your jewelry to carry.

args.summary:
This article from Mvraki (written by Elara Vance, a GIA Graduate Gemologist) examines emerging trends in jewelry material innovations for 2026, framing sustainability, performance, and transparency as converging into a single material-first approach reshaping design, sourcing, and manufacturing.

KEY THEMES:
1. **Sustainability as the Baseline**: Eco-friendly jewelry now centers on recycled metals, lab-grown diamonds, ethically sourced gemstones, and upcycling/repair programs. Supported by standards bodies including the Responsible Jewellery Council (RJC), Fairmined, Fairtrade, and the Kimberley Process. Consumer demand is strong—roughly seven in ten global consumers are willing to pay more for products from companies with positive environmental impact. Lab-grown diamonds reportedly use far less water than mined stones, and recycled precious metals deliver lower carbon footprints without quality loss.

2. **Material Comparisons**: The article provides a comparison table of leading materials:
   - Recycled gold/silver: avoids new mining, preserves quality, but chain/findings harder to source in fully recycled form
   - Fairmined gold/silver: small-scale verified mining improving livelihoods, though not all sellers are certified
   - Lab-grown diamonds: chemically identical to mined, lower impacts, but energy intensity varies by producer
   - Ethically sourced gemstones: verified provenance, reduced social harm
   - Vintage/secondhand: circular by default, unique aesthetics
   - Titanium and stainless steel: durable, lightweight, hypoallergenic, strong value
   - Platinum and palladium: exceptional durability, fully recyclable, but primary mining energy-intensive
   - Moissanite: diamond-like alternative at lower cost, requires disclosure

3. **Four Pathways Guiding Material Innovation** (from a Sustainability journal academic framework mapping natural vs. lab-created and design-driven vs. invention-driven): (a) designing sensibly (circular design, repairable settings, design for disassembly); (b) reshaping waste (agricultural byproducts, industrial offcuts, ocean plastics); (c) modeling nature (bio-based inputs like wood, shell, fibers, bio-derived composites); (d) making in lab (mycelium "leathers," algae-based polymers, lab-grown diamonds).

4. **Digital Design and AI**: A peer-reviewed study trained an artificial neural network to predict carbon footprint, water usage, and recyclability based on material type and design configuration. The model showed strong carbon prediction performance and found streamlined, modular pieces have lower impacts; ligno-cellulosic biomaterials generally emit less than precious metals. This enables simulating environmental consequences before production.

5. **Economics of the Golden Squeeze**: Rising gold prices compress margins and drive weight-efficient designs. Stakeholder responses include designers favoring hollow/open-backed settings, manufacturers hedging and diversifying into recycled metals, retailers using transparent dynamic pricing, and consumers exploring alternatives. Buying advice: ask what percentage of a piece's value is in raw metal vs. craftsmanship.

6. **Ethics and Traceability**: Documents risks of mining in low-income regions including child labor, unsafe conditions, and cyanide/mercury harms. Diamonds, gold, and silver have funded conflict. Fairmined, Fairtrade, and RJC support progress; mercury-free extraction initiatives protect miners and waterways.

7. **Factory and Bench Practices**: Safer studio chemistry (galvanic etching replacing acids; pickle bath of 20% citric acid/80% water; piped oxygen/natural gas instead of tanked acetylene). Scrap and "sweeps" collection, reused packaging, and verifying recycled content with suppliers. Environmental marketing claims are regulated and must be substantiated.

8. **Thailand Spotlight**: Thailand remains a premier silver jewelry hub, with eco-certification becoming non-negotiable and digital supply chains compressing launch cycles. Silver prices forecast around mid-thirties per ounce in early 2026, driving daintier, lightweight designs. Gen Z customers actively seek transparency.

9. **Care and Buying Tips**: Gold/platinum clean with soft cloth and mild dish soap; plated pieces avoid harsh abrasives; titanium/stainless steel respond to gentle soap and water. Professional maintenance (prong retipping, solder joints, pearl stringing) extends longevity. Buyers should request proof—lab-grown producers should disclose energy sources, recycled metals should have documentation, gemstones need traceability.

10. **Definitions**: Circular economy, slow fashion, eco-certification, Fairmined, RJC, Kimberley Process, conflict-free/ethical, MOQ, fancy-colored diamonds, moissanite.

The FAQ addresses whether lab-grown diamonds are "real" (yes, chemically and physically diamond), whether recycled gold matches mined quality (yes), certifications to request, best materials for sensitive skin (titanium, stainless steel, palladium, platinum), and how gold volatility affects buying.

The takeaway recommends three actions: ask for proof and read it, choose repairable and timeless designs, and match materials to lifestyle and values. Ten references are cited including academic and industry sources.
args.key_excerpts: "In 2026, the biggest shifts in materials are driven by two forces moving in parallel. On one side, brands, studios, and consumers increasingly prioritize recycled metals, lab-grown and ethically sourced stones, and traceable supply chains. On the other, price volatility—especially in gold—pushes makers toward weight-efficient forms, diversified material mixes, and agile, digital supply networks."

With the new year coming up, it’s time to cover the top jewelry trends that will dominate the fashion scene in 2026. Unique and authentic looks are major themes running through each of these trends.

From vintage-inspired brooches to misshapen baroque pearls, we’ll cover all you need to know to update your collection, along with styling tips and examples. Learn more about this year’s trending jewelry below.

## Vintage-Inspired Elegance

First on our list is modern jewelry with vintage charm. These pieces have historical details that could pass as family heirlooms or be found in a vintage store. Expect to see Victorian-inspired opulence like [cocktail rings](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/rings/cocktail-rings), gold chains and intaglio pendants (gemstones engraved with images, often of busts) alongside geometric Art Deco pieces like bezel rings.

Bag charms and body charms have been popular in 2025, and we foresee the next evolution of this trend to include vintage-inspired charm necklaces and bracelets. Brooches have been making a big wave since the [2025 Met Gala](https://www.vogue.com/slideshow/best-brooches-2025-met-gala-red-carpet), acting as personal charms that add subtle details to an outfit.

To achieve the look of a perfectly accrued, well-loved collection, style your vintage-inspired pieces together. Pin brooches on an oversized blazer or on your handbag. For everyday wear, try balancing historical details with more playful contemporary pieces, like beaded bracelets and T-shirts.

## Chunky and Sculptural Shapes

As an evolution of the quiet luxury trend, we’re seeing a growing love for sophisticated wearable art in classic golds and silvers. To complement those understated, luxurious pieces, bolder, organic-shaped jewelry will continue to enter the scene. Think abstract, fluid, asymmetrical, and melted-looking earrings, wide cuff bangles and [chunky wedding rings](https://www.bluenile.com/wedding-rings/wide-band-wedding-rings). Plus, we’ll see more unique and misshapen pearl pieces—more on that trend below.

Whichever standout sculptural jewelry you choose, pair it with more delicate pieces to balance your look and keep chunkier pieces from competing for attention. Pair a statement necklace with a large gold pendant, for example, with softer and more delicate gold chains.

## Nature-Inspired Themes

Thanks to an increased cultural focus on sustainability and authenticity, we’re expecting pieces with natural themes to dominate this year. People will adorn themselves with [flower earrings](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/earrings/flower-earrings), vine rings, leaf necklaces, and other whimsical, plant-inspired jewelry. Jewelry that is sustainably sourced and focuses on organic, raw stones and repurposed metals reflects a greater awareness of the environment.

Looking beyond botanical themes, we expect to see more pieces inspired by other areas of the natural world—namely, insects and animals. Playful snake, tiger, spider, and butterfly pendants can be eye-catching and meaningful pieces to add to a collection.

Style natural and organic jewelry with flowing fabrics and natural fibers, like linen, in earthy tones. If your jewelry features strong nature motifs (say, a large animal pendant), pare back on heavy patterns and stick to minimal color palettes.

## Personalized and Meaningful Pieces

This year, people are seeking jewelry that’s unique and emotionally resonant rather than generic and mass-produced. We’re embracing jewelry that symbolizes family, memories, connection, faith, milestones, and anything else close to the heart. More people are [customizing their jewelry](https://www.bluenile.com/blog/fashion/custom-jewelry-tips) and reaching for pieces with their [initials](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/collections/initial-collection), angel numbers and [zodiac signs](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/collections/zodiac-collection). There’s also a gravitation toward [lockets](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/necklaces/locket-necklaces) and [engravable rings](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/rings/engravable-rings). All of these personality pieces help tell your story through your look. They also make perfect gifts for special milestones and celebrations for loved ones.

Consider choosing one personalized piece—perhaps a locket or initial necklace—and make it your signature piece. Experiment with incorporating it into different types of outfits, from everyday workwear to evening attire, by layering it with both matching staples and contrasting materials.

## Mixed Metals

Once a fashion faux pas, [mixing metals](https://www.bluenile.com/blog/fashion/mixed-metals-guide) is now an art. Today, we’re moving beyond matching sets and embracing complementary contrasts. We’ll see more gold paired with silver in bracelet stacks, mixed metal chains and wrapped rings.

[Mixed metal jewelry](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/mixed-metal-jewelry) makes a statement, but also pairs well with both cool- and warm-toned outfits. If you’re unsure where to start, select one statement piece in a cool-toned silver or platinum, and then use smaller gold pieces for accents. Although their colors may contrast, the pieces can tie together in other ways, like shape, texture or finish. For example, choose gold and silver pieces that all share a polished finish instead of mixing polished with matte pieces.

## Bold Gold

While cool-toned metals like white gold, platinum and silver have been popular in recent years, yellow gold is making a comeback in jewelry trends for women. Following the dominance of the minimalism trend, we expect to re-embrace bolder gold pieces, like chunky rings and big chain necklaces. Expect to see standout [yellow gold statement pieces](https://www.bluenile.com/jewelry/gold-jewelry/yellow-gold-jewelry) this year.

Choose one gold focal point, like a chunky gold cuff, and let it be the highlight of your outfit. You can still wear other pieces, but keep them minimal—pair the gold cuff with stud earrings, for example, and leave your opposite wrist bare. Earthy tones, cream and black all look elegant with gold jewelry.

## Colored Gemstones

Vivid, unusual gemstones are another trend we expect will satisfy the hunger for individuality this upcoming year. Options like emerald, sapphire, amethyst, and topaz add unique pops of color and provide yet another way to personalize your look. [Gemstone jewelry trends](https://www.bluenile.com/blog/fashion/gemstone-jewelry-trends) point to greens and blues as particularly popular tones. Fancy-colored diamonds, which are unusual diamonds with hues ranging from yellow to pink, are becoming popular choices for engagement rings.

Different [gemstone colors](https://www.bluenile.com/education/gemstone/color) have unique meanings. For example, pink tourmaline, which is growing in demand, symbolizes love, care and compassion. Combining your birthstone with those of your loved ones is another way to personalize your jewelry. We may even see a resurgence of vintage gemstone trends like acrostic jewelry, which uses different gemstones to spell out secret messages.

Style colored gemstones with saturated hues. Or dress up your everyday white button-up and jeans with opal earrings or a topaz ring. Mismatched gemstone earrings, like an amethyst stud in one ear and a ruby pendant in the other, add a creative edge to any outfit.

The article covers the major jewelry trends expected to dominate the fashion scene in 2026, emphasizing unique and authentic looks.

The key trends covered include:

1. **Vintage-Inspired Elegance**: Victorian-inspired opulence like cocktail rings, gold chains, intaglio pendants, and geometric Art Deco pieces (bezel rings). Brooches have surged in popularity since the 2025 Met Gala, and vintage-inspired charm necklaces and bracelets are expected to evolve from 2025's bag/body charm trend.

2. **Chunky and Sculptural Shapes**: An evolution of quiet luxury, featuring abstract, fluid, asymmetrical, and "melted-looking" earrings, wide cuff bangles, chunky wedding rings, and misshapen pearl pieces. These should be paired with delicate pieces for balance.

3. **Nature-Inspired Themes**: Flower earrings, vine rings, leaf necklaces, and plant-inspired jewelry driven by sustainability and authenticity. Also includes insect and animal motifs (snake, tiger, spider, butterfly pendants), plus organic raw stones and repurposed metals.

4. **Personalized and Meaningful Pieces**: Customized jewelry with initials, angel numbers, zodiac signs, lockets, and engravable rings. People seek pieces that symbolize family, memories, faith, and milestones.

5. **Mixed Metals**: Gold paired with silver in bracelet stacks, mixed metal chains, and wrapped rings. Styling tip: pick a statement piece in one tone and use smaller pieces in the contrasting tone, tying them together through shared shape, texture, or finish.

6. **Bold Gold**: Yellow gold is making a comeback with chunky rings and big chain necklaces, following the minimalism trend. Pair with earthy tones, cream, and black.

7. **Colored Gemstones**: Emerald, sapphire, amethyst, and topaz are popular; greens and blues are particularly on-trend. Fancy-colored diamonds are becoming popular for engagement rings. Pink tourmaline (symbolizing love, care, compassion) is growing in demand, and acrostic jewelry (gemstones spelling secret messages) may see a resurgence.

8. **Unique and Misshapen Pearls**: Baroque (asymmetrical) pearls popularized by celebrities like Harry Styles, moving away from uniform pearl strands. Baroque pearls are created from disruptions in mollusk formation and align with the demand for authenticity.

9. **Quiet Luxury and Subtle Details**: Minimalist, timeless pieces with high-quality materials like platinum and gold—tennis bracelets, knot pendants, bangles, petite necklaces, and stud earrings.

10. **Bracelet Stacking and Necklace Layering**: Carefree, curated layered looks mixing lengths, textures, and metals with a "thrown on" appearance. Styling tip: start with three necklaces of various lengths; for bracelets stick to two or three pieces of varied thicknesses and textures.

De Beers shares latest research on US consumer trends

![Pair of hands held with an engagement ring on one ](/~/media/Images/D/debeers-v2/content-images/news-insights/news/the-diamond-report-engagement-ring-image.jpg?w=992)

 11 Jun 2026 

*The Diamond Report includes insights on who is buying diamonds and why, based on a study of 18,500 women across the industry’s largest consumer market*

Natural diamonds are the most desired luxury jewellery product, average purchase prices have increased 25%, Gen Z is now the second largest generation buying diamonds, and non-bridal occasions account for three-quarters of overall US demand. These are some of the key findings of De Beers Group’s latest US Diamond Acquisition Study, featuring responses from 18,500 women aged 18 – 74 across the industry’s largest consumer market.

Completed in 2026, the biannual study also found that Gen Z is spending almost double what Baby Boomers spend when buying natural diamonds – at $4,080 per piece vs $2,250 – and that while love-related purchase motivations remain the core driver of demand, personal motivations such as celebrating a new job, getting a promotion, recognising an achievement or ‘just because’ are increasingly driving diamond jewellery purchasing.

The study highlights that US consumers rank natural diamonds as their top preference for a luxury jewellery item, with 11% of women ranking natural diamond jewellery their most desired luxury gift. This places natural diamond desirability ahead of synthetic lab-grown diamonds (8%), other gemstones (5%) and plain gold jewellery (4%).

Average prices for natural diamond jewellery also increased significantly in 2025, rising to $4,063 per piece compared with $3,242 in 2023. This growth is being driven by consumers buying larger carat weights, with average total carat weight increasing to 1.86 carats, up from 1.65 carats in 2023.

When it comes to the industry’s youngest generation, the study found that Gen Z punches above its weight: the generation now accounts for just under a quarter (23%) of natural diamond demand value despite representing just 18% of the population. Gen Z consumers also buy or receive diamonds for more occasions than any other generation – at 1.83 occasions per year compared with an overall average of 1.7. While bridal occasions lead Gen Z demand at 45% of total purchases, gifting from relatives also plays an important role. Birthdays are particularly significant, representing 17% of all Gen Z diamond acquisitions compared with 13% across all generations. Gen Z also highly values self-expression and associates diamonds with being a symbol of identity more than any other generation, while also having the greatest reliance on social media for researching their purchases.

Diana Mitkov, lead researcher within Diamond Demand Insights & Analytics at De Beers Group, said: “The study findings highlight that today’s consumers aspire to own natural diamonds just as much as the generations that came before them, and ahead of any other jewellery product. And they are spending more per piece than ever before. But how and why consumers buy diamonds is evolving. Traditional life milestones such as getting engaged are no longer the only value driver for the industry; consumers are increasingly marking a wide range of occasions with natural diamonds and are looking for distinct pieces that feel personal to them.

“As unique miracles of nature, the attributes of natural diamonds play directly into these shifting consumer trends. The opportunity for the diamond industry is to ensure that natural diamonds continue to capture the value of this strong underlying desire in an increasingly competitive landscape by offering compelling designs across all sizes, colours and price points and for occasions that go well beyond traditional engagement or wedding jewellery.”          

These findings feature in a new publication from De Beers, *The Diamond Report*, which also includes an editorial on the key forces shaping a positive future for natural diamonds by EVP Corporate Affairs & Strategy and Chief Economist, Eirik Wærness; an analysis of US jewellery retail trends; perspectives from leading US designers and retailers on how the diamond buying experience is evolving; and reflections on the role natural diamonds can play in supporting socioeconomic progress for the people and places where they are discovered.

The report also notes that natural diamond sales are increasing across US independent jewellers, with Point of Sales data from 950 retailers showing sales grew 4% and 9% year-on-year in Q4 2025 and Q1 2026, respectively. Coloured and low-coloured diamonds (those in the K – Z colour range) promoted by De Beers Group’s ‘Desert diamonds’ campaign outperformed, with sales growth of 15% and 19%, respectively.

The same data shows that while synthetic lab-grown diamond jewellery sales are increasing in volume, declining retail prices mean their value share of demand remains relatively low at 15% of independent jewellers’ diamond sales, compared with 85% for natural diamonds in 2025. In addition, there is a noticeable drop-off in sales once synthetic lab-grown diamonds reach 3 carats or larger in size, suggesting that consumers may feel synthetic lab-grown diamonds beyond this size could look too big. The report notes this could mean that as synthetic lab-grown diamond prices continue to decline in line with the multi-year trend already experienced, retailers may be unable to upsell to larger sizes, which could result in lower overall sales and impact long-term gross profits.

Eirik Wærness said: “The diamond industry is evolving at pace with both supply and demand-side dynamics shaping the industry’s future. On the supply side, declining global production of natural diamonds is expected to support an improved supply-demand balance over the coming years. On the demand-side, a resilient US economy and stabilisation of demand in China saw global natural diamond demand return to growth in 2025 while the industry’s marketing efforts are showing encouraging signs of momentum. With retail returns from synthetic lab-grown diamonds likely to come under pressure in the future, we expect retailers will increasingly differentiate them from natural diamonds in their sales strategies. As these fundamentals continue to stabilise, the industry has a significant opportunity to reinforce the value of natural diamonds and support long-term growth.”

# Half of millennial and Gen Z couples pick engagement rings with lab-grown diamonds— ‘well beyond what the mining industry had expected,’ McKinsey says

![Sydney Lake](https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Lake_bio.jpg?format=webp&w=1440&q=100)

By 

[Sydney Lake](/author/sydney-lake/)

Sydney Lake

Associate Editor

![Sydney Lake](https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Lake_bio.jpg?format=webp&w=1440&q=100)

By 

[Sydney Lake](/author/sydney-lake/)

Sydney Lake

Associate Editor

November 18, 2025, 1:21 PM ET

![couple posing with engagement ring](https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/GettyImages-806217602-e1741638536286.jpg?format=webp&w=1440&q=100)

Ring buyers can get a bigger stone for their buck when choosing a lab-grown diamond.Getty Images—filadendron

Add Fortune on Google for similar content.

* **More than half of couples** have reported buying a lab-grown diamond for their engagement rings for the first time in history, according to a study by The Knot. That’s because lab-grown diamonds typically have better value in terms of size and price. While lab-grown diamonds were originally touted as a more environmentally friendly option, they still require large amounts of energy to produce.

More carats at a lower price sounds like a great deal. That’s why many couples are choosing lab-grown diamonds over natural mined diamonds for their engagement rings. Plus, there’s a perception lab-grown diamonds are better for the environment.

Recommended Video

---

For the first time ever, more than half of couples reported their engagement ring features a lab-grown stone, according to The Knot’s [2025 Real Weddings Study](https://www.theknot.com/content/wedding-data-insights/real-weddings-study). Lab-grown diamonds have grown increasingly popular in the past several years, with 6% more couples buying them than last year and 40% more since 2019.

“The increasing popularity of lab-grown diamonds can be attributed to being conscious of budget, perceived value and ethical production practices,” Lauren Kay, executive editor at [The Knot](https://www.theknot.com/), told *Fortune*. They’re “a great and viable option for those unwilling to sacrifice stone size due to budget constraints.”

Since lab-grown stones are typically cheaper than natural diamonds and there’s been such a massive increase in the number of lab-grown diamonds purchased, engagement ring prices are down, according to The Knot, which found the current average price is $5,200, a 5.7% drop from 2023 and a more than 15% decline from 2021.

And in some cases, ring purchasers could expect to spend 1.5 times more on a natural diamond ring than a lab-grown one.

“Design is absolutely the most important aspect of your purchase decision on a product—and the second criterion is price,” Alexander Lacik, CEO of jewelry giant Pandora previously [told](https://fortune.com/europe/2024/12/26/gen-z-millennials-lab-grown-diamonds-sustainable-price-bigger-ring-design/) *Fortune*’s [Orianna Rosa Royle](https://fortune.com/author/orianna-royle/).

Younger generations, specifically, find it less important for the stone to be natural (22% for Gen Z, 28% for millennials), Kay said.

Natural diamond producers have tried to keep up with the lab-grown diamond craze. In late 2024, De Beers, the world’s biggest producer of natural diamonds, [slashed its prices](https://fortune.com/2024/12/02/lab-grown-diamonds-gen-z-millennials-de-beers/) by 10% to 15%.

“The massive success of lab-grown diamonds has reduced prices for natural stones well beyond what the mining industry had expected, driven largely by consumers who want more affordable options,” according to a [report](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/metals-and-mining/our-insights/the-diamond-industry-is-at-an-inflection-point) by McKinsey & Co., which also called lab-grown diamonds “likely the biggest challenge facing diamond producers today.”

Still, ring buyers can get a bigger stone for their buck when choosing a lab-grown diamond. The average center-stone weight for lab-grown diamond rings in 2024 was 2.0 carats, compared to 1.6 carats for natural diamonds, Kay said. Meanwhile, the average carat weight of an engagement ring in 2021 was 1.5 carats, which jumped to 1.7 in 2024, according to The Knot.

“Customers—when it comes to the bridal engagement space—are opting for spending the same or similar amount of money, but for a significantly larger stone,” Lacik said.  “Women like bigger stones. That’s the way the world works, whether we like it or not.”

## Are lab-grown diamonds sustainable?

Although lab-grown diamonds have been touted as a more environmentally friendly option—which appeals to younger generations—they’re not exactly green. Producing these stones requires [subjecting carbon](https://fortune.com/article/disadvantages-lab-grown-diamonds-gen-z-millennials-environment-cost-price-coal-china/) to high pressure and high temperatures over several weeks. It’s an energy-intensive process, [Ulrika D’Haenens-Johansson](https://www.gia.edu/gia-researcher-ulrika-dhaenens-johansson), senior manager of diamond research at the [Gemological Institute of America](https://www.gia.edu/), told [*ABC News*](https://abcnews.go.com/Business/lab-grown-diamonds-sustainable-advertised/story?id=109046877), and most lab-grown diamond producers use electricity from fossil fuels, including coal.

More than 60% of lab-grown diamonds are produced in regions where coal is the primary source, according to the [International Diamond Center](https://shopidc.com/blogs/news/the-environmental-impact-of-naturally-mined-diamonds-vs-lab-grown-alternatives?srsltid=AfmBOop7i02hfJmSrF-8t-xrEA3uncc4IN0w4xosXSVbiy5zI9c4QqDD) (IDC). China and India are two of the largest lab-grown diamond producers and rely on coal-fired power plants to produce the gems. This results in a “high level of greenhouse gas emissions associated with lab-grown diamonds, which challenges the perception that they are a more sustainable option,” according to IDC.

However, the International Grown Diamond Association [claims](https://www.growndiamondcorp.com/blog/cvd-diamonds-vs-earth-grown-diamonds-differences/) lab-grown diamonds “do not lead to ecological damage.” Depending on production methods, lab-grown diamonds can have a much smaller footprint than natural diamonds, watchmaking experts [told](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/05/fashion/lab-grown-diamonds-watches-breitling-oris.html) *The New York Times.*

But at the end of the day, “environment doesn’t matter” to the consumer, Paul Zimnisky, a New York diamond analyst, told *NYT*. “Consumers don’t care about that as much as the media talks about it. Consumers are buying lab diamonds because they’re so cheap. It’s all about the price.”

7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.

args.summary:
This Fortune article (by Sydney Lake, Associate Editor, originally published November 18, 2025) reports on the historic rise of lab-grown diamonds in engagement rings. For the first time ever, more than half of couples reported their engagement ring features a lab-grown stone, according to The Knot's 2025 Real Weddings Study. This represents a 6% increase over the previous year and 40% growth since 2019. The trend is driven by budget consciousness, perceived value, and ethical production practices, particularly among younger generations (22% of Gen Z and 28% of millennials say natural stones are less important).

Key data points include: average engagement ring prices have dropped to $5,200 (a 5.7% decline from 2023 and over 15% from 2021); natural diamond rings can cost 1.5 times more than lab-grown ones; lab-grown diamond rings averaged 2.0 carats center-stone weight in 2024 versus 1.6 carats for natural diamonds. Natural diamond producer De Beers slashed prices by 10-15% in late 2024 to compete. McKinsey & Co. called lab-grown diamonds "likely the biggest challenge facing diamond producers today" and noted their success "reduced prices for natural stones well beyond what the mining industry had expected."

The article also addresses the sustainability question, noting that while lab-grown diamonds are marketed as more environmentally friendly, production requires energy-intensive high-pressure/high-temperature processes. Over 60% of lab-grown diamonds are produced in regions where coal is the primary energy source (notably China and India), resulting in significant greenhouse gas emissions that challenge the sustainability narrative. However, the International Grown Diamond Association claims lab-grown diamonds don't cause ecological damage, and production methods can yield a smaller footprint than natural mining. Ultimately, analyst Paul Zimnisky notes consumers buy lab diamonds primarily because they are cheap, not for environmental reasons.
args.key_excerpts: "The increasing popularity of lab-grown diamonds can be attributed to being conscious of budget, perceived value and ethical production practices," Lauren Kay, executive editor at The Knot. "The massive success of lab-grown diamonds has reduced prices for natural stones well beyond what the mining industry had expected, driven largely by consumers who want more affordable options," according to a report by McKinsey & Co.

# Luxury Redefined: Why Gen Z Loves Lab Grown Diamonds

![Luxury Redefined: Why Gen Z Loves Lab Grown Diamonds](//www.rockher.com/cdn/shop/articles/Screenshot2025-01-28124012_94db50ef-75de-4c9a-ab66-6353ea0153c8.png?v=1768814875&width=1840)

## Table of Contents

* [Introduction](#introduction)
* [Gen Z and the Redefinition of Luxury](#gen-z-luxury)
* [Affordable Luxury: Price & Value](#affordable-luxury)
* [Ethical & Sustainable Sparkle](#ethical-sustainable)
* [Personalization and Customization](#personalization)
* [Social Media’s Influence](#social-media-influence)
* [RockHer’s Lab-Grown Diamonds: The New Luxury](#rockher-new-luxury)

## Introduction

For Gen Z and young Millennials, **luxury** is being radically redefined. No longer is it solely about big brand names or hefty price tags – it’s about values, authenticity, and making smart choices. One clear example is the rise of [lab-grown diamonds](https://www.rockher.com/apps/diamondsearch/lab-grown-diamonds/) in the jewelry market. In fact, recent data shows that roughly **70% of Gen Z and Millennials prefer lab-grown diamonds** over mined ones for reasons ranging from ethics to affordability. This generational shift is transforming diamonds from a traditional status symbol into a statement of conscious consumerism.

## Gen Z and the Redefinition of Luxury

Gen Z has grown up in an era of social awareness and sustainability, and it shows in how they define “luxury.” For their generation, true luxury isn’t just about rarity or a famous logo – it’s about aligning purchases with personal principles. They ask: Is this product sustainable? Was it ethically sourced? Does it reflect who I am? In the realm of jewelry, young consumers are challenging the old guard. A sparkling diamond is not automatically seen as desirable unless it comes with a clean conscience and a meaningful story. This mindset has paved the way for lab-grown gems to shine. Lab-created diamonds check all the boxes for this new definition of luxury: they are visually identical to mined diamonds, yet carry none of the ethical baggage. For a generation that values transparency and positive impact, that difference is priceless.

## Affordable Luxury: Price & Value

One of the biggest drivers behind Gen Z’s love for lab-grown diamonds is **affordability**. Lab-grown stones typically cost significantly less than their mined counterparts, putting larger and higher-quality diamonds within reach for young buyers. A [1-carat lab-grown diamond ring](https://www.rockher.com/collections/1-carat-lab-grown-diamond-rings), for example, might be a fraction of the price of a smaller mined diamond of similar quality. This price advantage means Gen Z can get more sparkle for their money – an especially compelling point for a generation facing student loans and high living costs. But it’s not just about being “cheaper.” It’s about *value*: why pay more for a mined stone when a lab-grown gem offers the same beauty and durability? Young shoppers see lab-grown diamonds as a smart luxury – one where they don’t have to compromise on size or quality to stay within budget. In their eyes, being financially savvy is part of being luxurious.

## Ethical & Sustainable Sparkle

Beyond price, Gen Z cares deeply about **ethical and sustainable** sourcing. Traditional diamond mining has long been associated with environmental damage and human rights issues. Many young consumers are well aware of concepts like “blood diamonds” and the ecological toll of mining. Lab-grown diamonds offer a clean alternative: they are inherently *conflict-free* and can be produced with far less environmental impact. There’s no need to dig up the earth or fuel questionable supply chains to obtain these gems. For eco-conscious youths, that’s huge. Choosing a lab-grown diamond means they can wear their jewelry guilt-free, knowing it didn’t come at the cost of communities or ecosystems. In online conversations, you’ll often see lab-grown gems hailed as the choice for “conscious consumers” – a badge of honor for those who want their luxury to reflect their values. The fact that a lab-grown diamond has the same chemical and physical makeup as a mined one, but with a smaller carbon footprint, makes the decision even easier. Ultimately, sustainability is stylish: a sparkling stone that aligns with Gen Z’s environmental and ethical ideals truly lets them shine.

## Personalization and Customization

Another hallmark of Gen Z’s shopping habits is the desire for **personalization**. This is the generation of custom playlists, bespoke sneakers, and unique social media profiles – they love to put their personal stamp on everything they own. Jewelry is no exception. Lab-grown diamonds are empowering young buyers to get creative with their bling. Because these stones are more affordable and readily available in a variety of sizes and even colors, it’s easier than ever to design a piece that’s perfectly “you.” Many are opting to create custom engagement rings or mix-and-match designs that express their individuality. With tools available to [build your own engagement ring](https://www.rockher.com/collections/build-an-engagement-ring), Gen Z can choose every detail – from the diamond’s shape to the setting – without feeling constrained by cost. The result is a piece of jewelry that feels one-of-a-kind and deeply meaningful. Whether it’s adding a lab-grown diamond accent to a modern necklace or choosing a non-traditional gemstone color for a ring, younger consumers relish the chance to break the mold. In their eyes, a luxurious item is not just expensive; it’s personal. Lab-grown diamonds, with their versatility and accessibility, are the perfect medium for this self-expression.

## Social Media’s Influence

It’s impossible to talk about Gen Z trends without mentioning **social media**. Platforms like Instagram and TikTok play a huge role in shaping opinions and showcasing lifestyle choices – including jewelry. Lab-grown diamonds have sparkled across these platforms as symbols of savvy, forward-thinking style. Influencers and everyday users alike are posting engagement stories and jewelry hauls featuring lab-grown gems, often highlighting the fact that they’re eco-friendly and budget-friendly. This online buzz has helped normalize lab-created diamonds as equal (if not superior) to mined ones. On Instagram, a bigger, brilliant diamond ring can rack up likes, and thanks to lab-grown options, young couples can afford that show-stopping rock for the camera. TikTok videos touting “ethical engagement rings” or side-by-side comparisons of mined vs. lab-grown diamonds have gone viral – spreading awareness that you can get the glam without the guilt. In essence, social media has turned lab-grown diamonds into the *it* accessory for the conscious generation. The narrative is clear: wearing a lab-grown sparkler isn’t just fashionable, it signals that you’re part of a new wave of luxury that cares about the planet and people. Gen Z buyers love to share that message with pride.

## RockHer’s Lab-Grown Diamonds: The New Luxury

As this movement gains momentum, RockHer is at the forefront, delivering what we can truly call “new luxury.” RockHer’s collection of lab-grown diamonds represents the pinnacle of this ethos, combining stunning visual appeal with environmental responsibility. Each of our lab-created diamonds is meticulously grown and cut to unleash maximum brilliance – they are real diamonds in every sense, graded and certified for quality just like any mined stone. But unlike many mined gems, **RockHer’s lab-grown diamonds** come with the peace of mind that they are 100% conflict-free and crafted with sustainability in mind. We pair these gorgeous stones with recycled precious metals and expert craftsmanship, so your jewelry doesn’t just look good – it *does* good. In choosing a RockHer lab-grown diamond piece, you’re embracing a luxe experience without compromise. It’s an engagement ring that sparkles with meaning, a pair of [lab-grown diamond studs](https://www.rockher.com/collections/lab-grown-diamond-studs) you can flaunt proudly, or a bespoke creation that tells the world luxury and responsibility go hand in hand. For Gen Z and beyond, this is what modern luxury looks like: a beautiful keepsake that reflects both your style and your values.

# What does Gen Z want from jewellery?

From hyper-personalised designs to recycled materials, brands are adapting to a new generation of jewellery consumers.

By [Amy Francombe](/contributor/amy-francombe)

Photo: Courtesy of Loveness Lee

When Loveness Lee launched her eponymous jewellery brand in 2017, it was out of creative frustration with the existing jewellery scene. “The general public had access to high street jewellery, traditional fine pieces [or] vintage styles,” says the London-based designer. “But there wasn’t anything bold, creative and recognisable at an accessible price point.”

Drawing on her background in abstract painting, Lee began casting intricate forms from elements like cactus skeletons and barnacle shells, transforming them into sculptural, wearable art. That organic irregularity is now the brand’s signature — pieces that feel deeply personal and never identical due to the nature of the casting process. “No one else has it. They have a piece of nature to themselves,” Lee says of the brand’s appeal. Pieces retail from £75 to £650.

This year, Lee expanded the offering with a bespoke service, inviting customers to repurpose heirloom pieces — whether a mother’s engagement ring or a childhood trinket — into custom designs that preserve memory while aligning with the Loveness Lee aesthetic. The approach is paying off. Lee declined to share exact revenue figures, but without increasing her team or her marketing budget, the company has seen revenues double this year.

Loveness Lee is not alone in tapping into the growing appetite of younger consumers for jewellery that feels meaningful and expressive. Once tucked away in the accessories corner, jewellery has stepped into the spotlight in recent years — both in stores and on the cultural radar, as fresh brands reinvigorate the market, attracting younger consumers.

This year, Lee expanded the offering with a bespoke service, inviting customers to repurpose heirloom pieces.

Photo: Courtesy of Loveness Lee

According to data analytics firm Euromonitor, the global jewellery market was valued at approximately $369 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $416 billion by 2029. While fine jewellery continues to lead that growth, the broader category is expanding rapidly, driven by shifting consumer values and new expressions of status and style, particularly among Gen Z and millennial shoppers.

At Selfridges’s Oxford Street flagship, its ‘Jewellery Destination’ is set to open in August 2025, integrating jewellery with womenswear at the third-floor atrium, alongside a similarly expanded jewellery and accessories space at the Manchester Exchange Square outpost. “Selfridges is responding to a demand and shift in behaviour, one that’s rooted in intentional purchase and styling,” says Sara Wong, director of buying, accessories and the retailer’s pre-loved initiative Reselfridges. “Ring sales are up 34 per cent, with many pieces being self-gifted — Gen Z aren’t waiting for someone else to buy jewellery for them.” Meanwhile, at Dover Street Market, jewellery is taking centre stage this summer with a four-week exhibition spotlighting 36 emerging designers, including Alice Biolo, Martina Kocianova and Carolina Andrade.

“Jewellery is surging in popularity among Gen Z, driven by a desire for affordable luxury, personal expression and a shift away from traditional status symbols,” says Jane Collins, head of footwear and accessories at trend forecaster WGSN. “This generation is seeking out [‘little luxuries’](https://www.voguebusiness.com/story/beauty/charms-sunglasses-and-scents-can-small-luxuries-carry-the-industry-long-term) and ‘glimmers’ as a form of selfcare, tapping into accessible indulgences and mood-boosting optimism during economic uncertainty.”

So what’s driving the shift? And which jewellery brands are winning as young consumers lean in?

## **The personal touch**

Customisation has become a key driver of demand in the jewellery category as consumers increasingly seek out personal, expressive pieces. Trend forecasters link this shift to what WGSN calls “[chaotic customisation](https://www.voguebusiness.com/story/fashion/gen-zs-want-chaotic-customisation-in-2025-how-can-brands-tap-in)” — a popular aesthetic that pushes personalisation to the extreme through [bag charms](https://www.voguebusiness.com/story/fashion/bag-charms-and-brooches-are-back-as-luxurys-new-entry-point), DIY embellishments and other playful ways to accessorise accessories.

Read More

[Bag charms and brooches are back as luxury’s new entry point](/article/bag-charms-and-brooches-are-back-as-luxurys-new-entry-point)

Momentum has built on embellishments, which offer a gateway to luxury ownership and a means for cultivating personal style.

By [Madeleine Schulz](/contributor/madeleine-schulz)

“Gen Z’s approach to jewellery is notably more experimental, value-driven and expressive than previous generations,” says Collins. “They seek out unique, customisable and sentimental pieces that reflect individuality, align with their values and allow for playful, personal style.”

“Customisation has been huge for us — we’ve built an entire category around it. Our engraving collection is now one of our best-performing ranges, especially for gifting,” says Olivia Jenkins, founder of UK brand D Louise, which hit £6.6 million in sales in 2024 — a 183.5 per cent increase over three years. Customised pieces now make up over 25 per cent of the brand’s total sales.

UK brand D Louise hit £6.6 million in sales in 2024 — a 183.5 per cent increase over three years.

Photo: Courtesy of D.Louise

Personalisation is also evolving in terms of form and meaning. “Signet rings, for example, are being reimagined with engraved initials, zodiac symbols or meaningful motifs like suns and eyes, reflecting this generation’s desire for individuality and self-expression,” says Fflur Roberts, head of luxury goods at Euromonitor. “Often gender-neutral and worn as statement pieces, these rings encapsulate identity, values and even astrological beliefs, making them powerful vehicles for personal storytelling.”

One standout in the reimagined signet ring space is Cece Jewellery, the London‑based atelier founded by Cece Fein Hughes. Known for its richly symbolic, hand-enameled signets featuring everything from zodiac animals and angel wings to celestial motifs, the brand has seen remarkable growth since its launch three years ago — scaling from £14,000 in revenue to £3 million, and even crafting a custom ring for Taylor Swift in 2024.

“I often liken my jewellery to ‘luxury tattoos’ — a sentiment many of my bespoke clients share,” says Fein Hughes. “Commissioning a custom symbolic piece is a bit like choosing a tattoo: it’s deeply personal, a reflection of identity and rich with meaning.” Whether it’s star and Chinese zodiac signs or pup portraits, herbs and flowers with hidden symbolism, each design is a visual narrative for the consumer, she says. “Gen Z is all about self-expression, and choosing a Cece signet ring is a playful, colourful way to infuse your daily uniform with meaning.”

Cece Jewellery, the London‑based atelier, is known for its richly symbolic, hand-enameled signets.

Photo: Courtesy of Cece

## **Playing with new materials**

The jewellery sector is beginning to explore more responsible materials and manufacturing processes in response to Gen Z’s desire for value-driven brands, says Alice Crossley, senior foresight analyst at consultancy The Future Laboratory. “This transition includes a focus on atypical and raw materials like glass, wood, Tetra Pak, soda cans, 3D printing and even electronic waste.”

This ethos is also fuelling the popularity of upcycled and non-traditional materials, as designers rethink what constitutes a ‘precious’ object. UK-based designer Tega Akinola, for example, is known for using discarded cables and electronic components to create sculptural, one-off pieces that straddle the line between jewellery and wearable art. US-based KBH Jewels focuses on heirloom-style upcycled fine jewellery crafted entirely from reclaimed materials, tapping into both the circular economy and the emotional longevity Gen Z values.

UK-based designer Tega Akinola is known for using discarded cables and electronic components to create sculptural, one-off pieces.

Photo: Courtesy of Tega Akinola

“All of what I do comes under the branch of upcycling or repurposing. Then, I have two different sub-branches: one is conceptual and experimental work that explores the process of transforming something from waste to treasure, or using different and innovative materials and making them into a clothing piece or accessory piece,” says Akinola, “the other is selling products that are related to that [conceptual art].” She notes that the product resonates with younger consumers because it aesthetically stands out on saturated social media feeds and aligns with their desires to make more responsible and unique purchasing decisions.

Gen Z are also gravitating towards vintage jewellery resale. For instance, Accessories of Old, a vintage jewellery shop in West London specialising in deadstock pieces from the 1940s through the 1990s, has become a Gen Z sensation. Its [TikTok‑fuelled charm bar](https://www.tiktok.com/@accessoriesofold/video/7375958394584304928), where customers assemble custom vintage charm necklaces, draws long queues and viral social media content every weekend.

#### TikTok content

“By using responsibly sourced and recycled materials, we’ve cultivated a community that values intentionality and timelessness over trends,” says Sophie Howard, founder of By Pariah, a London-based fine jewellery brand that uses 100 per cent recycled materials, and has been worn by the likes of Michelle Obama and Hailey Bieber. “Our customers see each piece as more than jewellery; it’s a conscious choice that aligns with their own values.”

London-based brand By Pariah uses 100 per cent recycled materials.

Photo: Courtesy of By Parriah

Howard notes that growth didn’t happen overnight. “It wasn’t instant — it happened gradually, the more we leaned into storytelling. We started sharing not just the pieces themselves, but the process, the materials and the people behind them,” she says. The brand declined to share revenues but sales are now up 40 per cent year-on-year.

As the jewellery market continues to grow, so too will the opportunities for designers who prioritise meaning, material innovation and individuality. Jewellery is shedding its role as a mere finishing touch and emerging as a powerful medium of self-expression. For a generation navigating economic uncertainty and digital saturation, the brands succeeding are offering something tangible and deeply personal.

- In the bridal space, Gen Z is moving toward "just because" rings and moissanite engagement styles — less about legacy status and more about "aesthetic storytelling, values alignment, and emotional expression" (Andie T.).

- Brands winning with Gen Z are positioning pieces as "accessible indulgences rather than major investments" and selling stories, not just shine.
- Gen Z buys jewellery "to feel" — pieces that tell a story, feel personal, and "don't scream status" (Krishan Anand).
- The jewellery Gen Z buys "isn't just worn—it's posted, layered, gifted, and emotionally tied to identity" (The Art Angels).
