<webpage_content>
[Vogue Business is now in the Vogue App](https://vogue.smart.link/au4sikdbz)

[DOWNLOAD NOW](https://vogue.smart.link/au4sikdbz)

[Fashion](/business/fashion-industry)

# The Long View by Vogue Business: Can luxury jewellery reach Gen Z?

Fine jewellery is one of the fastest-growing categories in luxury, but sustaining momentum may be a challenge.

By [Laure Guilbault](/contributor/laure-guilbault)

ARTWORK BY *VOGUE BUSINESS*

*This article is part of our Advanced Membership package. To enjoy unlimited access to The Long View from Vogue Business and bi-monthly Market Insights Reports and webinars, sign up for Advanced Membership* [*here*](https://www.voguebusiness.com/membership)*.*

Never mind the pandemic — fine jewellery is on a roll. Its pace of growth is even set to outstrip handbags, a product category that is a traditional sales driver for the luxury industry.

Antoine Belge, analyst at investment company Exane, expects a growth rate for fine jewellery of 10-12 per cent per annum over the next five years, compared to 7-9 per cent for leather goods and approximately 6-7 per cent for the luxury industry.

However, doubts remain over the long-term buoyancy of the sector. “Everyone remains very upbeat on the category, and rightly so. What could go wrong?” says Citi luxury goods analyst Thomas Chauvet.

He answers his own question, pointing out that the category has yet to prove its allure to the emerging [Gen Z](https://www.voguebusiness.com/tag/gen-z) consumer. Potential stumbling blocks in the pursuit of Gen Z include jewellery’s longer product lifespan with a slower pace of development than fashion, much lower [e-commerce](https://www.voguebusiness.com/consumers/e-commerce) penetration and more conservative communications.

Read More

[The demi-fine jewellery boom: Is luxury next?](/article/the-demi-fine-jewellery-boom-is-luxury-next)

By [Lucy Maguire](/contributor/lucy-maguire)

All of these factors may contribute to the current surge flattening out — already likely to feel the impact of a softening of government backing for recovering economies. “Later this year, there could be some normalisation in demand due to government support and stimulus potentially fading,” says Chauvet, also noting the likely “wallet shift to experiences as the world reopens and international travel resumes”.

For the time being, the financial indicators for branded jewellery are positive. Sales at Richemont’s [jewellery maisons](https://www.voguebusiness.com/companies/richemont-shares-jump-on-jewellery-rebound-kering-approach), including Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, rose 62 per cent in the quarter ending 31 March, while LVMH’s [watches and jewellery division](https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/lvmhs-rebound-louis-vuitton-dior-and-e-commerce-drive-growth), including Bulgari and [Tiffany & Co.](https://www.voguebusiness.com/tag/tiffany-and-co), posted sales up 35 per cent. Tiffany & Co.’s comparable sales returned to growth as early as its third quarter of 2020 (ending 31 October), with the US jewellery brand enjoying an “excellent” start to the year, according to [new owner LVMH](https://www.voguebusiness.com/companies/why-the-new-lvmh-tiffany-deal-makes-sense).

Chanel’s Coco Crush fine jewellery collection saw double-digit revenue growth in 2020. At Chaumet, the average basket went up 20 to 25 per cent within less than a year as consumers indulged in precious pieces, with brides and grooms splurging on jewellery. “As people couldn’t travel or host very large wedding ceremonies, they reallocated their budget to wedding bands and solitaires,” Chaumet chief executive Jean-Marc Mansvelt says.

“The average basket clearly went up in e-commerce,” Van Cleef & Arpels chief executive Nicolas Bos says. “Online sales were focusing on entry-level ranges. Today, it’s all price points.” Despite a lack of social occasions to wear high jewellery, “there’s a notion of perennity with jewellery that resonates particularly in troubled times,” Bos adds.

Van Cleef & Arpels, photo by Patrick Swirc

Many consumers see jewellery as a reassuring purchase. “The global crisis has reinforced the safe haven status of jewellery,” says Boucheron chief executive Hélène Poulit-Duquesne. “This phenomenon also strengthened emerging trends such as the fact that women purchase more and more for themselves, resulting in a more emotional relationship to high jewellery compared to the status or the investment it used to represent.”

## **Appealing to Gen Z**

Gen Z customers can be demanding. They have tighter wallets, are constantly eager for novelty and express a strong preference for brands that reflect inclusivity and respond to sustainable values.

Persuading them to return for repeat visits is a challenge, says Poulit-Duquesne. “The key is to keep them coming back after that one ring.” She also emphasises how Gen Z needs to be guided to enjoy the experiential nature of a luxury purchase. “Our mission is not simply to make products, but to make our universe understandable so that people feel part of it.”

Jewellers are betting on the allure of iconic, Instagrammable collections. “There’s an amplifying effect of social media,” Bos says. He notes that the Alhambra line, created in the 1960s, continues to seduce across generations and periods. Even novelties are very branded and recognisable. Van Cleef & Arpels just launched Lucky Spring, incorporating the codes of the house such as the ladybugs, flowers and leaf motifs. According to industry sources, iconic collections make up the lion’s share of Cartier, Bulgari and Van Cleef & Arpels sales. They represent a much smaller share of Tiffany’s sales, hinting at potential to exploit. Chaumet, which had 12 jewellery collections a decade ago, now focuses on three main collections: Bee My Love, Liens and Joséphine. “There was a risk of dilution,” says Mansvelt. “Chaumet’s ultimate icon is the tiara, and it was also transformed into a ring.”

There are plenty of positive indicators for continued growth. Morgan Stanley analyst Edouard Aubin identifies three major growth drivers. “First, female empowerment — including in Asia — with self-purchase is on the rise. Second, while unbranded jewellery still represents the lion’s share of the industry’s sales, branded jewellery led by four global megabrands is gaining market share. Third, social media are turbo-charging the globalisation of jewellery as consumers favour recognisable, iconic lines. Chinese consumers notably gravitate towards established brands.”

The competition between the luxury giants boosts brands all-round. “It’s co-conquest,” says industry veteran Stanislas de Quercize, referring to the growth in market share by brands owned by Richemont and LVMH over unbranded jewellery.

## **High jewellery rebound**

Even high jewellery sales are looking up. That’s despite the pandemic-related cancellation of [VIP customer events](https://www.voguebusiness.com/companies/private-broadcasts-are-luxury-brands-new-secret-weapon), red carpets, press previews and a general lack of occasions to wear high-end pieces. Cartier CEO Cyrille Vigneron described the high jewellery recovery in the quarter ending 31 March as “quite promising” during Richemont’s earnings call. Van Cleef & Arpels’s Bos says the brand has shifted the way it presents from major international events to smaller, more local, intimate, regional events.

“We won't be able to host global events for a bit. We are having an important event for the Sous Les Étoiles collection in China right now, but nobody else from outside China can attend. This is the first great event I am missing in 20 years, which is a little strange,” Bos says. “Starting this autumn, we’ll have events with Europeans and progressively with Americans.”

Lavish events are coming back too. Bulgari unveiled its new high jewellery collection Magnifica at Milan’s Teatro alla Scala, Cartier held its Sixième Sens collection in June in Lake Como, Louis Vuitton is set to present its high jewellery collection in Monaco later this week, and Dior is hosting an event later in July. “We will go back to supporting our maison in terms of communications,” Richemont chairman Johann Rupert said during the recent earnings call. Red carpet is also back: jewellers are returning to the Cannes Film Festival, which takes place from 6-17 July. Kering, owner of Boucheron, will host its Women in Motion talk and dinner, while Diane Kruger will walk the red carpets in Chaumet.

## **The recommerce opportunity**

Resale, once shunned by luxury, is proving a hot trend. Kering is embracing resale and has taken a 5 per cent stake in French luxury resale platform Vestiaire Collective. Kering-owned Alexander McQueen is the first fashion brand to join Vestiaire Collective’s Brand Approved programme, which allows customers to sell their Alexander McQueen items, once verified, and receive vouchers to buy new products from the brand.

Boucheron chief executive Hélène Poulit-Duquesne and Chaumet chief executive Jean-Marc Mansvelt.

Courtesy of Chaumet and Boucheron

In jewellery, Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels are offering archive pieces, Cartier with Cartier Tradition for jewellery — including its first event in China dedicated to the archival pieces — and Vintage for watches in selected stores, and Van Cleef & Arpels’ Heritage. “We authenticate, repair, clean and offer to the clients in stores,” says Bos. “They are emblematic pieces of the house from different periods, between the 1920s and 1995. For example, we like to buy animal brooches from the 1950s because it gives a nice flair to the store. It is bound to develop, but our approach is curated; it’s a selection.” He sees auction houses and merchants like Thomas Faerber and Richemont-owned secondhand online luxury watch retailer Watchfinder as more relevant for broader resale because of the multi-brand offering.

Tiffany & Co. allows its US clients to upgrade their original Tiffany diamond engagement rings. Upon review, customers receive a credit up to the original purchase price, which can be used toward the purchase of a new Tiffany engagement ring.

“There’s a major opportunity in the secondhand market,” says de Quercize, who is a board member, president and founder of family office SAVIH and a former CEO of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels. “Incorporating high jewellery resale in your business has been done by Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels. Why not integrate the resale business of all jewellery pieces and watches? Recommerce is good for the planet, growth and profits. It's a great way to offer a decarbonised product to the clients, keep in touch with your consumer on a permanent basis, moving from transaction to relationship.”

Chaumet is taking note. “We are looking at it closely; we haven’t ruled [on it] yet,” says Mansvelt. “I am not sure that there are that many Chaumet pieces available on the secondhand market, in proportion. Is it passed from hand to hand within the families? I believe we have to listen to the market.”

Meanwhile, on Vestiaire Collective, the jewellery category is growing by 173 per cent year-on-year, faster than handbags (up 171 per cent). Sales are hugely up for top-selling jewellery models, such as Elsa Peretti for Tiffany & Co. and Clic H from Hermès, up by 324 per cent and 291 per cent, respectively, and hoops across brands up 207 per cent.

A note of caution is voiced by some experts. Analyst Thomas Chauvet recalls that following the global financial crisis of a decade ago, a similar sense of euphoria rippled through the luxury watches’ sector. However, demand slowed within a few years following a political change of leadership in China and a crackdown led by president Xi Jinping on gift-giving and extravagant displays of personal wealth. Besides the political shift in China, the watch sector was also hampered by a perfect storm of internal issues identified by Chauvet as “limited product innovation and reluctance to embrace technology, oversized wholesale distribution, inadequate pricing architecture and an old-style communication”.

This Vogue Business article examines whether luxury fine jewellery can sustain its current growth momentum and appeal to Gen Z consumers. Key points include:

- **Growth projections**: Exane analyst Antoine Belge expects fine jewellery to grow 10-12% annually over the next five years, outpacing leather goods (7-9%) and the luxury industry overall (6-7%).

- **Current performance**: Richemont's jewellery maisons (Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels) saw sales rise 62% in the quarter ending March 31. LVMH's watches and jewellery division (Bulgari, Tiffany & Co.) posted 35% sales growth. Chanel's Coco Crush collection saw double-digit growth in 2020, and Chaumet's average basket rose 20-25% within a year.

- **Gen Z challenges**: Citi analyst Thomas Chauvet warns the category has yet to prove its allure to Gen Z. Stumbling blocks include jewellery's longer product lifespan, slower development pace than fashion, lower e-commerce penetration, and more conservative communications. Gen Z customers have tighter wallets, seek novelty, and prefer brands reflecting inclusivity and sustainability. Jewellers are betting on iconic, Instagrammable collections (e.g., Van Cleef & Arpels' Alhambra and Lucky Spring lines, Chaumet's Bee My Love, Liens, and Joséphine collections).

- **Growth drivers**: Morgan Stanley analyst Edouard Aubin identifies three drivers: rising female self-purchase (including in Asia), branded jewellery (led by four global megabrands) gaining share over unbranded, and social media turbo-charging the globalisation of jewellery. Chinese consumers gravitate toward established brands.

- **High jewellery rebound**: Despite cancelled VIP events during the pandemic, high jewellery sales are recovering. Brands shifted to smaller, local, intimate events and are now returning to lavish events and red carpets (Cannes Film Festival, Bulgari's Magnifica at Teatro alla Scala, Cartier's Sixième Sens in Lake Como).

- **Recommerce opportunity**: Resale is a growing trend. Kering took a 5% stake in Vestiaire Collective. Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels offer archive pieces. Tiffany allows US clients to upgrade engagement rings with credit up to original purchase price. On Vestiaire Collective, jewellery category grew 173% year-on-year, faster than handbags (171%). Industry veteran Stanislas de Quercize advocates for integrating resale as it's "good for the planet, growth and profits."

- **Cautionary note**: Chauvet recalls that after the 2008 financial crisis, luxury watches saw similar euphoria that collapsed due to China's political shift, anti-gift-giving crackdown, limited innovation, inadequate pricing, and old-style communication. He warns "there could be a reset at some point after a decade of very high growth."

1. Identify and preserve the main topic or purpose of the webpage.
2. Retain key facts, statistics, and data points that are central to the content's message.
3. Keep important quotes from credible sources or experts.
4. Maintain the chronological order of events if the content is time-sensitive or historical.
5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

```
}
```

This is a YouTube video by Amanda Weldon (channel "belowtheblonde," ~77,000 subscribers) published on February 15, 2025, presenting the top 10 jewellery trends for 2025. The video synthesizes trend reports from Vogue, Who What Wear, and Glamour magazines and has 2,859 likes and 120,023 views.

The 10 jewellery trends for 2025 covered in the video are:
1. **Mixed Metals** – Moving away from single-metal-only styling; layering necklaces and bracelets with alternating gold/silver tones (and possibly rose gold), two-in-one earrings that create the illusion of multiple piercings, and pairing mixed metals with monochromatic outfits (black, brown, navy, cream, camel, burgundy).
2. **Bangles and Cuffs** – Chunky, oversized bracelets inspired by brands like Tiffany & Co., including unexpected materials like resin and acrylic (a "quirky art teacher aesthetic"); layering chunky cuffs with thinner bangles for depth and personality.
3. **Bountiful Beads** – A refined boho resurgence; earthy-toned, polished beads crafted from gemstones like jade, emerald, and quartz; works seasonally with flowy dresses or chunky knits and layers well with silver/gold chains.
4. **Cord Necklaces** – Nostalgic early-2000s-inspired pendants on soft leather or satin cords; great for layering or wearing solo, pairing well with v-necks and button-downs.
5. **Colourful Gemstones** – Vibrant gemstones (aqua blues, cobalt tones, rich garnets) making bold statements; pieces designed to look like one-of-a-kind treasures and serve as conversation starters; styling tip is to balance with neutral pieces.
6. **Freshwater Pearls** – Modern artistic Baroque pearl styling with irregular, organic shapes; green-hued pearls and pearls paired with gold beads; recommended to pair with tailored blazers; spotlights Canadian designer Pamela Card (Vancouver-based, woman-owned business).
7. **Sculptural Studs** – Seashell-inspired designs and bold geometric shapes adding whimsy; from quiet luxury to more playful maximalism; Pamela Card highlighted as leading this trend; versatile with sleek ponies or loose hair.
8. **Chunky Necklaces** – Heavyweight statement pieces, gold pendants, and layered chains that demand attention around the neck; not about 2012-era costume jewellery but beautifully crafted bold pieces worn with turtlenecks and plunging necklines.
9. **Vintage-Inspired Watches** – Return to timeless watch styles (quiet luxury), led by Cartier-inspired designs; accessible alternatives and dupes on the high street; two-toned watches cross-reference the mixed metals trend.
10. **Colourful Watches** – Vibrant dials and unexpected materials like wood and stone; vintage-inspired but more genderless in style; unisex designs blending bold cases with sleek minimalist faces.

The video includes product links for each trend, video chapters, and styling advice. Amanda also shares personal touches, including coveting the Stevie hoops from Maui, and recommends Pamela Card as a standout designer for freshwater pearls and sculptural studs.

Jewelry Resilient in 2024 Even As Luxury Sales Slipped, Says Bain & Co.

[Surveys](/industry/surveys)Feb 10, 2025

# Jewelry Resilient in 2024 Even As Luxury Sales Slipped, Says Bain & Co.

Bain & Co.’s latest report on the luxury market examines why the market’s customer base is shrinking and how to appeal to consumers in 2025.

[![](https://uploads.nationaljeweler.com/uploads/7aa17c3727ee24de764af5c00ad5b62b.jpg)](/search_by_authors?query=Lenore+Fedow)[Lenore Fedow](/search_by_authors?query=Lenore+Fedow)[lenore.fedow@nationaljeweler.com](mailto:lenore.fedow@nationaljeweler.com)

An 18-karat yellow gold “Stilla” ring set with marquise and round diamonds by Tacori ($2,990). Bain & Company’s new “Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study” examines how the market performed in 2024 and what’s ahead in 2025.

New York—Bain & Company’s “Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study,” released last month in collaboration with Altagamma, shared insights into the 2024 luxury market and the outlook for the year ahead.  
  
According to the study, sales in the global luxury goods market dipped to €1.48 trillion ($1.54 trillion) in 2024, down 1 to 3 percent year-over-year at current exchange rates.  
  
This slight decline signifies a normalization after the strong growth seen in 2022 and 2023, said the report, with 2024’s performance still surpassing pre-COVID levels.  
  
Bain & Co.’s report delves into the reasons behind the decline in sales last year, how the jewelry category is performing, U.S. market trends, and more.  
  
Here are five takeaways from the report.  
  
**The luxury market’s customer base is shrinking.**  
For the first time in the 23-year history of this report, the luxury market’s customer base contracted.  
  
Bain estimated the market lost about 50 million customers globally between 2022 and 2024, declining from 400 million to around 350 million customers by the end of 2024 driven by a decline in demand for personal luxury goods, particularly among younger consumers.  
  
The market for personal luxury goods (e.g., jewelry, watches, clothes, cosmetics), which Bain called “the core of the core” of luxury segments, saw its first contraction in 15 years, excluding the pandemic period.  
  
“Global luxury consumers, grappling with macroeconomic uncertainty and continued price elevation by brands, cut back slightly on discretionary items,” said the report.  
  
The size of the market for personal luxury goods dipped 2 percent year-over-year at current exchange rates to €363 billion ($377 billion) in 2024.  
  
“This trend—particularly acute among Generation Z, whose advocacy for luxury brands continued to decline—has caused the [overall] luxury customer base to shrink,” the reported noted.   
  
The slowdown in the market led to polarized performances among luxury brands.  
  
The report estimated only about one-third of brands saw growth in 2024, compared with 95 percent from 2021 to 2022 and 65 percent in 2023.  
  
“The average profitability of personal luxury goods brands eroded, reflecting the limited room for further price increases and rising costs of serving the consumer, from marketing to distribution,” said the report.  
  
By region, sales in the Americas totaled €100 billion ($103.86), down 1 percent year-over-year at current exchange rates.   
  
The U.S. luxury market was on a “generally upward” quarterly trajectory throughout the year despite [ebbs and flows in consumer confidence](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13604-consumer-confidence-slips-for-second-consecutive-month).  
  
Aspirational customers are facing financial pressure, with more shoppers opting for value-for-money luxury and non-luxury brands, turning to department stores and outlet malls to do their shopping.  
  
Shoppers, particularly younger ones, value “hyper-personalized” customer service and are looking for unique items.  
  
A few factors should help to sustain the U.S. market’s performance in the future, said the report, including potential interest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve, the conclusion of the presidential election, easing inflation, and the prospect of tax cuts and enhanced economic growth.  
  
**Jewelry was the “most resilient” of the core luxury segments.**  
Though the overall market for personal luxury goods struggled, jewelry was a top performer, particularly in the United States.   
  
Jewelry “proved to be the most resilient core luxury category in 2024,” said the report, flat to up 2 percent at current exchange rates to reach €31 billion ($32.2 billion) in sales.  
  
“This performance was driven by consistent high-low brand strategies and enhanced customer-centric approaches,” said the report.  
  
High jewelry did especially well, outperforming the “less-elevated” parts of the market.  
  
“Competition intensified, with luxury fashion houses expanding their presence in the segment and rising local giants seeking to grow beyond their domestic markets,” it said.  
  
Chanel, for example, introduced its [“Haute Joaillerie Sport” high jewelry collection](https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13498-chanel-to-receive-gem-award-for-high-jewelry-excellence) in 2024.   
  
The report also noted that secondhand luxury is increasingly becoming a “gateway” to luxury for aspirational consumers who cannot afford new items, with growth in sales of pre-owned jewelry particularly strong and sales of secondhand clothing accelerating.  
  
The success of the jewelry category is impressive when considering that few luxury categories posted growth in 2024.  
  
The report said most, “experienced elevation-related volume declines due to list price increases and an emphasis on higher price categories in the mix of products sold.”   
  
Outside of jewelry, luxury beauty and eyewear performed the best, up 3 to 5 percent year-over-year as customers opted for small indulgences and responded well to “renewed creativity” in the eyewear category.

 Related stories will be right here …

**The watch category struggled as consumer interest waned.**  
Watches had a tough year, posting sales declines of 5 to 7 percent at current exchange rates to around €51 billion ($52.97 billion) in 2024.  
  
“The segment exited its recent growth cycle amid reduced consumer interest, and prices dropped in the secondary market,” said the report.  
  
Only top-performing brands saw positive results, it said, with demand for unique shapes and precious materials growing.  
  
Notably, gender-specific designs were less common.  
  
The report also noted that the “retailization” trend in distribution continued, with brands looking to build connections with customers in their own stores instead of relying on multi-brand distributors.  
  
**Outlet stores did well as shoppers looked for deals.**  
The outlet channel outperformed the market in 2024, posting a growth rate of 0 to 3 percent at current exchange rates, the report said.  
  
While most physical luxury stores suffered from “plummeting” foot traffic, the outlet channel gained popularity as an entry point into the luxury market, driven in part by shoppers looking for more for their money.  
  
“Aspirational consumers faced increased financial pressure, leading to a shift toward value-for-money luxury and non-luxury brands, particularly in department stores and outlet malls,” said the report.  
  
As for the other channels, monobrand stores saw sales declines of 1 to 4 percent at current exchange rates, due in part to a decrease in foot traffic.  
  
Multi-brand stores also struggled, with department store sales down 2 to 4 percent and specialty stores down by 4 to 8 percent.  
  
As for online sales, the report said the channel is normalizing after post-pandemic swings, posting declines of 1 to 4 percent at current exchange rates. It maintained a 20 percent share of the luxury market.  
  
Notably, off-price online platforms saw growth because they, “[serve] as a gateway to luxury purchases and an appealing alternative for affluent consumers trading down.”  
  
**To succeed in 2025, luxury retailers need a solid strategy.**  
Last year was a challenging one for the luxury sector, but this year could see growth.  
  
The personal luxury goods segment is forecast to grow moderately in 2025, with sales estimated to be flat to up 4 percent.   
  
The report said solid market fundamentals should lead to growth between 4 to 6 percent annually until 2030, reaching an estimated total value of €460 billion to €500 billion ($477.75 billion to $519.29 billion) by the end of the period.  
  
Demographic and macroeconomic tailwinds should bolster the sector because, it said, there are more than 300 million new customers likely to emerge in the next five years in China and other markets.  
  
Retailers may have some tough choices to make to navigate the issues facing the luxury industry, such as deciding whether to seek exclusivity or change course to reach a broader audience, but deciding on a strategy is the way forward, the report said.  
  
“Across all the potential strategic choices, there’s a common need to rebuild luxury foundations by refocusing on the basics that have always characterized luxury, such as the highest quality and creativity; by fostering a relationship with consumers that goes beyond individual transactions, connects with multiple audiences, and transcends short-term hype; and, lastly, by delivering flawlessly, drawing on new technology such as generative AI along the whole value chain,” the report said.  
  
Read the full report [on the Bain & Company website](https://www.bain.com/insights/luxury-in-transition-securing-future-growth/).

This is a National Jeweler article (published Feb 10, 2025, by senior editor Lenore Fedow) reporting on Bain & Company's "Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study," released in collaboration with Altagamma. The study examines 2024 luxury market performance and the 2025 outlook.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Luxury market customer base is shrinking.** For the first time in the 23-year history of the report, the luxury customer base contracted, losing about 50 million customers globally between 2022 and 2024 (declining from 400 million to ~350 million). The personal luxury goods market (jewelry, watches, clothes, cosmetics) saw its first contraction in 15 years (excluding the pandemic period), dipping 2% year-over-year to €363 billion ($377 billion) in 2024. Only about one-third of luxury brands saw growth in 2024, compared with 95% in 2021-2022 and 65% in 2023. Gen Z's advocacy for luxury brands continued to decline.

2. **Jewelry was the "most resilient" core luxury segment.** Jewelry was flat to up 2% to reach €31 billion ($32.2 billion) in 2024 sales, driven by "consistent high-low brand strategies and enhanced customer-centric approaches." High jewelry performed especially well. Secondhand luxury is increasingly a "gateway" to luxury for aspirational consumers, with pre-owned jewelry sales growth particularly strong. Luxury beauty and eyewear also performed well (up 3-5%).

3. **Watches struggled.** Watch sales declined 5-7% to around €51 billion ($52.97 billion) in 2024, exiting its recent growth cycle amid reduced consumer interest and falling secondary market prices.

4. **Outlet stores outperformed.** The outlet channel grew 0-3% as aspirational consumers sought value-for-money options. Monobrand stores declined 1-4%, department stores fell 2-4%, specialty stores dropped 4-8%, and online sales declined 1-4% while maintaining a 20% market share.

5. **2025 outlook.** Personal luxury goods are forecast to grow modestly (flat to up 4%) in 2025, with growth of 4-6% annually expected until 2030, reaching €460-500 billion ($477.75-519.29 billion). More than 300 million new customers are expected to emerge in China and other markets in the next five years. The report emphasizes rebuilding luxury foundations by refocusing on quality and creativity, fostering consumer relationships beyond transactions, and leveraging generative AI.

**U.S. Market:** Sales in the Americas totaled €100 billion ($103.86 billion), down 1% year-over-year. The U.S. market was on a "generally upward" quarterly trajectory, supported by potential Fed rate cuts, the conclusion of the presidential election, easing inflation, and prospects of tax cuts.

The article includes related National Jeweler content on Valentine's Day jewelry spending, holiday sales, and other industry news, as well as site navigation and recent headlines covering topics like the Plumb Club board election, Jewelers Mutual CEO transition, Spinelli Kilcollin's trade-in program, and more.
args.key_excerpts: "Global luxury consumers, grappling with macroeconomic uncertainty and continued price elevation by brands, cut back slightly on discretionary items," said the report.

# Luxury jewelry sales mixed amid consumer pullback

The category is down at LVMH and Kering, while Richemont is seeing increased sales.

![](/static/img/social_icons/share-icon.svg?313321260226)

![A view of a Buccellati store interior as seen from above.](https://imgproxy.divecdn.com/X3aW8qiqoUi-jCtKeTkvNpX6c3-FKbuBHdyHaVIgeW0/g:nowe:0:205/c:3000:1694/rs:fill:1200:675:1/Z3M6Ly9kaXZlc2l0ZS1zdG9yYWdlL2RpdmVpbWFnZS9HZXR0eUltYWdlcy0xODQ3MzM5MTkuanBn.webp)
![](/static/img/play.svg?313321260226)

Against a background of tariff uncertainty and global macroeconomic tensions, many [luxury consumers are pulling back on purchases](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/hsbc-july-2025-luxury-earnings-predictions/752812/). 

One bright spot amid the pressure in the global luxury goods market was the overall jewelry category, which includes both high jewelry and fine jewelry. The category demonstrated notable resilience in 2024, according to Bain & Company. Last year, the sector grew between 0% and 2% to reach an [estimated value of 31 billion euros](https://www.bain.com/insights/luxury-in-transition-securing-future-growth/), or about $36 billion. 

However, even during an economic downturn, wealthy shoppers tend to trust certain categories, [such as high jewelry](https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/complete-guide-to-collecting-high-jewelry-or-haute-joaillerie), meaning expertly crafted, one-of-a-kind pieces featuring complex, artistic designs and rare gemstones. By contrast, fine jewelry is made of precious materials and is mass produced and easily recognizable.

High jewelry led market growth, outshining more accessible segments, while competition intensified due to the entry of luxury fashion houses and ambitious regional players, according to Fredrica Levato, senior partner at Bain & Company and co-author of [the firm’s 2024 Altagamma annual Luxury Goods Market Study](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/bain-luxury-spending-flat-worst-2024/733451/).

“This made [jewelry] the most stable segment within the core luxury categories, outperforming others such as the watch industry, which saw a 5% to 7% decline amid cooling consumer interest,” Levato said in an email. 

Richemont jewelry brands fared best in recent earnings reports. The company owns Buccellati, Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and Vhernier, and posted an [overall Q1 revenue increase of 3% to 5.4 billion euros](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/jewelry-richemont-earnings-cartier/753306/). In its earnings release, Richemont said sales at its jewelry houses increased 7% year over year, while its specialty watchmaker division fell 10%.

“Richemont jewelry brands…have been outperforming the broader industry and peers for a number of quarters, since the pandemic, but now this outperformance is more pronounced,” Jelena Sokolova, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said in an email. 

By contrast, recent revenue figures at LVMH have been less positive. The company owns nine combined watch and jewelry houses, including Bulgari, Tiffany & Co., Chaumet, Repossi and Fred.

The company posted [overall revenue of 39.8 billion euros](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/lvmh-first-half-profit-revenue-decline-2025-dior-loewe/754098/) for the first half of fiscal 2025, representing a 4% decline year over year. Revenue at its watches and jewelry division was down 1% for the period.

Meanwhile, rival luxury conglomerate Kering owns jewelry brands Boucheron, Pomellato, DoDo and Qeelin. Kering doesn’t separate its jewelry category in its earnings reports, but instead includes it under the “other” category, alongside fashion houses Balenciaga, McQueen and Brioni. 

Sales in that category declined 15% in the second quarter, while overall [revenue at Kering](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/kering-steep-losses-gucci-q2-2025-h1/756227/) was down 16% year over year.

The jewelry category may be part of what plays into the widening earnings gap as the overall luxury sector continues to navigate challenges.

“For the luxury industry [jewelry] is one of the fastest growing segments with very high entry barriers [such as] working capital requirements, gifting and investment demand which tends to be brand loyal,” said Sokolova.

args.summary:
This article from Fashion Dive reports on mixed luxury jewelry sales amid consumer pullback caused by tariff uncertainty and global macroeconomic tensions. The jewelry category (high jewelry and fine jewelry) showed notable resilience in 2024, growing 0-2% to reach an estimated value of 31 billion euros (~$36 billion), according to Bain & Company. High jewelry—expertly crafted, one-of-a-kind pieces with rare gemstones—led market growth, outperforming mass-produced fine jewelry. Bain's Fredrica Levato noted jewelry was "the most stable segment within the core luxury categories," outperforming the watch industry, which declined 5-7%.

Performance varied by conglomerate: Richemont (owner of Buccellati, Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, and Vhernier) posted a 3% overall Q1 revenue increase to 5.4 billion euros, with jewelry houses up 7% year-over-year while its specialty watchmaker division fell 10%. LVMH posted overall first-half fiscal 2025 revenue of 39.8 billion euros (down 4% year-over-year), with watches and jewelry revenue down 1%. Kering (owner of Boucheron, Pomellato, DoDo, and Qeelin) reported a 15% decline in its "other" category (which includes jewelry alongside Balenciaga, McQueen, and Brioni) in Q2, with overall revenue down 16% year-over-year.

Morningstar senior equity analyst Jelena Sokolova noted Richemont jewelry brands have been outperforming the broader industry since the pandemic, with the outperformance now more pronounced. Sokolova also highlighted jewelry as one of the fastest-growing luxury segments with high entry barriers, working capital requirements, and brand-loyal gifting and investment demand.
args.key_excerpts: "This made [jewelry] the most stable segment within the core luxury categories, outperforming others such as the watch industry, which saw a 5% to 7% decline amid cooling consumer interest," Levato said in an email.

## **Market Drivers**

### **Rising Demand Driven by High-Net-Worth Individuals and Expanding Affluent Classes**

The Luxury Jewelry Market benefits from the steady rise in high-net-worth individuals and the expanding affluent classes in both developed and emerging economies. Consumers with significant disposable income invest in fine jewelry to showcase wealth, heritage, and social standing. It reflects a preference for exclusivity, rarity, and craftsmanship in purchase decisions. Global wealth growth drives consistent demand for premium collections, rare gemstones, and bespoke designs. Luxury brands strengthen their positioning through private showrooms and exclusive launches targeted at elite buyers. This factor elevates the overall growth trajectory of the market.

### **Increasing Consumer Preference for Branded and Authenticated Jewelry Pieces**

The Luxury Jewelry Market gains momentum from a rising preference for branded products that guarantee authenticity and enduring value. Buyers prioritize traceability of materials, certified gemstones, and hallmarking processes to ensure credibility. It strengthens trust and promotes loyalty toward established luxury houses. Brands highlight heritage, craftsmanship, and innovation to reinforce exclusivity. Authentication technologies, including blockchain-based certification, enhance buyer confidence. This driver enhances the market’s resilience against counterfeit products.

### **Expansion of E-Commerce Channels and Digital Client Engagement Platforms**

The Luxury Jewelry Market adapts to changing consumer behavior through digital retail and personalized online experiences. E-commerce platforms introduce wider product visibility, curated catalogs, and secure purchasing frameworks for global clients. It enables international expansion of luxury brands by reaching customers beyond traditional flagship stores. Virtual try-on solutions, AI-driven recommendations, and live consultations replicate the luxury experience online. High-value transactions through secure digital platforms create strong trust among consumers. This factor broadens access to luxury collections and elevates sales opportunities.

### **Heightened Focus on Sustainability and Ethical Sourcing Practices**

The Luxury Jewelry Market evolves through growing emphasis on sustainability, transparency, and ethical sourcing. Consumers seek responsibly mined diamonds, recycled metals, and environmentally conscious practices in jewelry manufacturing. It compels brands to disclose sourcing methods and adopt traceability measures. Government regulations and industry standards reinforce this direction, ensuring compliance with ethical benchmarks. Leading luxury houses integrate sustainability into brand narratives, appealing to socially responsible consumers. This shift strengthens the long-term trust and value perception of the market.

## **Market Trends**

### **Growing Influence of High Jewelry Collaborations and Limited-Edition Collections**

The Luxury Jewelry Market observes strong momentum from collaborations between heritage brands and renowned designers or artists. These partnerships create limited-edition collections that heighten exclusivity and attract elite buyers. It strengthens brand prestige while catering to consumers seeking originality and cultural connection. Limited availability reinforces desirability and premium positioning. Collaborations often integrate unique craftsmanship with modern aesthetics to appeal to younger high-net-worth audiences. This trend elevates luxury jewelry into collectible art forms.

### **Digital Transformation through Virtual Retail Experiences and Immersive Tools**

The Luxury Jewelry Market adapts to digital transformation with technologies that enhance engagement. Virtual try-on solutions, augmented reality, and immersive platforms replicate the in-store luxury experience. It provides consumers with confidence in high-value purchases without physical presence. Brands invest in AI-driven personalization to create tailored product recommendations. Secure digital channels support global expansion while maintaining exclusivity. This trend accelerates the adoption of omnichannel strategies in luxury retail.

### **Increasing Popularity of Gender-Neutral and Customizable Jewelry Designs**

The Luxury Jewelry Market evolves with rising acceptance of gender-neutral collections and customizable pieces. Consumers value personal expression over traditional design boundaries. It drives brands to release versatile collections suited for diverse audiences. Customization options, including engraving and modular designs, strengthen emotional connection and individuality. Younger consumers view jewelry as both an investment and a lifestyle accessory. This trend reshapes creative direction and expands customer inclusivity.

### **Strong Emphasis on Ethical Luxury and Sustainable Craftsmanship Standards**

The Luxury Jewelry Market witnesses a marked shift toward ethical sourcing and sustainable craftsmanship. Responsible mining practices, recycled metals, and lab-grown diamonds gain acceptance among conscious consumers. It compels leading brands to integrate transparency into supply chains and marketing strategies. Certifications and blockchain traceability assure buyers of ethical authenticity. Consumers increasingly favor brands that align with sustainability and social responsibility values. This trend reinforces long-term trust in luxury jewelry investments.

## **Market Challenges Analysis**

### **Rising Impact of Counterfeiting and Market Saturation in Key Luxury Hubs**

The Luxury Jewelry Market faces persistent challenges from counterfeit products and unauthorized replicas that undermine brand integrity. Counterfeiting erodes consumer trust and diverts significant revenue from legitimate channels. It compels brands to invest heavily in authentication technologies and legal enforcement. Market saturation in mature regions further intensifies competition, reducing growth opportunities for established players. Rising consumer expectations for innovation and exclusivity pressure brands to continuously refresh collections. These factors complicate long-term stability in competitive markets.

### **Escalating Raw Material Costs and Vulnerability to Regulatory Scrutiny**

The Luxury Jewelry Market confronts rising costs of precious metals and gemstones, which directly impact margins and pricing strategies. It forces brands to balance between premium positioning and affordability for high-net-worth buyers. Regulatory scrutiny on ethical sourcing, environmental compliance, and labor practices intensifies the operational burden. Transparency requirements demand robust traceability systems, adding cost and complexity to global supply chains. Currency fluctuations further complicate procurement for brands dependent on international sourcing. These challenges place sustained pressure on profitability and operational efficiency.

## **Market Opportunities**

### **Expansion Potential through Emerging Markets and Wealth Growth in New Economies**

The Luxury Jewelry Market holds significant opportunities in emerging economies where rising disposable incomes and expanding affluent classes stimulate demand. It benefits from the growing number of first-time luxury buyers seeking premium products that symbolize status and investment value. Urbanization and lifestyle shifts in Asia-Pacific, Middle East, and parts of Latin America create untapped avenues for luxury brands. Strategic retail expansion into these regions provides access to a wider consumer base. Exclusive boutiques, pop-up experiences, and personalized services can strengthen loyalty in these new markets. This creates a foundation for sustained revenue growth across underpenetrated geographies.

The Luxury Jewelry Market can leverage innovation in sustainable materials and digital platforms to attract younger, socially conscious buyers. It gains momentum from rising demand for lab-grown diamonds, recycled metals, and ethically sourced gemstones. Transparent supply chains and certification systems reinforce consumer trust. # Luxury Jewelry Market By Raw Material (Gold, Platinum, Diamond, Precious Pearls, Gemstones, Others), By Product (Ring, Necklaces , Earrings, Bracelets, Others), By Application (Women, Men, Children), By Distribution channel (Offline, Online), By Region and Companies - Industry Segment Outlook, Market Assessment, Competition Scenario, Trends and Forecast 2024-2033

## Report Overview

The **Global Luxury Jewelry Market** size is expected to be worth around **USD 105.7 Billion** by 2033, from **USD 47.6 Billion** in 2023, growing at a **CAGR of 8.3%** during the forecast period from 2024 to 2033.

Luxury jewelry, a symbol of status and opulence, encompasses finely crafted pieces adorned with precious metals and gemstones, such as gold, [diamonds](https://market.us/report/diamond-market/), and pearls.

These items are not merely accessories; they represent a high level of craftsmanship and exclusivity, often associated with renowned brands and heritage craftsmanship.

The luxury jewelry market refers to the commercial arena where these high-value pieces are bought, sold, and traded. It includes both primary sales from brands to customers and secondary markets where items are resold or auctioned. This market is characterized by its high price points, limited production quantities, and significant consumer investment, both financially and emotionally.

![Luxury Jewelry Market By Size](https://market.us/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Luxury-Jewelry-Market-By-Size.jpg)

![Luxury Jewelry Market By Size](https://market.us/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Luxury-Jewelry-Market-By-Size.jpg)

The luxury jewelry market is poised for substantial growth, driven by increasing disposable income among the affluent population and a growing appreciation for artisanal craftsmanship. This sector has seen a resurgence of interest in unique, handcrafted jewelry that offers personal expression and maintains value over time.

Government policies play a pivotal role in shaping the luxury jewelry market. Regulations concerning the sourcing and distribution of materials like diamonds and gold often governed by international agreements such as the Kimberley Process—are crucial for maintaining the market’s integrity and sustainability.

According to the World Gold Council, China emerged as the world’s largest gold producer in 2023, contributing approximately **10%** to the total global production. This substantial share underscores China’s pivotal role in the luxury jewelry market, influencing global gold supply and pricing dynamics.

Furthermore, the total gold demand in 2023, inclusive of significant over-the-counter and stock flows, reached a record high at **4,899 tons**. This surge in demand is reflective of gold’s enduring appeal as a key component in luxury jewelry, supporting its market growth and investment allure.

In 2023, the average gold price set a new record at **US$1,940.54** per ounce, **8%** higher than the previous year, indicating robust market conditions and investor confidence. Additionally, the recycled gold supply, which increased by **9%** year-over-year to total **1,237 metric tons**, was driven by these high gold prices, highlighting a mature recycling market that contributes to sustaining gold supply without additional mining.

On another front, the stability in global natural industrial diamond production, with Russia leading at **41%** of the output, showcases the steady demand for these precious stones in luxury jewelry, supporting the industry’s supply chain resilience and continuous growth potential.

## Key Takeaways

## Raw Material Analysis

**Gold Dominates 2023 Luxury Jewelry Market with 39.2% Share**

In 2023, gold held a dominant market position in the By Raw Material Analysis segment of the Luxury Jewelry Market, securing a 39.2% share.

This significant market presence reflects gold’s enduring appeal and status as a preferred material among luxury buyers. Platinum followed, appreciated for its rarity and durability, appealing to a niche segment that values its unique properties.

Diamonds, synonymous with luxury, continued to captivate consumers, emphasizing their importance in high-value jewelry. Precious pearls also maintained a notable share, favored for their natural beauty and elegance in classic jewelry designs. Gemstones saw varied interest due to their wide range of colors and types, catering to diverse consumer tastes and preferences.

The Others category, which includes materials like silver and high-end metals, captured the remaining market portion, indicating a varied consumer base with specific preferences for less traditional luxury materials. This segmentation highlights the diverse materials that luxury jewelry buyers consider, with gold leading due to its traditional appeal and substantial investment value.

## Product Analysis

**Rings Lead 2023 Luxury Jewelry Market with 32.5% Share**

In 2023, Ring held a dominant market position in the By Product Analysis segment of the Luxury Jewelry Market, capturing a significant 32.5% share. This prominence underscores the enduring appeal and significant consumer investment in rings as a cornerstone of luxury adornment.

Following closely, necklaces commanded a robust market presence, favored for their versatility and the statement they make in both casual and formal settings.

Earrings, always a staple in personal jewelry collections, maintained a steady demand, reflecting consumer preferences for both classic and contemporary designs. Bracelets also saw appreciable traction, attributed to their increasing popularity as both standalone pieces and in combination with other jewelry types for a layered look.

The Others category, which includes items like brooches and luxury [cufflinks](https://market.us/report/cufflinks-market/), although smaller in market share, catered to niche consumer tastes, highlighting the diverse consumer base and the broad spectrum of products that define the luxury jewelry landscape. This segmentation reveals not only the varying consumer preferences but also highlights areas with potential growth opportunities within the luxury jewelry sector.

## Application Analysis

**Women Lead Luxury Jewelry Market with 69.8% Share in 2023**

In 2023, women held a dominant market position in the By Application Analysis segment of the Luxury Jewelry Market, accounting for a 69.8% share. This significant majority is attributed to the increasing purchasing power of women and the growing fashion consciousness that drives demand for luxury jewelry.

Contrastingly, men’s participation in the luxury jewelry market has been gradually increasing, driven by a rise in fashion trends that include [luxury watches](https://market.us/report/luxury-watch-market/) and branded jewelry. However, men’s share remains considerably lower than that of women, reflecting more traditional purchasing patterns in [luxury goods](https://market.us/report/luxury-goods-market/).

The children’s segment of the luxury jewelry market is relatively small but is beginning to gain traction. This growth is spurred by the trend of gifting expensive, keepsake jewelry to mark significant life events such as birthdays and graduations. While this segment represents a niche market, it is expected to grow as parents and family members increasingly view high-quality jewelry as a long-term investment for children.

## Distribution Channel Analysis

**Offline Dominates Luxury Jewelry Distribution with 82.6% Market Share**

In 2023, Offline held a dominant market position in the By Distribution Channel Analysis segment of the Luxury Jewelry Market, with an 82.6% share. This segment’s substantial market share can be attributed to consumer preferences for a tactile buying experience, where they can physically inspect and try on high-value items before purchasing.

The tactile aspect is crucial in the luxury market, where the feel, fit, and immediate gratification of luxury goods play a significant role in the buying decision. Furthermore, offline channels offer personalized services and expert advice, enhancing consumer confidence in expensive purchases.

Conversely, the Online segment, although smaller, is growing as technology improves and consumer habits shift. Online platforms are increasingly incorporating augmented reality (AR) and high-definition visualization tools to mimic the in-store experience, making them more appealing, especially to tech-savvy younger demographics.

However, despite these advancements, the need for physical interaction in luxury jewelry shopping keeps the Offline segment in the lead. As digital tools evolve and consumer trust increases, the online segment is expected to gradually capture more market share, introducing a dynamic shift in consumer buying patterns in the luxury jewelry sector. ![Luxury Jewelry Market Share](https://market.us/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Luxury-Jewelry-Market-Share.jpg)

### Brands Drive Jewelry Desires

The luxury jewelry market is propelled by several key factors that contribute to its ongoing growth and appeal. Firstly, consumer preference for branded and exclusive jewelry as a status symbol continues to rise, reflecting an increasing emphasis on brand aspirations that align with personal identity and social status.

Additionally, jewelry holds enduring cultural and religious significance, especially in regions like South Asia, where it plays a crucial role in ceremonies and rituals, thus maintaining its demand across diverse demographics. Technological advancements are also pivotal, as the integration of [3D printing](https://market.us/report/3d-printing-market/) and computer-aided design (CAD) technologies allows for the creation of intricate and customizable designs.

These technologies not only enhance the aesthetic appeal of luxury jewelry but also enable manufacturers to meet specific consumer preferences, thereby broadening the market’s scope and accessibility. This combination of brand prestige, cultural depth, and technological innovation forms a robust foundation for the market’s expansion.

## Restraints

### Counterfeit Jewelry Impacting Market

The luxury jewelry market faces significant challenges, primarily due to the widespread issue of counterfeiting. Counterfeit luxury jewelry significantly damages brand reputation and reduces revenue for authentic manufacturers.

As counterfeit pieces become more sophisticated, it becomes increasingly difficult for consumers to distinguish them from genuine articles, undermining consumer trust and loyalty.

Additionally, changing consumer preferences pose a notable restraint. Today’s consumers are increasingly drawn to minimalistic or alternative jewelry styles, which diverges from traditional luxury offerings. This shift could lead to a decrease in demand for classic luxury jewelry pieces, as consumers opt for simpler, often less expensive options that resonate more with contemporary fashion trends.

Together, these factors create a challenging environment for luxury jewelry brands, compelling them to innovate and adapt to maintain relevance and market share.

## Growth Factors

### Personalized Jewelry Drives Consumer Engagement

The luxury jewelry market is poised for significant growth, driven by evolving consumer preferences and strategic industry movements. A primary opportunity lies in personalized jewelry, catering to a rising demand for unique, custom-made pieces that reflect individual styles and stories. This trend not only enhances consumer engagement but also elevates brand loyalty and perceived value.

Furthermore, collaborations with renowned fashion brands present a lucrative avenue for introducing exclusive, trend-setting collections that merge the allure of high fashion with the prestige of luxury jewelry. Additionally, the expanding interest in men’s luxury jewelry opens a new demographic frontier, offering diverse designs that resonate with modern male consumers seeking sophistication and statement pieces.

These opportunities collectively underscore a dynamic shift towards more personalized, diverse, and fashion-forward offerings in the luxury jewelry sector.

## Emerging Trends

### Minimalism Elevates Luxury Jewelry Appeal

In the evolving landscape of the luxury jewelry market, minimalist designs are becoming increasingly popular, aligning with consumer preferences for understated elegance and lightweight accessories. This shift highlights a broader trend towards simplicity in luxury aesthetics, allowing for versatile and timeless pieces that blend seamlessly with various styles.

Additionally, there is a resurgent interest in vintage and antique jewelry, with consumers drawn to heirloom-inspired collections that embody historical significance and craftsmanship. Another significant trend is the rise of lab-grown diamonds, which are gaining traction as sustainable alternatives to traditional mined diamonds.

These lab-created gems cater to the growing consumer demand for eco-friendly and ethically sourced luxury products, providing a blend of modern technology and classic allure that appeals to environmentally conscious buyers. Together, these trends are shaping a new era in the luxury jewelry market, where sustainability, heritage, and minimalism converge to redefine consumer preferences and market dynamics.

## Regional Analysis

### Asia Pacific region dominant in the luxury jewelry market

The Asia Pacific region, now the dominant force in the luxury jewelry market, claims a staggering **65.3%** market share, amounting to USD **31.08 billion.**

This dominance is fueled by rising disposable incomes, expanding middle-class populations, and growing brand awareness among consumers. Countries like China and India not only lead in consumption but are also significant producers of luxury jewelry, leveraging centuries-old crafts combined with modern designs.

--- SOURCE 1: Luxury in Transition: Securing Future Growth - Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/luxury-in-transition-securing-future-growth

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Bain & Company 23rd annual Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study, co-released with Fondazione Altagamma, published on January 17, 2025, by authors Claudia D'Arpizio, Federica Levato, Andrea Steiner, and Joëlle de Montgolfier. The report analyzes the global luxury market's performance in 2024 and forecasts growth through 2030.

**Key Findings for 2024:**
- Overall luxury spending totaled €1.48 trillion globally in 2024, a slight decrease of 1-3% at current exchange rates vs. 2023 (flat to +1% at constant exchange rates), though still above pre-Covid levels.
- Personal luxury goods experienced their first contraction in 15 years (excluding the Covid period), dipping 2% at current exchange rates to €363 billion.
- Only about one-third of brands experienced growth in 2024 (down from 95% in 2021-22 and 65% in 2023).
- The global luxury customer base shrank by approximately 50 million people (from 400 million to ~350 million) between 2022 and 2024 — the first contraction in the 23-year history of the report.
- Top customers (VICs, just over 2% of the customer base) now account for 45% of global luxury purchases, up from 35% in 2021.

**Regional Performance:**
- Japan was the growth champion: +12-13% at current exchange rates to €33 billion, driven by favorable currency and tourist spending.
- Europe grew 3-4% to €110 billion, retaining position as largest region, driven by tourism (Chinese tourist purchases grew 40% and US tourists 10% in the first 10 months).
- Americas declined 1% to €100 billion; US showed upward quarterly trajectory.
- Mainland China declined sharply by 20-22%, dropping to 4th position; only ~5% of brands achieved positive revenue growth in China in the first 10 months.
- Rest of Asia-Pacific declined 1-2%; South Korea improved relatively.
- Rest of world grew 3-4% to €22 billion; UAE showed robust growth.

**Segment Performance (2024):**
- Luxury cars: declined 5% to €579 billion (largest segment).
- Luxury hospitality: rose 4% to €242 billion.
- Fine wines and spirits: stable at €99 billion.
- Gourmet food and fine dining: grew 8% to €72 billion.
- High-end furniture: eroded 2% to €51 billion.
- Fine art: dropped 7% to €36 billion.
- Private yachts and jets: grew 13% to €31 billion.
- Luxury cruises: grew 30% to €5 billion.
- Personal luxury goods categories: Beauty grew 3-5% to €79 billion; eyewear grew 3-5% to €17 billion; jewelry grew 0-2% to €31 billion (most resilient core category); leather goods declined 3-5% to €78 billion; apparel eroded up to 2% to €76 billion; watches declined 5-7% to €51 billion; shoes declined 5-7% to €25 billion (weakest category).

**Distribution Trends:**
- Outlets outperformed, growing 0-3%, as consumers sought value.
- Monobrand stores declined 1-4%; online channel declined 1-4% but maintained 20% market share.
- Secondhand luxury market grew 7% to €48 billion, outpacing new luxury goods.
- Net store openings in 2024 were one-third of 2023 levels.

**Profitability & Outlook:**
- Personal luxury goods profit margins (EBIT) expected at 18-19% in 2024, down from 21% in 2021-22.
- 2025 forecast: personal luxury goods growth of 0-4% (moderate).
- Through 2030: overall luxury spending expected to grow 5-9% per annum to €2-2.5 trillion; personal luxury goods to grow 4-6% annually to €460-500 billion.
- More than 300 million new addressable consumers expected globally in next five years; emerging markets (Latin America, India, Southeast Asia, Africa) expected to add more than 50 million upper-middle-class luxury consumers by 2030.
- Brands are urged to shift toward the "post-elevation era," rebuilding luxury foundations through creativity, craftsmanship, meaningful customer connections, and flawless tech-enabled execution (including generative AI). Key strategic dilemmas include exclusivity vs. broader audience, desire vs. love, and continuing price elevation vs. "high-low" strategies.

**Customer Insights:**
- Generation Z's advocacy for luxury brands continued to decline; their NPS is 25-30 points lower than millennial shoppers.
- More than 50% of consumers consider luxury brands overpriced.
- Customer satisfaction with luxury brands has dipped below pre-Covid levels.
- Experiences grew faster (5%) than goods (down 2%), as consumers prioritized travel and social events.

The study is based on triangulated data from more than 280 luxury companies, macroeconomic data, expert interviews (100+), and sources available as of November 10, 2024.

URL: https://nationaljeweler.com/articles/13928-state-of-colored-stones-the-big-three-in-the-modern-world

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Jeweler article (published May 19, 2025) examines the state of the "Big Three" colored gemstones—sapphires, emeralds, and rubies—in the modern U.S. market. Written by Lauren McLemore, associate editor for gemstones, the piece first appeared in the 2025 State of the Majors print edition.

KEY THEMES AND FINDINGS:

**Pricing Dynamics:** The finest untreated sapphires, rubies, and emeralds continue to command the highest prices of any gemstone. Since the pandemic, untreated fine sapphires have tripled in price. The mid-range market segment is "dying," according to gemstone dealer Simon Dussart of Asia Lounges, as mines struggle with profitability and shift toward treated materials for the low end. Rubies above 3 carats have become effectively inaccessible for many dealers.

**Ruby Market:** Untreated fine-quality ruby is exceedingly rare and now a specialized market. Myanmar's Mogok Valley remains the benchmark for quality but production has decreased significantly—over 90% of rubies over $50,000 per carat auctioned at Christie's (as of 2009) came from Mogok. Today, northeast Mozambique is the main source of ruby production, though quality and quantity are decreasing. Gemfields set a record per-carat price of $321.94 at its December 2024 Montepuez mine auction. Ethical sourcing alternatives include Columbia Gem House's "Pomme Ruby" from Madagascar and Virtu Gems' Kenyan rubies. Trading Afghan rubies remains legally complex due to Taliban sanctions.

**Sapphire Market:** Sapphire represents a smaller market value than ruby and emerald and is unique among the Big Three for its rainbow of colors. Over 90% of sapphires are treated. Overall sapphire quantity has decreased significantly since the 1980s. While classic "royal blue" (Princess Diana-style) sapphires command premium prices, buyers have shifted toward teal sapphires from Australia and denim-blue Montana material, with some movement back to Ceylon blue tones at 2025 trade shows.

**Emerald Market:** Emerald has benefited from the popularity of green gemstones and colorful engagement rings. Colombia, Brazil, and Zambia dominate global supply. There have been no major new discoveries in 40 years. Finer-quality untreated material is becoming rarer—demand for no-oil emeralds outstrips supply. Zoe Michelou of Imperial Colors Ltd. (Bangkok) notes prices keep climbing, sometimes changing within two months. Colombian emeralds still command premium prices due to history. The Swat district in Pakistan produces extremely clean, highly saturated small crystals (dubbed "the Rolls-Royce of emeralds" due to luxury watch company usage). Gemfields temporarily suspended mining at Zambia's Kagem mine (December, up to six months) citing oversupply of commercial-quality emeralds, then resumed focused open-pit mining in early May. Grizzly Mining offered 1.93 million carats at its December emerald auction.

**Role of Brands:** Luxury brands like Van Cleef & Arpels are becoming more "country agnostic" in sourcing and are seen as better positioned to market ultra-expensive fine-quality material (e.g., "unicorn" stones) to buyers with significant purchasing power.

**Market Share Growth:** Colored gemstones now account for more than 9-11% of the fine jewelry market, which was the previous long-standing range, according to GemWorld International President Stuart Robertson. Higher prices are encouraging buyers to embrace inclusions, unusual colors, and non-traditional cuts (e.g., Navneet Gems' portrait-cut Mozambican rubies in kite and hexagon shapes). Some in the trade speculate about a new "Big Three" emerging—rare garnet, spinel, and Paraíba tourmaline, per gemologist Jason Stephenson of Pala International.

**Key Quote:** "Gems, by definition, are freaks of nature. Once you understand that part, you understand that whatever comes out in gem form and gem quality is rare." — Simon Dussart, Asia Lounges
</summary>

Key details include: substantial emerald crystals were offered, including one weighing 479 g and three combined weighing 106 g. Production was offered in pre-graded parcels created by experienced sorters, with size being the first sorting factor. Emerald quality is determined by green color richness and clarity, while ruby grading focuses on color intensity, color orientation, and secondary color components (orangy or purplish), ranging from bright pinkish red to darker "closed" burgundy red. Ruby inclusions, especially dense silky bands, add complexity to grading.

All products were offered untreated except for oiling (used for inspection only). Gemfields previously offered treated parcels but discontinued this practice. Emerald valuation is complex due to abundant fractures (one crystal can yield many polished gems), while one ruby rough typically yields one finished gem.

A notable 500 g parcel of small (0.5 g, 2.8-4 mm average) but unusually clean, richly colored emeralds attracted significant attention due to their rarity and high demand. The article emphasizes that winning or losing parcels can hinge on variations as small as 0.5% of total price. Larger parcels of smaller gems often have greater economic impact than single large stones, as their profits sustain cutting workshops. Buyers bring teams including heat treaters, preformers, and polishers to inspect stones, with preforming/cutting being the most critical value-determining step.

Treatment considerations factor into valuation: fracture filling affects emerald value, and certain ruby grades require heating to improve color (e.g., those with strong purple tint). Results: ruby sales totaled nearly US$69 million with 97% of goods sold; emerald sale (higher quality rough only) totaled US$35 million with 93% of lots sold.

--- SOURCE 1: Jewelry Leads Luxury Spending in 2025 – Bain ---
URL: https://rapaport.com/news/jewelry-leads-luxury-spending-in-2025-bain

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Jewelry was the top-performing category in global luxury spending in 2025, according to a report by Bain & Company released jointly with Italian luxury goods industry organization Altagamma. The overall global luxury market reached EUR 1.44 trillion ($1.64 trillion) in 2025. Other strong categories included apparel, eyewear, and fragrances, while cosmetics remained weak and leather goods and footwear faced challenges but showed upward trajectories. In watches, collectors prioritized craftsmanship and rarity over hype, boosting the resale market.

Personal luxury spending dipped slightly to EUR 358 billion ($408.18 billion) in 2025, down from EUR 364 billion ($415 billion) in 2024. However, sales for 2026 are projected to grow 2% to 4% to between EUR 365 billion and EUR 373 billion ($416.32 billion and $425.44 billion), with a 70% probability, assuming Middle East stabilization, resilient local spending, and gradual Chinese recovery. A more optimistic 4% to 6% growth scenario has a 20% chance, while a flat to 2% growth outcome has a 10% probability.

Regional performance is diverging sharply: sales in the Americas are rising but lagging in Europe and the Middle East. Luxury spending in China is cautiously recovering, with online luxury sales up 25% to 35% year on year in the first quarter. Younger US consumers under 35 are increasing spending about four percentage points faster than older generations. The resale market continues gaining momentum, with about half of luxury consumers considering secondhand purchases before buying new items.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The luxury market is stabilizing, but this is not a return to the old rhythm – it is the emergence of a new one," said Claudia D’Arpizio, Bain & Company senior partner and global leader of the firm’s fashion and luxury practice. "Consumers are not stepping back from luxury. They are stepping forward into a new relationship with it – one defined by meaning, not just by product."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market | Bain & Company ---
URL: https://www.bain.com/insights/the-2025-chinese-personal-luxury-goods-market

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The 2025 Chinese Personal Luxury Goods Market report by Bain & Company (published January 28, 2026, authored by Bruno Lannes, Priscilla Dell'Orto, and Elle Yang) examines the state of China's personal luxury market. Key findings:

**Market Performance:** The mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%-5% in 2025, easing after a steep 17%-19% decline in 2024. The slowdown persisted through H1 (with only a modest Spring Festival boost), but recovery emerged in Q3 supported by favorable base effects, a robust stock market, and resurging consumer confidence. Q4 confirmed the recovery trajectory, particularly in fashion and leather categories.

**Category Performance:** Beauty rebounded with 4%-7% growth, the strongest segment, driven by demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances. Fashion demonstrated stronger resilience than leather goods due to innovation, digitalization, and shorter product life cycles. Leather goods declined 8%-11%, hurt by price increases and limited innovation. Jewelry improved (decline narrowed to 0%-5%) as consumers sought value preservation. Watches remained under severe pressure with a 14%-17% decline, as consumers shifted to other investment assets and secondhand or smart-device alternatives.

**Overseas Shopping:** Only 35% of mainland Chinese luxury purchases were made abroad in 2025 (down from 2024), as a weaker renminbi narrowed cross-market price gaps, and domestic mall promotions and domestic tourism boosted consumption repatriation. Inbound foreign tourists' purchases represented a very small portion of the market.

**Daigou (gray market) Sales:** Daigou activity remained elevated but uneven. Top 45 tracked brands showed a slight 3% sales increase (vs. 5% in 2024). Brands with tightly controlled wholesale overseas channels saw daigou sales decline to 5%-15% of official sales (vs. 15%-25% in 2024). Brands with larger, less regulated wholesale channels saw daigou sales reach 65%-75% or more of total mainland sales. Brand desirability remains the decisive factor in daigou demand.

**Secondhand Market:** The secondhand luxury market grew 15%-20% in 2025, remaining under 10% of total luxury market (vs. 20%-30% in developed markets). Online platforms dominate, with livestreaming playing a critical role in building consumer confidence in authenticity and reaching lower-tier cities. Top players are expanding into offline channels for verification, personalized services, and as recycling hubs. Leather goods and bags account for 50%-55% of the secondhand market, watches 25%-30%, and jewelry and ready-to-wear each 10%-15%. The market has strong potential to mirror Japan's mature model where resale reaches 30%-35% of the primary market.

**Consumer Segments:** Three key segments shape the market: top consumers (large share of sales for premium jewelry and ready-to-wear), middle-aged upper-middle-class consumers (deeply rooted, with incremental buyers from lower-tier cities), and next-generation aspirational consumers who face limited economic opportunities and delayed luxury entry—the key factor curbing new consumer acquisition.

**Local Brands:** Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers, differentiating through understanding of unmet local demand, digital-first go-to-customer strategies, and local access to raw materials enabling lower price points.

**Outlook:** The market is expected to show more positive signs in 2026, supported by domestic policy and geopolitical factors directing consumption back to the mainland. Growth remains highly category- and brand-dependent, with "true value" brands capturing stronger advocacy. China remains a cornerstone of global luxury growth despite macroeconomic challenges.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2025, the mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3%–5% but showed signs of recovery, starting in Q3." "The beauty sector, a standout performer, rebounded with 4%–7% growth... The demand for ultra-premium skin care and fragrances has kept steady as consumers increasingly seek emotional and sensory experiences." "In 2025, the secondhand luxury market in China remained significantly underpenetrated, accounting for less than 10% of the total luxury market (well below the levels seen in developed markets: 20%–30%)... Yet it reshaped the luxury landscape... maintaining a 15%–20% growth rate in 2025." "Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers. They are transforming the China luxury landscape with their distinctive fusion of global appeal and authentic Chinese identity." "Looking ahead, China will remain a cornerstone of global luxury market growth, despite ongoing macroeconomic challenges and broader societal shifts."
</key_excerpts>
